design.sizes: Older: small, about 5 x 3.5 to 6.5 x 4.5 ft; later: all sizes to 10 x 14 ft and larger.

look_alikes.name: Kashan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same structure; Kashan usually finer, shorter pile, more border stripes.

look_alikes.name: Lilihan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lilihan is single-wefted, about 65 kpsi, with a Hamadan-like back; Sarouk is double-wefted with depressed warps and blue wefts.

look_alikes.name: Mahal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mahals are coarser (Stone: 30-65 kpsi) with less depressed warps and longer pile.

look_alikes.name: Josan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Josan (Malayer) Sarouk-type rugs are symmetric-knotted.

rows.trade_use: 'Sarouk' is a trade name for rugs of certain designs woven in Arak and its district; 'Sarouk Farahan' has no unambiguous definition; 'Mohajeran Sarouk' for large fine 1910-1930 Sarouks that were not washed and painted; 'Royal Sarouk' is not a grade on any Persian invoice. Today Sarouk designs are woven in India, Romania and China.
rows.what_it_tells: A tightly woven, double-wefted asymmetric rug on cotton with deeply depressed warps and blue wefts, in a floral medallion or spray design, fits the Arak-district Sarouk.
rows.cautions: Hawley (1913) says hardly any 'Sarouks' were woven in Saruq village itself. See 'American Sarouk' for chemically washed and painted rugs.

facts.text: 'Sarouk' is a trade name for rugs of certain designs woven in Arak, nearby villages and the Farahan plain, not only in the village of Saruq.
facts.quote: probably not one in a score, perhaps not one in a hundred, of the Sarouks now offered for sale in this country was woven there

facts.text: Sarouks are tied with the asymmetric knot on a cotton foundation, with blue wefts and deeply depressed warps.
Hawley's Sarouk count is 12-18 knots per inch across and 12-20 down; Lewis gives 48-440 per square inch.
In the late 19th century, Sarouk workshop rugs imitated Tabriz floral-medallion models.
Nineteenth-century Sarouks of the Farahan area often used all-over Herati or Gol Hennai designs at about 100 knots per square inch.
Until 1914 about 85 per cent of the Arak district's output was in the lower Mahal, Mushkabad and Sultanabad grades; by about 1960, 60-70 per cent was Sarouk quality.
Mohajeran Sarouks were large, fine Sarouks woven between 1910 and 1930 with lustrous wool, a deep orange-red, and no chemical washing or painting.
No Sarouk was ever invoiced from Persia as 'Royal Sarouk'; the phrase is a sales embellishment.

says.text: Some Farahan rugs may be called Farahan Sarouks, but there is no unambiguous definition.
A few very old Feraghans are called Sarouks and a few Sarouks Feraghans.

museum_examples.title: Prayer Carpet (Sarouk Style)
museum_examples.shows: whole rug, front; cotton and wool, asymmetric ('Sehna') knots

rows.name: American Sarouk (washed and painted)
rows.region: Woven in Arak and its villages; finished (bleached and painted) in New York.
rows.made_by: Arak-district workshops and home looms to importers' orders in five grades (Sarouk Extra I, Extra II, I, II and bazaar quality, per Jacobsen).
rows.date_note: Detached-spray design adopted about 1915 or after World War I; painting most common 1920s-1930s; Jacobsen says about a third were still painted in 1960 and Europeans took over the Sarouk market from 1960.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric, as Sarouk.
structure.kpsi_note: Jacobsen: 9 x 10 to 14 x 15 knots per inch.
structure.wefts_note: As Sarouk.
structure.pile_note: Thick, heavy pile; colors bleached by a chemical bath and the red or rose ground repainted by hand on the front.
structure.sides: Double overcast in dark wool.
structure.ends: Narrow web and short fringe.
structure.back: Fine grain; on painted rugs the back shows faded rose or pink where the front is deep red or plum (Jacobsen).

design.field: Detached floral sprays on a rose, rosy-red or (before World War II) dark blue field, or a floral medallion with corners on a plain field.
design.border: Navy blue main border with floral design.
design.colors: Deep rose-red, raspberry or plum field (painted) with navy border.
design.sizes: Standard American sizes from 2 x 3 ft to 10 x 14 ft and larger.

look_alikes.name: Lilihan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lilihans were also washed and painted but are single-wefted with a Hamadan-like back.

look_alikes.name: American-market Kerman (1920s-1950s)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 1925-1937 Kermans copied this design; Kerman wool and often three wefts.

look_alikes.name: Mahal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mahals were also painted before World War II but are coarser.

rows.trade_use: Called simply 'Sarouk' in American stores; collectors call it 'American Sarouk'.
rows.what_it_tells: A thick Sarouk with detached floral sprays on a raspberry or plum field and a navy border fits the American-market Sarouk of about 1910-1960; a front much darker than the back shows it was painted.
rows.cautions: Painting is not damage to look for only on worn spots: Jacobsen says nearly all Sarouks sold in America from about 1910 to 1945 were washed and painted. Painted color can run when wet-cleaned.

facts.text: From about 1915 Sarouks for America were woven in detached floral sprays, usually on rose or rosy-red fields with navy borders.
During the 1920s and 1930s the dyes of most imported Sarouks were partly stripped and the rugs repainted in darker shades in New York.
Jacobsen says 98 per cent of Sarouks sold in American stores in the forty years before 1962 were chemically washed and painted.
Hawley (1913) says over ninety per cent of Sarouks, Kashans, Tabriz, Mahals and Muskabads sold in America had been treated by some artificial process to soften their colors.
facts.quote: Over ninety per cent of the Kermanshahs, Sarouks, Kashans, Tabriz, Muskabads, Mahals, and Gorevans ... have been treated by some artificial process

facts.text: Chemical washes use agents such as chlorine compounds, lime, acids or alkalis; harsh washes weaken and embrittle wool.
A painted Sarouk is darker on the pile side than on the back, where the field looks faded rose or pink.
A. Cecil Edwards (1953) criticized New York importers for painting color back into chemically stripped Sarouks; Jacobsen quotes him.

says.text: Fifty years before 1962; about a third of Sarouks still painted in 1960.
During the 1920s and 1930s.
Quoting Edwards (1953): twenty-five years.

rows.name: Sultanabad
rows.region: Sultanabad (renamed Arak in the 1930s) and over a hundred villages within a day's journey; Ziegler worked with 111 villages by 1894.
rows.made_by: Village and town weavers working for European and American firms (Ziegler & Co. from about 1877-1883, later OCM, Castelli, PETAG and others) through local agents who supplied wool, dyes and cartoons.
rows.date_note: Ziegler's Sultanabad agency was set up between 1877 and 1883; the large early trade ended with the Depression. Jacobsen uses 'Sultanabad' for good old (pre-war) carpets of the district.

structure.knot_note: Disputed: Lewis 'generally the Ghiordes, sometimes the Senna'; Hawley's table puts Sultanabad with the Ghiordes group but notes some are Sehna; Jacobsen says Arak-district rugs use the same Persian knot as Sarouk and later jufti knots; Stone's Mahallat entry: asymmetric.
structure.kpsi_note: Lewis: 5-8 down x 6-14 across = 30-112. Hawley's Muskabad/Mahal block: 7-14 x 8-12 = 56-168. Stone (Mahallat): 30-65.
structure.wefts_note: Two passes of medium to coarse cotton (Hawley, for Muskabad/Mahal).
structure.pile_note: Good wool of medium length (Lewis; Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Overcast (Lewis; Hawley: double overcasting).
structure.ends: Short web and loose warp fringe (Lewis).
structure.handle: Medium weight, durable, not finely woven (Jacobsen).

design.field: Large-scale all-over floral designs with Shah Abbasi palmettes, rosettes and large leaves; large Herati; the Mustaphi design on blue; Gol Hennai; medallions; European-taste designs drawn by the firms' designers.
design.border: Usually three stripes, often a Herati main border.
design.colors: Rose or red fields, about one in twenty blue; Lewis: bright reds, browns, blues, pinks, greens with white; Mumford: pale yellowish grounds in the early 'Savalan' type.
design.sizes: Carpet sizes only (Lewis 8-15 x 10-20 ft; Jacobsen mostly 10.8 x 14 and 11 x 17 ft).

look_alikes.name: Farahan (Feraghan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Farahans are finer and mostly small; large 'Feraghans' are usually Sultanabads.

look_alikes.name: Mahal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same family; Jacobsen calls better old pieces Sultanabad and poorer ones Mahal.

rows.trade_use: Old American trade names: 'Savalan' (after the mountains north of the district) and 'Extra Modern Persian'; grades 'Sultanabad', 'Mahal', 'Mushkabad'. Today many dealers call old pieces 'Ziegler', 'Sultanabad' or 'Mahal' interchangeably.
rows.what_it_tells: A large, coarse-to-medium carpet with large-scale floral or Herati design on cotton, from the Arak district, made c.1880-1940, fits the Sultanabad family.
rows.cautions: The knot type is reported differently by different authors; check. Many were chemically washed.

facts.text: Sultanabad became the center of a large rug industry controlled by European and American firms, which supplied wool and dyes and dictated patterns.
facts.quote: the centre of a great rug industry controlled by Europeans and Americans

facts.text: In the American market Sultanabads were often called 'Savalans', after the mountains to the north of the district.
facts.quote: In the American markets the Sultanabads are often called “ Savalans,” after the range of mountains

facts.text: Sultanabad carpets were graded by the trade as Muskabad, Mahal and Savalan (or Sultanabad).
facts.quote: Classed as Muskabad, Mahal and Savalan, according to grade.

facts.text: Sultanabad (Arak) carpets come only in carpet sizes and are rather coarsely woven.
The firms altered traditional palettes, dimensions and designs to Western specifications and produced standard sizes such as 8 x 10 and 9 x 12 ft.
The city of Sultanabad was renamed Arak.

says.text: Generally the Ghiordes, sometimes the Senna.
Listed with Ghiordes-knot classes; 'some of the Sultanabads have the Sehna knot'.
These coarser types use the same Persian Senna knots as the Sarouk.
Mahallat rugs: asymmetric.

rows.name: Ziegler (Ziegler & Co. carpets)
rows.region: Sultanabad (Arak) and its villages; the firm's first Persian agencies were at Tabriz and Rasht.
rows.made_by: Village weavers working through local agents ('amels) for Ziegler & Co., Manchester-based merchants, who supplied dyed wool and cartoons and inspected and packed the rugs in Sultanabad.
rows.date_note: Agencies at Tabriz and Rasht in 1867; Sultanabad agency between 1877 and 1882 or 1883; 111 villages by 1894; about 3,000 looms by World War I; production ended after the post-war slump and Depression.

structure.knot_note: Not specified for Ziegler production by these sources; see Sultanabad.
structure.kpsi_note: As Sultanabad/Mahal (Stone: 'medium quality').
structure.wefts_note: As Sultanabad.
structure.pile_note: Wool dyed by the firm's dyers.
structure.sides: As Sultanabad.
structure.ends: As Sultanabad.

design.field: Large-scale floral and palmette designs, medallion-and-corner designs fashionable in the West, vase designs; cartoons drawn for the firm (some survive from the manager Emil Alpiger, 1883-1896).
design.colors: Palettes altered to Western taste.
design.sizes: Western standard sizes.

look_alikes.name: Sultanabad
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ziegler carpets are Sultanabad/Mahal carpets; no structural test separates firm from firm.

rows.trade_use: Dealers use 'Ziegler' for decorative large Arak-district carpets of c.1880-1930 in spacious palmette designs, whether or not documented as Ziegler's; the name is also used for modern reproductions made outside Iran (no source here documents those).
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Ziegler' label says a dealer places the carpet in the Sultanabad export trade of about 1880-1930; documentation of the firm is almost never possible.
rows.cautions: Without archival evidence a 'Ziegler' attribution is a style label.

facts.text: Ziegler & Co. was a firm of Manchester-based merchants who imported European cotton goods to the Near East and exported Persian goods.
Ziegler's first Persian agencies were at Tabriz and Rasht in 1867; Stone dates its Tabriz office to 1883.
Ziegler set up a Sultanabad agency between 1877 and 1883 and organized village weaving through local agents who supplied dyed wool, cartoons and cash advances.
By 1894 Ziegler worked with 111 villages around Sultanabad; by World War I it bought the product of about 3,000 looms.
Ziegler's medium-quality carpets were known in the trade as Mushkabads or Mahals.
Ziegler handled the famous Ardabil carpets before their sale to the West.
Jacobsen says old Ziegler carpets made in Tabriz and Sultanabad used the vase design.

says.text: Persian agencies at Tabriz and Rasht in 1867; Sultanabad agency between 1877 and 1882; Alpiger manager 1883-1896.
In 1883 Ziegler set up an office in Tabriz for importing Persian rugs, then placed orders around Sultanabad.

rows.name: Mahal
rows.region: Villages of the Arak district: Mushkabad, Farahan, Dulakhor, Japalak and Mahallat. There is no town called Mahal.
rows.made_by: Village weavers working for exporting firms and Arak merchants.
rows.date_note: In use for Arak-district carpets since the Sultanabad export trade of the 1880s; still used as a grade name.

structure.knot_note: Hawley's table puts Mahal with the Sehna (asymmetric) group, noting some are Ghiordes; Stone (Mahallat): asymmetric; Jacobsen: Persian knot, with jufti knots in newer rugs.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone (Mahallat): 30-65. Hawley's Muskabad/Mahal block: 7-14 x 8-12 = 56-168; he says Mahals are slightly better woven than Muskabads.
structure.wefts_note: Two passes of medium to coarse cotton (Hawley).
structure.pile_note: Medium length, longer than Farahan (Hawley).
structure.sides: Double overcasting (Hawley).
structure.ends: Very narrow web and short fringe at the lower end, short fringe at the upper (Hawley, Muskabad block).
structure.handle: Coarse, of average thickness, lighter than Sarouk (Jacobsen).

design.field: Large-scale all-over designs with Shah Abbasi palmettes and florals; Herati; concentric medallions; Sarouk patterns.
design.border: Three to five stripes, often the turtle pattern.
design.colors: Red fields with blue or ivory borders in new rugs; older ones often blue with Herati.
design.sizes: Carpet sizes only, mostly 9 x 12 to 11 x 17 ft.

look_alikes.name: Farahan (Feraghan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'a fine Mahal is identical to a coarse Feraghan'; Mahals are carpet-size and coarser.

look_alikes.name: Mushkabad
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mushkabad is the next grade down; there is no sharp line between them.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mahals are less densely knotted with less depressed warps.

rows.trade_use: A grade or quality name for Arak-district carpets: Sarouk (best), then Arak, Mahal, Mushkabad. Many old Mahals were sold as Feraghans.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Mahal' is a coarse-to-medium Arak-district room-size carpet; the label gives a grade, not a village.
rows.cautions: Up to World War II most new Mahals sent to America were chemically washed and painted. Some new ones use skin ('dead') wool.

facts.text: Mahal is a trade name for second-quality Arak-district carpets, not the name of a town.
Hawley names Mahals as one of the grades of the Sultanabad industry.
facts.quote: Some take the name of the city, others are called Savalans, from a range of mountains that lie to the north, and others are known as Mahals.

facts.text: Mahallat-area rugs are less densely knotted, about 30-65 asymmetric knots per square inch, with less depressed warps than other Sarouks.
Mahals come only in carpet sizes.
Ziegler's medium-quality production was known in the trade as Mahals or Mushkabads.

says.text: Persian for 'Made to Order'; but a trade name.
Mahal means village rug (or 'a place or village').
A trade term for second-quality Sarouks; separately, Mahallat is a city whose villages weave these rugs.

rows.name: Mushkabad
rows.region: Mushkabad, a village district near Arak (Hawley: northwest of Sultanabad; Stone: east of Arak); the name is also a grade.
rows.made_by: Village weavers.
rows.date_note: Used since the Sultanabad export trade; Hawley (1913) describes the type; still a grade name.

structure.knot_note: Hawley: Ghiordes or Sehna.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 7-14 across x 8-12 down = 56-168; rows not firmly pressed down.
structure.wefts_note: Two passes of medium to coarse cotton (Hawley).
structure.pile_note: Soft wool of medium length (Hawley).
structure.sides: Double overcasting (Hawley).
structure.ends: Lower end a very narrow web and short fringe; upper end short fringe (Hawley).

design.field: Two or more concentric medallions covered with small Herati, large leaf and floral forms.
design.border: Three to five stripes, often the turtle pattern.
design.colors: Red, blue and ivory with green and brown; new ones red.
design.sizes: Large, nearly square: 10-18 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Mahal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mahals are slightly better woven.

look_alikes.name: Mashhad (Meshed)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Some writers confused 'Meshed' and 'Muskabad' (Norton's heading 'Meshed or Muskabad'); Jacobsen points out Meshed is in eastern Iran and Muskabad in western.

rows.trade_use: The lowest of the Arak grades: Sarouk, Arak, Mahal, Mushkabad.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'Mushkabad' is a coarse Arak-district carpet; the label is a grade.
rows.cautions: Many old Mushkabads were sold as Feraghans or Mahals. Some new ones use skin wool and wear quickly.

facts.text: Mushkabad carpets are very like Mahals, in large nearly square carpet sizes with cotton warp and weft, but less closely woven.
facts.quote: on account of their excellent quality of material and stoutness of weave they are very serviceable.

facts.text: Mushkabad is used in the trade for the lowest grade of Arak-district carpets.
Many Farahan-design rugs, including many sold as 'Feraghans', were woven at Mushkabad.
Ziegler's medium-quality carpets were known in the trade as Mushkabads or Mahals.

says.text: A trade designation for the lowest grade of modern Sarouks; 'the term does not refer to a place of origin' (though the headword also names an area east of Arak).
A district a short distance northwest of Sultanabad.
Woven principally in the town of Mushkabad and in Farahan villages; also a quality name.
Named after the village of that name.
Northwest of Sultanabad.
An area east of Arak.

rows.name: Lilihan
rows.region: Lilihan and nearby villages of the Kamareh (Kemereh) district near Khomein, south of Arak, inhabited by Persian Armenians.
rows.made_by: Armenian village weavers.
rows.date_note: Thousands exported to the United States 1923-1935 and 'through the 1930s'; few after World War II.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 65.
structure.wefts_note: Single-wefted (Stone); Jacobsen describes a 'basket weave' back like Hamadan or Senneh-Kurd rugs.
structure.pile_note: Not stated by these sources.
structure.sides: Not stated.
structure.ends: Not stated.

design.field: Sarouk-style all-over floral sprays; some older medallion designs.
design.colors: Red or rose fields, bleached and painted plum or rose-red for the American market.
design.sizes: 5 x 3.5, 7 x 5 and 9 x 12 ft.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lilihan is single-wefted and coarser; Sarouk is double-wefted with deeply depressed warps and blue wefts.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hamadan-area rugs are symmetric-knotted; Lilihan asymmetric.

rows.trade_use: Known in the American trade as 'the poor man's Sarouk'.
rows.what_it_tells: A single-wefted asymmetric rug with a Sarouk-like spray design, often painted, fits Lilihan.
rows.cautions: Like Sarouks, most were chemically washed and painted.

facts.text: Lilihan rugs resemble Sarouks in design and, like Sarouks, were often washed and painted for the American market.
Lilihan rugs are single-wefted, unlike Sarouks.
Large numbers of Lilihans were exported to the United States in the 1920s and 1930s.
Lilihan rugs have about 65 asymmetric knots per square inch on cotton, and the wefts may be red.
The Lilihan villages were inhabited by Persian Armenians.

says.text: Lillihan entry: a town south of Arak, about ten miles west of Khomein. Kemereh entry: several villages south of Hamadan, including Lillihan.
About 25 miles south of Sultanabad (Arak), principal town of the Kemereh district.

rows.name: Arak (modern)
rows.region: Arak city (formerly Sultanabad) and its villages, Markazi province.
rows.made_by: Home workshops and village weavers supplied by middlemen (mahalchi) who provide materials and credit in return for the right to buy the rugs; the Iran Carpet Company also had an Arak office.
rows.date_note: Rugs invoiced as 'Arak' first appeared about 1920, stopped about 1932 and resumed about 1948.

structure.knot_note: As Sarouk (Jacobsen: the Arak grade is next to Sarouk).
structure.kpsi_note: No source gives a count for the Arak grade.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Heavier nap than Sultanabad, Mahal or Mushkabad (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Not stated.
structure.ends: Not stated.

design.field: Sarouk-like all-over florals, or an open rose to red field with floral center and corners; Sultanabad and Mahal designs.
design.colors: Rose to red fields.
design.sizes: 9 x 12, 9 x 15, 9 x 17 ft and other large sizes; no small rugs.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Arak is the grade below Sarouk; the better ones approach Sarouk quality.

rows.trade_use: 'Arak' is used as a quality name, second to Sarouk in the district; weaving units in Arak piece-work are the char'ak (a quarter of a zar' of 104 cm).
rows.what_it_tells: An 'Arak' label names an Arak-district carpet of the grade below Sarouk.
rows.cautions: Pre-1932 Araks were invariably chemically washed and painted in New York.

facts.text: Arak is the modern name of the city and province formerly called Sultanabad, center of a large workshop rug industry.
In the Arak area, middlemen (mahalchi) supply all raw materials and credit to weavers in exchange for the right to buy the finished carpets.
In 1975, 3,440 of Arak's business establishments were carpet-weaving workshops, mostly household workshops.
Rugs invoiced as 'Arak' appeared about 1920, were made until about 1932, and resumed about 1948; pre-1932 Araks were washed and painted in New York.

rows.name: Ardabil design
rows.region: The original pair is dated 946 AH (1539-40) and is associated with the shrine of Sheikh Safi at Ardabil; place of weaving disputed (Ardabil, Kashan, Tabriz, Mashhad). Modern copies are woven in Tabriz, Mashhad, Kerman, Nain, India and elsewhere.
rows.made_by: Original: a Safavid court workshop under Shah Tahmasp; copies: city workshops.
rows.date_note: The originals are 1539-40; dates here are for modern rugs in the design, made since the originals reached London in 1893 and widely copied in the 20th century.

structure.knot_note: Originals: asymmetric on silk warps and wefts (Stone). Copies use their own center's structure.
structure.kpsi_note: Originals: about 300 (Stone); Jacobsen gives about 340. Copies vary.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated by these sources.
structure.pile_note: Originals: wool pile on silk foundation.
structure.sides: Not relevant to copies.
structure.ends: Not relevant to copies.

design.field: A large central yellow sunburst medallion with sixteen radiating ogival panels and two mosque lamps on a dark blue field of scrolling floral tendrils; quarter medallions in the corners.
design.colors: Dark blue field, yellow medallion, red, green.
design.sizes: Originals about 34.5 x 17.5 ft; copies all sizes.

look_alikes.name: Ardabil (modern town rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rugs from the town of Ardabil are Caucasian-style geometric rugs, a different thing.

rows.trade_use: 'Ardabil' on a modern rug means a copy of the medallion design; Jacobsen says dealers called any Mashhad or Tabriz rug with a similar medallion an 'Ardabil'.
rows.what_it_tells: The name identifies the design source; the rug's own structure tells where it was woven.
rows.cautions: No Ardabil-design rug outside the V&A and LACMA pair is an Ardabil carpet; dealers' phrase 'Ardabil Mosque carpet' for a new rug is a misuse.

facts.text: The two Ardabil carpets carry an inscription with an ode by Hafiz, the name Maqsud of Kashan, and the date 946 AH (1539-40).
facts.quote: The work of the slave of the threshold, Maqsud of Kashan, in the year 946.

facts.text: The Ardabil carpets have silk warps and wefts and wool pile with asymmetric knots at roughly 300-340 per square inch.
One Ardabil carpet, repaired with parts of its twin, is in the Victoria and Albert Museum (acquired 1893); a large part of the other is at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

Where the Ardabil carpets were woven is disputed: Kendrick thought Ardabil itself; others propose Kashan, Tabriz or Mashhad; Walker notes the weaver's name 'Kashani' need not mean the place of weaving.
Ziegler & Co. handled the Ardabil carpets before their sale in the West.
The Ardabil medallion is widely copied in Mashhad (Turkbaff and other grades), Tabriz and Nain carpets.

says.text: Most likely at Ardabil, with the weaver brought there.
Origin assigned variously to Ardabil, Kashan, Mashhad, Tabriz and other places; function conjectural.
Most authorities believe Kashan; some Tabriz or Isfahan.
Maksoud of Kashan was ordered to weave it; evidence of Kashan technique.

rows.name: Vase design (vase carpets)
rows.region: Originals: Safavid Persia, most often attributed to Kerman, by Pope (1926) to Joshaghan. Modern copies: Tabriz, Kerman, Qom, Kashan, Joshaghan, Ziegler Sultanabad, Bulgaria and elsewhere.
rows.made_by: Originals: Safavid workshops; copies: city workshops.
rows.date_note: Originals late 16th to 18th century; dates here are for later rugs in the design.

structure.knot_note: Originals: asymmetric open to the left ('vase technique', Stone after Thompson; Iranica iii). Copies use their own center's structure.
structure.kpsi_note: No count given for the group.
structure.weft_color: first and third passes in mixed or brindle wool (Walker)
structure.wefts_note: Originals: three wefts after each row of knots, two of wool and one of cotton or silk; warps completely offset (Stone; Walker).
structure.pile_note: Originals: wool.
structure.sides: Not relevant to copies.
structure.ends: Not relevant to copies.
structure.handle: Originals: distinctive feel and wear pattern (Walker).

design.field: Two or three superimposed lattices of vines and blossoms, often with vases, oriented to one end; also garden, sickle-leaf and shrub-row designs in the same technique.
design.colors: Originals often red fields.
design.sizes: Varies.

look_alikes.name: Kerman
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kerman rugs of c.1900-1914 used a vase-and-lattice 'vase technique' design derived from shawls (Iranica Kerman).

rows.trade_use: 'Vase carpet' or 'vase design' on a modern rug means the design; Jacobsen says Tabriz used it more than all others combined.
rows.what_it_tells: The name identifies a design family; the structure tells the rug's real center and date.
rows.cautions: In scholarship 'vase carpet' means a technical group (triple-wefted Safavid carpets), whether or not a vase appears.

facts.text: 'Vase carpets' are Safavid carpets with floral designs springing from vases in superimposed lattices, viewed from one direction; the group is defined by technique, not only by vases.
Vase-technique carpets have cotton warps, three weft passes after each row of knots (two wool, one cotton or silk), completely offset warps and asymmetric knots open to the left.
Vase carpets have most often been attributed to Kerman.
Pope (1926) attributed vase carpets to Joshaghan.
facts.quote: The so-called Vase carpets, the true Shah Abbas palace carpets, were woven in Joshaghan Ghali and its immediate environs

facts.text: The vase design was copied in modern Tabriz, Kerman, Qom and Kashan rugs and in old Ziegler carpets.

says.text: Origin problematic; attributed to Kerman.
Most often attributed to Kerman; produced from the reign of Shah Abbas I into post-Safavid times.
Woven in Joshaghan and its environs.
Believed by some authorities to be Isfahan.

museum_examples.shows: fragment, front; museum attribution: probably Kirman, Iran; Cotton (warp), wool (weft and pile); asymmetrically knotted pile

museum_examples.title: Vase-technique Carpet with Overlapping Cartouches
museum_examples.shows: whole item, front; museum attribution: probably Kirman or Isfahan, Iran; Cotton (warp), silk (weft), wool (weft and pile); asymmetrically knotted pile

museum_examples.shows: whole item, front; museum attribution: Isfahan or Kirman, Iran; Cotton (warp and weft), silk (weft), wool (weft and pile); asymmetrically knotted pile

rows.name: Polonaise design
rows.region: Originals: 17th-century Persia, probably Isfahan or Kashan.
rows.made_by: Safavid court and commercial workshops.
rows.date_note: Originals 17th century; dates here are for later silk rugs in the style.

structure.knot_note: Originals: asymmetric knot (Met records).
structure.kpsi_note: Not given by these sources.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Originals: silk pile with gold and silver brocading.
structure.sides: Not relevant to copies.
structure.ends: Not relevant to copies.

design.field: Large palmettes, curving leaves and vines on compartments of different ground colors, with metal-thread brocaded areas.
design.colors: Now muted pastels (originally brilliant): pinks, greens, yellows, silver and gold.
design.sizes: Many small pieces; some large.

look_alikes.name: Qom (Qum)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Modern silk Qom and Isfahan rugs sometimes copy Polonaise palmettes, without metal brocading.

rows.trade_use: 'Polonaise' on a modern rug means a silk rug in the 17th-century Shah Abbas palmette style.
rows.what_it_tells: Identifies a design source only.
rows.cautions: The name has nothing to do with Polish weaving.

facts.text: Polonaise carpets are 17th-century Persian silk carpets brocaded with gold and silver; more than 200 are known.
The name comes from carpets shown by Prince Czartoryski at the 1878 Paris Exhibition with his family's arms, which led to a mistaken belief that they were Polish-made.
facts.quote: The appellation of "Polish," given to carpets of this class in consequence, clung to them for many years.

facts.text: Polonaise carpets were probably woven in Isfahan or Kashan.
Many Polonaise carpets, though woven for use in Persia, were given or sold to Europeans in the 17th century.

Perhaps Joshaghan.

rows.region: Originals: 16th-century Safavid workshops (silk examples attributed to Kashan); modern copies: Tabriz, Qom, Isfahan, Kashan and elsewhere.
rows.made_by: Originals: court workshops; copies: city workshops.
rows.date_note: Originals 16th century (the Milan carpet dated 929 or 949 AH; the Vienna silk carpet of Shah Tahmasp's reign); dates here are for later rugs.

structure.knot_note: Originals asymmetric; copies use their center's structure.
structure.kpsi_note: Jacobsen gives the Vienna hunting carpet about 27 x 29 per inch (about 780); copies vary.

facts.text: Hunting carpets are Persian Safavid and Mughal carpets showing hunting scenes and animals within floral settings; many are attributed to Kashan.
The famous Vienna hunting carpet is silk with gold and silver brocade, from the court of Shah Tahmasp.
Hunting designs are among the designs used in modern Tabriz rugs.

rows.made_by: Various.

facts.text: Garden carpets show a Persian garden from above, with rectangular beds divided by water channels and pools.
A group of consistent design is attributed to Kurdistan (northwest Iran) about 1800.
The only documentary date for the Safavid vase-technique group comes from a garden carpet in Jaipur inventoried in 1632.

rows.name: Heriz
rows.region: The town of Heris (Heriz) and the villages around it in East Azerbaijan, east of Tabriz (Jacobsen names Bakhshaish, Gorevan, Mehriban, Asleh, Sarai and the Karaja section); marketed through Tabriz.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Heris district; in the 1900s often women working at home, later also contract looms.
rows.date_note: The Heris rugs readers own are mostly from the export trade that grew from the 1880s (Mumford describes it c. 1900) and from 20th-century contract weaving; a group of Heris silk rugs dates from the mid-19th century (Rasouli et al. 2025, Honar-ha-ye Ziba; AIC silk carpet c. 1875). Still woven.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Ghiordes/Turkish) per Hawley, Mumford, Kendrick & Tattersall, May (Gorevan group) and Stone; Lewis (1920) instead says the Herez-district classes are 'usually the Senna' knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley (Herez): horizontally 5-10, perpendicularly 6-12 = 30-120. Stone: 30-80. Lewis gives 48-180 for Gorevan and 30-180 for Bakhshis.
structure.weft_color: white; Kendrick & Tattersall and Lewis note wefts often dyed blue or brown in Gorevan-grade pieces
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: weft of cotton (seldom wool), moderately coarse, crossing twice between rows; for Gorevans 'only once, or frequently twice'. May: twice. Stone: Serapi-type Heriz rugs single-wefted, and single-wefted Heriz-area rugs may be called 'Ahar'.
structure.pile_note: medium length (Hawley); Lewis: rather coarse wool clipped short; Jacobsen: thick.
structure.sides: Hawley: a two-cord double selvage. Lewis: usually overcast, often in different colored wools.
structure.ends: Hawley: lower end a very narrow web and short warp fringe; upper end a short warp fringe. May: end webs of the Gorevan group may be colored.
structure.handle: Heavy, thick and fairly coarse; Hawley calls the texture loose. Mumford: not as heavy as Bijars.
structure.back: Very coarse grain (Hawley); the more visible half of each knot is longer than wide and the weft shows between rows.

design.field: A large angular medallion with pendants and big corner pieces on a red, rust or rose field covered with angular floral stems; also all-over angular florals, and a white-ground type with arch-like tendrils.
design.border: Main border usually dark blue with the turtle and rosette design, or large rosettes with serrated leaves.
design.colors: Red, rust or rose fields; dark blue, ivory, light blue, coppery red, green. Iranica: a medium indigo blue.
design.sizes: Mostly carpet sizes, often nearly square (Hawley: 9-15 ft, width 2/3-7/8 of length); after World War II also long narrow contract sizes.

look_alikes.name: Gorevan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same design; 'Gorevan' is a coarser grade name, not a different look.

look_alikes.name: Serapi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Older or finer Heriz-area carpets, usually lighter ivory, camel or light red fields and more open drawing; a US trade name.

look_alikes.name: Karaja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Small rugs and runners with a row of three hooked medallions; single weft.

look_alikes.name: Tabriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tabriz carpets use curving drawing and finer knotting; Heriz drawing is angular.

look_alikes.name: Bakshaish
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bakhshayesh is a Heriz-district village; older pieces with all-over Herati or angular palmettes and paler colors are sold under its name.

rows.trade_use: 'Heriz' covers the whole district. Within the trade, 'Gorevan' was the coarse grade, 'Mehriban' (contract quality) a better one, 'Ahar' (from 1958-59) a fine new grade, and 'Serapi' an American name for older or finer pieces.
rows.what_it_tells: A heavy, thick carpet with an angular medallion, a cotton foundation and symmetric knots points to the Heris district of Iranian Azerbaijan; the grade name on an invoice says more about quality than about the village.
rows.cautions: Grade names (Gorevan, Mehriban, Serapi, Ahar) are used differently by different authors and dealers. Jacobsen reports 'skin wool' and jufti knots in cheap Heriz-type carpets of 1954-60 that wore thin quickly. Heriz-style carpets were also woven in Tabriz in the 1980s.

facts.text: Herez carpets are made in a district east of Tabriz and sold in Tabriz.
Heriz-district rugs are mostly coarse weaves with the symmetric knot.
The warp is cotton and the knot is the symmetric (Turkish) knot.
facts.quote: The warp is cotton, as in most Persian carpets, but the knot is Turkish. (Mumford 1902, p. 179)

facts.text: Hawley gives 5-10 knots per inch across and 6-12 down for Herez (about 30-120 per square inch); Stone gives 30-80.
The usual design is an angular medallion with corner pieces; Iranica names the angular medallion-and-corner carpet as the design tied to Heris.
Before 1935 the name Herez meant a good quality in the American trade and Gorevan a thicker, coarser one.
In the late 1950s the Heris district had about 900 looms in Heris town, about 600 in Mehraban and about 500 each in Bakhshayesh and Gorevan (Jacobsen's figures).
Heris weavers formerly bought fine lustrous wool from the Shahsevan nomads and more recently buy wool from Ardabil.
Heris is a registered geographical indication for hand-knotted carpets.

says.text: Herez and Gorevan: Ghiordes (symmetric); Serapi: 'generally Sehna, frequently Ghiordes'.
Bakhshis, Gorevan and Serapi: 'usually the Senna, sometimes/occasionally the Ghiordes'.
All Herez varieties: Turkish knot.
Symmetric.
Herez: weft crosses twice; Gorevan: once, or frequently twice.
Gorevan group: crosses twice.
Serapi: single-wefted; 'single-wefted rugs of the Heriz area may be termed Ahar'.
Heriz is 'about forty miles west of Tabriz'.
The Herez district is about 40 miles east of Tabriz.
A little journey eastward of Tabriz on the road to Ardebil.

rows.name: Gorevan
rows.region: A village of the Heris district (Dehkhoda's c. 1950 gazetteer puts it about 28 km east of Ahar); the name is used for carpets from across the district.
rows.made_by: Heris-district village weavers.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Mumford (1902) says Tabriz shippers began invoicing Herez carpets as 'Gorevan' in the late 19th century; Hawley (1913) calls all Gorevans modern. The name stayed in use as a grade through the 20th century.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (symmetric) per Hawley, May and Kendrick & Tattersall; Lewis says usually Senna (asymmetric).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-8, perpendicularly 6-10 = 36-80. Lewis: 48-180. Jacobsen: in the coarsest grades over half the knots are jufti (tied over four warps).
structure.weft_color: Hawley: sometimes dyed blue; Kendrick & Tattersall: mostly dyed blue or brown; Lewis: sometimes dyed brown
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: coarse cotton weft crossing once, or frequently twice. May: twice.
structure.pile_note: Medium length (Hawley); coarse wool clipped short (Lewis); thick (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Hawley: a two-cord double selvage. Lewis: usually overcast, as a rule with different colored wool.
structure.ends: Hawley: short warp fringe at both ends. May: end webs may be colored, 'a feature found in but few Persian rugs'.
structure.handle: Thick and coarse; Hawley calls the texture rather loose.
structure.back: Very coarse grain; warp rarely fully hidden (Hawley).

design.field: Concentric angular (stepped hexagonal) medallions with large corners; heavy, archaic angular leaves and flowers; figures often colored in two strongly contrasting halves.
design.border: Main stripe usually the turtle design.
design.colors: Dull brick red, terracotta, buff, dark blue, dull green, yellow, ivory; terracotta, apricot and blue; copper-red, dark blue and buff.
design.sizes: Carpet sizes, rarely small rugs; Hawley 10-16 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same district and design; Gorevan is the coarser grade name.

look_alikes.name: Serapi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Serapis are often mistaken for Gorevans but are as a rule better woven, with lighter ivory or buff fields.

rows.trade_use: A quality name inside the Heriz family: Jacobsen says New York importers bought the cheaper Heriz grade as 'Gorevan' and retailers sold it as 'Heriz'; Stone says a very coarse rug in a Heriz pattern may be called Gorevan.
rows.what_it_tells: The name says the rug is from the Heris district and, in most trade use, that it is a coarser grade; it does not point to the village of Gorevan.
rows.cautions: The meaning has shifted: Mumford (1902) says the name was first used for Herez carpets and then for a new, finely woven Tabriz-style medallion type with an ivory ground; later authors use it for the coarse grade.

facts.text: Gorevan is the name of a small village in the Herez district.
Gorevans have concentric medallions and a turtle-pattern main border.
The knot is the symmetric (Ghiordes) knot and the warp is cotton.
Hawley gives 6-8 knots per inch across and 6-10 down (about 36-80 per square inch).
Gorevans come in carpet sizes and are rarely small rugs.
In the trade 'Gorevan' denotes a quality, the poorer grade of rugs sold as Heriz.
In 1954-60 many cheap Gorevans were woven with ready-dyed 'skin wool' bought in Tabriz and wore thin in a few years (Jacobsen).
Gorevan is listed as a proposed (not yet registered) carpet geographical indication, separate from Heris.

says.text: Ghiordes.
Ghiordes.
Usually the Senna, occasionally the Ghiordes.
First used by Tabriz shippers for Herez carpets; then for a new, finely woven medallion type of Tabriz drawing with an ivory ground.
A comparatively modern, moderately priced carpet of stout weave.
The lowest quality grade of Heriz.
Once, or frequently twice.
Twice.

rows.name: Mehriban (Heriz district)
rows.region: Mehraban village in the Heris district of East Azerbaijan. Not the same as the Mehraban district north of Hamadan (see Mehriban (Hamadan district)).
rows.made_by: Heris-district village weavers; from the 1940s-50s much of it contract weaving for importers.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen describes 'Mehrevan' contract-quality Heriz carpets reaching New York after World War II; the village is older.

structure.knot_note: As for Heriz (symmetric); no author gives a separate analysis.
structure.kpsi_note: No separate count found; Stone and Jacobsen rank it as a grade within the Heriz range.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated separately.
structure.pile_note: Thick, rather tightly woven (Jacobsen).

design.field: Geometric Heriz medallion designs with red fields, usually rosy or bluish reds rather than rust.
design.colors: Rosy red or deep bluish red fields.
design.sizes: Many sizes up to about 11 x 23 ft, including long narrow sizes made to importers' orders.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same family; Mehriban is a grade or village name within it.

look_alikes.name: Mehriban (Hamadan district)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A different place: Mehraban north of Hamadan weaves single-wefted village rugs, often with camel-colored fields.

rows.trade_use: 'Mehriban' or 'contract quality' was the trade's better grade of new Heriz in the 1940s-50s.
rows.what_it_tells: On an older American invoice the name points to a better-grade Heriz-district carpet; it does not by itself say Hamadan.
rows.cautions: Two different places share the name; Stone also ranks it differently in two entries.

facts.text: There are two places called Mehraban whose rugs reach the market: one in the Heris district and one in the Hamadan district.
Mehraban (East Azerbaijan) is a registered carpet geographical indication, listed with Heris, Bakhshayesh and Sarab.
Mehraban had about 600 looms in the late 1950s, second only to Heris town (Jacobsen).
The trade called Mehrevan carpets 'contract quality Herez'.

says.text: Mehriban entry: a grade of Heriz between Heriz and Gorevan in quality. Heriz entry: Mehraban and Serapi refer to the finer, more densely knotted rugs.
Mehrevans were among the best qualities of new Herez; some made in Herez town were better.

rows.name: Ahar
rows.region: The town of Ahar, north of the Heris district (Jacobsen; Stone: a town in the Heriz region).
rows.made_by: Weavers of Ahar and its district.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen says Heriz-type carpets marketed as 'Ahar' first appeared in 1958-59.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 65 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: single-wefted Heriz-area rugs may be termed 'Ahar'.

design.field: Medallion and corner designs. Jacobsen: a large medallion, partly geometric with some curvilinear effect, on rose or red fields with large ivory corners.
design.colors: Red, rose or brick fields with much ivory.
design.sizes: Mostly about 9 x 12 ft when introduced.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ahar carpets are a Heriz-family type; Stone treats 'Ahar' as a name for finer, more curvilinear or single-wefted Heriz-area rugs.

rows.trade_use: From 1958-59 'Ahar' or 'Ahar Herez' was used for a superior grade of new Heriz-type carpet; Stone uses it as a designation of fine weave or curvilinear design in Heriz rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A Heriz-type medallion carpet sold as Ahar is most likely from after the late 1950s.

facts.text: Most inhabitants of Ahar county work in agriculture, animal husbandry, and carpet and gelim weaving.
Ahar rugs use the symmetric knot.
Contemporary Ahar rugs have medallions and spandrels on a cotton foundation at about 65 knots per square inch.
Heriz-type carpets sold as 'Ahar' first appeared in 1959 and were among the best new Heriz qualities.
Ahar is listed as a proposed carpet geographical indication.

rows.name: Bakshaish
rows.region: A village of the Heris district east of Tabriz (East Azerbaijan).
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Heris district.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen describes old Bakshis of 1800-1900; a Negareh study (Mohammadi et al. 2016) traces weaving there to the Safavid period; since about 1900 the village has woven Heriz-type medallion carpets sold as Heriz or Gorevan.

structure.knot_note: Ballard's Bakshi rug and Stone: symmetric. Lewis: usually Senna, sometimes Ghiordes.
structure.kpsi_note: Ballard No. 4: Ghiordes, 9-10 vertical x 6 horizontal = 54-60. Lewis: 30-180.
structure.wefts_note: Not stated.
structure.pile_note: Ballard No. 4: long pile; Lewis: trimmed short.
structure.sides: Lewis: nearly always overcast with different colored yarns, occasionally finished flat.
structure.ends: Lewis: short fringe with loose warp threads at each end, occasionally knotted.
structure.handle: Ballard No. 4 is loosely woven with a long pile.

design.field: Older pieces: all-over Herati or angular palmette patterns in pale, faded blues, buffs and mauves; later: Heriz medallion designs. The Negareh study (Mohammadi et al. 2016) names three current designs, all medallion-and-corner.
design.border: Two narrow and one wide stripe, the wide one often with the Herati design.
design.colors: Old pieces pale blue, buff, mauve, faded magenta.
design.sizes: Old ones: runners about 3.5 ft wide and long narrow carpets 6 x 11 to 7 x 16 ft.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Modern Bakhshayesh carpets are sold as Heriz; the older all-over Herati or palmette pieces with pale colors are what collectors call Bakshaish (Jacobsen, Stone; Negareh study, Mohammadi et al. 2016).

look_alikes.name: Farahan (Feraghan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old Bakshis followed the small all-over Herati design of Feraghan rugs; Feraghans are asymmetric-knotted and finer.

rows.trade_use: Collectors use 'Bakshaish' for older Heriz-district pieces with all-over designs; new carpets woven there are sold as Heriz or Gorevan (Jacobsen; Negareh study, Mohammadi et al. 2016).
rows.what_it_tells: An older Heriz-district rug with an all-over angular design and soft, pale colors is the kind sold as Bakshaish.
rows.cautions: The name is applied loosely to old Heriz-area pieces; Mumford (1902) and Hawley (1913) describe the Bakshis of their day as hasty, poor weaving, the opposite of today's collector use.

facts.text: Bakhshayesh (Bakshis) is a weaving village of the Heris district east of Tabriz.
Because of Heris's fame, Bakhshayesh rugs are mostly sold as Heris rugs, though they have their own designs.
Older Bakshaish rugs used the Herati pattern; contemporary ones use the Heriz design.
A Ballard collection 'Bakshi rug' (catalogue No. 4) has Ghiordes knots at 54-60 per square inch, is loosely woven and has a long pile.
facts.quote: The rug is loosely woven and has a long pile. (Ballard catalogue, No. 4)

facts.text: Around 1880 a Sultanabad firm promoted weaving in Bakhshis; when quality fell the trade moved the name 'Herez' to other village work (Mumford's account).
Bakhshayesh is a registered carpet geographical indication.

says.text: Fifty miles southeast of Tabriz.
Southwest of Heriz.
The first day's stage east of Tabriz.
c. 1950: Bostanabad district of Tabriz county.
Usually Senna, sometimes Ghiordes.
Ghiordes (one rug).
Symmetric.
Those exported in his day were of little artistic value and carelessly woven.
Old Bakshis of 1800-1900 were rare and highly priced even 40 years before 1962.

rows.name: Serapi
rows.translit: Sarāb (the trade name 'Serapi' is not used in Persian)
rows.region: Heris district, East Azerbaijan. The name is said to come from Sarab (Sirab), a town between Tabriz and Ardabil, but the carpets sold as Serapi are Heriz-district work.
rows.made_by: Heris-district village weavers.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Mumford (c. 1900) describes Serapi as a then-new Heriz-district type; Jacobsen says nothing was imported under the name after the 1930s. The trade still applies it to older Heriz carpets (Stone: some define a Serapi as a Heriz 100-200 years old).

structure.knot_note: Hawley: 'generally Sehna, frequently Ghiordes'; Lewis: usually Senna, the finest Senna; Mumford and Stone: symmetric (Turkish).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-10, perpendicularly 7-12 = 42-120. Lewis: 80-216.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: coarse cotton weft crossing twice. Stone: single-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Medium length (Hawley); rather coarse but durable, generally clipped short (Lewis).
structure.sides: Hawley: a double selvage of two cords or double overcasting in figure-eight, usually red or buff. Lewis: nearly always overcast.
structure.ends: Hawley: lower end a narrow web and warp loops or short fringe; upper end a narrow web and fringe.
structure.back: Coarse grain; warp hidden; one warp of each pair much depressed or doubled under (Hawley).

design.field: Medallion with pendants and corners on an ivory, camel, light buff, light madder-red or light blue field, with more open ground and more floral detail than Gorevan; inscriptions occur.
design.border: Like Gorevan; three to five stripes.
design.colors: Light grounds (ivory, buff, camel, light red, light blue) with soft medium blues and coppery reds.
design.sizes: Hawley 10-18 ft, width 2/3-3/4 of length; Lewis 8-15 by 10-25 ft.

look_alikes.name: Heriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same district; trade usage reserves Serapi for older or finer pieces with lighter fields.

look_alikes.name: Gorevan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Large Serapis are often mistaken for Gorevans but are better woven, with lighter ivory or buff fields.

look_alikes.name: Sarab
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rugs actually woven in Sarab are camel-ground runners, not carpets.

rows.trade_use: An American trade term for Heriz-district carpets of better or older quality; Jacobsen says no rugs ever arrived on invoices as Serapi and that dealers used it in place of Gorevan or Heriz.
rows.what_it_tells: 'Serapi' on a label says an older Heriz-district carpet with a light field; it is a market label, not a place of weaving.
rows.cautions: Not a place name a buyer can check; it is applied generously to older Heriz carpets. The Sarab town product is something else.

facts.text: The name Serapi is derived from Sarab (Sirab), between Tabriz and Ardabil.
facts.quote: The rugs known as Serapis are named after the village of Sirab in the mountainous district between Tabriz and Ardebil (Hawley 1922, p. 148)

facts.text: Serapi is a trade term used only in America.
No carpet-size rugs were made in Sarab itself; its looms were too narrow (Jacobsen).
Serapis have the medallion of the Heriz group with a light ivory, camel or buff field and often inscriptions.
Lewis calls the Serapi the best grade of the Herez products.
facts.quote: The best grade of the Herez products. (Lewis 1920, p. 177)

facts.text: Hawley gives 6-10 knots per inch across and 7-12 down (about 42-120 per square inch); Lewis 80-216.

says.text: Generally Sehna, frequently Ghiordes.
Usually the Senna.
Turkish.
Symmetric.
Twice.
Single-wefted.
In Sirab and the country farther east.
Sometimes in the Herez district, sometimes on Tabriz or Sultanabad looms.
All so-called Serapi carpets are Herez or Gorevan; none made in Serab.

rows.name: Karaja
rows.region: The village of Karaja and several surrounding villages in the northern part of the Herez district; between Tabriz and Ahar.
rows.made_by: Village weavers.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen describes large numbers of new Karajas in the 1950s and a few prewar carpet sizes; earlier dating is not given by the sources.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 65-130 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Single weft (Jacobsen: 'Only one weft thread is used'; Stone: single-wefted). Stone: rugs of the same design that are double-wefted may be called Karadagh.
structure.pile_note: Clipped shorter than Heriz in small sizes (Jacobsen).

design.field: Two to four (usually three) hooked or stepped hexagonal medallions in a row on a red field, the center one blue, the end ones green, with small angular flowers between.
design.colors: Red, rose or brick fields; blue and green medallions; some runners with ivory fields.
design.sizes: Mats 2 x 2.8 ft, scatter rugs to about 6.4 x 4.10 ft, runners to 14 x 3 ft; a few carpets before World War II.

look_alikes.name: Karadagh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rugs of the Karadja design that are double-wefted may be called Karadagh; Jacobsen: weave differs but both are sold as Karaja.

look_alikes.name: Karaje (old-book name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old books' 'Karaje' is a Kurdish wool-warp runner from near Hamadan; Karaja has a cotton warp and geometric medallions.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'the Kazaks of Persia'; Caucasian Kazaks have wool warps and red or wool wefts.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Also single-wefted on cotton; the row of hooked hexagon medallions points to Karaja.

rows.trade_use: Small rugs and runners of Heriz type from the Karaja villages were sold as Karaja or as Heriz.
rows.what_it_tells: A small rug or runner with a row of hooked hexagon medallions, a cotton warp and a single weft points to the Karaja villages north of Heriz.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse Karaja (Azerbaijan, cotton warp) with Karaje (old trade name for Kurdish runners) or with Karadagh (the mountain region).

facts.text: Karaja rugs are made in the village of Karaja (Qarajeh) and several nearby villages north of the Heriz district.
Karaja rugs have hooked (geometric) medallions in a row on a long format.
Karajas are single-wefted with the symmetric knot on a cotton foundation.
Stone gives about 65-130 knots per square inch.
A very dark, double-dyed indigo blue is characteristic of Bijar, Karaja and Karadagh carpets (Iranica).

says.text: Same design; Karadagh when double-wefted.
Weave differs; Jacoby (1952) calls Karadjia merely a dialect form of Karadagh; Jacobsen disagrees because Karaja is a town.

rows.name: Karadagh
rows.region: The Qaradagh mountains of northern Iranian Azerbaijan between Tabriz and the Aras river, bordering the Caucasian Karabagh.
rows.made_by: Mountain village and tribal weavers; Iranica notes Kurdish tribes of Qaradagh weaving work very like the Shahsavan's.
rows.date_note: Old books (1900-1922) describe Karadagh rugs; Jacobsen says none were imported under the name after about 1910 and the name passed to Karaja and, he thinks, to the new Ardabil rugs.

structure.knot_note: Ghiordes (Hawley, Lewis, May).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 7-11, perpendicularly 7-11 = 49-121. Lewis: 64-154. Kendrick & Tattersall plates: 50-100.
structure.weft_color: Natural brown or dyed wool (Lewis, Mumford); occasionally dyed (Hawley)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley, May: crosses twice. Lewis: usually extra weft threads.
structure.pile_note: Medium (Hawley); sometimes camel hair (Lewis).
structure.sides: Hawley: a double selvage of two or three cords; Lewis: usually selvaged, occasionally overcast; May: two- or three-cord double overcasting.
structure.ends: Hawley: narrow web and short fringe at both ends. Lewis and Mumford: one end selvaged and turned back, the other selvaged with loose warp fringe; selvage usually red.
structure.handle: Moderately firm (Hawley); Kendrick & Tattersall: pliable and soft.
structure.back: Rather coarse grain; warp shows and weft is prominent (Hawley).

design.field: Small repeating patterns: diagonal rows of conventional flowers, hexagons, Herati or Mina Khani-like lattices; sometimes pole medallions; Caucasian devices common.
design.border: Mechanical vines or Caucasian geometric borders; reciprocal trefoil guards.
design.colors: Blue or camel-hair yellow fields, sometimes rose; natural camel hair in the ground.
design.sizes: Hawley 5-9 ft long; Lewis 3-4 x 5-7 ft and runners 2.5 x 8-15 ft.

look_alikes.name: Karabagh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Caucasian Karabagh rugs are similar; Hawley and Mumford say Karadagh designs keep more Persian floral character.

look_alikes.name: Karaja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karaja rugs have cotton warps and a single weft.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurdish rugs with Caucasian designs are incorrectly termed Karadagh.

rows.trade_use: An old-book and collector name; Kendrick & Tattersall say such rugs were also sold as Feraghan, Karabagh or Shiraz. Stone uses Karadagh for double-wefted rugs of Karadja design.
rows.what_it_tells: A wool-foundation, geometric northwest Persian rug that looks Caucasian may be what older books call Karadagh.
rows.cautions: The name is a guess for many geometric runners; attributions such as the Rijksmuseum's 'Karadagh (possibly)' show the doubt.

facts.text: Karadagh means 'black mountain(s)' and is a range in northern Azerbaijan between Tabriz and the Aras.
Karadagh rugs resemble the rugs of Karabagh across the Aras.
Karadagh warp and weft are wool, the knot Ghiordes, the weft crossing twice.
Hawley gives 7-11 knots per inch each way (about 49-121 per square inch); Lewis 64-154; Kendrick & Tattersall 50-100.
No rugs were imported under the name Karadagh for about fifty years before 1962 (Jacobsen).
Kurdish tribes of the Qaradagh region weave carpets very like Shahsavan work.

disagreements.about: what the name means in the trade

says.text: Double-wefted rugs of the Karadja design; Kurdish rugs with Caucasian designs are incorrectly called Karadagh.
Rugs of this kind were also sold as Feraghan, Karabagh or Shiraz.
Collectors used it as a guess for geometric runners.
Moderately firm.
Pliable and soft to the touch.

museum_examples.title: Medaillonkleed, versierd met botehs tegen blauw fond en geometrische motieven en dierfiguren. Kersrode rand met s-vormige ranken en rozetten.
museum_examples.shows: one image (whole piece, front)
museum_examples.attribution: maker: anonymous, Karadagh (possibly); maker: anonymous, Koerdistan (possibly)
museum_examples.note: Production: Karadagh (possibly) / Kurdistan (possibly) - doubtful. Medallion rug with botehs, geometric motifs and animal figures; cherry-red border; probably cut down from a longer runner. 186 x 98 cm.

museum_examples.title: Oosters tapijt
museum_examples.shows: one image (whole piece, front)
museum_examples.attribution: maker: anonymous, Hamadan (possibly); maker: anonymous, Karadagh (possibly); maker: anonymous, Noordwest-Perzië (possibly); maker: anonymous, Zuid-Kaukasus (possibly)
museum_examples.note: Production: Hamadan (possibly) / Karadagh (possibly) / Northwest Persia (possibly) - doubtful. Runner of repeated lozenge medallions on dark blue; shortened. 210 x 90 cm.

rows.name: Sarab
rows.region: The town and district of Sarab between Tabriz and Ardabil, East Azerbaijan.
rows.made_by: Village and Shahsavan weavers of the Sarab district (Iranica: Shahsavan pieces from around Sarab).
rows.date_note: Jacobsen saw old, semi-antique and new Serab runners (about 100 old ones a year around 1960); no earlier date is given by the sources.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 50 per square inch. Jacobsen: slightly coarser than a Bijar.
structure.weft_color: Iranica: the Shahsavan used cotton for wefts
structure.wefts_note: Iranica: Sarab-area Shahsavan pieces usually have two weft shots after each row of knots (unlike single-wefted Hamadan camel-hair pieces).
structure.pile_note: Undyed camel hair or camel-colored wool in the field (Jacobsen, Stone, Iranica).
structure.handle: Thick and tightly woven, heavier than a Bijar (Jacobsen).

design.field: A row of repeating diamond or hexagon (often octagonal) medallions on a camel-colored field; the field around them may be filled with a lattice or short angled hatch lines.
design.border: Main border cream with blue, rose and green.
design.colors: Shades of undyed camel with red, green, blue and ivory.
design.sizes: Runners 5 x 3 ft to 14 x 3 ft, rarely larger; no carpet sizes.

look_alikes.name: Hamadan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old 'Hamadan' camel-hair pieces look alike in color and design but have one weft per row; Sarab pieces usually two.

look_alikes.name: Serapi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Despite the name, Serapi carpets are Heriz-district work, not Sarab runners.

rows.trade_use: 'Serab' in the trade means a camel-ground runner; 'Serapi' means a Heriz carpet.
rows.what_it_tells: A thick camel-ground runner with a row of medallions points to the Sarab district.
rows.cautions: The Saint Louis Art Museum's 'Serab Long Carpet' places Serab in Hamadan province; Sarab is in East Azerbaijan.

facts.text: Sarab weavers produce runners with repeating diamond or hexagon medallions on a camel-colored field.
Serab rugs come only in runner sizes and a few small rugs; no carpet sizes are made.
Shahsavan pieces from around Sarab use much undyed camel hair and usually have two weft shots after each knot row.
Stone gives about 50 symmetric knots per square inch on an all-wool or wool-and-cotton foundation.
Sarab is a registered national carpet geographical indication (East Azerbaijan).
The Shahsevan summer pastures lay in the Ardabil, Meshkin and Sarab districts.

says.text: Registers Sarab separately from Heris.
Treats the Serab district as part of the Herez district but describes its rugs separately.

museum_examples.title: Serab Long Carpet
museum_examples.shows: one image (whole carpet)
museum_examples.attribution: Persian, Qājār dynasty; made in Serab, Hamadan province, Iran
museum_examples.note: Wool; 340.4 x 87.6 cm (runner/long carpet). DOUBTFUL PLACE: SLAM puts Serab in Hamadan province; Sarab town is in East Azerbaijan province (Hawley's 'Serab' camel-ground runners). Gift of Nellie Ballard White.

rows.name: Meshkin and Ardebil-area village rugs
rows.region: Meshkin Shahr, Ardabil and villages of Ardabil province near the Caucasian border.
rows.made_by: Village weavers.
rows.date_note: The new Ardebil rug came on the market only after 1950; Meshkin rugs reached New York in the 1960s.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Jacobsen: Ghiordes).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Meshkin about 65; Ardabil up to 160.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: Meshkin double-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Jacobsen: usually good wool, though some with 'dead' (skin) wool.
structure.handle: Jacobsen: Ardebils thin like Kuba or Shirvan rugs; Meshkins heavier.

design.field: Copies of 19th-century Caucasian designs (Kuba, Shirvan, Kazak, Karabagh), red or ivory fields.
design.colors: Red or ivory fields with blue, ivory, green, canary.
design.sizes: From 2.5 x 4 ft to about 8.5 x 11 ft, a few 9 x 12 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 19th-century Caucasian rugs have wool warps; these have cotton warps.

look_alikes.name: Ardabil (modern town rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The persian_city topic covers town production of Ardabil; village rugs in Caucasian designs overlap with it.

look_alikes.name: Ardabil design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Unrelated to the 16th-century Ardabil carpets.

rows.trade_use: 'Ardebil' for thin, cotton-warp rugs in Caucasian designs; 'Meshkin' for heavier ones.
rows.what_it_tells: A Caucasian-looking rug on a cotton foundation is likely a 20th-century northwest Persian copy such as Ardebil or Meshkin, not an old Caucasian rug.
rows.cautions: Sold in used-rug sales as 'collector's items' in the 1960s; they are post-1950 Persian rugs.

facts.text: Rugs of the Ardabil area employ Caucasian designs with symmetric knots on a cotton foundation.
The Ardebil rug in Caucasian designs is a new type that came on the market only after 1950.
Meshkin rugs have symmetric knots, are double-wefted on a cotton foundation at about 65 per square inch, and are similar to contemporary Ardabil rugs.
Meshkin rugs are heavy rugs in geometric designs copying Kazak, Karabagh and Kabistan rugs (Jacobsen 1969).
In 1972 the Ardabil carpet industry employed about 5,500 weavers, 60 percent of them men, with weaving shifting to villages.
Ardabil is a registered carpet geographical indication; Meshkin is proposed.

rows.name: Zanjan
rows.region: Zanjan and its villages (the old Khamseh district) between Tabriz and Tehran: Qoltuq, Bidgeneh, the Afshar villages, and Kurdish villages.
rows.made_by: Kurdish, Afshar and Shahsavan villagers.
rows.date_note: Mumford (1902) mentions a Zenjan dealer collecting Koultuk and Zenjan runners; Jacobsen describes coarse 'Zenjan' rugs until about 1958.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Stone; Mumford for Koultuk: Turkish).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Khamseh-district small rugs 30-65; Qoltuq about 130.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: both single- and double-wefted rugs are woven around Zanjan; Qoltuq double-wefted; Khamseh-district small rugs single-wefted. Mumford: Koultuk runners cotton warp, wool weft.
structure.ends: Mumford (Koultuk): one end plain selvage, the other selvage and loose ends.

design.field: Kurdish village designs; medallions with pendants and spandrels (Qoltuq); coarse red-field medallion rugs.
design.sizes: One general size, about 6.5 x 3.5 ft, in the coarse grade.

look_alikes.name: Bidjar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone notes rugs woven around Zanjan in imitation of Bijars, and Bidgeneh rugs similar to Bijars.

look_alikes.name: Mosul (trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Coarse Zanjan scatter rugs were sold as 'Zenjan Mosuls'.

rows.trade_use: Coarse scatter rugs as 'Zenjan' or 'Zenjan Mosul'.
rows.what_it_tells: A Bijar-looking rug may be a Zanjan-area imitation.
rows.cautions: 'Khamseh' here is the old province around Zanjan, not the Khamseh confederacy of Fars.

facts.text: Zanjan is a source of Kurdish village rugs and of rugs woven in imitation of Bijars.
Both single-wefted and double-wefted rugs are woven around Zanjan, with the symmetric knot on a cotton foundation.
Qoltuq, southwest of Zanjan, is a Kurdish source of medallion rugs, double-wefted on cotton at about 130 knots per square inch.
Koultuk runners have a cotton warp, wool weft and the Turkish knot; a Zenjan dealer marketed them as Koultuk or Zenjan (Mumford).
Coarse Zenjan rugs of about 6.5 x 3.5 ft were marketed as 'Zenjan Mosuls' in Zenjan and Tabriz (Jacobsen).
Afshar groups have lived in Khamseh around Zanjan probably since Safavid times.
Qoltuq, Bidgineh and 'Khamseh Zanjan' are registered carpet geographical indications.

rows.name: Shahsavan
rows.region: Northwest Iran: the Moghan plain, Ardabil, Meshkin, Sarab, Hashtrud, Mianeh, Khamseh (Zanjan), Bijar, Qazvin, Saveh and Varamin.
rows.made_by: Turkic-speaking Shahsavan tribes, nomadic and settled; women's domestic and dowry weaving.
rows.date_note: Museum bags date from about 1800 onward (Met 2015.490.24, about 1800-25); Iranica dates Shahsavan weaving to the 17th century. The trade recognized much 'Kurdish' or 'Caucasian' weaving as Shahsavan only in the 1970s.

structure.knot_note: Mostly flatweaves (soumak and tapestry); pile pieces rare (Stone). No source in hand states the pile knot.
structure.kpsi_note: No counts found.
structure.weft_color: Iranica: cotton used for wefts, occasionally warps
structure.wefts_note: Pile pieces from around Sarab usually have two wefts (Iranica).
structure.pile_note: Flatweave bags: soumak (weft wrapping) on wool warps, often with white cotton details (Met records).
structure.back: Iranica notes reverse soumak used as a ground weave particularly in Shahsevan flatweaves; Met records describe the backs of khorjin as weft-faced plain weave or slit tapestry.

design.field: Bold geometric medallions, hooked lozenges and stars on bags and bedding bags.
design.sizes: Saddle bags about 20 in. square per half; bedding bags (mafrash) four-sided.

look_alikes.name: Soumak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone attributes soumak bags and mafrash to Kurdish weavers in the Caucasus and similar pieces to the Shahsavan in Iran.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Much weaving sold as 'Kurdish' was later recognized as Shahsavan.

rows.trade_use: Used for soumak bags, mafrash panels and kilims from northwest Iran; pile rugs under the name are uncommon.
rows.what_it_tells: A soumak bag or bedding-bag panel from northwest Iran with bold geometric designs is the kind attributed to the Shahsavan.
rows.cautions: Attribution between Shahsavan, Kurdish and Caucasian work is often uncertain.

facts.text: The Shahsavan are a confederation of Turkish-speaking tribes of northwest Iran.
Shahsavan weavings are mainly flatweaves and flatwoven bags; pile carpets are rare.
The Shahsavan have made gelims, soumaks and knotted pile since the 17th century, with geometric designs.
Shahsevan weavers used cotton for wefts and occasionally for warps.
Reverse soumak appears as ground weave and decoration particularly in Shahsevan flatweaves.
Shahsevan mafrash (bedding bags) in Kurdistan are decorated only on the front sides; in Azerbaijan on all four sides.
In the 1970s the trade recognized that much 'Kurdish' or 'Caucasian' tribal weaving was Shahsevan.
Met Shahsevan saddle bags of about 1850-1880 are recorded as wool and cotton in soumak technique.
'Shahsavan' is proposed as a carpet geographical indication (East Azerbaijan).

rows.name: Bidjar
rows.region: The town of Bijar and about forty villages around it in Kurdistan province (the old Garrus district); Bijar-type rugs are also woven by Afshar villages north of Bijar and near Zanjan.
rows.made_by: Kurdish townspeople and villagers (Bijar's population is predominantly Kurdish); Afshar villagers north of Bijar. Cottage industry without factories (Iranica, after Edwards).
rows.date_note: Old Bijars with wool warps reached the West in large numbers until about 1930; after World War II the foundation changed to cotton. Still woven.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Ghiordes) in every source.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally 6-10, perpendicularly 8-12 = 48-120. Lewis: 48-120. Stone (later rugs): about 100-160.
structure.weft_color: Old: wool, often dyed red (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall); later fine cotton
structure.wefts_note: Hawley and May: twice. Mumford: a heavy two-strand wool 'filling' laid straight across between the front and back wefts after every row, with a thin dyed weft. Stone: early rugs usually three wefts hammered down, one very heavy; later rugs two. Iranica: triple-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Medium length, heavy and lustrous (Hawley, Kendrick & Tattersall); camel hair partly in some (Hawley, May, Lewis).
structure.sides: Hawley: double overcasting in red or purple. Lewis: overcast.
structure.ends: Hawley: web, sometimes colored, or a narrow braided selvage; upper end web with loose fringe; web occasionally turned back and hemmed. Lewis and Mumford: one end's web often turned back and hemmed.
structure.handle: Very stiff and heavy; 'board-like' (Jacobsen). Should be rolled, not folded (Lewis).
structure.back: Coarse grain; warps fully hidden because one of each pair lies under the other (Hawley, May); rows tightly packed.

design.field: Herati all over or with a small medallion and corners; open-field medallion and corners; Mina Khani; Shah Abbas; the 'Garrus' split-leaf arabesque; rose-cluster 'gol-farang' compartments; willow-and-cypress; samplers.
design.border: Three stripes and often a plain outer edging.
design.colors: Red, blue, ivory, camel; a very dark double-dyed indigo; bright, strongly massed colors.
design.sizes: Old: about 7 x 4 ft most often, also carpets 8 x 12 to 11 x 18 ft and wide runners; Hawley 6-16 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kurdish village and tribal rugs (Persian Kurdistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Persian Kurdish rugs one warp of each pair is depressed at an acute angle; in Bijars it is doubled under at a right angle, so the rug is much stiffer.

look_alikes.name: Senneh
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Senneh rugs are thin, short-piled, single-wefted and soft-handled; Bijars are thick, stiff and double- or triple-wefted.

look_alikes.name: Zanjan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone notes rugs woven around Zanjan in imitation of Bijars, and Bidgeneh rugs similar to Bijars.

look_alikes.name: Neyriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bijars are much stouter than Niris and have one warp more completely doubled under; Niris end webs are much longer.

rows.trade_use: 'Bijar' covers the town and the surrounding villages; 'Kurdish Bijar' is used in the trade for village and tribal pieces of the area (the term itself was not found in the sources read).
rows.what_it_tells: A very stiff, heavy rug that will not fold easily, with symmetric knots and hidden warps, points to Bijar or a close imitation; a wool foundation suggests an older piece, cotton a later one.
rows.cautions: Bijar designs and the heavy build are copied nearby (Zanjan, Afshar villages) and in India; old books' names 'Sarakhs' and 'Lulé' refer to the same rugs.

facts.text: Bijar rugs use the symmetric (Ghiordes) knot.
One warp of each knot is doubled under the other, so the warps are fully offset and hidden at the back.
facts.quote: in Bijars one of the two threads of warp encircled by a knot is doubled under the other so as to be at right angles to that plane (Hawley 1922, p. 143)

facts.text: Old Bijars had wool warps; cotton has been used for the foundation since World War II.
Bijars are so stiff they should be rolled, not folded.
facts.quote: Many of them are so thick and heavy that they cannot be folded but must be rolled up. (Lewis 1920, p. 186)

facts.text: Kurdish rugs often have a heavy wool filling laid straight across between front and back wefts after every row, held by a thin dyed weft; Bijars show this method.
facts.quote: a coarse, heavy, two-strand wool yarn is passed straight across, between front and back weft-threads, after every row of knots, as filling. (Mumford 1902, p. 187)

facts.text: Hawley gives 6-10 knots per inch across and 8-12 down (about 48-120 per square inch); Stone gives 100-160 for later rugs.
Bijar is a town of Kurdistan surrounded by weaving villages; in 1976, 44 percent of the district's labor force worked in carpet weaving.
Bijar samplers are relatively common compared with other Persian areas.
Bijar kilims are slit-tapestry weaves; small ones resemble Senneh kilims.
Bijar is a registered carpet geographical indication (Kurdistan province).
A stylized willow-and-cypress design was woven in Bijar in the early 20th century.

says.text: Twice between rows.
Twice.
Early rugs usually three, one very heavy; later rugs two.
Bijar-area carpets are triple-wefted.

disagreements.about: who wove them / the name Sarakhs

says.text: Turkomans from Sarakhs are said to have settled near Bijar, hence the name 'Saraks' for Bijar rugs, though the rugs have no Turkoman features.
Sarakhs are the true 'Lulés', made by settlers from old Sarakhs around Bijar.
The population of the Bijar district is predominantly Kurdish.
