rows.name: Medallion Ushak (design)
rows.region: Uşak workshops (Stone, TÜRKPATENT Uşak); similar carpets near İzmir.
rows.made_by: Workshop weavers of western Anatolia (attribution of some groups is debated).
rows.date_note: Sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the Uşak registration says the group developed into the eighteenth century and continued to about its middle.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Kendrick & Tattersall: Uşak carpets 'invariably woven with the Ghiordes knot'; Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Kendrick & Tattersall: Uşak carpets averaged about 70 to 85 knots per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Kendrick & Tattersall: red wool weft, two shoots after each row.
structure.sides: multi-cord selvages where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.ends: wide colored webs where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.spin: Kendrick & Tattersall (1922, p. 101) describe the white wool warp of Uşak carpets as having 'the usual left-handed twist' (the S-plied, Z-spun yarn usual in Anatolia).

design.field: A large round or oval central medallion with pendants and quarter-medallions, cut from an endless repeat; red field with dark blue medallion or the reverse, filled with yellow floral scrolls (Stone; TÜRKPATENT Uşak).

look_alikes.name: Oushak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nineteenth-century and later Oushak carpets descend from these designs but are coarser and in fewer colors.

rows.trade_use: 'Medallion Ushak (design)' is used today as a design name; reproductions are woven in Turkey, India, Pakistan, Romania and elsewhere.
rows.what_it_tells: This is a design of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries; a rug a family owns in this design is almost certainly a later reproduction or revival, and the design alone says nothing about where it was made.
rows.cautions: Treat as a design only. Originals are museum pieces; reproductions are common.

facts.text: Medallion Ushaks have a circular or oval central medallion with pendants on a red (or dark blue) field, in a long format.
The Uşak registration says medallion Uşaks were sometimes made up to 10 m long.
Kendrick & Tattersall describe the Oushak carpet as 'the real forerunner of the Turkey carpet of to-day', much in demand in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Western Europe.
facts.quote: The "Oushak" carpet, the real forerunner of the "Turkey carpet" of to-day, was much in demand in Western Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

rows.name: Lotto (design)
rows.region: Usually attributed to the Uşak area (Stone; Cleveland's record says Ushak).
rows.made_by: Workshop weavers of western Anatolia (attribution of some groups is debated).
rows.date_note: Early sixteenth through eighteenth century.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Kendrick & Tattersall: Uşak carpets 'invariably woven with the Ghiordes knot'; Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Kendrick & Tattersall plate analysis of a sixteenth-century arabesque rug: 95 knots per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Kendrick & Tattersall: red wool weft, two shoots after each row.
structure.sides: multi-cord selvages where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.ends: wide colored webs where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.spin: Kendrick & Tattersall (1922, p. 101) describe the white wool warp of Uşak carpets as having 'the usual left-handed twist' (the S-plied, Z-spun yarn usual in Anatolia).

design.field: An all-over yellow angular arabesque tracery on a red (rarely blue) field, usually with a Kufesque border.

look_alikes.name: Oushak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nineteenth-century and later Oushak carpets descend from these designs but are coarser and in fewer colors.

rows.trade_use: 'Lotto (design)' is used today as a design name; reproductions are woven in Turkey, India, Pakistan, Romania and elsewhere.
rows.what_it_tells: This is a design of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries; a rug a family owns in this design is almost certainly a later reproduction or revival, and the design alone says nothing about where it was made.
rows.cautions: Treat as a design only. Originals are museum pieces; reproductions are common.

facts.text: Lotto rugs have a red field covered by a yellow arabesque tracery and usually a Kufesque border; they are named after the painter Lorenzo Lotto.
facts.quote: The arabesques, too, are often seen — more especially in the paintings of the Venetian Lorenzo Lotto

facts.text: These rugs were woven from the early sixteenth through the eighteenth century and are usually attributed to Uşak (Stone).

rows.name: Holbein (design)
rows.region: Originally attributed to Uşak; Stone says large-pattern Holbeins were probably woven in the Çanakkale area and the origin is being reconsidered.
rows.made_by: Workshop weavers of western Anatolia (attribution of some groups is debated).
rows.date_note: Fifteenth to seventeenth centuries (dates of the paintings in which they appear).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Kendrick & Tattersall: Uşak carpets 'invariably woven with the Ghiordes knot'; Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Kendrick & Tattersall (plate analysis of a sixteenth-century Asia Minor carpet with squares): 70.
structure.wefts_note: Kendrick & Tattersall: red wool weft, two shoots after each row.
structure.sides: multi-cord selvages where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.ends: wide colored webs where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.spin: Kendrick & Tattersall (1922, p. 101) describe the white wool warp of Uşak carpets as having 'the usual left-handed twist' (the S-plied, Z-spun yarn usual in Anatolia).

design.field: Small-pattern: rows of small octagons with interlace, separated by vine-and-floret lozenges, Kufesque border. Large-pattern: large octagons inside squares.

look_alikes.name: Oushak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nineteenth-century and later Oushak carpets descend from these designs but are coarser and in fewer colors.

rows.what_it_tells: This is a design of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries; a rug a family owns in this design is almost certainly a later reproduction or revival, and the design alone says nothing about where it was made.
rows.cautions: Treat as a design only. Originals are museum pieces; reproductions are common.

facts.text: Holbein carpets are named for Turkish rugs shown in paintings by Hans Holbein and his contemporaries; their attribution to Uşak is being reconsidered, and large-pattern examples were probably woven in the Çanakkale area (Stone, p. 129).
The name comes from Turkish rugs shown in paintings by Hans Holbein and other painters of his time; Jacobsen describes their designs as squares and stars.
facts.quote: A very good example is Holbein's great painting of the "Ambassadors" in the National Gallery, London

rows.name: Transylvanian (design)
rows.region: Western Anatolia; the name comes from the many examples found in Transylvanian (Romanian, Hungarian) churches.
rows.made_by: Workshop weavers of western Anatolia (attribution of some groups is debated).
rows.date_note: Sixteenth through eighteenth centuries.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Kendrick & Tattersall: Uşak carpets 'invariably woven with the Ghiordes knot'; Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Kendrick & Tattersall: average 70.
structure.wefts_note: Kendrick & Tattersall: red wool weft, two shoots after each row. For the Transylvanian group they say the warp is mostly dyed yellow and the weft more often yellow than red.
structure.sides: multi-cord selvages where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.ends: wide colored webs where preserved (Kendrick & Tattersall)
structure.spin: Kendrick & Tattersall (1922, p. 101) describe the white wool warp of Uşak carpets as having 'the usual left-handed twist' (the S-plied, Z-spun yarn usual in Anatolia).

design.field: Often a double-ended niche (opposed arches) with vases or lamps, spandrels with floral or geometric fillers, a border of cartouches; about a third of published examples are Lotto designs.

look_alikes.name: Oushak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nineteenth-century and later Oushak carpets descend from these designs but are coarser and in fewer colors.

rows.trade_use: 'Transylvanian (design)' is used today as a design name; reproductions are woven in Turkey, India, Pakistan, Romania and elsewhere.
rows.what_it_tells: This is a design of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries; a rug a family owns in this design is almost certainly a later reproduction or revival, and the design alone says nothing about where it was made.
rows.cautions: Treat as a design only. Originals are museum pieces; reproductions are common.

facts.text: Transylvanian rugs are Turkish rugs found in Protestant churches of Transylvania, imported from western Turkey; of about 300 published, about a third are double-niche prayer designs and a third Lotto designs (Stone, p. 287).
They are named for the accident that many were found in Transylvania, which lay on a trade route for them.
facts.quote: They have acquired the name of Transylvanian carpets from the accidental circumstance that considerable numbers have been found in that province

facts.text: Kendrick & Tattersall say the warp of Transylvanian carpets is mostly dyed (usually yellow) and the weft more often yellow than red, about 70 knots per square inch.

rows.name: Ghiordes
rows.region: The town of Gördes (Manisa province), north-east of İzmir in western Anatolia (Hawley: a day's journey east of Bergama).
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers; later export workshops (Hawley: about a thousand looms in the Gördes and Kula districts together).
rows.date_note: Rugs woven in the area since the eighteenth century; Hawley (1913) says pieces seventy-five to one hundred and fifty years old could still be bought, and that modern Gördes production was quite different. Copies were woven in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries in Kayseri, Hereke, Bandırma and elsewhere.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot; the trade name 'Ghiordes knot' for the symmetric knot comes from this town. A 2025 Turkish study (Öztürk) argues the names 'Gördes knot' and 'Sine knot' are Western misnomers.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally seven to twelve, perpendicularly eight to sixteen = 56-192. Lewis 1911: 64-168. Stone: early prayer rugs 100-200. Ballard 1924 catalogue: Ghiordes prayer rugs about 77 to about 260 (OCR uncertain at the top). TÜRKPATENT Gördes (present-day standard): 1,050 per dm2 = about 68.
structure.warp_color: Hawley: wool or cotton, a few raw silk; Lewis: usually wool, antiques occasionally cotton or silk
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of wool or cotton; Lewis: usually cotton, occasionally wool or linen.
structure.pile_note: Clipped very short, harsh to the touch (Hawley); 'the shortest nap of any of the Turkish rugs' and lustreless (Lewis); sometimes cotton pile for white.
structure.sides: A weft selvage of two or three cords, or an added silk selvage (Hawley); 'frequently finished with an added silk selvage in pale colors' (Lewis).
structure.ends: A narrow web and warp fringe; some have an added silk fringe at the corners (Hawley); Lewis says the upper fringe is often a separate piece sewn on.
structure.back: Very fine grain but slightly rough (Hawley); one warp of each pair usually slightly depressed.

design.field: Prayer rugs with a narrow arched (often stepped) niche, sometimes a hanging lamp, one or two cross panels above and below, spandrels with floral arabesques; the field often plain red, blue or ivory; borders of six to nine stripes; later Mejidian-style naturalistic floral designs.
design.border: Six to nine stripes, often alternating light and dark.
design.colors: Red, blue, yellow and white; light blues, yellows, reds and greens with ivory.
design.sizes: Usually 5-7 ft long, two thirds to three quarters as wide.

look_alikes.name: Kula
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kulas have less elaborate borders, lower arches, rarely the corner fringe or more than one panel, floral fields in formal order, spandrels extended down the sides, always subdued colors; Lewis: Kulas always have fine wool warps.

look_alikes.name: Kayseri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kayseri copies are on cotton foundations, often with mercerized cotton, art silk or silk pile.

look_alikes.name: Hereke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hereke copies are much finer, often all silk, with a very short pile.

rows.trade_use: 'Ghiordes' was also a Smyrna trade grade name for heavy carpets and Jacobsen says the poorest 1920s Turkish carpets were sold in London as 'Ghiordes'.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted, very short-piled Turkish prayer rug with a narrow niche, cross panels and many narrow borders matches the Gördes type; age and place depend on foundation and dyes because Gördes designs were widely copied.
rows.cautions: Copies of Gördes prayer rugs were woven in Kayseri, Hereke, Bandırma and elsewhere, some treated to suggest great age. Bandırma (Panderma) copies on cotton foundations were made until the end of the Second World War.

facts.text: Ghiordes rugs are symmetric-knotted, fine (Hawley 56-192, Lewis 64-168 knots per square inch) and very short-piled.
facts.quote: Pile, wool, and occasionally some cotton, clipped very short so as to be harsh to the touch.

facts.text: Ghiordes warps are usually wool, sometimes cotton or silk; wefts wool or cotton.
facts.quote: Warp, wool or cotton and in a few pieces raw silk.

facts.text: Some Ghiordes rugs have an added silk selvage or silk fringe.
facts.quote: Frequently finished with an added silk selvage in pale colors.

facts.text: Hawley dated pieces by color: reds of rugs under a century old (in 1913) have a pinkish or magenta tinge, older ones a deep red.
In the nineteenth century, copies of Gördes prayer rugs were woven in Kayseri, Hereke, Bandırma and other places, some treated to look old.

The present-day Gördes registration (1997) specifies the Turkish double knot at 1,050 knots per dm2 (about 68 per square inch), all-wool foundation, pile 5-7 mm, prayer-rug sizes with mihrab and corner-medallion designs.
Ballard's 1924 catalogue (rugs later given to museums) records knot counts for Ghiordes prayer rugs ranging from about 77 to over 200 per square inch.

A 2025 Turkish study argues that the names 'Gördes (Ghiordes) knot' and 'Sine (Senneh) knot' are Western coinages that do not describe where the knots are used; 'symmetric' and 'asymmetric' are the structural terms.

says.text: Weft, wool or cotton.
Usually cotton, occasionally wool or linen.

disagreements.about: dates of old Ghiordes prayer rugs

says.text: Catalogues most Ghiordes prayer rugs as seventeenth or eighteenth century.
Rugs have been woven in the area of Gördes since the eighteenth century.

rows.name: Kula
rows.region: The town of Kula (Manisa province), about eighty miles east of İzmir, south-east of Gördes; Demirci rugs are related.
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers; later workshop production for export.
rows.date_note: Eighteenth-century rugs are attributed to Kula; after 1920 quality declined. Hawley says the modern factory-like production of his day mixed mohair with the wool.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally five to ten, perpendicularly seven to twelve = 35-120. Lewis 1911: 64-168. Stone: early about 120, later about 50. Ballard 1924: about 48-126. TÜRKPATENT Kula (present-day standard): 1,500 per dm2 = about 97.
structure.weft_color: sometimes dyed yellow (Hawley); Lewis: generally dyed yellow
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: in most rugs two wefts of wool; in others, even very old, a coarse jute weft crossing once alternating with a thin jute and a wool weft side by side.
structure.pile_note: Short or medium; lacks lustre (Hawley); mohair mixed in some later rugs (Hawley, Lewis).
structure.sides: A colored mixed selvage of two to four cords (Hawley); antiques always selvaged, moderns usually overcast (Lewis).
structure.ends: A colored web and warp fringe (Hawley); narrow web with loose warps (Lewis).
structure.back: Moderately coarse grain; one warp of each pair noticeably depressed (Hawley).

design.field: Prayer rugs similar to Gördes but with lower arches, formal floral fields (often a vase of flowers), the spandrel color carried down the sides in two narrow stripes; also 'mazarlık' (graveyard or landscape) designs with houses and trees.
design.border: Six to nine stripes, many narrow, with a characteristic stripe of tiny repeated figures.
design.colors: Mellow red or golden-brown 'apricot' fields with light-blue spandrels, dark-blue panels, green, brown and canary yellow.
design.sizes: 5-7 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Ghiordes
look_alikes.how_to_tell: See Ghiordes: Kula borders are simpler and arches lower; colors always subdued.

look_alikes.name: Kayseri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kayseri copies are on cotton foundations.

rows.trade_use: 'Kula' (Koula) names western Anatolian prayer rugs of this type; Jacobsen says new rugs sold as 'Kula' in 1960 bore no resemblance to the old type.
rows.what_it_tells: A Turkish prayer rug with wool foundation, a depressed warp, mellow yellow-brown colors and many narrow border stripes points to Kula.
rows.cautions: Kula and Gördes rugs are hard to tell apart. Graveyard (mazarlık) designs were woven in Kula, Gördes and Kırşehir.

facts.text: Kula prayer rugs resemble early Gördes prayer rugs, often with a vase of flowers in the field (Stone); Hawley says even experts sometimes cannot tell old Kulas and Ghiordes apart.
facts.quote: even the most experienced are sometimes at a loss to distinguish between them.

facts.text: Early Kula rugs have about 120 knots per square inch and later ones about 50 (Stone); Hawley gives 35-120 and Lewis 64-168.
Some Kula rugs, even old ones, have jute wefts.
facts.quote: the weft consists of a coarse thread of jute crossing once between two rows of knots

facts.text: Later Kula rugs sometimes have mohair mixed into the pile.
facts.quote: with the wool of many is mixed mohair, so that rapid deterioration follows slight usage.

facts.text: After 1920 Kula rugs declined, with coarse weaves and garish colors (Stone).

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Kula El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 13) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,500 knots per square decimeter (quality 30x50), about 97 knots per square inch (1,500 / 15.5), pile 7-10 mm, wool warp and wool wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row).

says.text: About 120 in early rugs, about 50 in later.
Sometimes dyed yellow.
Generally dyed yellow.

rows.name: Ladik
rows.region: The town of Lâdik north-west of Konya in central Anatolia, site of ancient Laodicea. Several Turkish towns are called Lâdik.
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers.
rows.date_note: Attributed from the eighteenth century, production declining after the First World War; a recent boom makes Lâdik a major center of Persian-design rugs today.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally nine to twelve, perpendicularly ten to thirteen = 90-156. Lewis 1911: 64-168. Ballard 1924: 64-112. Stone: contemporary Persian-design rugs 140-160.
structure.warp_color: fine wool, dyed the predominating color (Lewis)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of fine wool, generally red.
structure.pile_note: Medium (Hawley); in antiques fine lustrous wool cut short (Lewis).
structure.sides: A red added selvage of two or three cords (Hawley); a fairly wide colored selvage (Lewis).
structure.ends: A narrow web and warp fringe (Hawley); usually a 2-3 inch red web at each end, often striped yellow or blue (Lewis).
structure.back: Medium grain; one warp of each pair generally depressed (Hawley); Stone: offset warps in older rugs.

design.field: Prayer rugs with stepped, triple-arch or two-column niches and a cross panel of tulips on stems rising from 'vandykes'.
design.border: Four stripes; main stripe of lilies alternating with rosettes.
design.colors: Strong unshaded red and blue fields; shades of red and blue.
design.sizes: 4.5-7 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Konya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Konya prayer rugs vary more in their arches and have earth tones; Ladik's tulip panel is the marker.

rows.trade_use: 'Ladik' names old prayer rugs with tulip panels; new Lâdik production is mostly Persian floral designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A wool-foundation Turkish prayer rug with a row of tall tulips in a panel below or above the niche points to Lâdik.
rows.cautions: Tulip-panel designs are copied; check foundation and dyes.

facts.text: Ladik prayer rugs have a cross panel of tulips (or pomegranates) on stems rising from vandykes.
facts.quote: Between the fields and the borders of the ends are generally spacious panels, on which are represented rows of Vandykes.

facts.text: Older Ladik rugs are wool throughout with offset (depressed) warps.
facts.quote: One of the two threads encircled by a knot is generally depressed below the other at the back.

facts.text: Ladik is relatively finely knotted: Hawley 90-156, Lewis 64-168, Ballard 64-112 knots per square inch.
Lâdik is today a major weaving center producing Persian floral designs at 140-160 knots per square inch (Stone).

rows.name: Konya
rows.region: The city of Konya and the surrounding villages of south-central Anatolia, including Lâdik, Karapınar, Obruk, Keçimuhsine.
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers, Yörük and Turkmen groups in the province.
rows.date_note: Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century rugs in earth tones; Hawley and Mumford say Konya's modern (c. 1900) output was heavy carpets of the Oushak and Ghiordes grades.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally five to eight, perpendicularly six to ten = 30-80. Lewis 1911: 56-120.
structure.warp_color: fine wool in antiques, coarse in later ones, frequently dyed (Lewis); Mumford: later warps of very many colors, sometimes two colors in one yarn
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of medium wool dyed red. Mumford describes an old Konya with two wefts thrown together.
structure.pile_note: medium length
structure.sides: Generally a selvage of two or three cords, occasionally overcast (Hawley); antiques selvaged, moderns overcast (Lewis).
structure.ends: A web and warp fringe (Hawley, Lewis).

design.field: Prayer rugs with the greatest variety of arches (sharp, flat or stepped, with latch hooks into the spandrel), sometimes a lamp, a row of three-petal sprigs along the sides; geometric borders. Stone: earth tones (brown, green, mustard), some apricot fields; modern red-ground prayer rugs.
design.colors: Rich reds or blues in the field; yellow, green and white in the borders; earth tones and apricot.
design.sizes: 4.5-6 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Ladik
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lâdik's tulip panel.

look_alikes.name: Karapınar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karapınar rugs are runners or long rugs with Caucasian-like geometry.

rows.trade_use: Used for central Anatolian prayer rugs and large carpets marketed at Konya.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to central Anatolia.
rows.cautions: Konya is a market name covering many villages.

facts.text: Konya rugs are symmetric-knotted on wool, with red-dyed wefts.
facts.quote: Weft, wool, of medium diameter, dyed red.

facts.text: Konya prayer rugs show more variety in their arches than any other Anatolian prayer rug.
facts.quote: Probably in no other Asia Minor rug is such latitude in the drawing of the prayer arch.

facts.text: By about 1900 Konya produced heavy carpets in the Oushak and Ghiordes grades.
facts.quote: The modern Konieh manufacture is almost wholly of the heavy carpet order.

facts.text: Rugs have been woven in and around Konya since the Seljuk period; eighteenth- and nineteenth-century rugs are in earth tones, some with apricot fields (Stone).

rows.name: Karapınar
rows.region: The town of Karapınar, Konya province, south-central Anatolia.
rows.made_by: Village weavers (Turkmen and Yörük background).
rows.date_note: The 2026 registration describes eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Karapınar carpets as well as present production; Stone describes older rugs.

structure.knot_note: Turkish (symmetric) knot (Stone; TÜRKPATENT Karapınar).
structure.kpsi_note: No density given in the sources at hand.
structure.wefts_note: Not given.
structure.pile_note: Pure wool, hand-spun and plied, natural dyes (registration).
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: Geometric: one or three medallions (often eight-pointed stars in octagons or four-armed hooked medallions linked by small medallions), a single 'comb' border, and narrow end bands of house motifs; designs similar to Caucasian rugs.
design.border: A single border with comb (tarak) motifs (registration).
design.colors: Shades of red with mustard yellow; white in all, indigo and red most striking (registration).
design.sizes: Many in runner format; often large (registration).

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Designs look Caucasian; Karapınar rugs are often long runners with a single comb border and house-motif end bands.

rows.trade_use: Used for central Anatolian village runners and long rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to the Konya region.
rows.cautions: Structure data are thin in the sources at hand.

facts.text: Karapınar rugs are all wool, often runners, red with mustard yellow, with geometric medallions such as eight-pointed stars in octagons; designs resemble Caucasian rugs (Stone, p. 151).
The 2026 Karapınar registration describes pure hand-spun wool, natural dyes ('çöpboya'/'kökboya'), the Turkish knot, one or three medallions, a single comb border and house motifs in the end bands.
Karapınar rugs are pure wool with the Turkish knot.

rows.name: Obruk
rows.region: A town of south-central Anatolia (the Konya plain). Note: the 2017 geographical indication 'Obruk (Arısama) Halısı' belongs to a different Obruk village, in Bor, Niğde province.
rows.made_by: Village and nomadic weavers.
rows.date_note: Prayer kilims from the late nineteenth century.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Anatolian norm).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 'coarsely woven'; no figure.

design.field: Coarsely woven pile rugs of nomadic character; fine kilims, including prayer kilims with pointed, hooked mihrabs and a tree of life in each spandrel.

look_alikes.name: Konya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Obruk is one of the Konya-area villages.

rows.trade_use: A village name used mostly for kilims and coarse pile rugs of the Konya plain.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to the Konya region.
rows.cautions: Single source; do not confuse with the Niğde-Bor 'Obruk (Arısama)' registration.

facts.text: Obruk is a source of coarsely woven pile rugs of nomadic character and of fine kilims; from the late nineteenth century, prayer kilims with pointed, hooked mihrabs and a tree of life in each spandrel (Stone, p. 208).

rows.name: Mudjur
rows.region: The town of Mucur near the Kızılırmak in Kırşehir province, central Anatolia, about 25 miles south of Kırşehir.
rows.made_by: Town and village weavers.
rows.date_note: Hawley and Stone describe nineteenth-century prayer rugs; Ballard catalogued one as eighteenth century.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally six to nine, perpendicularly seven to twelve = 42-108. Ballard 1924: 63-72.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two wefts of medium to coarse wool dyed red or brown.
structure.pile_note: medium, glistening (Hawley)
structure.sides: A three-cord selvage, frequently red (Hawley).
structure.ends: Colored webs and fringe (Hawley).
structure.back: Moderately coarse; one warp generally depressed (Hawley).

design.field: Prayer rugs and multi-niche saffs with stepped and pointed (sometimes nested) mihrabs and a cross panel above; main border of rectangles holding geometric blossoms, like mosaic.
design.colors: The most colors of any Asia Minor rug: red, yellow, green, blue, mauve and pink; earlier rugs muted red, green and brown.
design.sizes: 4-6 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Kirshehir
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kırşehir is 25 miles away and arches are similar; Mucur borders are broad tile-like rectangles in many colors.

rows.trade_use: Used for central Anatolian prayer rugs with tile borders.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to the Kırşehir-Mucur area.
rows.cautions: Often classed simply as 'Anatolian'.

facts.text: Mudjur prayer rugs have arches like Kırşehir's and broad borders of many colors resembling mosaic.
facts.quote: no other rug of Asia Minor contains as a rule so many colours, which appear in the broad borders of old, well-woven pieces with glistening wool almost like mosaic work.

facts.text: Mudjur rugs are symmetric-knotted on wool with two red or brown wefts, 42-108 knots per square inch (Hawley).

rows.name: Kirshehir
rows.region: The town of Kırşehir north of the salt desert in central Anatolia, with Turkmen groups in the countryside. Lewis 1911 wrongly places it near Smyrna.
rows.made_by: Town weavers and Turkmen of the surrounding country.
rows.date_note: Hawley describes old pieces free of Western influence; Cleveland dates its examples to the late nineteenth century.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally five to nine, perpendicularly five to ten = 25-90. Lewis 1911: 42-120.
structure.weft_color: often of different colors in one rug (Hawley)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two to six wefts, varying within a rug.
structure.pile_note: Medium (Hawley); 'long, fluffy' (Lewis); glossy (Stone).
structure.sides: A weft selvage of two to four cords of different colors (Hawley).
structure.ends: Lower end web and warp loops; upper end web and fringe (Hawley); small mats sometimes carry tufts of all the rug's colors on the webs (Lewis).
structure.back: Coarse grain; warp shows in places (Hawley).

design.field: Prayer rugs with steep serrated arches outlined by several colored lines, prayer runners (saffs) and yastıks; floral and geometric forms blended; grass green used lavishly.
design.colors: Red, green (especially grass green), blue, brown, white.
design.sizes: 4-6 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Mudjur
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mucur borders are tile-like rectangles; Kırşehir arches are outlined in many parallel colored lines.

rows.trade_use: Used for central Anatolian prayer rugs; graveyard designs were also woven here.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to central Anatolia.

facts.text: Kırşehir rugs make lavish use of grass green.
facts.quote: as well as grass-coloured green, for which they had a particular fondness

facts.text: Kırşehir rugs are all wool; the wool is usually glossy (Stone); prayer rugs, prayer runners and yastıks are woven there.
Kırşehir wefts may cross two to six times between rows and be of different colors in one rug (Hawley).

rows.name: Bergama
rows.region: Bergama (ancient Pergamon), İzmir province, north-west Anatolia; the name is also used loosely for west Anatolian village rugs of uncertain origin; nearby Yuntdağ, Kozak and the Yağcıbedir area are separate groups.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Bergama district.
rows.date_note: Hawley (1913) says good Bergamas fifty or more years old were still obtainable; Jacobsen dates the choice old Bergamos from the eighteenth century to the First World War; present production is registered (1997).

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally five and a half to nine, perpendicularly seven to eleven = about 39-99. Lewis 1911: 60-168. Ballard 1924: about 60-132. TÜRKPATENT Bergama (present-day standard): 1,280 per dm2 = about 83.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two to six wefts; Lewis: frequently several.
structure.pile_note: Medium to long, soft and lustrous (Hawley, Lewis).
structure.sides: A weft selvage of two to four cords, red or blue (Hawley); broad red selvages, often with small wool tassels along the sides (Lewis).
structure.ends: A wide red web (up to six or seven inches) crossed by blue or other stripes, often with charms against the evil eye attached; tasselled fringe (Hawley); webs may carry woven rosettes (Lewis).

design.field: Nearly square rugs with a large central medallion (often hexagonal with hooked ends) surrounded by balanced small motifs; prayer rugs are the exception; Caucasian-looking geometric designs in later rugs.
design.border: One to four stripes, most often three.
design.colors: Deep blue and madder red with ivory.
design.sizes: 3-7 ft long, nearly square.

look_alikes.name: Yağcıbedir
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yağcıbedir rugs are dark blue and red, coarser (40-50 knots), with plaited warp ends.

look_alikes.name: Çanakkale
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Çanakkale rugs are coarse with red wefts and red plain-weave ends; the trade may also call them Bergama.

rows.trade_use: Used broadly for west Anatolian village rugs; Jacobsen says cheap 1920s small rugs were sold as 'Pergamos', not to be confused with old Bergamas.
rows.what_it_tells: A near-square, long-piled all-wool rug with red wefts and wide red striped end webs points to the Bergama district.
rows.cautions: 'Bergama' is applied to west Anatolian rugs of indefinite origin.

facts.text: Bergama rugs are nearly square, and prayer rugs are the exception.
facts.quote: in shape they are nearly square, and prayer rugs are the exception rather than the rule.

facts.text: Bergama rugs have wide red end webs crossed by colored stripes, often with charms against the evil eye attached.
facts.quote: Both ends, a web, that is sometimes six or seven inches wide, coloured red and crossed by broad longitudinal stripes

facts.text: Bergama wefts are wool dyed red, two or more between rows.
facts.quote: Weft, wool of fine diameter, dyed red. A thread of weft crosses from two to six times between every two rows of knots.

facts.text: The name Bergama is sometimes applied to western Anatolian rugs of indefinite origin (Stone).

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Bergama El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 14) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,280 knots per square decimeter (quality 32x40), about 83 knots per square inch (1,280 / 15.5), pile 7-10 mm, wool warp and wool wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row).

says.text: About 39-99.
About 60-132 for the rugs catalogued.

rows.name: Yağcıbedir
rows.region: Villages of the Yağcıbedir Turkmen around Sındırgı, Balıkesir province, in the Bergama-Balıkesir area of north-west Anatolia (Stone; TÜRKPATENT registration filed by Sındırgı municipality).
rows.made_by: Villages of the Yağcıbedir (a Turkmen group).
rows.date_note: Stone describes older and current production, which is increasing; registered 1997.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric (Turkish double) knot (Stone; registration).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 40-50. TÜRKPATENT Yağcıbedir (present-day standard): 1,050 per dm2 = about 68.
structure.wefts_note: Registration: a thick and a thin wool weft.
structure.pile_note: 5-7 mm in the registration.
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: Warp ends plaited and tasseled (Stone).
structure.back: Stone: some older examples have a line of variously dyed Angora wool knotted on the back.

design.field: Hexagonal medallions with stepped ends filled with geometric flowers; prayer rugs with a stepped niche filled with eight-pointed stars; narrow runners of geometric blossoms on dark blue; contemporary copies of the Eagle Kazak; stylized plant and geometric motifs in double-ended mihrab layouts (registration).
design.colors: Dark blue and red dominant.

look_alikes.name: Chelaberd (Eagle Kazak)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yağcıbedir weavers copy the Eagle Kazak; dark blue grounds, plaited tasseled warp ends and newer wool separate them from Caucasian originals.

look_alikes.name: Bergama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same district; Yağcıbedir rugs are darker (blue and red).

rows.trade_use: Sold as 'Yagcibedir' or 'Yahyali' style dark village rugs; Stone notes production is increasing.
rows.what_it_tells: A dark blue and red, coarse, all-wool rug with plaited tasseled warp ends points to the Yağcıbedir villages.
rows.cautions: Contemporary Yağcıbedir rugs copy Caucasian designs (Eagle Kazak) and can be mistaken for Caucasian rugs.

facts.text: Yağcıbedir rugs are dark blue and red village rugs of the Balıkesir-Bergama area, knotted at 40-50 symmetric knots per square inch, with plaited and tasseled warp ends; contemporary designs include copies of the Eagle Kazak (Stone, p. 310).

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Yağcıbedir El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 17) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,050 knots per square decimeter (quality 30x35), about 68 knots per square inch (1,050 / 15.5), pile 5-7 mm, wool warp and wool wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row).
Yağcıbedir rugs are all wool with the symmetric knot.

says.text: 40-50 per square inch.
1,050 per dm2 (about 68 per square inch) as the registered standard.

rows.name: Çanakkale
rows.region: Çanakkale province on the Dardanelles, north-west Anatolia, including Ayvacık, Yenice, Çan and Ezine.
rows.made_by: Village weavers descended from semi-nomadic Yörük of the mountain villages (registration).
rows.date_note: Stone describes nineteenth- and twentieth-century rugs; registered 1997 (Çanakkale municipality), current text from a later amendment.

structure.knot_note: Turkish (Gördes) knot (Stone; registration).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 40-80. TÜRKPATENT Çanakkale (present-day standard): 672-1,000 per dm2 = about 43-65.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: the number of wefts varies between rows; registration: a thick and a thin wool weft.
structure.pile_note: Long: 8-10 mm in the registration.
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: Usually red plain weave (Stone).

design.field: Entirely geometric: octagons, hexagons, diamonds, hooks and stars; named motifs include the star dish (yıldız tabak), crane medallion (turna göbeği), plane-tree leaf, Turkmen rose; usually three borders (registration).
design.border: One wide and two narrow borders; carnation, scissors and water motifs (registration).
design.colors: Mostly natural dyes: blues, greens, browns, black and white; yellow more common in Ayvacık and Yenice (registration); red fields.

look_alikes.name: Bergama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone says the trade may call Çanakkale rugs 'Bergama'.

look_alikes.name: Ezine
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ezine is a collecting town south of Çanakkale for similar rugs.

look_alikes.name: DOBAG
look_alikes.how_to_tell: DOBAG cooperative rugs are woven in Ayvacık with natural dyes and carry a DOBAG label/certificate.

rows.trade_use: 'Canakkale' and 'Ezine' are used for coarse north-west Anatolian village rugs; Stone says the trade may call them Bergama.
rows.what_it_tells: A coarse all-wool rug with red wefts, red plain-weave ends and bold geometric medallions points to Çanakkale province.
rows.cautions: Also sold as Bergama; DOBAG cooperative rugs come from the same district.

facts.text: Nineteenth- and twentieth-century Çanakkale rugs are coarsely woven on a wool foundation with red wefts, about 40-80 symmetric knots per square inch, usually with red plain-weave ends; the trade may call them Bergama (Stone, p. 59).

The Çanakkale registration specifies the Turkish (Gördes) knot at 672-1,000 per dm2 (about 43-65 per square inch), pile 8-10 mm, wool warp and wefts, mostly natural dyes, and geometric designs with three borders; it traces Çanakkale weaving to semi-nomadic Yörük of the mountain villages.
Çanakkale rugs are coarse, all-wool, symmetric-knotted rugs.

rows.name: Ezine
rows.region: A town (formerly Avunya) south of Çanakkale serving as a collection point for rugs woven in the area.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Çanakkale district.
rows.date_note: Stone describes older rugs collected at Ezine.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (as Çanakkale).
structure.kpsi_note: No separate figure; see Çanakkale.

design.field: Red, blue and yellow complex geometric designs with arrows projecting from rectangular medallions, often within the leaf-and-goblet border.
design.colors: Red, blue, yellow.
design.sizes: Small sizes.

look_alikes.name: Çanakkale
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same district.

look_alikes.name: Shirvan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The leaf-and-goblet border is also typical of Shirvans; Ezine rugs are coarser and wool-wefted red.

rows.trade_use: A market name for Çanakkale-district rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to north-west Anatolia.
rows.cautions: Single source.

facts.text: Ezine, south of Çanakkale, served as a collection point for rugs woven in the area: red, blue and yellow geometric designs with arrows projecting from rectangular medallions, often with the leaf-and-goblet border; wool throughout and small (Stone, p. 105).

rows.name: Milas
rows.region: Milas (ancient Mylasa) and surrounding villages in Muğla province, south-west Anatolia; Lewis 1911 misplaces it 'a few miles southwest of Smyrna'.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Milas district (Stone: today weaving only in the surrounding villages).
rows.date_note: Weaving may have begun in the seventeenth century; Hawley describes old pieces and modern copies; registered 1997.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally five to eight, perpendicularly six to eleven = 30-88. Lewis 1911: 20-90. Stone: 55-75. TÜRKPATENT Milas (present-day standard): 1,040 per dm2 = about 67.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: generally four wefts of small diameter, dyed blue or red; Lewis: cotton or wool, mostly wool.
structure.pile_note: Medium, sometimes short (Hawley); coarse, lustrous, cut short (Lewis).
structure.sides: A selvage of two to four cords, usually red (Hawley); Stone notes a red-weft, all-wool construction.
structure.ends: Lower end a red web and loose fringe; upper end a red web, a braided selvage and fringe (Hawley).

design.field: Prayer rugs with a diamond-shaped (horseshoe-derived) mihrab; rugs with vertical panels like Makri; a column of boxes or diamonds; narrow fields between wide borders; 'thumb-like' cogwheel inner border; Mejidian floral rugs.
design.border: Several stripes; the central one as wide as the rest, palmettes and flowers.
design.colors: Dark red, ivory, yellow, green and a characteristic lavender or mauve; golden yellow.
design.sizes: 4.5-6 ft long.

look_alikes.name: Ladik
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Milas mihrabs fold inward to a diamond; Ladik has a tulip panel.

rows.trade_use: Used for south-west Anatolian prayer rugs and panel rugs; 'Carian' in old books.
rows.what_it_tells: A red-wefted all-wool rug with a diamond-shaped niche, mauve and golden yellow points to Milas.
rows.cautions: Makri (Fethiye) rugs with vertical panels are a neighboring group.

facts.text: Milas rugs are all wool with red wefts, mostly coarsely knotted at about 55-75 knots per square inch (Stone, p. 191).
Melez (Milas) prayer rugs have a mihrab whose sides angle in toward the field, forming an incomplete diamond.
facts.quote: The resulting drawing shows two equilateral triangles on each side of the field at the base of the mihrab

facts.text: A lavender or mauve tone is present in almost every old Melez.
facts.quote: a characteristic tone of lavender or mauve, which is present in almost every old Melez.

facts.text: The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Milas El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 15) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,040 knots per square decimeter (quality 26x40), about 67 knots per square inch (1,040 / 15.5), pile 7-8 mm, wool warp and wool wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row).

museum_examples.title: Carpet

rows.name: Döşemealtı
rows.region: Döşemealtı district just north of Antalya, south-west Anatolia.
rows.made_by: Teke Yörük settled in Döşemealtı (registration).
rows.date_note: The registration (2021) describes older and present weaving; Stone describes only a few small rugs.

structure.knot_note: Turkish (Gördes) knot (registration).
structure.kpsi_note: Registration: formerly 3x4 to 4x4 knots per cm2 (12-16 per cm2 = about 77-103 per square inch), today down to 2x2 (4 per cm2 = about 26 per square inch).
structure.weft_color: the color of the rug's ground (registration)
structure.wefts_note: Registration: after each row of knots a 'süzme' weft then a 'basma' weft.
structure.pile_note: 7-8 mm, handspun doubled wool (registration).
structure.sides: A kilim-woven edge 1-1.5 cm wide in wool of the field color (registration).
structure.ends: A kilim band 2-3 cm, the same color as the edge, and a plaited 'çiti' at the fringe (registration).

design.field: Small near-square prayer-size rugs: halelli (field of small symmetric motifs), toplu (two or three large cross-shaped motifs), akrepli (scorpion-filled lozenge), dallı (branch), camili (mosque) designs; many named borders ('su') (registration).
design.colors: Older: red, blue, dark blue, green and white; today red, burgundy, green, black, blues and natural yellow; natural dyes described (registration).
design.sizes: 71 x 120 cm to 143 x 196 cm (registration).

look_alikes.name: Yürük
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Döşemealtı is a settled Yörük weaving; small square-ish prayer-size rugs with kilim-woven edges.

rows.trade_use: Rugs from Döşemealtı are sometimes called 'Antalya'.
rows.what_it_tells: A small all-wool Turkish-knotted rug with kilim-woven side edges and ends in the field color points to Döşemealtı.
rows.cautions: The registration says new rugs are spread on fields in the sun to fade them to pastel tones, so fading alone does not indicate age.

facts.text: Döşemealtı rugs are woven by Teke Yörük with the Turkish knot on wool warps and wefts (registration).
The registration says knot counts fell from 3x4 or 4x4 per cm2 in older rugs to about 2x2 today.
Newly woven Döşemealtı rugs are laid out in fields in the sun to fade to pastel tones preferred by buyers (registration).
Only a few small rugs are woven in Döşemealtı; carpets made there are sometimes called Antalya (Stone).

says.text: Döşemealtı entry: rugs attributed to Döşemealtı may have been woven in Antalya. Antalya entry: carpets made in Döşemealtı are sometimes incorrectly termed Antalya.
Döşemealtı rugs are woven by Teke Yörük in Döşemealtı district and its neighborhoods.

rows.name: Yürük
rows.region: Pastoral nomads of Anatolia, moving between mountain summer pastures and coastal winter plains in western and southern Anatolia.
rows.made_by: Yörük pastoral nomads, of Turkmen origin.
rows.date_note: Hawley describes the rugs of his day and older pieces; Stone says the name is used very widely.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally five to seven, perpendicularly six to nine = 30-63. Lewis 1911: 56-120.
structure.warp_color: brown wool or goat hair, frequently dyed (Lewis)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two to four wefts, varying in the same rug.
structure.pile_note: Long, floccy, lustrous; sometimes goat hair mixed in (Lewis).
structure.sides: Generally a heavy double overcasting, sometimes a double selvage (Hawley); selvaged with goat hair or overcast with colored yarn (Lewis).
structure.ends: Colored webs, often with a parti-colored cord, warp loops or knotted or braided fringe (Hawley, Lewis).

design.field: Nomadic geometric designs: hooked lozenges, diagonal stripes, crude unrelated figures, sometimes boteh borrowed from Kurdish weavers.
design.colors: Dark madder, blue, green and brown, deeper and less bright than Kazaks.
design.sizes: 4-9 ft long, narrow.

look_alikes.name: East Anatolian Kurdish rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurdish rugs of Turkey have often been mislabeled 'Yörük'.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yürük rugs resemble Kazaks in their long pile and hooks but are darker and less brilliant.

rows.trade_use: Used loosely for any shaggy nomadic-looking Anatolian rug.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Anatolian pastoral weaving, but the label is loose.
rows.cautions: Kurdish rugs are often mislabeled Yörük.

facts.text: Yörük rugs resemble Caucasian Kazaks in their long pile and hooked designs but are darker in color.
facts.quote: resembling more than anything else the work of the wild Kazaks of the Caucasus

facts.text: Yürük warps and wefts may be brown wool or goat hair.
facts.quote: Warp. — Brown wool or goats' hair. Frequently dyed.

facts.text: Yörük weavings are all wool, made with many techniques, and strongly influenced by neighbors; Kurdish rugs have been mistakenly attributed to the Yörük (Stone).

rows.name: East Anatolian Kurdish rugs
rows.region: Eastern Anatolia: the Anti-Taurus foothills, the country around Lake Van (Lewis 1911's 'Mosul' rugs), Malatya, Hakkari, Kars and Sivas.
rows.made_by: Kurdish village and formerly nomadic weavers.
rows.date_note: Sources describe nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century rugs.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Lewis 1911 ('Mosul' rugs made by Kurds around Lake Van): 36-80.
structure.warp_color: coarse dark wool or goat hair, occasionally cotton (Lewis)
structure.wefts_note: Stone: Kurdish wefts are two-ply except in Turkey (where they are unplied).
structure.pile_note: Long, lustrous; camel or goat hair sometimes used (Lewis).
structure.sides: Corded edges overcast with dark wool or with wool of different colors 'after the Kurdish fashion' (Lewis).
structure.ends: A narrow web with stripes of colored yarn (red and blue); one end often turned and hemmed, the other braided and knotted (Lewis).

design.field: Crude geometric designs, often irregular in shape, with braided warp fringes; geometric motifs or abstract designs.
design.colors: Dark rich blues, yellows, greens, reds and browns.

look_alikes.name: Yürük
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurdish rugs of Turkey have often been mislabeled Yörük.

look_alikes.name: Kars
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurdish rugs of the Kars area are not generally distinguishable from other Kars rugs.

rows.trade_use: 'Kurdish' is used for rugs of Kurdish weavers in Turkey, Iran and Iraq; old American books used 'Mosul' for some.
rows.what_it_tells: A coarse, long-piled, irregular rug with dark wool or goat-hair warps and colorful overcast edges points to Kurdish village weaving.
rows.cautions: Kurdish weavers adopt local designs, so few overall characterizations hold.

facts.text: Kurdish tribes of the Anti-Taurus foothills wove coarse rugs with irregular shapes, crude geometric designs, long uneven pile and braided warp fringes (Hawley, p. 188).
facts.quote: for their usual unsymmetric shapes, crude geometric designs, long uneven nap, and braided fringe of warp at the ends are lacking in all elegance.

facts.text: Rugs sold as 'Mosul' were made by Kurds of the mountains north of Mosul around Lake Van, symmetric-knotted at 36-80 per square inch, with dark wool or goat-hair warps (Lewis 1911).
Kurdish wefts are two-ply except in Turkey; many Kurdish rugs of Turkey have been incorrectly described as Yörük (Stone, p. 167).

rows.name: Sivas
rows.region: The city of Sivas and surrounding villages in north-central Anatolia; Zara, Şarkışla and Kangal nearby.
rows.made_by: Town and village women; later a government weaving school and prisoners.
rows.date_note: Carpets were made before the First World War ('Smyrna-Sivas' the finest Turkish grade); registered 1997.

structure.knot_note: Hawley and the registration: symmetric (Turkish) knot. Stone: symmetric except at a government weaving school, where Persian-design rugs are woven with the asymmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: horizontally seven to eleven, perpendicularly nine to fifteen = 63-165. TÜRKPATENT Sivas (present-day standard): 2,500 per dm2 = about 161.
structure.warp_color: Hawley: cotton, well spun, of small diameter; Stone: older rugs all wool, cotton increasingly used
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two cotton wefts. Registration: thick and thin cotton wefts.
structure.pile_note: Short to medium (Hawley); 4.5-5 mm in the registration.
structure.sides: An added selvage of four or five cords attached in places (Hawley).
structure.ends: Narrow web and loose fringe (Hawley).
structure.back: Only slightly coarse; one warp depressed and sometimes doubled under the other (Hawley).

design.field: A large hexagon reaching the sides with an inner medallion on a white field, rosettes and floral figures, narrow borders; three rectangular panels of different colors each with a stepped medallion, broad vertical stripes, a carnation-vine border; Persian designs at the school.
design.colors: Red and white with dull blue, green and light yellow.
design.sizes: 3.5-6.5 ft long; carpet sizes.

look_alikes.name: Oushak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sivas carpets are finer, short-piled and on cotton foundations; Jacobsen says unidentified old Turkish carpets are often just called Sivas or Smyrna.

rows.trade_use: Any old Turkish carpet that cannot be called Oushak 'is invariably called Sivas or Smyrna'; pre-1914 'Smyrna-Sivas' meant the finest Turkish carpets.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted Turkish carpet with a cotton foundation and depressed warps points to Sivas or a similar central Anatolian workshop.
rows.cautions: Persian-design Sivas carpets with asymmetric knots exist.

facts.text: Sivas rugs have cotton warps and wefts, the warp well spun and one warp of each pair depressed.
facts.quote: not only are both warp and weft of cotton, but the warp is of small diameter and well spun, and one of the two threads to which a knot is tied is depressed below the other.

facts.text: Older Sivas rugs are all wool, with cotton increasingly used in the foundation (Stone).
Rugs with Persian designs woven at a government weaving school in Sivas use the asymmetric knot (Stone).

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Sivas El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 6) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 2,500 knots per square decimeter (quality 50x50), about 161 knots per square inch (2,500 / 15.5), pile 4.5-5 mm, cotton warp and cotton wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row).

says.text: Both warp and weft of cotton.
Older rugs of Sivas are all wool; cotton is increasingly used in the foundation.
Turkish (double) knot.
Symmetric, except asymmetric at the government weaving school for Persian designs.

rows.name: Kayseri
rows.region: Kayseri (ancient Caesarea) in central Anatolia and nearby Bünyan.
rows.made_by: Town workshops and village weavers.
rows.date_note: Mumford (1902) describes a recent large manufacture of Oushak-type carpets and silk and wool copies of Persian rugs; Bünyan registered 1997; production continues.

structure.knot_note: Mostly symmetric; Stone says a few Kayseri rugs are woven with the asymmetric knot. The Bünyan registration specifies the Turkish knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: contemporary wool rugs 80-120; silk up to 450. TÜRKPATENT Bünyan (present-day standard): 1,512 per dm2 = about 98.
structure.wefts_note: Registration (Bünyan): thick and thin cotton wefts.
structure.pile_note: Stone: wool, rayon (art silk), mercerized cotton or, rarely, silk; white cotton used as a design accent in nineteenth-century rugs; many saffs in mercerized cotton.
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.handle: Silk and art-silk pieces are thin and drape.

design.field: Copies of Turkish prayer designs (especially Gördes) and of Persian designs; multi-niche saffs; prayer rugs with Ghiordes-like arches.
design.colors: Often bright; anilines in Hawley's day.

look_alikes.name: Ghiordes
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kayseri copies of Gördes prayer rugs are on cotton foundations, often with mercerized cotton or art-silk pile.

look_alikes.name: Hereke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hereke silks are finer and the registered Hereke silk is silk throughout; Hawley says Kayseri silks were inferior to Hereke's.

rows.trade_use: 'Kayseri' is used for central Anatolian workshop rugs, including shiny 'silk' rugs that are often mercerized cotton or art silk.
rows.what_it_tells: A shiny Turkish prayer rug on a cotton foundation is consistent with Kayseri workshop production; test whether the 'silk' is silk.
rows.cautions: Art silk (viscose/rayon) and mercerized cotton are sold as 'silk'; Kayseri also copied Gördes prayer rugs, some made to look old.

facts.text: Kayseri (Caesarea) produced silk as well as wool rugs, including copies of Persian designs.
facts.quote: In Cesarea a large general manufacture has sprung up, both of big carpets of the Oushak type, and copies of the Persian sedjadeh, in both silk and wool.

facts.text: Kayseri rugs copied Turkish prayer designs such as Gördes.
facts.quote: prayer rugs with arches resembling the Ghiordes pattern, but their borders are more conventional.

facts.text: Kayseri rugs are woven on a cotton foundation with pile of wool, rayon, mercerized cotton or, rarely, silk; many saffs use mercerized cotton (Stone, p. 154).
Hawley says modern Kayseri products were generally inferior to Hereke's, often aniline dyed.

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Bünyan El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 5) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,512 knots per square decimeter (quality 36x42), about 98 knots per square inch (1,512 / 15.5), pile 5-6 mm, cotton warp and cotton wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row). Wool pile.

says.text: Turkish (double) knot for registered Bünyan rugs.
A few Kayseri rugs are woven with the asymmetric knot.

rows.name: Hereke
rows.region: Hereke on the Gulf of İzmit (Sea of Marmara), Kocaeli province (Millî Saraylar; Hawley).
rows.made_by: The Ottoman imperial factory (Hereke Fabrika-i Hümayunu), later state-run (Sümerbank), and since 1995 the National Palaces administration; private workshops in the town (Millî Saraylar; Stone).
rows.date_note: The factory was founded in 1843 and began producing upholstery and curtain silks in 1845; carpet weaving units were added under Sultan Abdülhamid II (r. 1876-1909) (Millî Saraylar). Stone says rug weaving began in 1864. The year 1891 often given elsewhere is not confirmed by the sources at hand.

structure.knot_note: Disputed: the Hereke registrations specify the Turkish (double, symmetric) knot; Stone says early Hereke production used asymmetric knots.
structure.kpsi_note: Kendrick & Tattersall: wool Hereke carpets 45-64. TÜRKPATENT Hereke wool: 3,600 per dm2 = about 232; Hereke silk: 10,000 per dm2 = about 645 (Stone: 'average grade about 645'). Stone: early production up to 800.
structure.warp_color: silk for silk rugs; cotton for wool rugs (registrations)
structure.wefts_note: Registrations: a thick and a thin weft (silk, or cotton for the wool grade).
structure.pile_note: Silk: 2-2.5 mm; wool: 3.5-4.5 mm (registrations). Later pieces often have metal-thread brocade fields (Stone).
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: Copies of classical Persian designs (Kirman designs, half of output per Jacobsen) and of Gördes prayer rugs; palace carpets and diplomatic gifts; post-war pieces with metal-brocade fields (Hawley, Jacobsen, Stone, Millî Saraylar).
design.colors: Soft, Persian-style palettes; silk sheen.
design.sizes: All sizes; very large palace carpets.

look_alikes.name: Kayseri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kayseri 'silks' are often art silk or mercerized cotton on cotton foundations and coarser.

look_alikes.name: Ghiordes
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hereke made fine silk copies of Gördes prayer rugs.

rows.trade_use: 'Hereke' is used today for the finest Turkish silk rugs from many workshops, not only the old imperial factory.
rows.what_it_tells: A very finely knotted, short-piled silk (or very fine wool) Turkish rug in Persian or Gördes designs is consistent with Hereke-type production.
rows.cautions: The name is used for fine silk rugs from other Turkish and foreign workshops; Chinese silk rugs in 'Hereke' designs are common.

facts.text: The Hereke factory was founded in 1843 and began production in 1845 as the 'Hereke Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu', making silk upholstery and curtains for the palaces.
Carpet weaving at Hereke was added later: under Abdülhamid II according to the National Palaces administration; in 1864 according to Stone.
Early Hereke weavers or master weavers were brought from Kirman, and many Hereke rugs copy Persian and Gördes designs.
facts.quote: As the early weavers were brought from Kirman to instruct the artisans of the Sultan, and the patterns have been largely copied from old Persian and Asia Minor pieces

facts.text: The registered standard for Hereke silk carpets is silk throughout, Turkish double knot, 10,000 knots per dm2 (about 645 per square inch), pile 2-2.5 mm.

Hereke wool carpets of about 1920 had 45-64 knots per square inch and were sold as the finest 'Smyrna' carpets (Kendrick & Tattersall); the registered Hereke wool standard is 3,600 per dm2 (about 232) on a cotton foundation.
Under the Republic the factory was run by Sümerbank and in 1995 passed to the National Palaces administration, where it works as a museum-factory (Millî Saraylar).

says.text: Early commercial production used asymmetric knots at densities reaching 800 per square inch.
Turkish (double) knot for the registered Hereke silk carpet.
Court workshops established about 1843; rug weaving did not begin until 1864.
Founded 1843, producing from 1845; carpet weaving units added under Sultan Abdülhamid II (reigned 1876-1909).

rows.name: Isparta
rows.region: Isparta in south-west Anatolia, a major finishing center and market; rugs also woven in Denizli and Afyon; Jacobsen says 'Spartas' were also woven in Smyrna, other Turkish towns and by Armenian refugees in Greece.
rows.made_by: Town workshops organized for export; Şahin & Akova trace the organized industry to 1891 and to the 'Şark Halı Kumpanyası' founded with İzmir entrepreneurs (Ispartalıoğlu Agop and Sons).
rows.date_note: Şahin & Akova (2019, citing Işık et al. 1992 and Sakarya 1992): a standardized Isparta carpet industry began in 1891 under the governor Babanzade Mustafa Zihni Pasha; 2,450 looms in 1924; peak output over 2 million m2 in 1978. Jacobsen: tens of thousands of 'Spartas' came to America 1924-1932.

structure.knot_note: Disputed: Stone says many use the asymmetric knot with some warp offset; the 'İnce Isparta (Hasgül)' registration specifies the Turkish (double) knot.
structure.kpsi_note: TÜRKPATENT İnce Isparta (present-day standard): 1,444 per dm2 = about 93.
structure.wefts_note: Registration: thick and thin cotton wefts.
structure.pile_note: 5-7 mm (registration); 1920s carpets 'long, high nap' and chemically washed (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: Copies of other Turkish, Caucasian and Persian designs; in the 1920s-30s Sarouk-style all-over floral designs on rose or blue grounds.
design.colors: Soft, chemically washed colors in 1920s exports; 'delicate tones'.
design.sizes: Carpet sizes.

look_alikes.name: Oushak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Oushaks are wool-foundation, coarse, with Turkish designs; Spartas are cotton-foundation Persian-design carpets.

rows.trade_use: 'Sparta' was the trade name; Jacobsen says these 1920s carpets were sold as 'Anatolians' or 'Spartas' under some 25 importers' trade names.
rows.what_it_tells: A Persian-design (often Sarouk-like) carpet on a cotton foundation with an Anatolian look and a soft chemically washed palette is consistent with 1920s-30s Isparta export production.
rows.cautions: Mistaken for Persian Sarouks; Jacobsen says many were not durable.

facts.text: Rugs woven in Isparta were known to the trade as 'Spartas'.
facts.quote: In the town of Isbarta in the southern part of the province of Konieh are woven rugs which are sometimes known to the trade as "Spartas."

facts.text: In the 1920s and 1930s Isparta carpets copied Persian Sarouk designs on cotton foundations.
The organized Isparta carpet industry dates from 1891 under the governor Babanzade Mustafa Zihni Pasha, followed by the 'Şark Halı Kumpanyası' founded with İzmir entrepreneurs (Şahin & Akova 2019).
Isparta carpets are woven on cotton warps and wefts.

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'İnce Isparta (Hasgül) El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 21) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,444 knots per square decimeter (quality 38x38), about 93 knots per square inch (1,444 / 15.5), pile 5-7 mm, cotton warp and cotton wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row). Wool pile.

says.text: Many using the asymmetric knot; some warp offset.
Turkish (double) knot for the registered 'İnce Isparta (Hasgül)' carpet.
Cotton warp and wefts.
The authors say all yarns of this carpet should be wool, although the registration names cotton for warp and weft.

rows.name: Yahyalı
rows.region: Yahyalı, Kayseri province, near Niğde in central Anatolia (Stone; registration filed by Yahyalı municipality).
rows.made_by: Village weavers.
rows.date_note: Stone describes current-style rugs; registered 1997.

structure.knot_note: Turkish (double) knot (registration).
structure.kpsi_note: TÜRKPATENT Yahyalı (present-day standard): 1,050 per dm2 = about 68.
structure.wefts_note: Registration: thick and thin wool wefts.
structure.pile_note: 5-7 mm (registration).
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: A hexagon or diamond medallion with pendants, sometimes shaped like hanging lamps, on a red field; very varied designs of Central Asian, Seljuk and Ottoman origin (registration).
design.colors: Red, blue and yellow.

look_alikes.name: Taşpınar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Taşpınar rugs have elongated medallions on dark blue.

rows.trade_use: Used for central Anatolian village rugs with red fields and lamp-pendant medallions.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to central Anatolia.

facts.text: Yahyalı rugs are generally red, blue and yellow, typically with a hexagon or diamond medallion with pendants (sometimes like hanging lamps) on a red field (Stone, p. 310).

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Yahyalı El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 18) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,050 knots per square decimeter (quality 30x35), about 68 knots per square inch (1,050 / 15.5), pile 5-7 mm, wool warp and wool wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row).

rows.name: Taşpınar
rows.region: The village of Taşpınar, Aksaray province, south-central Anatolia (Stone; registration filed by Taşpınar municipality).
rows.made_by: Village weavers.
rows.date_note: Registered 1997; Stone gives no dates.

structure.knot_note: Turkish (double) knot (registration).
structure.kpsi_note: TÜRKPATENT Taşpınar (present-day standard): 1,050 per dm2 = about 68.
structure.wefts_note: Registration: thick and thin wool wefts.
structure.pile_note: 5-7 mm (registration).
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: Elongated medallions on a dark blue field; corner-and-medallion layouts of stylized plant and geometric motifs (registration).
design.colors: Dark blue field.

look_alikes.name: Yahyalı
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yahyalı fields are usually red.

rows.trade_use: Used for central Anatolian village carpets.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Aksaray province.

facts.text: Taşpınar is the source of carpets most of which have elongated medallions and a dark blue field (Stone, p. 282).

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Taşpınar El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 7) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,050 knots per square decimeter (quality 30x35), about 68 knots per square inch (1,050 / 15.5), pile 5-7 mm, wool warp and wool wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row).

rows.name: Kars
rows.region: Kars and its district in north-east Anatolia on the old Caucasian border; Kağızman nearby.
rows.made_by: Village weavers of the Kars area, including Kurds; workshops.
rows.date_note: No source at hand dates the start of Kars production; it was registered in 1997 (two registrations: 'Kars El Halısı' and the coarser 'Sümer Kars El Halısı').

structure.knot_note: Turkish (symmetric) knot (Stone; registrations).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 60. TÜRKPATENT Kars: 1,050 per dm2 = about 68; Sümer Kars: 616 per dm2 = about 40.
structure.wefts_note: Registrations: a thick and a thin wool weft.
structure.pile_note: Kars 5-7 mm; Sümer Kars 10-14 mm (registrations).
structure.sides: not recorded in the sources at hand
structure.ends: not recorded in the sources at hand

design.field: Modified Caucasian (Kazak) designs; medallion compositions with stylized plant motifs (registration); the Lori-Pambak medallion is still used here.
design.colors: Reds tend to burgundy rather than Kazak brick red.

look_alikes.name: Kazak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kars rugs are similar to Kazaks in construction and design but their reds tend to burgundy rather than brick red; newer wool and Turkish design changes also help.

rows.trade_use: Sold in the trade as 'Kars Kazak' (the term is in wide use but is not documented in the sources at hand).
rows.what_it_tells: A Kazak-looking all-wool rug with burgundy reds is consistent with Kars (north-east Turkey) production.
rows.cautions: Easily confused with Caucasian Kazaks.

facts.text: Kars rugs have modified Caucasian designs on an all-wool foundation and are coarsely woven, similar to Kazaks in construction and design; reds tend to burgundy rather than brick red; about 60 knots per square inch (Stone, p. 151).
Kurds in the Kars area weave rugs not generally distinguishable from other Kars rugs woven outside workshops (Stone).

The Turkish geographical-indication registration 'Kars El Halısı' (TÜRKPATENT no. 8) specifies the Turkish (symmetric, 'double') knot at 1,050 knots per square decimeter (quality 30x35), about 68 knots per square inch (1,050 / 15.5), pile 5-7 mm, wool warp and wool wefts (a thick and a thin weft after each row). Medallion compositions.
The 'Sümer Kars El Halısı' registration (no. 12) specifies 616 knots per dm2 (about 40 per square inch) and a long pile of 10-14 mm, all wool.
Kars rugs are all wool with the symmetric knot, coarse like Kazaks.

rows.name: DOBAG
other_names: Doğal Boya Araştırma ve Geliştirme Projesi
Natural Dye Research and Development Project
rows.native: DOBAG (Doğal Boya Araştırma ve Geliştirme Projesi)
rows.translit: Doğal Boya Araştırma ve Geliştirme Projesi
rows.region: Weaving cooperatives in Ayvacık (Çanakkale province, the project's headquarters) and the Yuntdağ (Manisa).
rows.made_by: Village women in cooperatives.
rows.date_note: Production began in 1981.

structure.knot_note: Symmetric knot (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: Not given.
structure.pile_note: Natural-dyed, all wool (Stone).

design.field: Traditional local designs of the Ayvacık and Yuntdağ villages.
design.colors: Natural dyes only.

look_alikes.name: Çanakkale
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same villages; DOBAG rugs are cooperative-made with natural dyes (look for the project's label).

rows.trade_use: A cooperative label for natural-dyed village rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: A DOBAG rug is a post-1981 natural-dye revival rug, not an antique.
rows.cautions: Single source in hand; details of labels and certificates not confirmed.

facts.text: DOBAG (Doğal Boya Araştırma ve Geliştirme Projesi, 'Natural Dye Research and Development Project') rugs are natural-dyed, all-wool, symmetric-knotted rugs woven by cooperatives in Ayvacık and the Yuntdağ; production began in 1981 (Stone, p. 90).

rows.name: Tekke
rows.country: Turkmenistan; also northeastern Iran and around Herat, Afghanistan
rows.region: The Akhal oasis north of the Kopet Dagh and, from the mid-19th century, the Merv oasis; Tekke groups later also wove in northeastern Iran and northern Afghanistan.
rows.made_by: Tekke Turkmen women, in tents and settled villages
rows.date_note: Few Turkmen weavings that survive are older than the 18th century; the Tekke pieces readers meet are mostly 19th century. Tekke-design carpets continued in Soviet and present-day Turkmenistan and among Tekke in Iran and Afghanistan (see Soviet and present-day Turkmen carpets, Afghan (Ersari Turkmen carpets of northern Afghanistan), mauri).

structure.knot_note: Hawley and Lewis call it 'Sehna' (asymmetric). Iranica (Denny) and the TurkoTek guide (citing Loges 1980 and Mackie & Thompson 1980) say open to the right. None of these sources states from which side open left/right is judged; the field uses the labels consistently (Salor open left, Tekke open right).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 7-12 knots per inch across x 9-14 down = 63-168. Lewis: 40-400. Stone: about 150. Kendrick & Tattersall give 130-200 for Turkmen 'Bokhara' carpets in general. Present-day Türkmenhaly grades for Teke work run about 142-219 (see Soviet and present-day Turkmen carpets).
structure.warp_color: ivory to light brown wool (TurkoTek, Jourdan); Hawley and Kendrick & Tattersall also allow goat hair
structure.weft_color: brown (Jourdan via TurkoTek); Lewis: dyed red or brown
structure.wefts_note: Two shoots of two-ply wool of slightly unequal tension (Mackie & Thompson p. 96 via TurkoTek; Hawley). Stone: usually double-wefted, a few single-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Short, close-clipped, velvety wool; occasionally some silk (Lewis) or goat hair (Hawley).
structure.sides: Usually a simple overcast or selvage in dark blue wool (Mackie & Thompson p. 100 via TurkoTek; Stone). Hawley describes a three-cord double goat-hair selvage and Kendrick & Tattersall a three-cord selvedge; Lewis says overcast in wool of the field color.
structure.ends: A wide colored plain-weave band (Lewis: 10-12 inches, in the field color) with a long loose warp fringe; pieces made to hang (door rugs) may have braided cords at the top (Hawley, Lewis, Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.handle: Firm, with a short, close pile (Hawley: 'firm'; Lewis: close texture).

design.field: Rows (often three) of Tekke guls, a quartered octagon with indented sides, linked by dark lines, with smaller minor guls (chemche or gurbaghe) between.
design.border: Narrow main border, often rows of small octagons on red; elem (end panels) on main carpets.
design.colors: Reds from brick to purple-red and liver red, with dark blue, ivory and some green and yellow; older pieces dyed with madder and indigo.
design.sizes: Main carpets roughly 6 x 8 to 7 x 10 ft (Met 22.100.45 is 279 x 184 cm); bags and trappings much smaller.

look_alikes.name: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs (incl. Jaldar and Mori)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Pakistani 'Bokhara' or 'Mori' rugs copy the Tekke gul on a cotton foundation (cotton warps, so a cotton fringe); a Tekke has wool warps and wefts.

look_alikes.name: Salor
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Salor knots open to the left and alternate warps lie deeply depressed, so the back is ribbed; Tekke knots open to the right on nearly level warps.

look_alikes.name: Yomut
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Most Yomud main carpets are tied with the symmetric knot and have checkerboard two-color side cords; Tekke rugs use the asymmetric knot and dark blue sides.

look_alikes.name: Soviet and present-day Turkmen carpets
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Soviet and present-day state carpets repeat the Tekke gul with machine-even drawing and synthetic dyes; old Tekke pieces show natural-dye shading and tribal end finishes.

look_alikes.name: Bokhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'Royal Bokhara' is a trade name; authors disagree on whether it meant Tekke or Salor work.

rows.trade_use: Called 'Tekke', 'Tekke Bokhara' or 'Royal Bokhara' in the trade; 'Bokhara' alone is used for any rug with Turkmen guls, including new rugs from Pakistan, India, Iran, Afghanistan and China.
rows.what_it_tells: A wool-foundation rug with rows of quartered, indented octagons, asymmetric knots and nearly level warps points to Tekke Turkmen work. Whether it is a 19th-century tribal piece or later Soviet, Iranian or Afghan Tekke-design work depends on dyes, wear and finishes.
rows.cautions: The Tekke gul is the most copied Turkmen design in the world; the design alone says little. Hawley's 'Tekke' description covers mostly door rugs (katchli pattern), not main carpets.

facts.text: The Tekke were the dominant Turkmen tribe before the Russian conquest; their resistance ended with the fall of Geok Tepe in 1881.
The Tekke took the Merv oasis in the 19th century, displacing the Salor (Stone: about 1830; Hawley: some time after 1830; Jacobsen: 1856).
Tekke pile is tied with the asymmetric knot.
facts.quote: Knot, Sehna. Knots to inch horizontally seven to twelve; perpendicularly, nine to fourteen. (Hawley p. 240)

facts.text: Tekke knots open to the right, unlike Salor knots, which open to the left.
Tekke weavers use two shoots of wool weft between rows of knots.
Tekke side finishes are usually simple and in dark blue wool.
Typical Tekke main carpets have about 150 knots per square inch; Lewis gives a range of 40 to 400.
facts.quote: number to square inch forty to four hundred. (Lewis 1920, p. 282)

facts.text: The ends carry a wide colored band and a long fringe of loose warp ends.
facts.quote: the ends have a long, coloured web and a long fringe. (Kendrick & Tattersall p. 188)

facts.text: The Tekke gul is the main gul of Tekke main carpets; the minor gul is usually the chemche or gurbaghe.
Tekke torbas and other small bags may be very finely knotted.
The early Tekke palette came from madder, indigo and a yellow dye; green was dyed twice (blue over yellow) and later greens fade toward blue.
For nearly a century the American trade called Tekke rugs 'Royal Bokhara' and Tekke door rugs 'Princess Bokhara'.

says.text: One of the two warps under each knot is depressed below the other at the back (slight depression).
The warp lies on two levels slightly separated.
Almost always non-depressed (level) warps.
Usually simple, in dark blue wool (via TurkoTek).
A three-cord double goat's-hair selvage.
Overcast in wool dyed the main color of the rug; occasionally selvaged.
About 150.
Two shoots (via TurkoTek).
Usually two, a few single-wefted.
