rows.name: Salor
rows.region: The Merv oasis until their defeat by the Tekke and Persians in the mid-19th century; afterward scattered (Penjdeh, Sarakhs, northern Afghanistan).
rows.made_by: Salor Turkmen women
rows.date_note: The pieces scholars accept as Salor ('S group') date mainly from the late 18th and first half of the 19th century (Met 1974.149.46: late 18th-early 19th century). After the Salor were defeated, other tribes used the Salor gul.

structure.knot_note: Usual knot asymmetric open to the left; some later pieces are reported open to the right (TurkoTek/Howe). Same open-left/right convention as for Tekke; not defined by the sources.
structure.kpsi_note: TurkoTek (Howe): 2,000-5,000 knots per dm2 = about 129-323 per square inch. Jacobsen (a dealer) claims 225-500, without saying how he counted.
structure.warp_color: ivory, brown or gray wool, Z2S
structure.wefts_note: Two shoots of wool, one taut and one sinuous (TurkoTek/Howe).
structure.pile_note: Fine, lustrous wool with small areas of silk, often magenta, used as highlights.
structure.sides: Often two separate two-warp selvages wrapped in dark blue or green wool, or in a checkerboard (TurkoTek/Howe; single source).
structure.ends: Wrapped, or plain weave folded and sewn (TurkoTek/Howe; single source).
structure.handle: Not floppy; Jacobsen describes the pile of tent-bag faces as short with a 'frosty' feel.
structure.back: Ribbed, because alternate warps lie deeply depressed.

design.field: Main carpets: rows of the Salor gul (an octagon with turret-like projections, also called the 'turret gul' or 'Rose of Salor'), 4-7 rows of 10-13 guls (Mackie & Thompson p. 67 via TurkoTek); bags with the same gul or the gulli gul.
design.border: Geometric Turkmen borders; chuvals often with a flag border.
design.colors: Deep madder and insect-dye reds (lac and cochineal reported, especially in silk), dark blue, ivory, magenta silk.
design.sizes: Main carpets about 8 x 10 ft (Met 1974.149.46: 323 x 248 cm); chuvals about 2.5 x 4 ft.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tekke knots open to the right on nearly level warps; Salor knots open to the left on deeply depressed warps, giving a ribbed back.

look_alikes.name: Saryk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Saryk pile is tied with the symmetric knot; Salor with the asymmetric knot open left.

look_alikes.name: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs (incl. Jaldar and Mori)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Modern copies of the Salor gul on cotton foundations come from Pakistan and India.

rows.trade_use: 'Salor' and 'Salor Bokhara' in older books and the trade; Kendrick & Tattersall equate Salor rugs with the trade name 'Royal Bokhara'.
rows.what_it_tells: A Turkmen piece with asymmetric knots open to the left, deeply depressed warps and silk highlights fits the 'S group' that most scholars give to the Salor.
rows.cautions: The Salor gul alone does not prove Salor work; after the 1830s-50s other tribes (Tekke, Saryk) used it. Attribution of the 'S group' to the Salor is accepted by most but questioned by some.

facts.text: The Salor are thought to be the oldest Turkmen tribe; historical references to them go back to the 11th century.
Salor knots are asymmetric and open to the left.
In Salor weaving alternate warps lie on two levels (strongly depressed), so the back is ribbed.
Salor pieces often have small silk highlights in the pile.
Salor main carpets have 4 to 7 rows of guls with 10 to 13 guls in a row.
Knot density is about 129-323 per square inch (2,000-5,000 per dm2).
Treating the structural 'S group' as Salor work began with Jon Thompson's 1973 edition of Bogolyubov; some writers doubt it.
After the Salor were defeated, other tribes used the Salor gul in their own weavings.

says.text: Defeated by the Tekke and Persians in the 1830s.
The Tekke took Merv from the Salor in 1856.
Mid-19th century.
Salor rugs are 'known frequently as Royal Bokhara'.
Royal Bokhara = Tekke.
Royal Bokharas were made in and around the city of Bokhara.
225 to 500 (dealer, method not given).

rows.name: Saryk
other_names: Pinde, Pende, Penjdeh (in part; trade name for rugs from the Penjdeh oasis)
rows.region: Merv, then (from the later 19th century) the Penjdeh oasis on the Murghab; some groups settled in northern Afghanistan.
rows.made_by: Saryk Turkmen women
rows.date_note: Stone gives a color sequence: the earliest all-wool pieces with an orange-tan field, then crimson fields with cotton and silk highlights, and after about 1880 purple-brown fields. Cleveland dates its Saryk main carpet to the 1870s.

structure.knot_note: Saryk pile is almost always tied with the symmetric knot (Iranica; Cleveland records); Stone says very late pieces may have asymmetric knots.
structure.kpsi_note: Cleveland 2006.201 main carpet: 171 symmetric knots per square inch; Cleveland 2008.223 bag face: 252.
structure.wefts_note: Double-wefted (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Wool, with white cotton and magenta silk highlights in some pieces (Stone; Cleveland 2008.223).

design.field: Main carpets with the Saryk gul (a stepped octagon with a central hexagon), the temirchin gul in early carpets, or a gulli-type gul copied from the Salor; bags with quartered guls in staggered rows.
design.colors: Orange-tan, then crimson, then (after about 1880) purple-brown, purple or brown fields.
design.sizes: Cleveland 2006.201: 258 x 250 cm; bag face 2008.223: 89 x 127 cm.

look_alikes.name: Salor
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Salor knots are asymmetric open left; Saryk knots are symmetric.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tekke knots are asymmetric open right; Saryk knots symmetric.

look_alikes.name: Mauri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Afghanistan 'Sariq Mauri' rugs use the Salor (turret) gul in modern production.

rows.trade_use: 'Saryk' or 'Sariq'; Jacobsen's 'Pinde' (Penjdeh) rugs overlap with Saryk work woven at Penjdeh.
rows.what_it_tells: Symmetric knots in a red Turkmen piece with stepped octagons or quartered guls, sometimes with cotton or silk highlights, point to the Saryk.
rows.cautions: The Saryk used guls of other tribes; the knot is a better guide than the gul.

facts.text: Saryk pile is almost always tied with the symmetric knot.
facts.quote: Wool, silk; 171 symmetrical (Turkish) knots per square inch (Cleveland 2006.201, CC0 data)

facts.text: Early Saryk rugs have symmetric knots; very late rugs may have asymmetric knots.
Saryk rugs are double-wefted with offset warps.
Many Saryk settled around Penjdeh and others in northern Afghanistan.
The most common Saryk gul is a stepped octagon with a central hexagon; the temirchin gul appears in early Saryk main carpets.
Saryk pieces may have white cotton and magenta silk highlights in the pile.

says.text: Almost invariably symmetric.
Early pieces symmetric; very late ones may be asymmetric.

rows.name: Yomut
rows.region: The east coast of the Caspian, the Khiva oasis, and northeastern Iran (Gorgan plain, Gonbad-e Qabus); sub-groups include the Atabai, Jafarbai, Ogurjali and Igdyr.
rows.made_by: Yomut Turkmen women
rows.date_note: Most Yomut pieces readers meet are 19th century; Yomut in Iran and Afghanistan kept weaving into the 20th century, often in Tekke designs.

structure.knot_note: Yomut weavers used both knots, sometimes in one carpet (Iranica). Most surveyed pieces are symmetric (O'Bannon via Howe; Kendrick & Tattersall 'Ghiordes commoner'; Met and Cleveland records). Hawley says 'generally Sehna, occasionally Ghiordes'. Yomut weavers also shift knots by one warp (offset knotting) to draw smooth diagonals (Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 5-8 x 7-10 per inch = 35-80. Lewis: 56-180. Kendrick & Tattersall: 130-200 (and 150 in their price table). Stone: typically 100-150. Cleveland 2010.190: 128-136.
structure.warp_color: brown or undyed; some groups ivory
structure.weft_color: often brown; Lewis: frequently dyed red
structure.wefts_note: Two shoots of wool (Hawley; TurkoTek); camel hair or cotton occasionally.
structure.pile_note: Medium length, lustrous in old pieces.
structure.sides: A two-cord selvage wrapped in alternating colors (red/blue, red/brown, two reds) giving a checkerboard look; sometimes a goat-hair selvage of 3-4 cords (Lewis, Hawley, TurkoTek).
structure.ends: A broad red or reddish-brown plain-weave band, often with colored stripes, and a long warp fringe sometimes twisted into tassels; main carpets often have decorated elem (end panels) in pile.

design.field: Main carpets with dyrnak, tauk noska or kepse guls in offset rows (early pieces in columns), or latch-hooked diamonds; bags with diamond lattices and barber-pole stripes.
design.border: Main border usually on a white ground; running latch-hook, barber-pole and saw-tooth stripes.
design.colors: Brownish red, plum or aubergine fields, more white and a wider range of colors than other Turkmen.
design.sizes: Main carpets about 5 x 10 to 6 x 11 ft (Met 22.100.47: 331 x 192 cm); chuvals about 2.5 x 4 ft.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tekke pile is asymmetric with dark blue sides; Yomud pile is mostly symmetric, with checkerboard two-color side cords and white-ground borders.

look_alikes.name: Chodor
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chodor pieces use asymmetric knots open right and often cotton wefts; Yomud mostly symmetric knots and wool wefts.

rows.trade_use: 'Yomud' or 'Yomut'; older trade 'Yomud Bokhara'. New 'Yomud' rugs came from Afghanistan and Iran after 1945.
rows.what_it_tells: A red-brown Turkmen rug with white-ground border, latch-hooked guls or diamonds, symmetric knots and checkered side cords points to Yomut work.
rows.cautions: Knot counts given by early authors differ several-fold; do not rely on density alone.

facts.text: Yomut weavers used both the symmetric and the asymmetric knot, sometimes in the same carpet.
The symmetric knot is the more common knot in Yomut rugs.
facts.quote: The Ghiordes knot is commoner than the Sehna, whereas the latter is almost invariably found in other Central Asiatic rugs. (Kendrick & Tattersall p. 188)

facts.text: Yomud sides are often a two-cord selvage colored in alternating squares, a checkerboard effect.
facts.quote: A coarse selvage of two cords which are colored in alternate squares of red and blue, red and brown, or two shades of red (Lewis p. 285)

facts.text: Yomud weavers sometimes tie knots offset by one warp, like bricks in a wall, to draw smoother diagonal lines.
The main Yomud guls are the dyrnak, tauk noska and kepse.
Yomud warps are often brown wool or goat hair.
Main borders usually have a white ground, and Yomud work uses a wider range of colors than other Turkmen.
Yomut groups live along the southeastern Caspian in Iran and the eastern Caspian shore in Turkmenistan; sub-tribes include the Atabai, Jafarbai, Ogurjali and Igdyr.
Igdyr and Imreli groups use Yomut patterns rather than their own guls.

says.text: Generally Sehna (asymmetric), occasionally Ghiordes.
Ghiordes (symmetric) commoner than Sehna.
All three knot types, sometimes in one carpet.
128-136 symmetric (one carpet).

rows.name: Chodor
rows.region: The Khiva (Khorezm) oasis on the lower Amu Darya; earlier on the Mangyshlak peninsula.
rows.made_by: Chodor Turkmen women
rows.date_note: Most Chodor pieces in collections are 19th century; Moshkova says their original ertmen gul degenerated within 20-30 years once they wove for the Khiva and Bukhara markets.

structure.knot_note: Always asymmetric open to the right (Stone; TurkoTek citing Mackie & Thompson).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found; Türkmenhaly's present-day grade 3 (Ýomut and Çowdur designs) is about 112-150.
structure.weft_color: often brown wool plied with white cotton, or all cotton
structure.wefts_note: Two-ply wefts, sometimes wool, sometimes cotton or wool plied with cotton; most Chodor pieces have some cotton in the weft (Stone; Mackie & Thompson p. 119 via TurkoTek).
structure.sides: A flat selvage of about four cords wrapped in a two-color check (Mackie & Thompson p. 119 via TurkoTek; single source).

design.field: Main carpets with the tauk noska gul or the ertmen gul (a stepped diamond with ram's-horn projections); chuvals with three rows of guls.
design.colors: A distinctive purple-brown field; the oldest pieces a deep purple.

look_alikes.name: Yomut
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yomud pieces are mostly symmetric-knotted with wool wefts; Chodor asymmetric open right, usually with some cotton in the weft.

look_alikes.name: Arabachi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both use the tauk noska gul and purple-brown fields; Stone gives Arabachi knots as open left, Chodor as open right.

rows.trade_use: 'Chodor' or 'Chaudor'; Jacobsen lists it as a 'type of Yomut'.
rows.what_it_tells: An asymmetric-knotted Turkmen piece with a purple-brown field and white cotton showing in the wefts points to the Chodor.
rows.cautions: Chodor attributions rest on structure; designs overlap with Yomut and Arabachi.

facts.text: Chodor rugs are tied with the asymmetric knot open to the right.
Chodor wefts often contain cotton, plied with wool or alone.
The field color is often a distinctive purple-brown.
The ertmen is the Chodor tribal gul; on main carpets it was replaced by the tauk noska.
The Chodor lived in the Khiva area and brought carpets to the Khiva and Bukhara markets.
Chodor sides are a flat four-cord selvage wrapped in a two-color check.

rows.name: Arabachi
rows.region: The middle Amu Darya (Oxus) region of central Turkestan.
rows.made_by: Arabachi Turkmen women
rows.date_note: 19th century; few pieces are attributed.

structure.knot_note: Stone: asymmetric, open to the left (single source here).

design.field: Older main carpets carry the tauk noska gul.
design.colors: Purplish-brown field; outlines in natural brown wool.

look_alikes.name: Chodor
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone gives Arabachi knots as open left and Chodor as open right; both use the tauk noska gul and purple-brown grounds.

rows.trade_use: 'Arabachi' is a collector's attribution; the trade did not use it.
rows.what_it_tells: A purplish-brown Turkmen piece with the tauk noska gul and cotton in the weft might be Arabachi, but the attribution is disputed.
rows.cautions: Stone notes that attributing specific rugs to the Arabachi is questioned.

facts.text: Older main carpets attributed to the Arabachi carry the tauk noska gul.
Arabachi knots are asymmetric open to the left, with some warp offset and wefts of wool and white cotton.
The attribution of specific rugs to the Arabachi is questioned.

rows.name: Ersari
other_names: Afghan (trade name for coarse Ersari main carpets)
rows.region: The middle Amu Darya (Oxus) valley from Charjou to Kerki and across into northern Afghanistan (Andkhoy, Aqcha, Sheberghan).
rows.made_by: Ersari Turkmen women; sub-groups include the Kizil Ayak, Dali and probably the Chub Bash
rows.date_note: 19th-century Ersari pieces from the Amu Darya; Ersari weaving continues in northern Afghanistan (see Afghan (Ersari Turkmen carpets of northern Afghanistan)).

structure.knot_note: Hawley ('Afghans'), Kendrick & Tattersall and Stone (Andkhoy, Beshir) give the asymmetric knot; the open direction was not found in the sources read.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley ('Afghans'): 35-80. Lewis ('Khiva Bokhara'): 42-96. Kendrick & Tattersall ('Afghan'): 45-70. Türkmenhaly's present-day Beşir/Kerki grade: about 101-129.
structure.wefts_note: Two shoots (Hawley; Stone for Andkhoy).
structure.pile_note: Longer and coarser than other Turkmen pile.
structure.sides: Goat-hair selvage of several cords (Hawley; Lewis).
structure.ends: Broad red-brown plain-weave band with colored stripes and a long fringe (Hawley; Kendrick & Tattersall).

design.field: Main carpets with large gulli guls (quarters with clover-leaf motifs) or temirjin guls; also many non-tribal designs (boteh, mina khani, Herati, ikat patterns).
design.colors: Reds with dark blue, yellow, white.
design.sizes: Larger variety of sizes than other Turkmen.

look_alikes.name: Afghan (Ersari Turkmen carpets of northern Afghanistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same people; 'Afghan' is the trade name for the coarse Ersari main carpets with large guls, from either side of the border.

look_alikes.name: Beshir
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'Beshir' is used for Ersari-area rugs with floral, ikat-derived or prayer designs.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tekke rugs are finer, with smaller guls and dark blue sides; Ersari rugs coarser with goat-hair selvages.

rows.trade_use: 'Ersari' among collectors; in the trade, 'Afghan', 'Khiva', 'Beshir' or simply 'Bokhara'.
rows.what_it_tells: A coarse, heavy Turkmen rug with big quartered guls and goat-hair sides points to Ersari weaving of the Amu Darya or northern Afghanistan.
rows.cautions: Stone warns that rugs have been called Ersari when there is no reason to give them to another tribe.

facts.text: The Ersari moved from the eastern Caspian shore to the Amu Darya valley in the 17th century.
The Kizil Ayak and Dali are considered Ersari sub-tribes, and the Chub Bash may be one.
Ersari carpets are often more coarsely woven than those of other Turkmen groups.
Ersari who settled in villages along the Oxus took up Persian commercial designs such as the Herati.
The gulli gul and temirjin gul are the Ersari tribal guls.
The Ersari main carpet with the gulli gul was a major Afghan rug export in the late 19th century.

rows.name: Beshir
rows.region: Named after Beshir on the Amu Darya; the name covers rugs from around Bukhara and along the Amu Darya into northern Afghanistan.
rows.made_by: Mostly thought to be Ersari Turkmen and settled villagers of the Amu Darya (disputed)
rows.date_note: Kendrick & Tattersall (1922) say Beshir rugs had been exported only for about twenty years; old pieces are 19th century.

structure.knot_note: Hawley: Sehna (asymmetric). Lewis: either, usually Senna. Stone: asymmetric.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 7-12 x 7-12 per inch = 49-144. Lewis: 30-120. Kendrick & Tattersall: 50-100.
structure.wefts_note: Two shoots, medium or coarse (Hawley).
structure.pile_note: Medium to long and lustrous (Kendrick & Tattersall: very long and very lustrous).
structure.sides: Goat-hair selvage of two to four cords (Hawley; Lewis three or four cords).
structure.ends: A wide plain-weave band, usually red, crossed by blue, green and other colored stripes; loose or knotted fringe (Hawley; Lewis; Kendrick & Tattersall).

design.field: Floral and lattice designs unlike other Turkmen work: large cloud-like or 'vermiculated' scrolls, Herati and mina khani lattices, ikat-derived patterns, boteh, 2-1-2 medallions; prayer rugs with a large arch.
design.colors: Reds and browns with blue and much yellow; little white.
design.sizes: 4-12 ft long; Lewis: 3-8 by 5-12 ft; often long, narrow carpets.

look_alikes.name: Ersari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Beshir is a design-led trade name within Ersari-area weaving; tribal-gul pieces are called Ersari.

look_alikes.name: Afghan (Ersari Turkmen carpets of northern Afghanistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'Afghan' carpets carry rows of large octagons; Beshir carpets floral or lattice designs.

rows.trade_use: 'Beshir' or 'Beshire Bokhara' for Amu Darya rugs with floral, lattice or prayer designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A coarse, lustrous Turkmen-area rug with large floral scrolls or a lattice and much yellow points to the Beshir group of the Amu Darya.
rows.cautions: Giving all Beshir rugs to the Ersari is disputed.

facts.text: Beshir rugs are tied mostly with the asymmetric knot.
facts.quote: Knot, Sehna. Knots to inch horizontally seven to twelve; perpendicularly, seven to twelve. (Hawley p. 243)

facts.text: Beshir rugs have a goat-hair selvage of several cords and a wide striped web at the ends.
Beshir designs are more floral than other Central Asian rugs and often recall Persian designs; trellis patterns and vermiculated scrolls occur.
Most Beshir rugs are thought to be woven by Ersari Turkmen; this attribution is disputed.
Knot counts run from about 30 to 144 per square inch.

says.text: From 'Bech Schehr', 'five villages' west of Khiva on the Amu Darya.
A town on the Amu Darya in west Turkestan.
A district to the west of Khiva.
A small district on the Amu Daria not far from Afghanistan.

rows.name: Kizil Ayak
rows.region: The middle Amu Darya (Ersari area) and northern Afghanistan.
rows.made_by: Kizil Ayak Turkmen, thought to be an Ersari sub-group
rows.date_note: 19th-century pieces; the name is also a design grade in present-day Turkmen state production (Türkmenhaly grade 4).

structure.knot_note: Stone; Poullada via Howe (open right).
structure.kpsi_note: Poullada via Howe: about 95-150.

design.field: Main carpets with the tauk noska gul; minor gul the chemche.

look_alikes.name: Chub Bash
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone says some Kizil Ayak and Chub Bash pieces cannot be told apart.

rows.trade_use: Collector's attribution; Kendrick & Tattersall list 'Kisiliyak' among trade names for Turkmen carpets.
rows.what_it_tells: An Ersari-area piece with tauk noska guls, light wool warps and brown wefts may be Kizil Ayak.
rows.cautions: Hard to separate from Chub Bash and other Ersari groups.

facts.text: Kizil Ayak rugs use the asymmetric knot open to the right, light undyed wool warps and brown wefts.
The main gul of the Kizil Ayak is the tauk noska and the minor gul the chemche.
The Kizil Ayak are thought to be a sub-group of the Ersari.

rows.name: Chub Bash
rows.region: Northern Afghanistan (Ersari area).
rows.made_by: Chub Bash Turkmen, possibly an Ersari sub-tribe
rows.date_note: 19th-20th century; few attributed pieces.

structure.knot_note: Not stated separately; Stone says some Chub Bash and Kizil Ayak pieces share structure.

design.field: A variety of guls including the ertman and tauk noska; the dyrnak gul is also used.

look_alikes.name: Kizil Ayak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Because of similar structure and design, some Kizil Ayak cannot be told from Chub Bash weavings.

rows.trade_use: Collector's attribution only.
rows.what_it_tells: Little can be said beyond 'Ersari-area Turkmen'.
rows.cautions: Single-source attribution; use with care.

facts.text: The Chub Bash are a Turkmen tribe of northern Afghanistan, possibly an Ersari sub-tribe, whose weavings use the ertman and tauk noska guls.

rows.name: Bokhara
rows.country: Uzbekistan (the city); the rugs came from all over Turkmen Central Asia
rows.region: Bukhara was a market and shipping center for Turkmen rugs in the 19th century, not a weaving center for them.
rows.made_by: Turkmen tribes of all kinds; today also weavers in Pakistan, India, Iran, Afghanistan and China copying Turkmen designs
rows.date_note: In use in the Western trade by the late 19th century; still used for any rug with Turkmen-style guls.

structure.knot_note: Hawley's 'Royal Bokhara' and 'Princess Bokhara' analyses both give the Sehna (asymmetric) knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: Royal Bokhara 8-12 x 16-24 per inch = 128-288; Princess Bokhara 8-12 x 14-18 = 112-216. Kendrick & Tattersall: 130-200; Ballard No. 102 'Bokhara': 143-169.
structure.warp_color: Hawley: Royal, fine white wool; Princess, brown wool or goat hair
structure.wefts_note: Two shoots (Hawley).
structure.pile_note: Short; Hawley notes small patches of silk in some Royal Bokharas.
structure.sides: Royal: blue double overcasting; Princess: double overcasting or a three-cord goat-hair selvage (Hawley).
structure.ends: Narrow web and short fringe (Royal) or web and fringe (Princess) (Hawley).

design.field: Rows of octagonal guls ('Royal'); the four-panel katchli layout ('Princess', = Tekke ensi).
design.colors: Dark reds with blue, ivory and some orange.
design.sizes: Royal 4-10 ft long; Princess about 4.5-6 ft, nearly square.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Most 'Royal Bokhara' rugs in American homes before 1940 were Tekke main carpets.

look_alikes.name: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs (incl. Jaldar and Mori)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Since the late 1950s most new 'Bokhara' rugs are Pakistani, on cotton foundations.

look_alikes.name: Soviet and present-day Turkmen carpets
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Soviet-era factory carpets in Tekke designs were also sold as Bokhara.

rows.trade_use: Any rug with Turkmen-style guls, whatever its origin; 'Royal' and 'Princess' Bokhara are older American trade terms. A 'Bokhara' label says nothing about where the rug was made.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug sold as 'Bokhara' has a Turkmen-style design; the foundation (wool or cotton), knot and finishes tell whether it is Turkmen work or a later copy.
rows.cautions: Authors disagree on which tribe 'Royal Bokhara' meant. Never read 'Bokhara' as a place of weaving.

facts.text: Bokhara was a market where Turkmen and other tribes bartered their rugs, so the name was given to rugs of many groups: Royal, Princess, Tekke, Yomud and Khiva Bokharas.
facts.quote: Thus we hear of Royal Bokharas, Princess Bokharas, Tekke Bokharas, Yomud Bokharas, and Khiva Bokharas. (Hawley p. 235)

facts.text: Most rugs of Western Turkestan were called Bokhara though very few were made there.
facts.quote: Most of the rugs made in Western Turkestan are called Bokhara, though very few are made there. (Kendrick & Tattersall p. 187)

facts.text: Turkmen rugs are often erroneously called 'Bukhara' in the trade, and modern 'Bukhara' rugs from India, Pakistan and China imitate Turkmen patterns.
'Princess Bokhara' rugs have the four-panel (katchli) layout and are Tekke door rugs, often called prayer rugs.
Hawley's 'Royal Bokhara' analysis: asymmetric knot, 128-288 knots per square inch, fine white wool warps lying level, two wefts, blue double overcast sides.
facts.quote: Knot, Sehna. Knots to inch horizontally eight to twelve; perpendicularly, sixteen to twenty-four. (Hawley p. 236)

facts.text: Clark (1922) says names like 'Bokhara' and 'Khiva' were given to practically every type of Turkmen rug.
facts.quote: Some of these names, such as 'Bokhara' and 'Khiva,' are given promiscuously to practically every type of Turkoman rug (Clark, pp. 66-67)

says.text: Made in and around the city of Bokhara; the old ones are rare.
Salor rugs are 'frequently known as Royal Bokhara'.
Tekke rugs have been called Royal Bokhara for nearly 100 years.

rows.name: Soviet and present-day Turkmen carpets
rows.region: State carpet enterprises in Ashgabat and regional workshops across Turkmenistan.
rows.made_by: Women weavers employed by Soviet and, after 1991, Turkmen state enterprises
rows.date_note: Soviet collection and reorganization of Turkmen carpet making began in the 1920s; Jacobsen says almost no Turkmen rugs reached America for about 20-25 years before 1960, and old ones were sold off by the Soviets in 1924-35. Production continues under the state corporation Türkmenhaly.

structure.knot_note: Türkmenhaly describes 'double' (двойной) and 'one-and-a-half' (полуторный) knots; how these map onto symmetric and asymmetric was not settled.
structure.kpsi_note: Türkmenhaly grades (per m2 converted to per square inch): Ahal-Teke single-wefted 240-340k/m2 = 155-219; Teke and Pendi double-wefted 220-340k = 142-219; Ýomut and Çowdur 174-232k = 112-150; Beşir, Kerki, Gyzyl-aýak 156-200k = 101-129.
structure.wefts_note: Türkmenhaly lists an Ahal-Teke grade with a single weft and a Teke/Pendi grade with two.
structure.ends: Plain-weave band ('toprak') and fringe at both ends (Türkmenhaly).

design.field: Traditional tribal designs (Tekke gul above all, also Yomut, Chodor, Beshir), plus pictorial and portrait carpets.
design.colors: Turkmen reds with dark blue and ivory; synthetic dyes.
design.sizes: Standard metric sizes; very large showpieces.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Older Tekke pieces show natural-dye shading, tribal side and end finishes, and irregular drawing; state carpets are even, metric-sized and synthetic-dyed.

look_alikes.name: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs (incl. Jaldar and Mori)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Soviet/Turkmen state carpets are wool-on-wool or mixed; Pakistani Bokharas are on cotton.

rows.trade_use: Sold as 'Turkmen', 'Tekke', 'Russian Bokhara' or simply 'Bokhara'.
rows.what_it_tells: A Tekke-design carpet in metric sizes with even drawing and synthetic dyes may come from Soviet or present-day Turkmen state production.
rows.cautions: Back labels and stamps from Soviet enterprises exist but were not documented in the sources found.

facts.text: In 1918 Moscow's Museum of Oriental Cultures began collecting Turkmen carpets; in 1927 Turkmen carpet production was described as declining.
Between 1924 and 1935 many old Turkmen rugs reached New York and London after the Soviets collected them to raise hard currency.
Ashgabat is a center of commercial rug manufacture and of trade in Turkmen weavings.
Present-day Turkmen state production grades carpets by design group and knot density, from about 101 to 219 knots per square inch.
A giant carpet with the guşly göl field (193 m2) was woven in 1941-42.
Turkmen carpet making was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list on 12 December 2019.

rows.name: Afghan (Ersari Turkmen carpets of northern Afghanistan)
rows.country: Afghanistan; earlier also the Amu Darya side of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan
rows.region: Northern Afghanistan: Andkhoy, Aqcha (the chief market), Sheberghan, Labijar, Maimana, Mazar-e Sharif and their villages; in the early books also the eastern Bokhara khanate north of the Hindu Kush.
rows.made_by: Ersari Turkmen women in villages and tents; from the 1960s-70s also men in merchants' 'factories' of 50 or more looms
rows.date_note: 'Afghans' were sold in the West by about 1900. Export production grew strongly in the 1950s-70s; 'Afghan gold' rugs appeared about 1968-73 (Spooner 1973).

structure.knot_note: Hawley: generally Sehna (asymmetric), occasionally Ghiordes. Afghan weavers call the asymmetric knot yak pich ('one twist') and the symmetric do pich (Spooner 1973). The Ballard 'Afghan' rug No. 104 is symmetric.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 5-8 x 7-10 per inch = 35-80. Lewis: 42-96. Kendrick & Tattersall: 45-70. Ballard No. 104: 36-49.
structure.warp_color: dark wool or goat hair; gray (Jacobsen)
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two shoots. Spooner 1973: one, two or three wefts per row in Afghan carpets generally; Stone: Andkhoy rugs usually double-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Long, plush, lustrous wool, sometimes with goat fleece (Hawley; Lewis; Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.sides: A goat-hair selvage of three or four cords (Hawley), up to seven cords in black or dark brown (Lewis).
structure.ends: A broad red-brown plain-weave band crossed by narrow colored lines or a checkered stripe, and a long, shaggy fringe of the warp ends (Hawley; Lewis; Kendrick & Tattersall).
structure.handle: Heavy and thick; coarser than other Turkmen rugs (Hawley; Holt).
structure.back: Moderately coarse; Lewis says loosely tied so the back looks like the symmetric knot.

design.field: Usually three (sometimes more) vertical rows of large quartered octagons (gulli gul type) almost touching, with small diamonds between; the large octagon is called fil-pay ('elephant's foot') in Afghanistan.
design.border: Geometric; vine and crude floral forms.
design.colors: Dark red, maroon, mahogany or wine-red fields with blue, green, apricot ('burnt almond'), yellow and a little ivory; 'Golden Afghan' rugs in yellow-gold.
design.sizes: Mostly large and nearly square in older books (6 x 9 to 8 x 11 ft and larger); Jacobsen says many small sizes too.

look_alikes.name: Ersari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same weavers; 'Ersari' is the collector's tribal name, 'Afghan' the trade name.

look_alikes.name: Daulatabad
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'Daulatabad' is the modern trade name for the typical red carpet with large blue or black octagons, from Dawlatabad and other northern markets.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tekke rugs are finer, with smaller indented guls, short pile and dark blue sides; Afghans are coarse, long-piled, with large octagons and goat-hair sides.

rows.trade_use: 'Afghan' for coarse red carpets with big octagons; older books also say 'Khiva' or 'Khiva Bokhara'. 'Golden Afghan' for yellow-gold rugs (first bleached reds, later woven in gold).
rows.what_it_tells: A heavy, long-piled rug with rows of big quartered octagons on dark red, wool or goat-hair warps and a long shaggy fringe points to Ersari Turkmen weaving of northern Afghanistan or the Amu Darya.
rows.cautions: Many 20th-century Afghans were chemically washed; 'Golden Afghans' began as bleached red rugs. Pakistani and Indian copies exist on cotton foundations.

facts.text: The trade name 'Afghan' means a coarse Ersari main carpet with the gulli gul; older books also call these rugs 'Khiva' or 'Khiva Bokhara'.
facts.quote: KHIVA BOKHARA. Synonym.--Afghan. (Lewis 1920, p. 278)

facts.text: Hawley says these rugs are not strictly Afghan: they came from tribesmen on both sides of the Amu Darya, from the Hindu Kush across the eastern Bokhara khanate.
facts.quote: Nor are they strictly Afghans, since they come from the territory of mountain ridges and fertile valleys that stretches from the Hindu Koosh Mountains northward (Hawley p. 244)

facts.text: Most Turkmen living south of the Afghan-Soviet border were Ersari, who wove thicker and cheaper carpets than other Turkmen.

Hawley's analysis: asymmetric knot (occasionally symmetric), 35-80 knots per square inch, coarse wool or goat-hair warps, two wefts, goat-hair side selvage of three or four cords, broad red-brown end bands and a long fringe.
facts.quote: Knot, generally Sehna, occasionally Ghiordes. Knots to inch horizontally five to eight; perpendicularly, seven to ten. (Hawley p. 245)

facts.text: Lewis gives 42-96 knots per square inch, dark wool or goat-hair warps and a long, shaggy fringe of goat-hair warp.
facts.quote: The long, shaggy fringe of the loose goats' hair warp is a characteristic feature. (Lewis p. 278)

facts.text: Kendrick & Tattersall give 45-70 knots per square inch and describe broad webs divided into colored bands and long fringes.
Until shortly before 1973 Afghan carpets were wool throughout, foundation included, and woven on horizontal looms.
Andkhoy is a market for mostly Ersari rugs in red, indigo and white, asymmetrically knotted and usually double-wefted; Aqcha is the chief rug market.
Export production grew in the 1970s, with much lower-quality work; in the decade before 1973 Turkmen merchants set up 'factories' where men wove.
'Golden Afghan' rugs were red rugs bleached or treated to gold; later gold rugs were woven directly for the Western market.
By 1973 most carpets reaching the West had been chemically washed.

disagreements.about: date of the Turkmen settlement in Afghanistan

says.text: Most Turkmen tribes migrated to Afghanistan in the 1920s.
The best weavers came from Soviet Turkmenistan in the 1930s.
Ersari from Panjdeh founded Dawlatabad soon after 1876; Tekke refugees came in the 1930s.
The 'Kirzig' tribe of Bokhara and northern Afghanistan.
Tribesmen of both Bokhara and Afghanistan.
Ersari Turkmen.
Single-wefted without offset warps vs double-wefted with offset warps.
Single vs double strand of pile yarn; the knots are yak pich / do pich.
Originally bleached red rugs; later woven in gold.
Red Afghans faded to 'copperish gold' by treatment in London.
'Afghan golds' introduced about 1968-73 and woven on the looms.

rows.name: Daulatabad
rows.region: Two towns: Dawlatabad in Faryab (near Andkhoy and Maimana), grown from a settlement founded soon after 1876 by Ersari from Panjdeh, and Dawlatabad in Balkh province, settled by Tekke refugees in the 1930s and the main carpet center of the Mazar-e Sharif region.
rows.made_by: Turkmen (Ersari, Tekke) and Uzbek weavers of the surrounding villages
rows.date_note: Iranica (1994) says the name still stands for the typical modern Afghan Turkmen carpet; such rugs were exported in quantity from the 1960s-70s.

structure.knot_note: Not stated in the sources for Daulatabad specifically; Afghan Turkmen rugs of the area are asymmetric-knotted (Stone, Andkhoy).
structure.kpsi_note: No count found for Daulatabad specifically.

design.field: Large octagon guls (fil-pay) in rows, in dark blue or black on a red field, framed by several borders.
design.colors: Brownish red with dark blue or black.

look_alikes.name: Afghan (Ersari Turkmen carpets of northern Afghanistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same family of rugs; 'Daulatabad' is a later market name for the better-made modern pieces.

look_alikes.name: Khal Mohammadi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Khal Mohammadi rugs (a dealer category) are brighter red and finer, said to be on cotton foundations.

rows.trade_use: A trade name for the standard red Afghan Turkmen carpet with large octagons; one dealer says exporters used it for 'any better than average Afghan rug'.
rows.what_it_tells: A modern red Afghan rug with large blue-black octagons and several borders is the type the trade calls Daulatabad.
rows.cautions: Two towns share the name; the trade name does not prove the town of origin.

facts.text: There are two Dawlatabads with carpet weaving: one in Faryab founded soon after 1876 by Ersari from Panjdeh, and one in Balkh settled by Tekke refugees in the 1930s.
Weaving in Dawlatabad (Faryab) began in its Turkmen villages and spread to Uzbek villages; dealers from Kabul and Andkhoy control production.
'Daulatabad' also names a design of large octagon guls in multiple borders, brownish-red with dark blue.
The 'Taghan Daulatabad' is an Ersari-type Afghan rug with a large gul containing fork-like elements in each quarter.

says.text: Names the large octagons.
A secondary filler motif (dealer).

rows.name: Khal Mohammadi
rows.region: Said to be named after an Ersari master dyer of Kunduz; now also woven near Peshawar.
rows.made_by: Afghan Turkmen weavers (dealer accounts)
rows.date_note: Dealer accounts date the name to the late 1970s; another dealer says 150 years ago. Unsettled.

structure.knot_note: Dealer text only.
structure.kpsi_note: Dealer text: 100-200.

design.field: Rows of Turkmen guls, often large octagons, in navy on a bright red field.
design.colors: Bright red with navy.

look_alikes.name: Daulatabad
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are Afghan Turkmen trade names; dealers describe Khal Mohammadi as brighter red, on cotton, and finer.

rows.trade_use: A dealer category for a red Afghan Turkmen rug.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to modern Afghan (or Afghan-refugee Pakistani) production.
rows.cautions: Only dealer sources were found; treat every detail as unconfirmed.

facts.text: Khal Mohammadi is said to be named after an Ersari master dyer, Khal Mohammad, of Kunduz, and to have a red ground with navy guls on a cotton foundation at 100-200 knots per square inch.

says.text: Late 1970s.
Other dealer snippets say the dyer lived '150 years ago'.

rows.name: Mauri
rows.region: Turkmen settlements of Tekke origin at Barmazid, Shakh, Maurchaq (Maurichaq) and Herat; Sariq settlements in northern Afghanistan.
rows.made_by: Tekke and Saryk Turkmen whose families came from Merv (Soviet Turkmenistan) in the 1920s-30s
rows.date_note: Spooner (1973) says the Turkmen who came from Soviet Turkmenistan in the 1930s did not weave for 10-15 years and then improved steadily.

structure.knot_note: Not stated; Afghan Turkmen rugs are generally asymmetric-knotted.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Maurchaq Mauri about 175 knots per square inch.
structure.pile_note: Stone: pile of single (not plied) yarn.

design.field: Tekke guls (Maurchaq Mauri) or the Salor turret gul (Sariq Mauri).

look_alikes.name: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs (incl. Jaldar and Mori)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Pakistani 'Mori' is a different thing: Tekke-design rugs on cotton with level warps. Afghan 'Mauri' is a wool rug of Merv Turkmen weavers with slightly offset warps.

look_alikes.name: Tekke
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mauri rugs are 20th-century Afghan Tekke-design work; antique Tekke pieces come from Turkmenistan.

rows.trade_use: In Afghanistan the best grade of Turkmen rug; by 1973 all Turkmen varieties there were 'referred to as Mauri' (Spooner).
rows.what_it_tells: A fine Afghan rug in Tekke or Salor designs sold as 'Mauri' points to 20th-century Afghan Turkmen work of Merv origin.
rows.cautions: Not the same as Pakistani 'Mori'; both names come from Merv.

facts.text: 'Mauri' comes from Marv (Merv); by 1973 all Turkmen varieties in Afghanistan were generally called Mauri, because most of the best weavers came from Merv.
Mauri is a trade designation for the best grade of contemporary Afghan carpet, with slightly offset warps and pile of single yarn.
The finest Afghan carpets of the early 1970s came from Turkmen settlements of Tekke origin in Barmazid, Shakh, Maurichaq and Herat.
Maurchaq Mauri rugs are woven by Tekke and Sariq Turkmen in villages on Afghanistan's northern border, with the Tekke gul, at about 175 knots per square inch.
In Afghanistan the Sariq weave the 'Sariq Mauri' with the turret gul.
'Mori' in the Pakistani and Indian trade means rugs without warp offset, and also the Tekke-gul design.

rows.name: Afghan 'Kazak'
rows.region: Mostly woven by Afghan refugee weavers in Pakistan (Peshawar area) and in Afghanistan.
rows.made_by: Afghan Turkmen and other refugee weavers working for exporters
rows.date_note: A 1990s-onward revival of Caucasian Kazak-style designs; no non-dealer source found for its start.

structure.knot_note: Not documented in a non-dealer source.
structure.pile_note: Dealers describe hand-spun wool and natural dyes; not confirmed.

design.field: Bold geometric medallions and latch-hooks after 19th-century Caucasian Kazak rugs.

look_alikes.name: Afghan (Ersari Turkmen carpets of northern Afghanistan)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Afghan Kazaks copy Caucasian designs; traditional Afghan Turkmen rugs carry guls.

rows.trade_use: 'Kazak' or 'Afghan Kazak' for new rugs in Caucasian Kazak designs from Afghan producers.
rows.what_it_tells: A new-looking rug in Caucasian Kazak designs with hand-spun wool points to the Afghan/Pakistani revival production since the 1990s, not to the Caucasus.
rows.cautions: Old Caucasian Kazaks are all wool with symmetric knots, 40-60 per square inch and 2-8 wefts per row, often red-dyed; check the foundation and wefts. The revival's origins are known only from dealer accounts.

facts.text: Peshawar replaced Kabul as the center of the Afghan rug trade after Afghan dealers fled there in the 1980s.
From about 1989 the human-rights group Cultural Survival sponsored a rug project urging refugee weavers in Pakistan to use traditional designs and vegetable dyes.
Nineteenth-century Caucasian Kazak rugs are all wool with symmetric knots at about 40-60 per square inch, often with red-dyed wefts.

rows.name: Afghan war rug
rows.region: First in western Afghanistan (Herat, Farah) and in the refugee camps and bazaars of Peshawar; later in northern Afghanistan (Sheberghan) and Pakistan.
rows.made_by: Baluch weavers first (incl. Taimani Baluch of Farah), then Turkmen, Uzbek and Pashtun weavers, many of them refugees
rows.date_note: War imagery appeared soon after the Soviet invasion of December 1979; the earliest documented example was bought in Peshawar in June 1980. After 9/11 new designs show the World Trade Center attack.

structure.knot_note: Baluch-style pieces follow Baluch structure (asymmetric knots, double-wefted; see Baluch). Not documented per piece.
structure.wefts_note: Baluch rugs are double-wefted (Stone, Baluchi).
structure.pile_note: The 2003 Canberra catalogue lists most 1980s-90s Baluch-style war rugs on wool warps, some on cotton or silk, and 2002 rugs on cotton warps.

design.field: First a few weapons within traditional designs; later tanks, helicopters, Kalashnikovs and maps fill the field; after 1989 the Soviet withdrawal with English captions; after 2001 the World Trade Center, aircraft carriers, flags and maps.
design.sizes: Mostly small rugs.

look_alikes.name: Mushwani and Herat Baluch (note)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Herat Baluch rugs are the parent tradition; war rugs replace field motifs with weapons.

rows.trade_use: 'War rug' for any Afghan or Pakistani rug with weapons or war scenes.
rows.what_it_tells: Weapons, maps or dated war scenes woven into an Afghan or Baluch-style rug date it to 1979 or later.
rows.cautions: Many war rugs were made in Pakistan and sold as 'made in Afghanistan'; post-2001 pieces were often mass-produced and poorly made.

facts.text: War rugs began soon after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, first among Baluch weavers.
The design developed in stages: a few weapons within traditional fields and borders, then war imagery displacing most field motifs, then war imagery replacing field and border motifs entirely.
Peshawar was the main place war rugs were sold through the 1980s; many were made in Pakistan by Afghan refugees.
After the Soviet withdrawal in 1989, rugs showing the retreat along the Salang highway were the first with extensive English text, usually misspelled.
Rugs made after 11 September 2001 show the World Trade Center attacks, American aircraft carriers, maps of Afghanistan and US and Afghan flags.
Some post-2001 rugs name Sheberghan or Turkmen weavers, and many are poorly made.
Many war rugs made in Pakistan are sold as made in Afghanistan.

says.text: Baluch weavers in Herat.
The earliest documented one was bought in Peshawar in June 1980; Baluch made most of the first ones.
Inspiration from 1978; the earliest perhaps aimed at Soviet buyers.
The earliest may have been aimed at Soviet buyers.
Soviet demand was unproven; Western buyers in Peshawar mattered more.

rows.name: Uzbek pile rugs and julkhyrs
rows.region: Semi-nomadic Uzbek groups of Uzbekistan and northern Afghanistan; still made in Jizzakh region (Gallaorol, Bakhmal) and Samarkand region (Urgut).
rows.made_by: Uzbek semi-nomadic, livestock-herding groups (e.g. Kungrat, Lakai)
rows.date_note: 19th- and 20th-century pieces; the Uzbek national encyclopedia (2000) says julkhyrs are still made.

structure.knot_note: Stone: Uzbek strip rugs use the symmetric knot tied so it skips a warp, not on two adjacent warps; extra wefts lie behind and around each row, so the knots hardly show on the back (single source).
structure.wefts_note: Extra wefts behind rows of knots (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Very long, shaggy pile ('bearskin').
structure.sides: Separate strips sewn together; a striped edging strip sewn on (OzME).
structure.back: Knot nodes hard to see because of the extra wefts (Stone).

design.field: Rows of diamonds, hexagons or octagons, often in strips separated by thin stripes, on a dark ground; red, orange, black and natural colors.
design.colors: Red, orange, yellow, blue and black with natural white, gray and brown.
design.sizes: OzME: 2.0-2.5 x 1.0-1.4 m, from two 0.5 m middle strips and two 0.2 m edge strips; Stone: strips about 2.5 ft by 8-10 ft.

look_alikes.name: Kyrgyz pile rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kyrgyz pile carpets are woven in one piece on goat-hair warps; julkhyrs are long-pile rugs assembled from strips.

rows.trade_use: 'Julkhyr' or 'Uzbek rug' for long-pile strip rugs; 'Uzbek' also for flatweaves and suzanis.
rows.what_it_tells: A thick, shaggy rug sewn from narrow strips with bold diamonds or octagons points to Uzbek julkhyr weaving.
rows.cautions: The pile length printed in the encyclopedia copy (7-20 mm) may be a unit error; long-pile julkhyrs are described as much shaggier.

facts.text: A julkhyr ('bearskin') is an Uzbek carpet with very long pile, made of broad pile strips sewn together.
Julkhyrs are woven by semi-nomadic, livestock-herding Uzbek groups from camel, sheep and goat wool, and are still made in Jizzakh and Samarkand regions.
The Persian words jul ('horse-cloth, covering') and khirs ('bear') fit the meaning 'bearskin'.
Uzbek pile strip rugs use the symmetric knot tied so that it skips a warp, with extra wefts that hide the knots on the back.
Uzbek all-wool rugs have a long pile in red, orange and black geometric designs, often with the ram's-horn motif.

rows.name: Kyrgyz pile rugs
rows.country: Kyrgyzstan; also Eastern Turkestan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan (Pamir)
rows.region: Southern Kyrgyzstan (Leilek, Batken, Nookat) and Kyrgyz groups of Eastern Turkestan.
rows.made_by: Kyrgyz women
rows.date_note: 19th- and 20th-century pieces; most Kyrgyz floor coverings are felts.

structure.knot_note: Not documented in the sources found.

design.field: Diamonds, octagons and compartments ('tabak') in red with blue.
design.colors: Mostly red with blue; small white, black and yellow details.
design.sizes: Average about 3.5 x 2.5 m (Akmataliev).

look_alikes.name: Uzbek pile rugs and julkhyrs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are Central Asian red-ground geometric rugs; julkhyrs are strip-woven with very long pile.

rows.trade_use: 'Kirghiz' in older books; rarely seen as a trade name.
rows.what_it_tells: A red-and-blue geometric pile rug on goat-hair warps from Central Asia may be Kyrgyz; most Kyrgyz floor coverings are felts (shyrdak, ala-kiyiz).
rows.cautions: Kyrgyz and Kazakh weavers favored felts and flatweaves; pile pieces are fewer and less studied.

facts.text: The Kyrgyz and Kazakhs mostly made felts and flat-woven brocaded pieces rather than pile carpets.
The Kyrgyz also knotted small rugs, bags and animal trappings in pile.

Kyrgyz pile carpets (kilem) have goat-hair warps and wool wefts, are mostly red with blue, and average about 3.5 x 2.5 m; named kinds include very large ordo kilem, wall carpets (kaly), floor carpets (tör) and camel covers (töö).
The Kyrgyz felt carpets ala-kiyiz and shyrdak are on UNESCO's urgent-safeguarding list (2012).

rows.name: Mushwani and Herat Baluch (note)
rows.region: Herat and western Afghanistan (Baluch); northern Afghanistan (Mushwani).
rows.made_by: Baluch villagers; the Pashtun Mushwani tribe; Aimaq (Taimani)
rows.date_note: Note only: Baluch rugs are covered with the Persian village and tribal rugs.

structure.knot_note: Stone: Mushwani rugs often over 100 asymmetric knots per square inch (open left), some symmetric; Baluch rugs mostly asymmetric and double-wefted.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Taimani about 40; Mushwani often over 100.

design.field: Mushwani: dark latch-hooked diamond medallions; Baluch: dark blues and reds with white highlights, prayer designs, flat-woven end bands.

look_alikes.name: Afghan war rug
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Baluch weavers of Herat made the first war rugs.

rows.trade_use: 'Baluch', 'Herat Baluch', 'Mushwani'.
rows.what_it_tells: See the Baluch entry in the Persian village group.
rows.cautions: Aimaq (Taimani) rugs have often been confused with Baluch work.

facts.text: The Mushwani are a Pashtun tribe of northern Afghanistan who weave large, dark rugs with latch-hooked diamond medallions, often over 100 asymmetric knots per square inch.
Baluch rugs of western Afghanistan are generally smaller, less densely woven and cheaper than Turkmen rugs.
Herat is a market center for Baluch rugs.

rows.name: Khotan
rows.region: The Khotan (Hotan) oasis: Khotan town, Sampul (Shanpulu), the Yurungkash river villages and Lop County (Luopu).
rows.made_by: Uyghur weavers (village workshops; master and pupil)
rows.date_note: Forsyth's mission saw carpet making at Khotan in 1873; the craft continues and is listed as national intangible heritage (2008). Most pieces readers meet are late 19th or 20th century.

structure.knot_note: Kendrick & Tattersall (Sehna) and Stone (asymmetric) for East Turkestan rugs; Lewis notes occasional symmetric knots in Samarkand-type rugs.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: wool rugs about 40-100, silk up to 200. Kendrick & Tattersall: about 40-65 for East Turkestan rugs.
structure.wefts_note: Early Khotan rugs often have three wool wefts per row, two taut and one sinuous (Stone); later ones cotton.
structure.pile_note: Wool of medium length; some silk rugs and some with metal-thread grounds.
structure.handle: Loosely woven, rather floppy (Hawley; Kendrick & Tattersall).

design.field: Round medallions (often three, or five with corners), pomegranate trees growing from vases, lattice and fret grounds, and long multi-niche saffs.
design.border: Several narrow stripes with swastika, fret and wave-and-rock patterns.
design.colors: Reds, yellows and blues; much yellow and apricot; strong contrasts.
design.sizes: Long formats: about 6-14 ft by half that width (Hawley's 'Samarkand' sizes).

look_alikes.name: Kashgar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hard to separate; Stone says Khotan was the source of most East Turkestan medallion rugs; modern Kashgar rugs use the symmetric knot on cotton.

look_alikes.name: Samarkand (trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 'Samarkand' is a trade name; most rugs sold under it were woven in Khotan, Kashgar or Yarkand.

look_alikes.name: Ningxia
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ningxia rugs use Chinese motifs on cotton too, but with yellow-and-blue palettes, Chinese foot sizes and small formats; Khotan rugs are long, with three-medallion and pomegranate designs.

rows.trade_use: 'Khotan', 'Samarkand' or 'Kashgar'; modern Hotan rugs are sold under their own name.
rows.what_it_tells: A long rug with round medallions or a pomegranate-and-vase design, Chinese border stripes and a cotton foundation points to East Turkestan, most often Khotan.
rows.cautions: Old dealers' 'Samarkand' and 'Kashgar' labels do not prove the town.

facts.text: In 1873 Khotan carpets were made at Sampul (Shanpulu), Yurungkash and other villages, in wool or silk and sometimes with gold thread; patterns were passed from master to pupil.
facts.quote: The patterns do not exist on paper, but are passed on from master to pupil (Forsyth 1875)

facts.text: Some Khotan carpets have the pattern in wool pile on a ground of gold or silver metal thread.
Khotan is thought to be the source of most East Turkestan medallion rugs.
Early Khotan rugs may have three wool wefts between rows of knots; later ones have cotton foundations and about 40-100 asymmetric knots per square inch.
East Turkestan rugs usually have a cotton warp on two levels, cotton weft and the asymmetric knot, at about 40-65 knots per square inch.
facts.quote: They have usually a cotton warp on two levels and a cotton weft. The Sehna knot is used, and the texture is coarse and rather loose with from about 40 to 65 knots to the square inch. (Kendrick & Tattersall p. 190)

facts.text: Uyghur carpet weaving, filed by Lop County in Hotan, has been national intangible heritage of China since 2008; pattern names end in nusxa.

museum_examples.licence: Public Domain (Met Open Access; collection API isPublicDomain: true)
museum_examples.title: Carpet
museum_examples.shows: front, whole carpet; Met place: 'present-day China, Khotan'; silk warp, weft and pile, asymmetrically knotted; Met gives the 18th-century date

rows.name: Kashgar
rows.region: Kashgar oasis, western Xinjiang.
rows.made_by: Uyghur weavers
rows.date_note: Forsyth (1873) reports that the Kashgar carpet trade had declined after the wars of the 1860s; Stone mentions 18th-century silk and metal-thread carpets. Modern Kashgar rugs are still made.

structure.knot_note: Lewis and Hawley: Sehna (asymmetric). Stone: contemporary Kashgar rugs use the symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Lewis: 4-7 x 5-9 per inch = 20-63.
structure.wefts_note: Lewis: four-stranded cotton weft. Stone: contemporary rugs double-wefted.
structure.pile_note: Wool of medium length, often partly silk (Lewis).
structure.sides: An added yarn selvage (Lewis).
structure.ends: A web of varying length and a fringe of loose warp ends (Lewis).

design.field: Chinese-style fret or trellis grounds with bats, butterflies, cranes, dragons and fish; medallions.
design.colors: Strong yellow, blue, red, pink, green, orange, pale terracotta.

look_alikes.name: Khotan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Very similar; modern Kashgar rugs use the symmetric knot.

look_alikes.name: Samarkand (trade name)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Old Kashgar rugs were often sold as 'Samarkand'.

rows.trade_use: 'Kashgar'; old pieces often sold as 'Samarkand'.
rows.what_it_tells: A Chinese-looking rug with Indo-Persian colors on cotton points to East Turkestan; Kashgar is one possible center.
rows.cautions: Attribution to a single oasis is rarely certain.

facts.text: Kashgar and Yarkand were the chief inland centers of East Turkestan rug making, with Indo-Persian color influence.
Lewis gives Kashgar rugs 20-63 asymmetric knots per square inch, coarse cotton warps and four-strand cotton wefts.
facts.quote: Knot.--Senna. Number vertically five to nine; number horizontally four to seven; number to square inch twenty to sixty-three. (Lewis p. 287)

facts.text: Silk carpets with gold and silver thread were woven in Kashgar in the 18th century; in 1873 they were no longer made for want of buyers.
Contemporary Kashgar rugs use the symmetric knot on a cotton foundation and are double-wefted.

says.text: Senna (asymmetric).
Contemporary Kashgar rugs: symmetric.

museum_examples.licence: Public Domain (Met Open Access; collection API isPublicDomain: true)
museum_examples.title: Carpet
museum_examples.shows: front, whole carpet; Met place: 'present-day China, Kashgar'; cotton warp and weft, silk pile, asymmetrically knotted; 23 additional images

rows.name: Yarkand
rows.region: Yarkand oasis, between Kashgar and Khotan; Forsyth names Khiwaz, a village about 5 miles from Yarkand.
rows.made_by: Uyghur weavers
rows.date_note: Late 19th and 20th century; a lesser center than Khotan and Kashgar.

structure.knot_note: Lewis (Senna); Stone (asymmetric).
structure.kpsi_note: Lewis: 20-63.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: two blue wefts on a cotton foundation. Lewis: generally four strands between rows.
structure.pile_note: Coarse wool of medium length, sometimes with silk (Lewis).
structure.sides: A selvage of two cords (Lewis).
structure.ends: A web of varying length and loose warp ends (Lewis).

design.field: Like Kashgar and 'Samarkand' rugs: fret grounds with animals, dragons, bats, butterflies, circles and octagons; old rugs with a pomegranate-and-vase design have been given to Yarkand.
design.colors: Brownish-red or tan fields with blue, red, green, yellow, pink and terracotta.

look_alikes.name: Khotan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The pomegranate-and-vase design once given to Yarkand is now questioned; Khotan made most such rugs.

rows.trade_use: 'Yarkand', rarely used now.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to East Turkestan; Yarkand as the exact center is seldom provable.
rows.cautions: The Yarkand attribution of pomegranate-vase rugs is questioned.

facts.text: Carpets were made at Khiwaz, near Yarkand, in 1873, and were judged inferior to Khotan carpets.
Yarkand rugs usually have asymmetric knots and two blue wefts on a cotton foundation; older ones have highly offset warps.
Lewis gives Yarkand rugs 20-63 asymmetric knots per square inch on coarse wool or cotton.

rows.name: Samarkand (trade name)
rows.region: Rugs sold under this name were mostly woven in the East Turkestan oases (Khotan, Kashgar, Yarkand) and traded through Samarkand; Hawley and Lewis thought they were woven near Samarkand.
rows.made_by: Uyghur and other Central Asian weavers
rows.date_note: The name was common in the trade c. 1890-1930; Jacobsen (1962) says none had been imported for 28 years.

structure.knot_note: Hawley: Sehna. Lewis: nearly always Senna, seldom Ghiordes. Ballard Nos. 105 and 106: Sehna.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: 6-8 x 5-8 per inch = 30-64. Lewis: 30-70. Ballard Nos. 105-106: 42-56.
structure.warp_color: Lewis: usually dyed blue or yellow
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: two, occasionally three; Lewis: three or four.
structure.pile_note: Medium-length, loose, lustrous wool; sometimes silk or silk mixed with wool.
structure.sides: Red or pink overcasting (Hawley); antiques a narrow added selvage, modern pieces overcast (Lewis).
structure.ends: Lower end web and warp loops, upper end web and fringe (Hawley); wide web with loose or twisted fringe (Lewis).

design.field: Round medallions (one, three or five), Chinese scrolls, dragons, birds, fish, butterflies; frets in the corners; pomegranate and vase designs.
design.border: Relatively wide, several stripes: an undulating vine, a swastika band, frets, barber-pole or wave-and-rock.
design.colors: Red or madder fields, or blue, brown, gray, tan; strong yellow and blue.
design.sizes: 6-14 ft long, half to three-fifths as wide.

look_alikes.name: Khotan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Most 'Samarkands' are East Turkestan rugs, the majority from Khotan.

look_alikes.name: Kashgar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kashgar rugs were sold as Samarkand in Constantinople.

rows.trade_use: An old trade name for East Turkestan rugs; still seen on old labels and in auction text.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug labeled 'Samarkand' is almost certainly an East Turkestan rug, not one made in Samarkand.
rows.cautions: Samarkand was a market, not a major weaving center; 'Malgaran' was used for an inferior grade.

facts.text: Hawley grouped Samarkand, Kashgar and Yarkand rugs as 'Turko-Chinese' rugs with Chinese ornament.
Hawley's Samarkand: asymmetric knot, 30-64 knots per square inch, cotton (occasionally wool) warps with one warp doubled under the other, two or three wefts, red or pink overcast sides.
facts.quote: Warp, generally cotton, occasionally wool; one of the two threads encircled by a knot is doubled under the other. (Hawley p. 247)

facts.text: Lewis gives 30-70 knots per square inch, warps of wool, cotton or silk often dyed blue or yellow, and three or four wefts per row.
Rugs woven in Kashgar, Khotan and Yarkand have been wrongly attributed to Samarkand, which was a market rather than a weaving center.
Eastern Turkestan rugs may be called 'Samarkand' because Samarkand was once a trading center for them.
Ballard's two 'Samarkand' rugs (now at the Met) are asymmetric-knotted at about 42-56 knots per square inch.
Hawley and Lewis say 'Malgaran' was a name for these rugs or for an inferior grade of them.

says.text: Woven in a district somewhat east of the city of Samarkand.
In the vicinity of Samarkand.
Samarkand was a market, not a weaving center; the rugs came from Kashgar, Khotan and Yarkand.
All Chinese carpets were long assigned to East Turkestan because those reached Europe first.
Two, occasionally three.
Three or four.

museum_examples.shows: front, whole rug; Met place: 'present-day Uzbekistan, probably Samarqand'; cotton warp, wool weft and pile, asymmetrically knotted; 13 additional images

rows.name: Ningxia
other_names: Ningxia palace carpet (see Qing palace carpets with woven hall names)
rows.region: Ningxia (today Yinchuan) in the Yellow River plain, then part of Gansu province; also other Gansu towns.
rows.made_by: Workshop weavers, men and women; wool bought from Mongols
rows.date_note: Ningxia rugs are recorded from the 1690s (Gerbillon, 1697), but most pieces readers meet are 19th or early 20th century; machine-spun cotton warps came in about 1920. The craft continues (national intangible heritage extension, 2021).

structure.knot_note: Mostly the asymmetric ('single') knot with some symmetric ('double') knots, especially at the edges (Leitch; Stone; Hali). Hali says open left; Leitch calls it 'right-hand' by his own definition; the two are not comparable.
structure.kpsi_note: Hali: antique pieces about 25-35. Stone: about 40 for c. 1900 rugs. Leitch: rarely over 120 per foot (about 100 per square inch). Gansu rugs generally about 36 (Stone).
structure.warp_color: white; often only two-ply (Leitch); 3-ply machine-spun after 1920, 6-8 ply in the late period (Stone)
structure.wefts_note: Usually two, up to four, never thicker than the warps (Leitch); Gansu rugs sometimes have wool wefts (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Wool of Mongolian or Tan sheep (滩羊); shorter pile than other Chinese rugs.
structure.sides: Weft selvage, sometimes double-overcast (Leitch).
structure.ends: Fringed warp ends, some knotted (Leitch); Hawley: lower end often warp loops, upper end fringe (Chinese rugs generally).
structure.handle: Loose, supple (Hawley: Chinese rugs generally more loosely woven).
structure.back: Double wefts often prominent on the back (Hali).

design.field: Blue designs on yellow, apricot or tan fields; medallions, frets, all-over lattices, Buddhist and Daoist emblems, pastoral scenes.
design.border: Narrow; T-fret, swastika or key patterns; a gray-brown outer margin on the group attributed to 18th-century Ningxia.
design.colors: Yellow or tan fields with blue (three shades of blue, 三蓝, are the Ningxia signature), touches of red, brown, green.
design.sizes: Small formats measured in Chinese feet: k'ang covers about 5 x 8 or 6 x 10 ft (Stone; Rockhill).

look_alikes.name: Baotou and Suiyuan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Baotou rugs are more densely knotted, use more blue and often have no border; Ningxia rugs are yellow-and-blue with a narrow border.

look_alikes.name: Peking (Beijing)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Peking rugs are larger, made for export in English-foot sizes with 6-8-ply cotton warps; Ningxia rugs small, in Chinese-foot sizes.

look_alikes.name: Khotan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: East Turkestan rugs are long, with three-medallion or pomegranate designs and more red.

rows.trade_use: 'Ningxia' or 'Ninghsia' for older northwestern Chinese rugs, especially yellow-and-blue ones; also a modern regional brand.
rows.what_it_tells: A small, loosely knotted Chinese rug on cotton with blue designs on yellow or tan and sizes in Chinese feet points to Ningxia or nearby Gansu work, mostly 19th-early 20th century.
rows.cautions: The 18th-century dating of some Ningxia groups is disputed; Hawley's Ming and Kangxi datings are not accepted. Chinese-design rugs from India and Japan copy the look.

facts.text: In January 1892 Rockhill found sixteen carpet workshops in Ningxia, most with six to ten vertical looms worked by men and women; the wool was bought from Mongols.
facts.quote: (there are sixteen in the city), in most of which we found between six to ten looms at which both men and women worked. (Rockhill 1894, p. 41)

facts.text: Ningxia dyers in 1892 used brazilwood red, pagoda-tree-seed yellow, safflower and indigo; aniline dyes were on sale but used mainly for purple.
Ningxia rugs were mentioned by Gerbillon in 1697; a 1736 Gansu gazetteer praised Ningxia pile carpets, and court records of 1727-28 show carpets woven there to palace patterns.
Before the late Qing, rug making in China was mainly a craft of the northwest, with Ningxia and the Kweihwa (Guihua) district noted.
Chinese rugs use the asymmetric knot, with occasional symmetric knots at the edges and ends of early examples.
facts.quote: All are woven with the Sehna knot. In all but the earliest rugs the warp and weft are of cotton; each thread of warp is equally prominent at the back (Hawley p. 265)

facts.text: Late 19th- and early 20th-century Ningxia rugs are coarse, about 40 asymmetric knots per square inch on a cotton foundation.
Ningxia rugs are small, measured in Chinese feet, for the k'ang (heated platform), travel or hanging.
facts.quote: The usual size of the rugs is that necessary to cover a k'ang, say ten feet by six. (Rockhill 1894, p. 42)

facts.text: Ningxia hand-carpet weaving is a national intangible-heritage item (VIII-110 extension, 2021); its signature is three shades of blue and the wool is from Tan sheep.
Some Ningxia pillar rugs made for monasteries carry Tibetan inscriptions naming the donor.
Ningxia and Peking had a name for making the best Chinese carpets around 1920.

says.text: Gerbillon saw Ningxia rugs in 1697.
Literary references from 1692.
About 25-35 (antique).
About 40.
Rarely over 120 per foot (about 100 per square inch).
A group with gray-brown margins has been attributed to 18th-century Ningxia; the attribution is disputed.
Hawley dated many Chinese rugs to the Ming and Kangxi periods.

rows.name: Qing palace carpets with woven hall names
rows.region: Woven for halls of the imperial palaces in Beijing; some wool carpets ordered from Ningxia to palace patterns; silk-and-metal pieces probably from Beijing workshops.
rows.made_by: Imperial and court-commissioned workshops
rows.date_note: Court records show Ningxia carpets woven to palace patterns in 1727-28. A group of silk-and-metal-thread carpets with a woven hall name in the top border is dated variously from the Qianlong reign (1736-95) to 1920-40.

structure.knot_note: As other Chinese pile rugs.
structure.pile_note: Silk pile with metal-thread (silver or gold-wrapped) brocaded grounds in the inscribed group; wool in Ningxia palace carpets.

design.field: Imperial dragons, clouds and waves; a short woven inscription of three to five characters at one end naming the palace hall (e.g. 乾清宫, Hall of Heavenly Purity).
design.colors: Imperial yellow, blues; silver or gold metal-thread grounds.

look_alikes.name: Ningxia
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Wool Ningxia court carpets carry no hall name in the sources found; the hall-named carpets found are silk and metal thread.

look_alikes.name: Chinese silk rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Modern Chinese silk rugs copy palace designs and inscriptions; the 1920-40 date the V&A gives its example shows how late such pieces can be.

rows.trade_use: 'Palace carpet' or 'imperial' is used loosely in the trade for any Chinese rug with dragons or yellow grounds.
rows.what_it_tells: A woven hall name in characters at one end belongs to a recognized group of silk-and-metal palace-style carpets; the date of the group is disputed.
rows.cautions: Many 'palace' carpets on the market are later copies; the V&A dates its inscribed example to 1920-40. Ballard's rug No. 93 was only 'purported' to come from the Imperial Palace.

facts.text: A group of silk and metal-thread carpets carries a woven inscription of a few characters naming a palace hall, such as 乾清宫 (Qianqing gong).
The date of the inscribed silk-and-metal carpets is disputed; the V&A dates its example to 1920-40.
Court records of 1727-28 show carpets woven in Ningxia to palace patterns.
The Ningxia intangible-heritage listing claims that Ningxia carpets make up more than half of the Palace Museum's thousand-plus carpets.
Kendrick & Tattersall (1922) say silk-and-gold Chinese carpets were commonly attributed to the Ming dynasty 'with small justification as a rule'.
facts.quote: commonly attributed to the time of the Ming dynasty, but with small justification as a rule. (Kendrick & Tattersall p. 63)

says.text: Late 19th-early 20th century, reporting an older Qianlong-period theory.

disagreements.about: where the Forbidden City carpets were woven

says.text: The Ming palace carpets were imperial commissions woven in Beijing.
More than half of the Palace Museum's carpets are Ningxia work.

rows.name: Baotou and Suiyuan
rows.native: 包头 / 绥远 / 归化
rows.region: Baotou and its villages in the great bend of the Yellow River, and Guihua (Kweihwa, today's Hohhot) in the former Suiyuan province.
rows.made_by: Workshop weavers; Leitch says Baotou's weavers came from Ningxia
rows.date_note: Late 19th and early 20th century; Stone says larger Kweihwa carpets were woven in the 1920s. Leitch (1928) ranks Baotou rugs first among inland Chinese rugs.

structure.knot_note: Leitch: the 'single' (asymmetric) knot throughout, tied either way.
structure.kpsi_note: Leitch: frequently more than 160 knots per foot (about 178 per square inch). Stone: more densely knotted than Ningxia. The Met's Baotou saddle rug is not counted.
structure.wefts_note: Two wefts of about the warp's size (Leitch).
structure.pile_note: Moderately short, fine wool from sheep of the Yellow River loop (Leitch).
structure.sides: Simple weft selvage (Leitch).
structure.ends: Narrow web; upper end looped, lower end fringed (Leitch).
structure.handle: Fine and supple; Leitch says some look more like tapestries than rugs.

design.field: Large, simple, often pictorial designs (Buddhist, mythological, landscapes), shaded colors, often no border (Leitch); early rugs with all-over repeats.
design.border: Usually absent (Leitch); one dealer says about four borders.
design.colors: Brilliant yellow, green, blue and red (Leitch); more blue than Ningxia.
design.sizes: Mats to carpets, measured in Chinese feet (Leitch).

look_alikes.name: Ningxia
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ningxia rugs are coarser, yellow-and-blue, with narrow borders; Baotou rugs finer, more colorful, often borderless.

rows.trade_use: 'Baotou' or 'Paotow'; 'Suiyuan' for the province.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted, brightly shaded Inner Mongolian rug on cotton, borderless or with a pictorial field, points to Baotou.
rows.cautions: Stone runs 'Guizhou, Kweichow, Kweihwa' together; Kweihwa is 归化 (Hohhot) in Inner Mongolia, not Guizhou province in the south.

facts.text: Baotou's weavers came from Ningxia, and Baotou rugs resemble Ningxia rugs but are more ornate.
facts.quote: the weavers of the latter migrated from the former place (Leitch 1928)

facts.text: Baotou rugs are more densely knotted than Ningxia rugs and use more blue.
Leitch's Baotou structure: cotton warp, two wefts, asymmetric knot, narrow web with the upper end looped and lower end fringed, simple weft selvage, sizes in Chinese feet.
Early Baotou rugs have all-over repeating patterns; later ones are more pictorial.
Suiyuan was a province of Inner Mongolia with rug production; its capital was Guihua (Kweihwa).
Pillar rugs are long, narrow rugs made to wrap a temple column so the design joins up; they have no side borders and often show coiling dragons.

says.text: A border is usually absent.
About four borders (dealer).
Frequently over 160 per foot (about 178 per square inch).
Chinese rugs in general 30-120.

rows.name: Peking (Beijing)
rows.region: Workshops and factories in Beijing; old trade lineages called east gate and west gate (东门/西门).
rows.made_by: Workshop weavers (male), in shops of about 20-100
rows.date_note: Rug weaving in Beijing is thought to have begun about 1860; the first export factory (继长永, Chi Chang Yung) followed; heaviest production 1880-1920, after which Tianjin led. Production stopped in the mid-1930s; resumed after 1960.

structure.knot_note: Mostly the 'single' (asymmetric) knot; symmetric ('double') knots at edges and ends of some pieces (Leitch). Hali: asymmetric. Leitch calls all Peking knots 'right-hand' by his own definition.
structure.kpsi_note: Leitch: 80-90 knots per foot, occasionally 100 (about 44-69 per square inch). Stone: current Beijing production 34-100.
structure.wefts_note: Two wefts, occasionally four, together equal to one warp in thickness (Leitch).
structure.pile_note: Wool, very rarely silk; no longer than half an inch (Leitch).
structure.sides: Double or triple overcasting (Leitch); Hali: flat wrapped sides.
structure.ends: Fringes (Leitch).

design.field: Blue fields with buff, white or gold designs; copies of older palace, court and temple rugs; Buddhist and Daoist symbols, often mixed; Hundred Antiques; during World War I some Persian-style designs.
design.border: Key and fret borders; often a plain outer band.
design.colors: Subdued blues, taupe, brown, red, mandarin yellow; blue-and-white nearly universal 1860-1920 (Hali).
design.sizes: Mats to very large carpets, round, oval or rectangular, in English feet (Leitch).

look_alikes.name: Tianjin (Tientsin)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tianjin rugs of the 1920s have the same foundation and count but longer pile of machine-spun wool, darker colors, very even wefting and sometimes symmetric knots throughout (Leitch).

look_alikes.name: Ningxia
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ningxia rugs are small, in Chinese feet, with 2-ply warps; Peking rugs in English feet with 6-8-ply warps.

look_alikes.name: japanese-export
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Japanese 'Peking' rugs of the 1950s are post-war Japanese copies in Chinese designs.

rows.trade_use: 'Peking' for older blue-and-white or antique-design Chinese export rugs; also 'Peking' as a name for Japanese and Indian copies in the 1950s-60s.
rows.what_it_tells: A Chinese rug on a white cotton foundation in an antique Chinese design, with sizes in English feet, points to Beijing export production of about 1880-1930.
rows.cautions: Jacobsen judged the 'Peking quality' of the 1920s inferior to Tianjin factory rugs; most were chemically washed.

facts.text: Rug weaving in Beijing is thought to have begun about 1860, with regular factory production from about 1880; heaviest production was 1880-1920.
The first Beijing export rug factory was Chi Chang Yung (继长永).
Beijing had 354 rug workshops in 1920.
Peking rugs of the 1920s have cotton warps of six or eight ply, two wefts, mostly asymmetric knots at 80-90 per foot, double or triple overcast sides and fringed ends.
Beijing rugs were usually woven with the asymmetric knot on warps without offset.
Peking weavers 'cut out' the pile around motifs to make them stand in relief.
facts.quote: A common practice among the Chinese carpet-weavers of cutting into the pile in order to round-off the angular contours (Kendrick & Tattersall p. 66)

facts.text: Beijing palace-carpet weaving (北京宫毯织造技艺) has been national intangible heritage since 2008; the style is called 京式 (Peking style).
Lewis (1920) ranked Pekin first, Tientsin second and 'Thibet' third among the Chinese rugs reaching America.

says.text: Gold medal at Paris 1900.
First prize at St. Louis (1903/1904).
St. Louis.
Brought from Tibet about 1860 (one account), or by Gansu weavers in the Qianlong reign (another).
From Baotou, or a Tibetan monk at Baoguo temple (dealer).
Two, occasionally four.
Heavy weft, up to four strands.

rows.name: Tianjin (Tientsin)
rows.region: Tianjin, the port of Beijing; about 300 workshops by 1929.
rows.made_by: Factory and workshop weavers working on contract for American and European firms
rows.date_note: Tianjin had no carpet making before 1860; it became the main production center about 1910-1930; the Depression and the Japanese invasion ended most production in the early to mid 1930s.

structure.knot_note: Usually the 'single' (asymmetric) knot; some pieces symmetric ('double') throughout for durability (Leitch). Jacobsen says the Chinese 'employed the double Persian knot' from about 1925.
structure.kpsi_note: Same thread count as Peking rugs (Leitch): about 80-120 per foot; '90-line' = about 56 per square inch.
structure.wefts_note: Very even wefting, beaten with a full-width metal comb (Leitch).
structure.pile_note: Longer than Peking pile; machine-spun or tightly hand-spun wool (Leitch); heavy, thick pile from about 1925 (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Single or double overcasting (Leitch).
structure.ends: Fringed (Leitch).
structure.handle: Heavy and stiff in the 'super' qualities.
structure.back: 'Closed back': wefts hidden because the warps are fully offset (Stone).

design.field: Open fields, often blue, with white, yellow or gold designs; asymmetrically placed floral sprays; small or large rounded medallions; borders absent or elaborate; copies of Aubusson and Savonnerie rugs; some pictorial rugs.
design.colors: Darker hues than Peking (Leitch); chemically washed to soft pastel tones for export.
design.sizes: Mostly 9 x 12 ft and other standard American sizes.

look_alikes.name: Chinese art deco rugs (Nichols, Fette)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nichols and Fette rugs were made in Tianjin and Beijing; the art deco label refers to their designs.

look_alikes.name: Chinese export rugs graded by line (1960s on)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Post-1960 export rugs are graded in lines with chrome dyes and steel looms; 1920s-30s rugs show hand-scissor carving, older wool and age wear (see that row).

look_alikes.name: Peking (Beijing)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Peking rugs have shorter pile and lighter colors.
