rows.trade_use: 'Tientsin' was used as a general trade name because so many Chinese carpets were exported through the port.
rows.what_it_tells: A heavy Chinese rug with an open, carved field in decorator colors on a cotton foundation, especially with a closed back, points to Tianjin export production of about 1910-1935.
rows.cautions: The name 'Tientsin carpet' was given to rugs merely exported through Tianjin.

facts.text: Tianjin became the major center for Chinese rugs from about 1910, with about 300 workshops and factories by 1929 weaving on contract for American and European firms.
Many carpets were exported through Tientsin, so 'Tientsin carpet' became a trade name, as 'Bokhara' did for Central Asia.
facts.quote: Many carpets find their way to Tientsin for export, and on that account the term 'Tientsin carpet' has come into use. (Kendrick & Tattersall p. 66)

facts.text: Tianjin rugs differ from Peking rugs by longer pile of machine-spun or tightly spun wool, darker colors and even wefting beaten with a full-width metal comb; some use the symmetric knot throughout.
facts.quote: the wool used is machine spun, or tightly hand spun. (Leitch 1928, p. 147)

facts.text: About 1925 factories multiplied and a much heavier, tighter Chinese rug with a thick pile appeared.
'Closed back' means asymmetric knots on fully offset warps so that wefts do not show on the back; it is used in Tianjin rugs.
Copies of Aubusson and Savonnerie rugs were woven in Tianjin in the 1920s-30s.
Nearly all Chinese rugs imported to America in the 1920s-30s were lightly chemically washed, mostly in the United States.
facts.quote: Most of the rugs washed are treated in the United States (Leitch 1928, p. 158)

facts.text: The Depression and the Japanese invasion ended most production in the early to mid 1930s; large-scale production did not resume until the 1960s.

says.text: About 300 in Tianjin by 1929.
303 registered factories, 2,749 looms.
About 600 factories (probably all of China).
Usually single (asymmetric); some double (symmetric) throughout.
From about 1925 'the double Persian knot'.

rows.name: Chinese art deco rugs (Nichols, Fette)
other_names: 美术式 (meishu shi, Chinese trade style)
rows.region: Tianjin and Beijing factories run by American firms.
rows.made_by: Factory weavers working for American-owned firms (Walter Nichols; Helen Fette and a Chinese partner, Li)
rows.date_note: Nichols launched his 'Super Chinese' rug in 1924; Fette rugs date from the 1920s and early 1930s; production ended in the mid 1930s.

structure.knot_note: Asymmetric on fully offset warps (Nichols closed back, Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: 'Super' = 90 line, about 56 per square inch (Stone); Fette rugs finer and lighter than Nichols (Jacobsen; Hali).
structure.pile_note: Nichols: heavy, thick pile; Fette: finer, thinner pile, never lime-washed (Jacobsen).
structure.sides: Wool selvages (Nichols, Stone).
structure.ends: Fringed.
structure.handle: Nichols: very heavy (about 1 lb per square foot, dealer text); Fette: lighter.

design.field: Open fields in strong, unusual color pairs (Nichols) or pastel shades (Fette) with asymmetric floral sprays, small vignettes, geometric art deco motifs, Chinese and Spanish motifs; round, oval and semicircular shapes.
design.colors: Nichols: saturated colors (purple, plum, emerald, mustard, black); Fette: soft natural-dye pastels.
design.sizes: Nichols standard 9 x 12 ft; Fette circles, ovals and semicircles.

look_alikes.name: Chinese export rugs graded by line (1960s on)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Modern 'art deco' reproductions (China, India, Nepal) are usually on modern line grades with electrically carved pile and chemically even colors; Nichols and Fette rugs show hand-scissor carving, back labels (Fette) and age wear.

look_alikes.name: Tianjin (Tientsin)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nichols and Fette rugs are a subset of 1920s-30s Tianjin/Beijing production.

rows.trade_use: 'Art deco' or 'Nichols' is used loosely for any 1920s-30s Chinese rug with bold colors and open fields, and for modern copies.
rows.what_it_tells: A heavy Chinese rug in strong deco colors with a closed back points to Nichols-type production of 1924-1930s; a lighter pastel rug, sometimes oval, with a back label, to Fette.
rows.cautions: Western 'art deco' (Nichols, Fette, 1920s-30s) is not the same as the Chinese trade style 美术式, which the Chinese dealer source dates to the 1930s-40s and links to French floral carpets. Modern reproductions are common.

facts.text: Walter Nichols, an American, founded his firm in Tianjin in 1924; its rugs were heavy and strong, on a cotton foundation with wool selvages and fully offset warps (closed back).
Many Nichols rugs were in the art deco style, and the style has been closely associated with his name.
Fette rugs were woven in Beijing and Tianjin in the 1920s and early 1930s to Helen Fette's designs by the Fette-Li Rug Company, in pastel natural dyes, often round, semicircular or oval.
Fette rugs were finer and lighter than other Chinese rugs of the time and were not lime-washed.
Fette rugs sometimes carry labels on the back.
'Esthetic' rugs were a 1930s Chinese design category of art deco and Aubusson designs.
Jacobsen says Chinese rugs of 1922-34 often show 'white knots' (warp joins) through worn plain fields, and that Fette rugs seldom do.

says.text: Nichols Super Yarn and Carpets.
Nichols Super Chinese rug Company.
Fette rugs not made since 1934.
Nichols and Fette worked until the Second World War.
Nichols closed in 1935.
Beijing and Tianjin.
Tianjin.
Beijing.

rows.name: Chinese export rugs graded by line (1960s on)
rows.native: 道; 片活/剪花; 京式, 美术式, 彩花式, 素凸式
rows.translit: dào (line); piànhuó/jiǎnhuā (carving); jīngshì, měishùshì, cǎihuāshì, sùtūshì
rows.region: State and cooperative factories in Tianjin, Beijing, Hebei, Shandong, Henan, Inner Mongolia and elsewhere.
rows.made_by: Factory weavers in cooperative and state carpet factories
rows.date_note: Large-scale commercial production resumed in the 1960s; Jacobsen saw new China-woven rugs in London in 1960 that could not then be imported into the USA.

structure.knot_note: The 'figure-8' knot (8字扣) is tied in two ways (抽绞 and 拉绞) (patent).
structure.kpsi_note: Line (道) = knots per foot across the width; the vertical count is assumed equal, so knots per square inch = (line / 12) squared: 70 line = 34, 80 = 44, 90 = 56, 120 = 100. Silk: 120-300 line (100-625). Wool grades of 150-250 line appeared by 2011.
structure.wefts_note: One thick and one thin weft (patent).
structure.pile_note: Pile heights 3/8, 1/2 or 5/8 inch for wool; 1/2 inch for silk (Stone).
structure.sides: Overcast.
structure.ends: Fringed.

design.field: Peking-style antique designs, open-field floral sprays, Aubusson and Savonnerie designs, plain fields with carved borders; four trade styles: 京式 (Peking), 美术式 (French-floral 'art'), 彩花式 (diagonal floral sprays), 素凸式 (one color, carved relief).
design.colors: Chrome dyes; pastel and decorator colors.
design.sizes: Standard Western sizes.

look_alikes.name: Tianjin (Tientsin)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 1920s-30s rugs show hand-scissor carving, hand-spun or early machine-spun wool and age; modern rugs carry line grades, chrome dyes, electric-scissor carving.

look_alikes.name: Chinese art deco rugs (Nichols, Fette)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Modern 'deco' copies are line-graded factory rugs.

look_alikes.name: japanese-export
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Japan made Chinese-design and Savonnerie-design wool rugs for the US in the 1950s-60s, while Chinese goods could not be imported.

rows.trade_use: Sold by line count ('90-line', '120-line'), as 'Super', and by style ('Aubusson', 'Savonnerie', 'Peking', 'carved').
rows.what_it_tells: A tag or invoice giving '70/80/90/120 line' points to post-1960 Chinese factory production; 90-line is about 56 knots per square inch.
rows.cautions: Line counts are per foot across the width, not per inch and not per square inch.

facts.text: The line (道) is the Chinese measure of knot density: the number of knots, one per pair of warps, in one foot across the width; the vertical count is assumed to be the same.
facts.quote: The usual standard of measure in China is the linear foot, the rugs being said to contain a certain number of knots to the foot. (Leitch 1928, p. 8)

facts.text: A 90-line rug has 7.5 knots per inch each way, about 56 knots per square inch; the square of the line number gives knots per square foot.
Warps per foot are twice the knots per foot, and in Peking and Tianjin 'threads' and 'knots' per foot were used as the same number.
Wool carpets are woven in 70, 80, 90 and 120-line qualities and silk rugs in 120 to 300 lines; 'Super' means 90-line, 5/8-inch pile and a closed back.
By 2011 most hand-knotted wool carpets on the Chinese market were 150 line, 200 was rare and 250 was new.
After weaving, Chinese carpets are leveled (平毯), carved along the design (剪花/片活, 'cutting out') and washed (洗毯).
Sculpting or carving the pile to make the design stand in relief is common in 20th-century Chinese rugs and in Indian copies of them.
Contemporary Chinese rugs are woven in cooperative factories with steel looms and chrome dyes.
Large-scale Chinese rug production resumed in the 1960s; Jacobsen saw new China-woven rugs in London in 1960.
Chinese trade style names include 京式 (Peking style), 美术式 ('art' style after French carpets), 彩花式 (floral sprays) and 素凸式 (one-color carved).

says.text: Number of warp and weft lines per square foot (the square of the dao gives knots).
Knots per foot across the width.

disagreements.about: Chinese 美术式 vs Western 'art deco'

says.text: 美术式 dates from the 1930s-40s and follows French floral carpets.
'Esthetic' rugs of the 1930s were art deco and Aubusson designs.

rows.name: Chinese silk rugs
rows.native: 真丝地毯; 柞蚕丝地毯
rows.translit: zhēnsī dìtǎn; zuòcánsī dìtǎn (tussah silk carpet)
rows.region: Henan (Nanzhao county, Nanyang), Hebei, Xinjiang (Urumqi, Hotan) and other provinces.
rows.made_by: Factory and home weavers
rows.date_note: Silk rugs were made in small numbers in the 1920s (mainly Beijing, coarse); the large modern production in Persian designs dates from the 1980s.

structure.kpsi_note: Silk grades of 120-300 line = 100-625 per square inch (Stone); Nanzhao typical 210 per foot = about 306 per square inch. 1920s silk rugs only 40-120 per foot (Leitch).
structure.pile_note: Mulberry or tussah (柞蚕) silk; Urumqi rugs with gold-wrapped thread grounds.

design.field: Persian city designs (Qum, Isfahan, Tabriz, Kashan), Hereke-style prayer and garden designs, Chinese pictorial designs.
design.sizes: Mostly small rugs.

look_alikes.name: Chinese export rugs graded by line (1960s on)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same factories and line grades; silk rugs are finer.

rows.trade_use: Sold as 'silk', 'Qum-style', 'Hereke-style' or simply 'Persian silk'.
rows.what_it_tells: A fine silk rug in a Persian or Hereke design on a cotton or silk foundation may be Chinese production since the 1980s; structure alone rarely tells it from Iranian or Turkish work.
rows.cautions: No source was found on Chinese silk rugs being sold as Iranian or Turkish; still, a 'Hereke' or 'Qum' design does not prove where a silk rug was made.

facts.text: In the 1920s Chinese silk rugs were coarse (40-120 knots per foot), on cotton foundations, often spun from waste silk, and made mainly in Beijing.
Nanzhao county in Henan has made knotted tussah-silk carpets in Persian-style designs since the 1980s.
Hebei (Tientsin province) is a source of contemporary silk rugs; Urumqi makes silk rugs with gold-wrapped thread grounds.
Silk rugs are woven in 120 to 300-line qualities.

rows.name: Tibetan rug (khaden and other traditional rugs)
rows.country: China (Tibet Autonomous Region and Tibetan areas); Tibetan weavers also in Ladakh and Sikkim
rows.region: Mainly Tsang in southern Tibet: Gyantse (the leading center), Shigatse, the Nyang valley, Gobshi near Gyantse; also Lhasa.
rows.made_by: Household and workshop weavers, men and women (Landon saw both at Gobshi in 1904)
rows.date_note: Reliable dating of Tibetan rugs begins in the 1880s; a few are tentatively dated to the 17th century; commercial production is recorded from the late 18th century. Traditional production in Tibet was disrupted after 1959.

structure.knot_note: Tibetan pile is a continuous supplementary weft looped around two warps and then around a gauge rod; after a run of loops the loops are cut and the rod removed. Stone calls this weft wrapping, not knotting; some Tibetan rugs use the symmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 20-140 per square inch; older rugs coarser.
structure.wefts_note: Rows of cut loops alternate with several rows of ground weft (Stone).
structure.pile_note: Thick, rather short highland wool; Leitch says the pile is shorter in Tibetan rugs than in Chinese ones.
structure.sides: Many older rugs have a red fabric edging (Stone).
structure.back: Many older rugs are backed with red fabric (Stone); the pile rows look like overlapping shingles (Stone).

design.field: Checkerboard designs, tiger stripes, dragons and phoenixes, lotus and peony, medallions, crossed vajras (dorje), plain orange or maroon fields.
design.border: Often a plain or pearl band; Chinese-derived frets.
design.colors: Orange and gold for religious use, maroon for monastery floors; strong reds, blues, yellows.
design.sizes: Narrow looms: Landon (1904) says pieces wider than about 30 inches were hard to weave; plain rugs were made in strips and sewn together.

look_alikes.name: tibetan-nepal-export
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Refugee export rugs (from 1960) have cotton foundations, modern dyes, Western sizes and are often carved after weaving; older Tibetan rugs are wool or wool-and-cotton, narrow, with red fabric edging or backing.

look_alikes.name: Ningxia
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chinese rugs tie each asymmetric knot separately on a cotton foundation; Tibetan rugs have cut-loop pile in rows separated by several ground wefts.

rows.trade_use: 'Tibetan rug' is used both for rugs woven in Tibet and for the Tibetan-style rugs of Nepal and India.
rows.what_it_tells: A narrow, thick rug with cut-loop pile in clearly separated rows, a wool or wool-and-cotton foundation and red cloth edging points to traditional Tibetan weaving, mostly 1880-1950s.
rows.cautions: Most 'Tibetan' rugs on the market since the 1960s were woven in Nepal or India.

facts.text: Tibetan pile is made by looping a continuous yarn around two warps and then around a gauge rod; the loops are cut and the rod removed, and rows of cut loops alternate with several rows of ground weft.
Some Tibetan rugs use the symmetric knot; knot densities run from about 20 to 140 per square inch, older rugs being coarser.
Older Tibetan rugs, with a few exceptions, are all wool, and many have a red fabric edging and backing.
Rugs from Tibet and other inland regions may have woolen warp and weft, unlike the cotton foundations of eastern Chinese rugs.
facts.quote: Occasional examples from Tibet and other inland regions may have woolen warp and weft. (Leitch 1928, p. 140)

facts.text: In 1904 Landon saw a rug workshop at Little Gobshi near Gyantse with men and women weaving native Tibetan patterns; looms limited pieces to about 30 inches wide, and plain orange and maroon rugs were woven in strips and sewn together.
facts.quote: The plain orange and maroon rugs are made in narrow strips and sewn together to any desired width (Landon 1905, p. 110)

facts.text: Gyantse is a site of rug production since the 19th century; Shigatse was the second center for higher-quality rugs.
Tibetan rug design was influenced mainly by China and to a lesser extent by East Turkestan.
The Chinese and the Tibetans used pile knotting for many purposes besides floor rugs: small mats, chair and seat covers, saddle cloths and temple hangings.
Lewis (1920) grouped 'Thibet' rugs with Chinese rugs as practically Chinese and ranked them third after Peking and Tientsin.
Tibetan terms for pile rugs include den (gdan) and drumze; a khaden is a rug for sleeping or sitting.

says.text: A weft-wrapping technique with cut loops; 'some Tibetan rugs are woven with the symmetric knot'.
Kendrick & Tattersall speak of Chinese and Tibetan 'pile-knotting' without distinguishing the technique.

museum_examples.licence: Public Domain (Met Open Access; collection API isPublicDomain: true)
museum_examples.title: Tantric Rug with Two Flayed Male Figures
museum_examples.shows: front; Tibet; wool, cotton, and dye; 166.4 x 81.3 cm; a ritual rug, not a household khaden

rows.name: Tibetan saddle rug
rows.country: China (Tibet); Mongolia and Inner Mongolia (related Chinese pieces)
rows.region: Tibetan plateau; related saddle rugs were woven in Ningxia and Baotou.
rows.made_by: Tibetan weavers
rows.date_note: Late 19th to mid-20th century for most surviving pieces.

structure.knot_note: As other Tibetan rugs.

design.field: Pairs of under- and over-saddle pieces; dragons, tiger stripes, lotus, checkerboard and floral designs.
design.sizes: Butterfly saddle rugs: trapezoid with rounded corners on the short side.

look_alikes.name: Baotou and Suiyuan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chinese saddle rugs from Baotou and Ningxia are knotted with the asymmetric knot on cotton; Tibetan ones use the cut-loop technique.

rows.trade_use: 'Tibetan saddle rug'; 'butterfly' for the trapezoid shape.
rows.what_it_tells: A trapezoid or notched small rug with a matching pair points to a Tibetan or Chinese saddle rug.
rows.cautions: Chinese (Baotou, Ningxia) saddle rugs look similar; check the technique.

facts.text: Butterfly saddle rugs are Tibetan saddle rugs in a trapezoid shape whose shorter edge may have rounded corners, suggesting a butterfly.
Tibetan saddles were set on a cloth and covered by several rugs, raising the rider eight or nine inches.
facts.quote: The saddles of the Tibetans are curious high structures, under which a beautiful cloth is placed, and the whole is then concealed by rug after rug. (Landon 1905)

facts.text: Saddle cloths in a curved shape were among the pile pieces of the Chinese and Tibetans.

museum_examples.licence: Public Domain (Met Open Access; collection API isPublicDomain: true)
museum_examples.title: Saddle Rug
museum_examples.shows: front; Met culture 'Inner Mongolian, probably Baotou' (a Chinese, not Tibetan, saddle rug, shown for comparison)

rows.name: Tibetan tiger rug
rows.region: Tibet.
rows.made_by: Tibetan weavers
rows.date_note: Older tiger rugs are late 19th-early 20th century; modern copies are made in Nepal and India.

structure.knot_note: As other Tibetan rugs.

design.field: A tiger pelt shown whole (with head and legs) or as abstract stripes over the whole field.
design.colors: Orange and yellow with black or dark brown stripes.

look_alikes.name: tibetan-nepal-export
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nepali export tiger rugs use cotton foundations, modern dyes and often carved pile.

rows.trade_use: 'Tiger rug'.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug woven as a tiger skin points to Tibetan weaving or its modern Nepali copies.
rows.cautions: Popular with collectors; many modern copies.

facts.text: Tiger rugs are a large group of Tibetan rugs woven in imitation of tiger skins; tiger skins were prized by Tibetan nobles and officials and older tiger carpets are thought to have been badges of authority.
A 'tiger skin' pattern of repeated waving lines also appears in the fields of older Chinese rugs.

rows.name: Wangden rug
rows.region: Wangden village in the Nyang river valley, south of Shigatse.
rows.made_by: Village weavers, originally for monasteries
rows.date_note: Older pieces late 19th-early 20th century; Wangden rugs are still woven.

structure.knot_note: Pile technique as other Tibetan rugs (not separately documented).
structure.back: The trade describes Wangden rugs by a warp-faced back (the warps, not wefts or knots, show on the back); no source other than Wikipedia was found for this in this pass.

design.field: Small square mats, often with an added heavy fringe; checkerboard and geometric designs.
design.sizes: Meditation mats about 1.5 ft square.

look_alikes.name: Tibetan rug (khaden and other traditional rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ordinary Tibetan rugs show the rows of pile loops and wefts on the back; Wangden pieces are known for a warp-faced back.

rows.trade_use: 'Wangden' in the trade for Tibetan rugs with a warp-faced back, wherever made.
rows.what_it_tells: A small Tibetan mat with a heavy fringe and a ribbed, warp-faced back is the type sold as Wangden.
rows.cautions: The structural description of the 'warp-faced back' needs a second source; the name is used as a type name.

facts.text: Wangden is a Tibetan village in the Nyang river valley and the source of meditation mats.
'Meditation mat' is a trade term for a small Tibetan pile mat about one and a half feet square, used in Buddhist meditation; some have an added heavy fringe.

rows.name: Nabeshima dantsu
rows.region: Saga (Hizen province), Kyushu; since 1954 the Yoshijima workshop also in Kurume, Fukuoka.
rows.made_by: Farm households taught by Koga Seiemon in the Edo period; later town workshops (e.g. the Yoshijima family, founded 1912)
rows.date_note: Begun in the late 17th century (Genroku era), but in the Edo period the Saga domain reserved the rugs for its own use and gifts and banned general sale; the ban was lifted in the Meiji era, so pieces readers own are mostly Meiji (1868-1912) or later.

structure.knot_note: Colored pile threads are tied by hand to the warps and the weft beaten in (Nihon Kokugo Daijiten); the exact knot type is not stated in the sources read.
structure.kpsi_note: Not found.
structure.pile_note: All cotton, dyed with plant dyes; hand-woven on an upright loom (Nichigai).
structure.handle: Dense and firm; cotton suits Japan's humid climate (maker).

design.field: Large peonies drawn like crabs ('kani-botan', crab peony), peony scrolls, karakusa scrolls and Chinese-derived medallions.
design.colors: Indigo, brown and green with red and ochre accents (maker).
design.sizes: Small square or rectangular rugs (dantsu are shorter and wider than jūtan).

look_alikes.name: Sakai dantsu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sakai dantsu was modeled on Nabeshima; Meiji-era Sakai export rugs may include jute; Nabeshima dantsu is all cotton.

look_alikes.name: Akō dantsu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Akō dantsu is also all cotton; the crab-peony design marks Nabeshima.

rows.trade_use: 'Nabeshima' or 'Nabeshima dantsu'; one of Japan's 'three great dantsu' with Sakai and Akō.
rows.what_it_tells: A Japanese cotton-pile rug with a crab-peony design points to Nabeshima dantsu of Saga, made from the Meiji era on.
rows.cautions: Japanese makers still weave Nabeshima dantsu; a design alone does not date a piece.

facts.text: Nabeshima dantsu began in Saga in the late 17th century when Koga Seiemon learned the technique from Chinese people (or from a servant taught by foreigners) and taught it to local households.
Japanese dantsu weaving was learned in the Edo period from Chinese techniques at Nagasaki and began with Nabeshima; Sakai and Akō dantsu followed its model.
The Saga (Nabeshima) domain encouraged the craft, made it an official domain product and banned its general sale; the ban was lifted in the Meiji era.
Nabeshima dantsu is made of cotton.
Its signature design is the kani-botan, a crab-like peony, with karakusa scrolls.
Nabeshima dantsu was shown at the Vienna World Exhibition of 1873.
It is designated a Saga Prefecture traditional local product (2003) and a Fukuoka Prefecture specialty craft (1981).

says.text: Mid-Edo period.
Late 17th century.
Genroku era (1688-1704), over 300 years ago.
Learned from Chinese people.
From a servant who learned it from foreigners; the technique traveled from Central Asia via Turkey and China.
Chinese weaving techniques learned in Nagasaki.

rows.name: Sakai dantsu
rows.region: Sakai (Izumi province, near Osaka).
rows.made_by: Town workshops; Holt (1901) mentions child weavers in the producing towns
rows.date_note: Created in 1831 (Tenpō 2) by the Sakai thread merchant Fujimoto Shōzaemon, modeled on Chinese and Nabeshima dantsu; flourished in the early and middle Meiji era, when Japanese cotton and jute rugs were sold in the United States.

structure.knot_note: Hand-knotted (手編込み) dantsu (Nihon Kokugo Daijiten); knot type not stated.
structure.pile_note: Holt (1901) says modern Japanese rugs are made of cotton or jute; Hawley that Japanese pile is largely jute and cotton. Sources do not say which Sakai rugs used jute.

design.field: Chinese-derived and Japanese designs; Holt says Persian designs once copied in Japan were being replaced by purely Japanese designs.
design.colors: Blue, white and sometimes pink (Holt, Japanese rugs generally).

look_alikes.name: Nabeshima dantsu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nabeshima dantsu is all cotton with the crab-peony design; Meiji export rugs from Sakai and elsewhere may have jute pile.

look_alikes.name: japanese-export
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Post-1950 Japanese export rugs are wool on cotton, in Chinese and Savonnerie designs.

rows.trade_use: 'Japanese rug' or 'Japan rug' in American usage around 1900.
rows.what_it_tells: A cotton- or jute-pile Japanese rug in blue and white points to Meiji-Taishō export production, Sakai being the leading center.
rows.cautions: Sources for Sakai's export volumes and decline were not found.

facts.text: Sakai dantsu was created in 1831 by the Sakai thread merchant Fujimoto Shōzaemon, imitating Chinese dantsu and Saga's Nabeshima dantsu.
Sakai dantsu flourished in the early and middle Meiji era.
Sakai and Akō, with Saga, were the Japanese dantsu centers; dantsu was also made in the Sakai area (Senshū) in the 1830s-40s.
Around 1900 Japanese rugs sold in the United States were made of cotton or jute and used in summer homes.
facts.quote: The modern Japanese rugs are made of cotton or jute, and are used extensively in the United States in summer homes. (Holt 1901, p. 91)

rows.name: Akō dantsu
rows.region: Akō, Hyōgo Prefecture (Harima province).
rows.made_by: Founded by Kojima Naka; today the Akō Dantsu preservation and producers' groups
rows.date_note: Founded in 1849 (Kaei 2) by Kojima Naka; flourished from the Meiji to the Taishō era, lapsed in the Shōwa era (after the Second World War), revived from 1999.

structure.knot_note: Not stated in the sources read.
structure.pile_note: All cotton (Heibonsha).

design.field: Strikingly drawn patterns (Hyōgo Prefecture); Chinese-derived motifs.

look_alikes.name: Nabeshima dantsu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are all-cotton dantsu; the crab-peony design marks Nabeshima.

rows.trade_use: 'Akō dantsu'; one of Japan's 'three great dantsu'.
rows.what_it_tells: An all-cotton Japanese dantsu may be Akō work; old pieces date from about 1850 to the 1930s, new ones from 1999 on.
rows.cautions: Production lapsed in the Shōwa era and revived in 1999; new pieces exist.

facts.text: Akō dantsu was founded in 1849 by Kojima Naka.
Akō dantsu flourished from the Meiji to the Taishō era and lapsed in the Shōwa era.
A society to pass on Akō dantsu was formed in 1999, from students of weaving courses taught by Sakaguchi Kirie.
Akō dantsu is a designated traditional craft of Hyōgo Prefecture (designated 30 March 2007).
Akō dantsu, like Nabeshima dantsu, is made entirely of cotton.

rows.name: Agra (jail and workshop carpets)
rows.region: Agra, Uttar Pradesh (in British times the North-Western Provinces), northern India; the Agra jail (today Agra Central Jail) and town workshops.
rows.made_by: In the 19th and early 20th centuries mostly prisoners in the Agra jail, working under British supervision, alongside town workshops; much earlier, Mughal court workshops (late 16th and 17th centuries).
rows.date_note: Carpet weavers were settled at Agra under Akbar (1556-1605), but the large jail-made 'Agra' carpets readers meet date from the mid-19th century into the early 20th. In 1962 Jacobsen wrote that none had been made for about 40 years; Stone (2013) says Agra weaves again and some rugs are still made by prisoners. A start year for the Agra jail looms was not found.

structure.knot_note: No source gives the knot for Agra jail carpets in particular. Mumford (1902) says both the Sehna (asymmetric) and Ghiordes (symmetric) knots were used in Indian carpets of his day, and only a twist of yarn around the warp in the cheapest grades; Jacobsen (1962) says Indian rugs used only the Persian (asymmetric) knot up to 1945.
structure.kpsi_note: No count found for Agra itself. Hawley calls Agra texture looser than Amritsar's (about 200 kpsi); Mumford gives 48 to about 100 kpsi for Allahabad carpets, which he calls similar in almost every respect to Agra's.
structure.pile_note: Wool pile; Mumford says the jails also made cotton-pile carpets as thick and heavy as the wool ones. Hawley calls the pile short, with tufts that blend well.
structure.handle: Very large, thick and heavy (Hawley, Mumford, Holt).
structure.back: Every warp shows equally on the back, i.e. the warps lie level rather than one of each pair being pushed under (Hawley).

design.field: Plain or open fields in one soft color with a small medallion and corners, or all-over small cone (boteh) or pineapple figures; Holt also describes a blue tree design on fawn.
design.border: Often the cone (boteh) set crosswise, as in some Khorasan borders.
design.colors: Fields of blue, green, fawn, olive or tan, often almost one color; later rugs add browns and purples.
design.sizes: 9 x 12 ft and larger, often oversized (Jacobsen; Hawley 'very large').

look_alikes.name: Amritsar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amritsar rugs have one warp of each pair pushed under the other and a closer weave (Hawley: about 200 kpsi); Agra warps show equally on the back and the weave is looser.

look_alikes.name: Lahore (Mughal workshop and jail carpets)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both were jail-made. Hawley gives Lahore the doubled-under warp of Amritsar and lighter shades; Agra warps lie level.

rows.trade_use: Jacobsen (1962) says dealers gave the name Agra to almost any old oversized estate rug in these soft colors when they did not know where it was made.
rows.what_it_tells: A very large, heavy carpet on a cotton foundation, with level warps and a soft, nearly single-color field, is consistent with Indian jail or workshop production of about 1850-1920, which British-era books tie above all to Agra.
rows.cautions: The name was used loosely for old, oversized Indian-looking carpets. A US law of 1890 barred convict-made goods from import (Tariff Act of 1890, sec. 51); Holt (1901) says more Agra rugs would have been imported but for that law, and Mumford (1902) says the prison output went mainly to England. Rugs sold as 'Agra' today are a different, current production.

facts.text: Akbar's chronicler Abul Fazl wrote that carpet weavers of all kinds had settled in every town, especially Agra, Fatehpur and Lahore.
facts.quote: All kinds of carpet-weavers have settled here, and drive a flourishing trade.

facts.text: Carpet workshops were working in Agra by 1619.
In the 19th century carpets were woven by convicts in the Agra jail.
facts.quote: Almost within sight of the minarets of the Taj Mahal are prison walls where convicts of Agra ploddingly weave.

facts.text: Two early-1900s books single out the Agra jail as the source of the best jail-made carpets.
facts.quote: The best jail-made carpets are manufactured at Agra

facts.text: Some rugs are still woven by prisoners of the Agra Central Jail, and Agra has an active carpet industry again.
After the 1947 partition many Muslim weavers left Agra for Pakistan.
Agra jail carpets mostly have a cotton foundation (warp and weft cotton, wool pile).
On the back of an Agra carpet each warp shows equally, and the weave is looser than Amritsar's.
Agra carpets are very large and heavy; Jacobsen says always 9 x 12 ft or larger, usually oversized.
Vincent Robinson explained the Agra looms by an early demand for carpets too large to be carried in by camels or elephants.
Fields were often nearly one soft color (blue, green, fawn; Jacobsen adds olive and tan); Mumford says browns and purples came in later.
The Agra jail also made cotton-pile carpets, as thick and heavy as the woollen ones.
US law barred convict-made goods from import from 1890; books of 1901-1905 say this kept Indian jail carpets out of the American market.
facts.quote: there is now a United States law prohibiting the importation of goods made in jail.

facts.text: Jacobsen (1962) wrote that no Agra rugs had been made in the previous 40 years and that the name was given to almost any old estate rug in these colors of unknown origin.

says.text: None made in the last 40 years (i.e. none since about 1920).
Agra has an active carpet industry again and some rugs are woven by prisoners of the Agra Central Jail.
Both Sehna and Ghiordes knots are used in Indian carpets, and a mere twist in cheap grades.
Only the Persian (asymmetric) knot was used in Indian rugs up to 1945.

rows.name: Lahore (Mughal workshop and jail carpets)
rows.region: Lahore, Punjab. Since the 1947 partition Lahore is in Pakistan.
rows.made_by: Mughal imperial workshops in the 17th century; in the 19th century prisoners in Lahore's central, district and female jails and a 'school of industry'; later private factories, some run by the same foreign firms as at Amritsar.
rows.date_note: The imperial workshop dates from about 1580 and the famous Girdlers' carpet from 1634, but those are museum pieces. Jail and factory carpets readers may own date from the 19th century to partition in 1947; after that, Lahore rugs are Pakistani production (see the Pakistan rows).

structure.knot_note: Hawley does not name the knot for Lahore but says the weave is like Amritsar's, for which he gives the Sehna (asymmetric) knot, with one warp of each knot doubled under the other.
structure.kpsi_note: Holt (1901): 40 to 100 knots per square inch. Mumford (1902) says the revived non-jail weaving seldom has more than 40. Hawley: fewer knots than Amritsar (about 200).
structure.pile_note: Both woollen and cotton carpets were made in the jails (Mumford, Holt, Hawley).
structure.sides: Finish like Amritsar's (Hawley: sides and ends resemble Amritsar products; Amritsar sides are overcast).
structure.back: One warp of each knot doubled under the other, as at Amritsar (Hawley).

design.field: Persian designs; Mumford describes an all-over pear (boteh) field arranged as in Herat or Saraband rugs.
design.border: Geometric figures in the guard stripes; Mumford: a border with 'Greek' (key-like) elements.
design.colors: Lighter shades than Amritsar.

look_alikes.name: Amritsar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same firms and similar finish; Lahore rugs come in lighter shades with fewer knots per inch.

look_alikes.name: Agra (jail and workshop carpets)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Agra warps lie level on the back; Lahore has one warp of each pair doubled under.

rows.trade_use: Since 1947 'Lahore' on a rug is a Pakistani origin; Stone says current Lahore production is mostly in Turkmen designs.
rows.what_it_tells: A Lahore attribution points to British-era Punjab jail or factory weaving (19th century to 1947) or, for modern rugs, to Pakistani export production.
rows.cautions: Seventeenth-century 'Lahore' carpets are court pieces in museums, not the jail or factory rugs found in homes. Old books' 'Lahore' covers jail work in wool and cotton of widely varying quality.

facts.text: Akbar's imperial carpet workshop was set up at Lahore around 1580, and Akbar's chronicler names Lahore among the towns where carpet weavers settled.
The Girdlers' Company carpet, dated 1634, was woven in the royal workshop at Lahore; it is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum.
Lahore carpets were among the first Indian carpets to reach England, through the East India Company in the 17th century; an agent wrote in 1617 of buying 30 fine Lahore carpets at Agra.
In the 19th century carpets were woven in Lahore's jails; Mumford counts a central jail of up to 2,000 prisoners plus district and female jails, a 'thug jail' and a school of industry.
facts.quote: The central jail there has held as many as two thousand prisoners, and in addition there are district and female jails, a thug jail and a 'school of industry,'

facts.text: Lahore jails made both woollen and cotton carpets.
Prison weaving was also set up in Karachi's jails; the Pakistani trade authority reproduces an 1873 photograph of carpet weavers in Karachi jail.
Later a factory system followed, and some foreign firms ran weaving works in both Lahore and Amritsar, so their products resemble each other.
Lahore rugs come in lighter shades and with fewer knots than Amritsar rugs, and often have geometric figures in the guard borders.
Holt gives Lahore jail rugs 40 to 100 knots per square inch.
Lahore has been in Pakistan since the 1947 partition; Stone says its current production is mainly rugs in Turkmen designs.

says.text: 40 to 100 knots per square inch (jail rugs).
Revived weaving outside the jails seldom exceeds 40 knots per square inch.

rows.name: Amritsar
rows.region: Amritsar, Punjab, India (near the Pakistan border).
rows.made_by: Men and boys, many of them Kashmiri, in large factories working for or owned by English and American firms; patterns read aloud from a written Kashmiri script (talim).
rows.date_note: Stone dates the start to about 1860; Hawley to after a change in shawl fashion about 1870. The rugs most readers meet were woven for Western firms from the 1880s to the 1930s. Stone says production fell in the 1920s depression and at partition (1947) and has since recovered.

structure.knot_note: Hawley: Sehna (asymmetric) knot. Stone: asymmetric.
structure.kpsi_note: Hawley: frequently 200 per square inch. Mumford: the same patterns made in every grade from 3 x 3 (9) to 12 x 12 (144) per inch, and the pashmina grade up to 14 x 14 (196). Stone: contemporary rugs about 200-400.
structure.wefts_note: Hawley: the wefts are pressed down very firmly. Langton (quoting Scidmore) describes looms strung with cotton warp; weft material for Amritsar specifically is not given (Langton says Indian rugs generally have cotton warp and weft).
structure.pile_note: Short pile (Hawley). The best grade, 'pushmina', uses pashm, the fine under-wool, and sometimes a silk warp (Mumford; Holt).
structure.sides: Overcast (Hawley).
structure.ends: As a rule a cotton web (plain-woven band) at the lower end and a web with fringe at the upper end (Hawley); Mumford says lower grades have a heavy, crude overcasting instead of fringes.
structure.back: One warp of each knot doubled under the other, as in Bijar rugs (Hawley).

design.field: Copies of Persian designs (Mumford: the Feraghan is a favorite), of European carpets and of Indian or Persian antiques; Stone says early production copied Turkmen designs and current rugs are floral Persian.

look_alikes.name: Lahore (Mughal workshop and jail carpets)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lahore rugs are lighter in color and less finely knotted.

look_alikes.name: Agra (jail and workshop carpets)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Agra warps lie level and the weave is looser.

rows.trade_use: Jacobsen (1962) says he had never seen a rug sold under the name Amritsar; Amritsar rugs went out under importers' trade names.
rows.what_it_tells: A firmly woven Indian rug with depressed warps, overcast sides and a Persian design is consistent with Punjab factory production for Western importers, of which Amritsar was the leading center from about 1880 to 1930.
rows.cautions: Hawley says Amritsar rugs in modern Persian patterns were often mistaken for Kermanshah or Sultanabad rugs. Grades ranged from very coarse to fine, so the name says little about quality.

facts.text: Amritsar's rug industry grew out of Kashmiri shawl weaving: shawl weavers who had come to Amritsar turned to rugs when shawl demand fell.
English and American firms ran large rug factories at Amritsar around 1900.
At Amritsar the pattern was written in a Kashmiri script and read aloud knot by knot to rows of boy weavers; Stone calls such written instructions a talim, used in Kashmir and Pakistan.
facts.quote: read off the directions for the pattern from pages of Kashmiri cipher

facts.text: Fine Amritsar rugs run about 200 asymmetric knots per square inch or more (Hawley: frequently 200; Stone: contemporary 200-400).
Amritsar rugs have one warp of each knot doubled under the other, firmly packed wefts, short pile and overcast sides.
Around 1900 Amritsar firms made the same patterns in every grade from 3 x 3 to 12 x 12 knots per inch; the best 'pushmina' grade reached 14 x 14 and sometimes had a silk warp.
'Pushmina' (pashmina) was a maker's grade name for rugs woven of pashm, the fine under-wool.
Hawley says US demand for Amritsar rugs began with the Indian rug exhibit at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.
Production declined in the 1920s depression and at partition, and has since recovered.
Early Amritsar production copied Turkmen designs; current rugs are floral, after Persian models.

says.text: Rug manufacturing began in Amritsar in about 1860, using unemployed shawl weavers.
Kashmiris settled in Amritsar about 1840 and made shawls until a change of fashion about 1870, when many turned to rug weaving.
Probably 5,000 men and boys in the Amritsar carpet industry, counting wool handlers and dyers.
Some twenty thousand men and boys at the looms (1913 text).

rows.name: Mirzapur and Bhadohi (the Uttar Pradesh carpet belt)
rows.region: Mirzapur and Bhadohi, near Varanasi (Benares), Uttar Pradesh. The district boundaries of the Bhadohi GI were not found.
rows.made_by: Mostly home (cottage) looms, plus factories; in the 1950s-60s large British and American import houses ran factories with their own dye works and yarn mills. In the 19th century some jail production.
rows.date_note: Mirzapur had a carpet industry before 1850; Stone says that since about 1900 it has been the source of a very large volume of coarsely woven rugs. Most rugs readers meet are post-1950 export production, which continues.

structure.knot_note: Stone (Mirzapur and Bhadohi entries).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Bhadohi rugs 30-225 kpsi; his Uttar Pradesh entry gives most contemporary rugs about 120-245. Tags use the local 'a/b' notation (e.g. 5/40, 9/60), which must be converted (see knot counts).
structure.wefts_note: Stone's India entry: contemporary Indian rugs are woven on a cotton foundation with double wefts.
structure.pile_note: Cheaper grades may mix jute into the pile (Jacobsen; Holt notes vegetable fiber in Mirzapur rugs c.1900). Rugs are often sculptured (pile cut lower along design outlines).

design.field: Persian floral copies, Chinese designs and Aubusson/Savonnerie designs; around 1900 Mumford describes round floral figures in rows on a cream or pale yellow ground.
design.colors: Around 1900, dark red figures on pale yellow or cream. Later, pastels for the Savonnerie types.

look_alikes.name: Indian rugs in Savonnerie, Aubusson and Chinese designs (Indo-Savonnerie, carved one-color rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Many post-war Indo-Savonnerie and Chinese-design rugs were themselves woven in the Mirzapur district.

rows.trade_use: The area's rugs are sold under design names ('Indo-Kashan', 'Indo-Tabriz') and importers' trade names more often than as 'Mirzapur' or 'Bhadohi'.
rows.what_it_tells: A cotton-foundation Indian rug with a Persian, Chinese or French design and an 'a/b' quality number on the tag is consistent with Uttar Pradesh export production, most likely after 1950.
rows.cautions: Holt (1901) says Mirzapur rugs were sometimes sold as Turkish. Quality runs from very coarse to fine. The GI is a protected name for rugs from the registered area; a rug without a GI mark is not thereby from elsewhere.

facts.text: Mirzapur was a notable carpet center before the mid-19th century; its quality fell afterward, which Mumford and Hawley blame on prison labor and cheap trading.
Since about 1900 Mirzapur has turned out a very large volume of coarsely woven rugs.

Uttar Pradesh is India's largest rug-producing area, with Bhadohi and Mirzapur as main centers; in 1960 the Mirzapur area was described as the world's largest hand-knotted rug industry, with about 60,000 home weavers.
In the 1950s-60s large import houses wove Savonnerie-design rugs in Mirzapur district factories with their own dye plants and yarn mills, while cheaper grades were woven in cottages.
'Hand Made Carpet of Bhadohi' is a registered Indian Geographical Indication (application no. 148, registered in the year April 2010-March 2011).
Bhadohi rugs are mostly copies of Persian floral designs, woven with the asymmetric knot on a cotton foundation at about 30-225 knots per square inch.
Mirzapur rugs are often sculptured (carved), and hand-carved borders were common on Indian export rugs from the 1950s.
Around 1900 the wool for Mirzapur carpets came mainly from western Rajputana and was treated with lime for brilliancy.
Holt (1901) says Mirzapur rugs were sometimes wrongly sold as Turkish, which they somewhat resemble.

says.text: Bhadohi rugs: 30-225 knots per square inch (p.47).
Uttar Pradesh rugs: mostly about 120-245 knots per square inch (p.295).

rows.name: Jaipur
rows.region: Jaipur, Rajasthan (the old Rajputana), with Bikaner and Ajmer nearby.
rows.made_by: In the 19th century prisoners in the Jaipur jail and students of the school of art; today export workshops and home looms.
rows.date_note: Stone dates Jaipur prison weaving from the mid-19th century. Jaipur weaving continues.

structure.knot_note: Stone: contemporary rugs use the asymmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: the finer contemporary Jaipur rugs about 200; his Rajasthan entry gives 144-225.
structure.wefts_note: Stone: single or double wefts; the single-wefted rugs are finer.

design.field: Persian-derived designs with vines, flowers, cypress trees and animals; prison rugs copied Mughal designs.
design.colors: Ivory, red or blue fields (Holt; Mumford: dark red, blue or ivory white).

rows.what_it_tells: A Rajasthan rug in a Persian or Mughal-style floral design with animals and cypress trees fits the Jaipur tradition; modern Jaipur rugs are general export production.
rows.cautions: Seventeenth-century Mughal carpets kept in the Jaipur palace (now the Jaipur museum) are a separate, classical group and are not what 'Jaipur rug' means in the trade.

facts.text: Some of the finest surviving Mughal carpets are in the Maharaja's palace (now museum) collection at Jaipur.
Rug weaving in the Jaipur prison began in the mid-19th century, copying Mughal designs.
Holt (1901) says Jaipur rugs were generally made in the schools of art.
Jaipur rugs follow Persian drawing, with vines, flowers, cypress trees and animals.
Fields are usually red, blue or ivory.
Contemporary Jaipur rugs use the asymmetric knot on a cotton foundation, single- or double-wefted; the finer ones have about 200 knots per square inch.

says.text: Rug weaving in prisons began in Jaipur in the middle of the 19th century.
Jaipur rugs are generally made in the schools of art.

rows.name: Kashmir (Srinagar) pile rugs, wool and silk
other_names: Cashmere (caution: old books use this for Soumak)
rows.region: Srinagar and the Kashmir valley (Jammu and Kashmir); weaving has spread from Srinagar to rural areas (CEPC).
rows.made_by: Town workshops and home looms working from written talim instructions.
rows.date_note: Stone says Kashmir pile rugs rose to prominence in the mid-19th century, and that rug production in Srinagar became significant in the late 19th century. Most rugs readers meet are 20th-century and later.

structure.knot_note: Stone: most contemporary Kashmir rugs are jufti-knotted (each knot over more than two warps) with design outlines in regular knots. The knot type (asymmetric) for Kashmir is our inference from Stone's general India entry, not stated in his Kashmir entry.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: the better contemporary rugs about 400-480. Holt (1901) saw a Kashmir factory reproduction at 16 x 16 per inch (256).
structure.wefts_note: Stone: double-wefted with offset warps.
structure.pile_note: Wool and silk pile; Stone says the finest contemporary Srinagar rugs are all silk or part wool, part silk. Old books praise the soft, silky Kashmir wool (Hawley, Holt).

design.field: Copies of early Persian carpets; some pictorial rugs with Hindu deities; Khamariah rugs after Isfahan models.
design.border: Old Kashmir carpets had borders hard to tell from the field (Hawley; Mumford quoting Birdwood).

look_alikes.name: Kashmir chain-stitch rugs (and gabba)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chain-stitch rugs are embroidered on cloth and have no pile; turn the rug over to see rows of stitches through a fabric.

rows.trade_use: 'Kashmir' and 'Srinagar' are used for silk and fine wool rugs from the valley.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted Indian rug in silk or very soft wool with a classical Persian design is consistent with Kashmir (Srinagar) workshop weaving, mostly 20th century or later.
rows.cautions: In older American books and the early trade, 'Kashmir' or 'Cashmere' rugs meant Caucasian Soumak flatweaves, not rugs from Kashmir. 'Jewel of Kashmir' was a 1950s-60s trade name for flat-stitch Aubusson-style rugs. Silk-looking Kashmir rugs may also be made of viscose (see the art silk row).

facts.text: Kashmir was famous for shawls; as shawl weaving declined, its wool and weavers turned to rugs.
Kashmir pile rugs rose to prominence in the mid-19th century; rug production in Srinagar became significant in the late 19th century.
Writers around 1900-1913 describe Srinagar rugs as woven of very soft, silky wool, many with vegetable or natural dyes.

Contemporary Kashmir rugs are mostly on a cotton foundation, double-wefted with offset warps; the better ones have about 400-480 knots per square inch, and most are jufti-knotted with outlines in regular knots.
Srinagar is the source of the finest contemporary Kashmir rugs, all silk or part wool and part silk.
'Kashmiri Hand Knotted Carpet' is a registered Indian Geographical Indication (application no. 527, registered April 2016-March 2017).
Kashmiri weavers work from a written talim that gives the colors knot by knot; the method went with Kashmiri weavers to Amritsar.
A training program of the All India Handicrafts Board spread carpet weaving from Srinagar to rural areas; CEPC gives about 48,000 workers by the end of the 1980s.
In older books 'Kashmir' or 'Cashmere' rugs are Caucasian Soumak (Shemakha) flatweaves, a dealers' name with no link to Kashmir.
Holt saw a Kashmir factory reproduction of a famous Persian rug woven at 16 x 16 knots to the inch.

rows.name: Kashmir chain-stitch rugs (and gabba)
rows.region: Kashmir (Jammu and Kashmir).
rows.made_by: Kashmiri embroiderers (commercial production).
rows.date_note: No source read gives a start date. Stone (2013) describes current commercial production in India; 'Kashmir Chain Stitch', 'Kashmir Crewel' and 'Gabba' were registered as Indian GIs in April 2024-March 2025.

structure.knot_note: Not knotted or woven: the pattern is embroidered in chain stitch (rows of interlocking loops) onto a cloth ground. Gabba rugs are appliquéd and embroidered (Stone).
structure.kpsi_note: No knot count applies.
structure.pile_note: No pile; the surface is covered with rows of chain stitches.
structure.back: The back shows the stitches passing through a cloth ground, not knots.

look_alikes.name: Kashmir (Srinagar) pile rugs, wool and silk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Pile rugs have tufts you can part down to knots; chain-stitch rugs have a flat stitched surface on a cloth.

look_alikes.name: Namda (felt rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A namda's ground is felt, not woven cloth.

rows.what_it_tells: A flat rug whose design is made of rows of looped stitches on cloth is an embroidered rug, of the kind made commercially in Kashmir.
rows.cautions: Jacobsen (1962) describes a different flat 'Jewel of Kashmir' rug of the 1950s-60s, a flat-stitch Aubusson-style rug like needlepoint, made in Kashmir and India for a British firm; do not confuse the two.

facts.text: Rugs embroidered with chain stitch are made commercially in India.
Gabba are appliquéd and embroidered rugs of Kashmir; 'Gabba' is a registered Indian Geographical Indication (application no. 902, registered April 2024-March 2025).
'Kashmir Chain Stitch' (application no. 1046) and 'Kashmir Crewel' (application no. 1047) were registered as Indian Geographical Indications in April 2024-March 2025.
In the 1950s-60s a British firm sold flat-stitch Aubusson-design rugs made in Kashmir and India under the trade name 'Jewel of Kashmir'.

rows.name: Namda (felt rugs)
rows.region: Kashmir is the registered GI; Stone calls namda a felt carpet of India generally.
rows.made_by: Felt makers.
rows.date_note: No dating source found. 'Kashmir Namda' was registered as an Indian GI in April 2024-March 2025.

structure.knot_note: Felt, not woven: wool fibers are matted together. Designs are appliquéd or laid in colored wool during felting (Stone).
structure.pile_note: No pile and no warp or weft.
structure.back: Felt on both faces; no threads or knots.

look_alikes.name: Kashmir chain-stitch rugs (and gabba)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chain-stitch rugs are embroidered on woven cloth; a namda is felt throughout.

rows.what_it_tells: A rug of matted wool felt with colored wool or appliqué designs is a namda-type felt rug.
rows.cautions: Embroidered namdas exist (embroidery on a felt ground), so stitches on top do not rule out a namda; look at the ground.

facts.text: A namda (numdah) is a felt carpet of India, its designs appliquéd or made with colored wool during felting.
'Kashmir Namda' is a registered Indian Geographical Indication (application no. 868, registered April 2024-March 2025).

rows.name: 'Indo-' trade names (Indo-Tabriz, Indo-Heriz, Indo-Kashan, Indo-Mahal, Indo-Gabbeh and older Indo-Sarouk, Indo-Kirman)
rows.region: Mainly Uttar Pradesh (Bhadohi-Mirzapur), also Jaipur, Agra, Amritsar and elsewhere.
rows.made_by: Indian export workshops and home looms working to importers' designs.
rows.date_note: Holt (1901) already reports importers giving their own names to Indian qualities. Jacobsen dates Indo-Sarouk, Indo-Kirman, Indo-Tabriz and similar names to about 1920-1945. The current 'Indo-' names continue the habit.

structure.knot_note: Stone: contemporary Indian rugs use asymmetric knots on a cotton foundation with double wefts.
structure.kpsi_note: Depends wholly on the quality ordered; Stone's common Indian qualities 4/30 to 12/60 convert to about 30-180 kpsi and Uttar Pradesh rugs run about 120-245.

design.field: The design of the Persian (or other) type in the name.

look_alikes.name: Mirzapur and Bhadohi (the Uttar Pradesh carpet belt)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Most 'Indo-' rugs are themselves Uttar Pradesh production.

rows.trade_use: 'Indo-' plus a Persian town name = woven in India in that town's design: an Indo-Kashan is an Indian rug in a Kashan design.
rows.what_it_tells: The name says where the design comes from, not where the rug was made: an 'Indo-' rug was woven in India.
rows.cautions: The names say nothing about quality, which varies widely. 'Indo-Persian' (or 'Indo-Herat') in museum writing means a 16th-17th century classical group of disputed origin, a different thing entirely. Jacobsen notes that a trade name could change meaning: 'Kandahar' meant a Persian-design Indian rug about 1930 and a Savonnerie-design one in 1960. The modern names Indo-Heriz, Indo-Kashan, Indo-Mahal and Indo-Gabbeh were not found in any source read this pass.

facts.text: The prefix 'Indo-' means the rug was woven in India in a design typical of some other region.
Around 1900 importers named Indian rugs by quality and the name did not show where the rug was woven.
facts.quote: the name borne by a rug does not necessarily indicate the district in which it was woven.

facts.text: From about 1920 to 1940 the main Indian types imported to the US were the Indo-Sarouk, Indo-Kirman, Kandahar and Laristan, brought in by two large New York firms.

The Indo-Sarouk was made in limited numbers about 1925-1938, mostly 9 x 12 ft with rose fields, and stopped by World War II; the Indo-Kirman stopped about 1945; no Indo-Tabriz, Indo-Feraghan or Indo-Ispahan was made after World War II.
Indian rugs in modern Persian patterns were often mistaken for Kermanshah or Sultanabad (Persian) rugs.
'Indo-Mir' rugs, woven mainly in Uttar Pradesh, have an all-over field of small botehs after Serabend (Mir) designs.
In museum writing, 'Indo-Persian' or 'Indo-Herat' names a 16th-17th century group of classical carpets attributed by different scholars to India, Herat or Isfahan.

says.text: p.74: 'This rug ceased being made about 1944.'
p.214: 'Only limited numbers were made prior to that time, in the period 1925-1938.'

rows.name: Indian rugs in Savonnerie, Aubusson and Chinese designs (Indo-Savonnerie, carved one-color rugs)
rows.region: Mainly the Mirzapur district factories and cottages.
rows.made_by: Factories of large British and American import houses and cottage weavers working to set designs.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen (1962) says these replaced the Persian-design Indian types after World War II; Stone says contemporary Indian rugs still copy Chinese, Aubusson and Savonnerie designs.

structure.knot_note: Stone: contemporary Indian rugs use the asymmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Many qualities, from the cheapest with jute mixed in to the heavy Kandahar and Chinda grades (Jacobsen).
structure.pile_note: Thick pile, often carved (sculptured) along the design or borders; plain one-color rugs with carved borders were common (Jacobsen; Stone).

design.field: French Savonnerie and Aubusson designs in pastels, or Chinese designs, often an open field with a floral spray in two or four corners; also plain one-color rugs with carved borders.
design.colors: Light pastels: ivory, rose, beige, soft green, light blue.
design.sizes: Standard US sizes from 5 x 3 to 12 x 20 ft; runners from 1959.

look_alikes.name: Japanese hand-made rugs (Imperial, Fuigi Royal, Peking)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Japan wove similar Chinese and Savonnerie-design rugs in the 1950s-60s ('Imperial', 'Peking'); the label or the importer's tag is the surest guide.

rows.trade_use: Sold under importers' trade names (Kandahar, Kalabar, Chinda, Bengali, Sirdar) and as 'Indo-Savonnerie' or 'Indo-Aubusson'.
rows.what_it_tells: A hand-knotted pastel rug in a French or Chinese design with carved pile and an Indian tag is consistent with Indian export production from 1945 onward.
rows.cautions: 'Indo-Aubusson' was a trade name for a thick pile rug, though a true Aubusson is flat-woven. Trade names were reused for different rugs over time. Carving alone does not mean Chinese.

facts.text: After World War II Indian export rugs switched to light pastel French Savonnerie and Aubusson designs, Chinese designs, and plain one-color rugs with hand-carved borders.
Sculpting (cutting the pile lower along design lines) is common in 20th-century Chinese rugs and in Indian copies of them.
In 1962 the leading trade names for these Indian rugs included Chinda, Kandahar, Kalabar, Indo-Aubusson, Bengali and Sirdar.
About 1930 'Kandahar' named a different Indian rug, in a Persian Mina Khani design on a rose field; the same firm later used the name for its best Savonnerie-design quality.
Some cheaper Indian rugs mixed jute or other plant fiber with the wool.
By 1969 tags on Indian rugs had to state the pile fiber content, such as 100% wool or 70% wool, 30% jute.

rows.name: Dhurrie (Indian cotton flatweave)
rows.region: Throughout India; registered GIs at Agra and Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh), Navalgund (Karnataka) and Warangal (Telangana).
rows.made_by: Village and town weavers; from about 1880 to 1920 also prisoners in Indian jails.
rows.date_note: Dhurries are an old Indian craft (Kendrick: the usual floor covering before Akbar). Those readers meet are mostly from the late 19th century on, including jail dhurries of about 1880-1920.

structure.knot_note: No pile. Stone: virtually every kilim structure is used: slit tapestry, interlocked and dovetailed wefts, eccentric wefts.
structure.pile_note: Pileless cotton (Hawley, Holt, Stone).
structure.ends: Some end in a fringe (Holt).

design.field: Stripes (blue, red, black; blue and white; Holt adds blue, brown or gray with narrow yellow and red lines) and simple geometric figures; some with prayer niches (saffs).
design.sizes: Some square; darbar dhurries are very large.

rows.what_it_tells: A flat, pileless cotton rug with stripes or simple geometric designs is consistent with an Indian dhurrie.
rows.cautions: Wool flatweaves from elsewhere (kilims) look similar; a dhurrie is typically cotton. Jail dhurries can be very fine.

facts.text: A dhurrie is a pileless (flat-woven) cotton rug of India.
facts.quote: They are pileless cotton fabrics, that may represent an indigenous craft old as the Aryan migrations.

facts.text: Dhurrie designs are mostly stripes, sometimes with simple geometric figures.
Between about 1880 and 1920 dhurries were woven in Indian prisons, many to the highest standards; Hawley says Multan's dari were made almost exclusively in the jails.
In the 19th century Calcutta jail served as a collection center for rugs and dhurries woven in other Indian jails.
Dhurries are also called satrangi and jamkhani; a darbar is a very large dhurrie for public buildings.
Holt names Agra, Cawnpore, Delhi, Lucknow and the Bombay area as main dhurrie centers.
Four dhurrie GIs are registered in India: Navalgund Durries (application 61, 2007-08), Agra Durrie (233, 2012-13), Mirzapur Handmade Dari (458, 2014-15) and Warangal Durries (523, 2017-18).

rows.name: Hand-tufted rugs (India, China and elsewhere)
other_names: hooked (Jacobsen's word for Hong Kong ones)
rows.country: India (also China, Hong Kong, the Philippines and others)
rows.region: Indian carpet centers (CEPC lists hand-tufted among Indian products); Stone names China and the Philippines.
rows.made_by: Workshop operators with hand-held tufting guns.
rows.date_note: The earliest dated mention found is Jacobsen (1969) on Hong Kong rugs with plastic-covered backs; when Indian hand-tufting began was not found.

structure.knot_note: No knots: yarn is shot through a backing cloth with a tufting gun, held by latex glue.
structure.kpsi_note: No knot count applies.
structure.pile_note: Cut or loop pile (CEPC).
structure.sides: Usually bound; see checks.
structure.ends: Fringe, if any, is added; see checks.
structure.back: Latex coat over the tufts, then a second backing cloth glued on (often a third cloth in finishing); the back looks like plain cloth with no knots visible (Stone; CEPC).

look_alikes.name: Mirzapur and Bhadohi (the Uttar Pradesh carpet belt)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hand-knotted rugs show the pattern and individual knots on the back; tufted rugs have a cloth back glued over latex.

rows.trade_use: 'Hand-tufted' on a label means gun-tufted and glued, not hand-knotted.
rows.what_it_tells: A cloth-covered back with a latex smell or rubbery layer points to a tufted rug, most likely made after the 1960s.
rows.cautions: Older British trade writing used 'hand-tufted' to mean hand-knotted (see checks); on modern labels it means gun-tufted.

facts.text: Tufted rugs are made by inserting wool or synthetic yarn into a backing cloth by hand or machine, coating the back with latex and adding a further fabric backing.
Tufted pile can be cut or looped.
In 1969 Jacobsen warned of Hong Kong rugs 'hooked' with thick wool yarn whose backs were covered with plastic, being bought as real oriental rugs.
Indian exporters make hand-tufted as well as hand-knotted carpets.
Stone names China and the Philippines as commercial producers of tufted rugs.

rows.name: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs (incl. Jaldar and Mori)
rows.region: Lahore, Karachi, Hyderabad, Peshawar; TDAP lists many centers incl. Lahore, Gujranwala, Multan, Karachi, Hyderabad, Peshawar and areas around Quetta.
rows.made_by: Factory and cottage weavers; TDAP credits Afghans as the master weavers of Jaldar rugs.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen dates the first Mori rugs to about 1955 and large-scale Pakistani export weaving to about 1957; TDAP says the industry was neglected for two decades after 1947 and boomed in the late 1970s and 1980s. Still made.

structure.knot_note: Sources disagree: Stone says Pakistani rugs use the asymmetric knot; TDAP calls Jaldars symmetric-knotted, and a Pakistani dealer says the symmetric knot is what Pakistanis call the 'single knot'.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Pakistani rugs 40-350. TDAP: Bokhara average about 200, Yomud Bokhara 250-550, Jaldar 100-250. Jacobsen: Mori 250-400, 'over 300'. Tag notation like 16/18 or 11/22 (knots per inch across / along).
structure.wefts_note: Stone: the cheapest grades may have jute wefts.
structure.pile_note: Local wool, or blended with New Zealand or Australian wool for finer grades (Stone); Jacobsen's 1950s Mori rugs had a pile of fine cashmere wool with a velvety look.

design.field: Rows of Turkmen-style guls (octagons), mostly after Tekke rugs; Jaldar has columns or lattices of diamond guls.
design.colors: Mostly reds (TDAP: red the most popular); Mori fields wine, burgundy, ivory or light tan.
design.sizes: Mori mostly about 6 x 4 ft, some to 9 x 12 ft.

look_alikes.name: Pak-Persian rugs (Pakistani rugs in Persian designs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Pak-Persian rugs copy Persian floral designs and have offset warps; Bokharas have gul designs and level warps.

rows.trade_use: 'Bokhara' (and 'Royal', 'Princess') in the trade means a Turkmen gul design, not the city of Bukhara; Pakistani Bokharas are the biggest group of modern rugs sold under that name.
rows.what_it_tells: A finely knotted modern rug with rows of Turkmen guls, a cotton foundation and level warps is consistent with Pakistani 'Bokhara' production after about 1955.
rows.cautions: Old Turkmen tribal rugs share the design but have wool foundations and different colors and structure (see the Turkmen rows). Indian and Iranian workshops also make 'Bokharas'. The Pakistani trade words 'single' and 'double' are used inconsistently (see knot counts).

facts.text: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs are modern rugs in Turkmen gul designs, woven for export.
'Bokhara' is a trade name for rugs in Turkmen designs; Turkmen rugs are not from the city of Bukhara.
Virtually all Pakistani pile rugs are woven for export (TDAP: more than 99%).
Pakistan's main weaving centers include Lahore, Karachi, Hyderabad and Peshawar.
Mori rugs, very finely woven Pakistani rugs in Tekke designs with a cashmere-wool pile, appeared in the London market about 1955; Jacobsen imported the first to America in 1960.
Jaldar is a Pakistani design of columns or lattices of diamonds; TDAP says Jaldar guls are angular diamonds where Bokhara guls are rounded.
TDAP gives Pakistani Bokharas an average of about 200 knots per square inch, Yomud Bokharas 250-550 and Jaldars 100-250.
Where Pakistani designs copy Turkmen 'Bokhara' models the warps are not offset; where they copy Persian models they are.
TDAP groups Bokhara, Jaldar and 'Silk Touch' as Pakistan's 'single knot' qualities.

'Royal Bokhara' is a trade term of indefinite meaning for a supposedly superior Turkmen-design rug, sometimes meaning Tekke main carpets; TDAP divides Pakistani Tekke Bokharas into 'Royal' and 'Princess'.
A Pakistani dealer describes Bokhara pile as New Zealand worsted blended with local Pakistani wool, on a cotton base, with synthetic dyes.

says.text: Rugs of Pakistan are woven on a cotton foundation with the asymmetric knot (p.211).
Jaldar rugs are symmetrical-knotted (p.9).
Dealer text: Bokharas use the symmetrical knot, which Pakistanis call the 'single knot'.
Mori rugs appeared about 1955 (p.262); large-scale Pakistani export weaving began about 1957 (p.90).
After independence the craft was neglected for more than two decades; the breakthrough came in the 1970s, with a boom in the late 1970s and 1980s.

rows.name: Pak-Persian rugs (Pakistani rugs in Persian designs)
rows.region: Pakistani export centers (Lahore and others).
rows.made_by: Factory and cottage weavers.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen saw Pakistani rugs in Tabriz designs in London from about 1957; Stone (2013) calls Persian copies a recent addition to Pakistan's Turkmen-design output. Still made.

structure.knot_note: Stone: asymmetric knot; offset warps where Persian models are copied.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone's range for Pakistani rugs; no separate figure for Pak-Persian found.
structure.pile_note: Local wool, or blended with New Zealand or Australian wool for finer grades (Stone).

design.field: Persian city designs: Tabriz and Kirman/Yazd designs in Jacobsen's day; Persian floral designs generally.
design.sizes: About 4 x 7, 5 x 8 and 7 x 10 ft in 1960-62.

look_alikes.name: Pakistani 'Bokhara' rugs (incl. Jaldar and Mori)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bokharas have Turkmen gul designs and level warps.

rows.trade_use: TDAP: the 'double knot' qualities are 'popularly known as Pak-Persian'.
rows.what_it_tells: A rug in a Persian city design with a Pakistani label or Pakistani-style tag notation is consistent with Pak-Persian production, 1957 or later.
rows.cautions: Jacobsen says these could be mistaken for Persian Tabriz rugs even by dealers. 'Double' on a Pakistani tag can mean this knot/quality group or a count with twice as many rows as knots across (see knot counts).

facts.text: Pakistan weaves rugs in Persian designs; the trade calls them Pak-Persian.
Jacobsen describes Pakistani rugs in Tabriz designs, first woven in West Pakistan about 1957, in the London market by 1960; none had reached the US by 1962.
Where Pakistani rugs copy Persian models, the warps are offset.
TDAP calls Pakistan's 'double knot' qualities 'Pak-Persian carpets'.

rows.name: Chobi and 'Ziegler' rugs (Pakistan, hand-spun, vegetable-dyed)
rows.region: Pakistan (TDAP gives no town); Afghan refugee weaving was concentrated in northern Pakistan around Peshawar (see the refugee row).
rows.made_by: Pakistani workshops using methods TDAP says were learned from Afghan refugees settled in Pakistan.
rows.date_note: Afghan refugees came to Pakistan after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979. A start date for chobi and 'Ziegler' production was not found; 1980 is a lower bound only.

structure.knot_note: TDAP heads this group 'Turkish knot' (symmetric) but says chobi rugs use a knot called 'seena' (probably Senneh, i.e. asymmetric). Unresolved.
structure.kpsi_note: TDAP: chobi knot density 'anywhere over 100'.
structure.pile_note: Hand-spun wool (TDAP).

design.colors: Light browns and tans, wood-like colors; vegetable dyes (TDAP).

rows.trade_use: 'Chobi' and 'Ziegler' are quality or style names, not places. Ziegler & Co. was the British firm that ordered carpets around Sultanabad, Persia, from 1883 to World War I; the Pakistani 'Ziegler' quality uses its name.
rows.what_it_tells: A soft-colored, hand-spun, vegetable-dyed rug with a Pakistani or Afghan label is consistent with refugee-influenced production of the 1980s onward.
rows.cautions: Old Ziegler-period Persian carpets (Sultanabad/Arak, 1883-1914) are a different and much older group. 'Ziegler', 'Kazak' and 'Gabbeh' made in Pakistan borrow the names of other rug types.

facts.text: 'Chobi' (Persian chub, 'wood') describes Afghan and Pakistani rugs in light browns and tans.
TDAP lists a group of hand-spun, vegetable-dyed qualities (Ziegler or Chobi, Kazak, Karghai, Khal Mohammadi, modern Gabbeh) as learned from Afghan refugees settled in Pakistan.
TDAP says chobi rugs are hand-spun wool on a cotton warp, over 100 knots per square inch, and sell mainly in North America.
Ziegler & Co. of Manchester opened a Tabriz office in 1883 and by World War I was buying the output of 3,000 looms around Sultanabad; the trade knew those carpets as Mahals.
A dealer gives rang-i-chub as the Afghan term for natural dyestuffs.

says.text: p.6: this group is 'Turkish Knot made with hand spun vegetable dyes'.
p.10: chobi rugs use 'a type of unique knot known as seena'.

rows.name: Afghan refugee weaving in Pakistan
rows.region: Refugee camps in northern Pakistan, around Peshawar.
rows.made_by: Afghan refugees (Turkmen, Baluch, Pashtun and others) and the Pakistani firms they wove for.
rows.date_note: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (December 1979) and the wars after it drove refugees into Pakistan; war rugs were seen in Peshawar by the late 1980s and refugees there were weaving export rugs by the 1990s. TDAP says many refugee weavers later went home.

structure.knot_note: Spooner: two knot types are used in Afghanistan; the knot follows the weaving group.
structure.kpsi_note: Wide range; Spooner says good Afghan carpets reach 400+ kpsi but many are under 100.

design.field: Traditional Turkmen and Baluch designs, and from about 1980 war imagery (weapons, tanks, helicopters, maps).

rows.trade_use: Rugs woven by Afghans in Pakistan were exported as Pakistani, so a 'Made in Pakistan' label does not rule out Afghan weavers.
rows.what_it_tells: An Afghan-style rug (Turkmen or Baluch design, or war imagery) with a Pakistani label points to refugee weaving in Pakistan, 1980 or later.
rows.cautions: Production of Baluch-type rugs had already spread to Pakistan in the 1970s, before the refugees (Spooner). The label shows the exporting country, not the weavers' origin.

facts.text: Soviet troops occupied Afghanistan in December 1979 and withdrew in February 1989.

A large share of Afghan war rugs probably came from refugee camps in northern Pakistan; war rugs were seen in Peshawar in the late 1980s, and refugees in Pakistan were weaving rugs for export by the 1990s.
When demand for Baluch rugs rose in the 1970s, their production spread to other parts of Afghanistan, to Pakistan and to eastern Iran.
A war rug in the Textile Museum of Canada (T2008.1.23) reads 'Afghanistan Welcome to Peshawar', which suggests refugee weaving near Peshawar.
TDAP says Pakistan learned its hand-spun, vegetable-dyed qualities from Afghan refugees, that Afghans were the industry's main labor force, and that many have gone back.

rows.name: Romanian rugs in Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs
rows.translit: covoare înnodate manual (tip oriental) — 'hand-knotted carpets, oriental type'
rows.region: Craft cooperatives across Romania. The trade grades are named after Romanian towns, rivers and mountains (Braila, Bran, Brasov, Bucharest, Dorna, Harmon, Milcov, Mures, Olt, Postavarul). One knotted-carpet cooperative documented by name is Munca si Arta in Galati on the Danube. Theodor Tuduc's reproduction workshop (1919-1945) was in Brasov.
rows.made_by: Mostly women weavers in state craft cooperatives (the UCECOM network) before 1989. Modern pile-rug weaving in Romania was begun by Armenian refugees after the First World War.
rows.date_note: Stone dates significant export pile-rug weaving from about 1950, growing after the United States lowered tariffs in 1975; Jacobsen first reports Romanian hand-made rugs on the market in 1969. Orders were already falling in 1994 (Moscow Times); whether any cooperative production continues is not established. Workshop copies of Caucasian and Turkish rugs (and Tuduc's forgeries) date from the 1920s-1940s.

structure.knot_note: Stone: the asymmetric knot for Persian designs, the symmetric knot for Turkish and Caucasian designs.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone gives 25-200 knots per square inch depending on grade, and a figure for each grade: Dorna 25 (cotton foundation); Bran about 60 (wool); Bucharest about 70 (cotton); Braila about 100 (cotton); Brasov about 100 (wool); Mures 129 (cotton; Persian designs); Harmon 130 (wool); Postavarul 155 (wool); Olt 160 (cotton); Milcov 194 (cotton; the highest commercial grade). Single source for the grade figures.
structure.pile_note: Jacobsen (1969) praised the wool as better than in most Persian rugs and expected the rugs to be durable.
structure.back: Very regular: steel-frame looms give straight sides, square corners and an even weave (Stone).

design.field: Copies of Persian designs (for example the detached floral sprays of Sarouk rugs), and of Turkish and Caucasian designs; some geometric designs.
design.colors: Jacobsen (1969) found the colors excellent but the drawing of most designs machine-like, as in many Tabriz rugs; he liked the geometric designs better than the floral ones.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Romania wove Sarouk designs. A Romanian piece points to itself through very even shape and weave from steel-frame looms, stiff drawing, and a grade-name label (Milcov, Olt, Mures and so on).

look_alikes.name: Bulgarian rugs in Persian designs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are Balkan export rugs in Persian designs. Romanian rugs are sold by grade name and also come in Turkish and Caucasian designs on the symmetric knot; the Bulgarian rugs Jacobsen saw were in Tabriz designs.

look_alikes.name: tuduc-reproduction
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A rug in an antique Transylvanian, Ottoman, Lotto or Spanish armorial design that is too perfect in pattern, has resolved corners and feels stiff may be a Tuduc reproduction (Textile Museum of Canada; Denny in AramcoWorld). Only a specialist can confirm.

rows.trade_use: Sold by grade name rather than by design name; each grade fixes the foundation and the knot density. 'Balkan rugs' covered Bulgarian and Romanian hand-made rugs in Jacobsen's classification.
rows.what_it_tells: A Romanian grade name, a very even weave and a Persian, Turkish or Caucasian design drawn with machine-like precision point to export production of the 1950s-1980s from a Romanian cooperative, not to Iran, Turkey or the Caucasus.
rows.cautions: The grade names are known from one reference; a dealer page repeats Stone word for word and does not count. 'Bessarabian' is used loosely for Polish, Romanian and Bulgarian hand-knotted rugs. Romanian kilims (scoarta) are flat-woven and are a different thing. In the 1920s-1940s Romanian workshops made fine copies of Caucasian and Turkish rugs, and Theodor Tuduc made forgeries of classical Ottoman, Transylvanian, Lotto and Spanish carpets that were aged and sold as old; some entered major museums. A rug with an 'antique' classical design can be a 20th-century Romanian copy.

facts.text: Modern pile-rug weaving in Romania was begun by Armenian refugees after the First World War; in the 1920s and 1930s Romanian workshops wove fine copies of Caucasian and Turkish rugs, some bought by major museums as old.
Significant pile-rug weaving for export began about 1950 and increased after the United States lowered tariffs in 1975.
Romanian hand-knotted rugs were made by craft cooperatives.
Romanian cooperatives wove a range of grades in Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs, on wool or cotton foundations.
Steel-frame looms are used, giving very regular shapes and a consistent weave.

Knot density runs from about 25 to 200 knots per square inch depending on grade; the grades are Braila, Bran, Brasov, Bucharest, Dorna, Harmon, Milcov, Mures, Olt and Postavarul, each with its own foundation and density (Milcov, 194 kpsi on cotton, is the highest commercial grade).

Before 1989 the central union of craft cooperatives (UCECOM) had 40 handicraft cooperatives employing about 50,000 people, three-quarters of them women; woven carpets were the main product and about 90% were exported; hand-knotted 'oriental type' carpets were also made.
Exports went mainly to the USA and Britain, and also to Italy, France, Sweden, Germany and Greece.
