In 1994 the Munca si Arta cooperative in Galati had almost 1,000 women knotting oriental carpets, about 12,000 square meters a year in 1992 and 1993, with a weaver knotting about 1.5 square meters a month; orders were falling against competition from Iran, Iraq, Pakistan and China.

Jacobsen (1969) saw hand-made rugs from Romania of excellent quality, color and wool, mostly with machine-like drawing like many Tabriz rugs and the post-WWI Turkish 'Sparta' rugs, and noted they were government-subsidized.
Jacobsen (1969) classed hand-woven rugs of Bulgaria and Romania together as 'Balkan rugs'.
Sarouk designs of detached floral sprays are used in rugs woven in Romania (as well as India and China).
Theodor Tuduc (1888-1983), a Romanian rug restorer and maker of reproductions, worked in Brasov; his copies of classical carpets were aged and sold as authentic, and some were displayed by museums.
Tuduc's work includes white-ground Chintamani, Transylvanian, Lotto and Spanish armorial carpets; he moved from Transylvanian fakes to Persian, Caucasian and Spanish ones.

Features used to spot a Tuduc: pattern too perfect and symmetrical, weak color palette (Denny); stiff rather than floppy handle, corners that resolve neatly where old rugs rarely do, and selvedges that look 'stapled on' (Textile Museum of Canada).
'Bessarabian' is used loosely in the trade for Polish, Romanian and Bulgarian hand-knotted rugs.

says.text: Most of his weaving was done in his Brasov workshop between 1919 and 1945 (p. 287).
He worked in Brasov between the two world wars.

disagreements.about: when Romanian export rugs reached the Western market

says.text: Significant export weaving began about 1950 (p. 237).
In 1962 Jacobsen lists Bulgaria as the only Balkan exporter in numbers (p. 178) and does not mention Romania; his first report of Romanian rugs is in 1969 (Check Points, p. 158).

rows.name: Bulgarian rugs in Persian designs
rows.translit: Persiyski kilim ('Persian carpet'; name of the Panagyurishte cooperative as rendered by Radio Bulgaria)
rows.region: Kotel and Panagyurishte; a labour production cooperative named 'Persian Carpet' in Panagyurishte and village workshops nearby, and a 'Persian Carpet' manufacturing enterprise in Plovdiv, in the 1960s (Radio Bulgaria).
rows.made_by: Women weavers in state cooperatives and enterprises working from colored paper design charts.
rows.date_note: Jacobsen saw them on the European market 'for several years' before 1962, so from the mid- or late 1950s; Radio Bulgaria documents the Panagyurishte cooperative in the 1960s and says its archives were destroyed in 1992-93. No end date found; Stone (2013) still calls Bulgaria a minor contemporary source.

structure.knot_note: Knot type not given by the sources read.
structure.kpsi_note: No count given. Jacobsen: tightly woven, 'about the same' fineness as a Sarouk, with a medium-thick pile like a Sarouk.
structure.pile_note: Jacobsen: good medium-heavy pile of excellent wool.

design.field: Persian floral designs, mostly Tabriz designs taken from Tabriz paper scale drawings; floral designs based on Persian models. Drawing is stiff and 'mechanical'.
design.sizes: Jacobsen saw carpet sizes about 7 x 10, 9 x 12 and 10 x 14 ft.

look_alikes.name: Tabriz
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jacobsen says most people, even dealers, would take them for Persian Tabriz rugs; the drawing is more mechanical than in Tabriz rugs. No structural test is given in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Romanian rugs in Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are Balkan export rugs; Romanian rugs are sold under grade names and also come in Turkish and Caucasian designs.

look_alikes.name: chiprovtsi-kilim
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chiprovtsi and Kotel are best known for flat-woven, two-sided kilims; a pile rug is not a Chiprovtsi or Kotel kilim.

rows.trade_use: Jacobsen filed them under 'Balkan rugs (made in Bulgaria)'. Western dealers today list them by the Persian design they copy, e.g. 'Bulgarian Tabriz design'.
rows.what_it_tells: A hand-knotted rug in a Tabriz-type design with a stiff, very regular drawing and a cotton foundation may be Bulgarian export work of the 1950s-1980s rather than Persian.
rows.cautions: Few were sold in the United States: in 1962 they paid 45% duty because Bulgaria lacked most-favored-nation status, so most went to Europe. Bulgarian 'kilims' (Chiprovtsi, Kotel, 'Thracian') are flat-woven and are a different thing. Stone also mentions 19th-century Bulgarian rugs made in imitation of Gördes prayer rugs.

facts.text: Bulgaria made hand-knotted pile rugs in Persian designs from the 1950s, notably at Panagyurishte.
Bulgaria is a minor source of contemporary pile rugs with floral designs based on Persian models, woven in Kotel and Panagyurishte.
Large numbers of hand-knotted rugs in Tabriz designs were being woven in Bulgaria and sold in the European market around 1960.

In the 1960s Panagyurishte had a labour production cooperative named 'Persian Carpet' that wove from colored paper design charts drawn by a staff draftswoman; Plovdiv had a 'Persian Carpet' manufacturing enterprise.
Bulgarian weavers worked from paper design charts (scale patterns).
The Bulgarian rugs were woven from Tabriz paper scale patterns and copied Tabriz texture as well as design.
Jacobsen saw them only in London, in carpet sizes of about 7 x 10, 9 x 12 and 10 x 14 ft; they were tightly woven, about as fine as a Sarouk, with a medium-thick pile of excellent wool.
Balkan rugs, like Indian, Chinese, Japanese and new Pakistani rugs, use cotton warps.
Jacobsen wrote that formerly some 'Balkan rugs' were made in Russia and Yugoslavia, but only Bulgaria exported great numbers.
US import duty on Bulgarian rugs was 45%, double the 22.5% on Persian rugs, because Bulgaria lacked most-favored-nation status; Jacobsen knew of none brought to America.
Jacobsen (1969) classed the hand-woven rugs of Bulgaria and Romania together as 'Balkan rugs'.
Chiprovtsi carpets are two-sided flat-woven carpets (tapestries) made on a vertical loom; the Chiprovtsi carpet-making tradition was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014.
Bulgarian kilims are mostly slit-weave tapestry, sometimes called 'Thracian'; 19th-century kilim centers include Chiprovtsi, Kotel, Samokov, Sliven and others.

rows.name: Albanian rugs in Persian designs
rows.region: State carpet factories and workshops in Korçë (Korça), Kukës and Kavajë, and the 'Migjeni' artistic enterprise in Tirana, which produced rugs for export (1975 state documentary). Designs were centralized in Tirana (Zoto).
rows.made_by: Women weavers in state factories and workshops under the communist government.
rows.date_note: A source 'since World War II'. The state factory system ended with communism (1990-91); in the early 1990s private workshops made carpets for tourists and export (Library of Congress). Exact factory dates not found.

structure.knot_note: Not given by the sources read; Stone calls them pile rugs.
structure.pile_note: Pile material not stated by the sources read.

design.field: Persian designs; copies and interpretations of Persian design styles alongside Albanian folk motifs studied by the Academy of Sciences (Zoto; 1975 documentary).

look_alikes.name: Bulgarian rugs in Persian designs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both are communist-era Balkan export rugs in Persian designs; no structural difference is given in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Romanian rugs in Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Romanian rugs carry grade names (Milcov, Olt...). No Albanian grade names were found.

rows.trade_use: Rarely named in the US trade; dealers list them as 'Albanian' plus the Persian design copied.
rows.what_it_tells: An Albanian label or provenance on a Persian-design pile rug points to state export production of about 1945-1990.
rows.cautions: Albanian factories also made flat-woven kilims for export (Zoto); 'qilim' covers both. Documentation is thin and split between periods (Zoto).

facts.text: Since the Second World War Albania has been a source of well-made pile rugs in Persian designs.
In communist Albania kilims and carpets were made by hand in factories for export, with designs centralized in Tirana; some designs were copies or interpretations of Persian styles.

A 1975 state documentary shows a carpet factory in Korça, a carpet factory in Kukës, a carpet workshop in Kavaja, and the 'Migjeni' artistic enterprise in Tirana producing rugs for export; ethnographers at the Academy of Sciences studied folk motifs for rugs.
After the Second World War Albania made hand-made carpets in Persian designs.
Albanian state factories made carpets for export.
In the early 1990s Albanian businessmen set up workshops producing handicrafts, carpets and weavings for tourist shops and export.

rows.name: Greek rugs woven by Asia Minor refugees (1920s-1930s)
rows.region: Athens and its refugee suburbs (Podonifti, later Nea Ionia; Polygono; Vyronas), Piraeus (Drapetsona), Corinth, Thessaloniki and other towns (Volos, Veria, Edessa, Komotini), and a factory at Agios Petros in Arcadia.
rows.made_by: Refugees from Asia Minor after 1922: Greek Orthodox weavers from Isparta (the 'Spartalides'), Smyrna and Kütahya, and Armenian refugees; mostly women and girls, in factories and as home weavers.
rows.date_note: First Greek carpet factory 1922 (Tzamou). End dates differ: Jacobsen says about 1931-32, Stone says up to the Second World War, Tzamou says the industry declined after 1940 though a few family workshops wove by hand into the mid-1970s. 1940 is used as the end of the main period.

structure.knot_note: Tzamou: the Isparta-type ('Sparta') carpets of the refugees were worked with the asymmetric knot.
structure.kpsi_note: Jacobsen (Sparta rugs, Turkish and Grecian, p. 298): the coarsest had not more than 36 knots per square inch, the best seldom over 150. Several qualities from very poor to good average.
structure.pile_note: Jacobsen (on the Group III Turkish and Greek factory rugs): long, high nap, colors softened by bleaching; Pergamo rugs lightly chemically washed, none painted.

design.field: The same designs as the Turkish factory carpets of the day, after Persian floral designs; Pergamo rugs also in Baluch, Caucasian and Turkish designs. Designs were drawn on millimeter graph paper (Tzamou).
design.sizes: Factory rugs mostly 6 x 9 ft and larger; Pergamo rugs in small sizes and runners.

look_alikes.name: sparta-isparta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Greek refugee rugs and Turkish Isparta rugs of the 1920s were sold under the same 'Sparta' and 'Anatolian' trade names in the same designs; the sources read give no structural test to separate them.

look_alikes.name: Sarouk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Turkish and Greek factory rugs copied Persian floral designs, but Jacobsen found their look 'domestic' and mechanical next to the Persian originals.

look_alikes.name: flokati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A flokati is a Greek wool rug with a very shaggy pile up to six inches long and no design: nothing like a knotted Persian-design rug.

rows.trade_use: In America these rugs were sold as 'Sparta' or 'Anatolian' rugs or under importers' own trade names. 'Grecian rug' and 'Grecian family' are Jacobsen's terms.
rows.what_it_tells: A worn, long-piled Persian-design carpet of 1920s-30s American provenance sold as 'Sparta' or 'Anatolian' may come from Greece or from Turkey; both point to the commercial weaving of the 1920s, not to an old village rug.
rows.cautions: 'Sparta' names both the Turkish town of Isparta and these Greek-made rugs; it does not mean Sparta in the Peloponnese. Greek kilims and flokati rugs are folk flatweaves and shag rugs, not knotted carpets. Jacobsen's dates and his statement that rugs were 'never woven in Greece' before 1922 are contradicted in part by Tzamou (carpet-knotting was taught on Samos and by exiles slightly earlier).

facts.text: Knotted carpet production in Greece began with refugees from Asia Minor after the Greco-Turkish war of 1922.
The first Greek carpet factory was founded in 1922 by Filippos Kachramanoglou at Polygono, Athens, with a second, larger one at Podonifti in 1923-24.

Factories centered on Podonifti (Nea Ionia) had about 2,000 looms and about 6,000 women workers, and home weaving employed about 30,000 more; the Greek state granted industrial plots next to refugee settlements.

Refugees from Isparta in Pisidia, where carpet weaving had grown in the 19th century, brought Isparta-type designs drawn on millimeter paper; within a few years Greek carpets competed with Turkish ones abroad.
The refugee carpets were tied with the asymmetric knot.

The Greek refugee rugs were tied to the name 'Sparta' (from Isparta): Jacobsen says they were generally sold as Sparta rugs; Tzamou calls them Isparta-type ('Sparta') carpets introduced by refugees from Isparta.
American interests set up small factories in Piraeus among Armenian refugees from Turkey, and considerable weaving was also done in and around Salonika.
Knotted pile carpets were woven in Athens and Corinth up to the Second World War.
Workshops also operated in Thessaloniki, Volos, Veria, Edessa, Komotini, Drapetsona (Piraeus) and Vyronas; more than fifty were founded by refugees from Isparta.
They were generally sold as 'Sparta' rugs, in America under many trade names, in several qualities, using the same Persian-style designs as the Turkish carpets of the day.
Jacobsen's Plate 132 shows a 'Sparta rug, Turkish or Grecian family', made in 1924-1932.

The industrial branch declined after 1940; surviving firms turned to machine-made carpets or wool spinning, while a few family workshops (e.g. in Komotini) wove hand-knotted carpets into the mid-1970s, and the state handicraft organization (named by Tzamou as EOMMEX) ran workshops in the 1950s-60s.
'Pergamo' rugs were made by Armenian refugees in Greece (Piraeus and Salonika) in small sizes and runners, mostly in Persian designs, lightly chemically washed and not painted.
A flokati is a Greek wool rug with very shaggy pile up to six inches long, without pattern.

says.text: Armenian refugees from Turkey, in small factories set up by American interests (p. 91; Pergamo, p. 270).
Greek weavers repatriated from Turkey after the 1922 war (p. 119).
Greek Orthodox refugees from Isparta, Smyrna and Kütahya, with refugee capital; Greek and Armenian women of Asia Minor had both woven carpets there.
Piraeus and in and around Salonika.
Athens and Corinth.
Above all Podonifti/Nea Ionia (Athens), also Drapetsona (Piraeus), Thessaloniki, Volos, Veria, Edessa, Komotini and Arcadia.
Made only 1923-1931 (p. 20); 'up to about 1932' (p. 91); plate 132 dated 1924-1932.
Up to the Second World War.
Decline after 1940, with some family workshops weaving by hand into the mid-1970s.
Says Pergamo rugs were made 'right after World War II', yet that most wore out in 30 years and the Depression ended them; WWI is probably meant (p. 270).

disagreements.about: whether carpets were knotted in Greece before 1922

says.text: Rugs were never woven in Greece until right after World War I (p. 91).
Carpet-knotting was taught slightly earlier, e.g. at a vocational school on Samos and by exiles from Isparta in 1918-19, though 1922 was the turning point.

rows.name: Egyptian hand-knotted rugs, including Mamluk-design rugs
rows.region: Not established by the sources read for modern knotted production; Cairo was the classical center.
rows.made_by: Workshops (details not found).
rows.date_note: Knotted-rug production in Egypt had all but ended by the late 17th century and began again in the 1950s, when imports were limited.

structure.knot_note: Not given for modern rugs. The classical Mamluk carpets they copy are asymmetrically knotted, all wool, with S-spun yarn (Stone; Met).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Egyptian knot counts are written as knots per centimeter across x knots per centimeter along, e.g. '4 x 5' = 20 knots per square centimeter, which is about 130 knots per square inch (20 x 6.45). That is Stone's example, not a range.

design.field: Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs; revivals of Mamluk designs: large geometric medallions and octagons on red with yellow, blue and green.

look_alikes.name: mamluk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Classical Mamluk carpets (late 15th-16th c.) are all wool with S-spun yarn and lac red; a modern copy will usually show modern dyes and a new foundation. Only a specialist can date one.

rows.trade_use: 'Mamluk' is used in the trade as a design name for modern rugs in the style of the classical Cairo carpets, wherever made.
rows.what_it_tells: A modern rug labeled Egyptian with a 'N x N' per-centimeter quality points to post-1950 Egyptian production; a Mamluk design on its own does not show where or when a rug was made.
rows.cautions: Egypt's best-known hand-weaving towns today (e.g. Fuwwa in Kafr el-Sheikh) are known mainly for flat-woven kilims, not knotted pile; Harrania and Wissa Wassef pieces are tapestries; 'assyuti' and 'helwan' are Egyptian kilims (Stone; Youm7; Sada El-Balad). Many so-called 'Mamluk' rugs are of uncertain origin; one group is attributed to the Maghreb.

facts.text: Knotted-rug production in Egypt began again in the 1950s because of limits on imports, after having all but disappeared by the late 17th century.
Contemporary Egyptian rugs are made in Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs and are not exported in significant numbers.
Egyptian knot counts are expressed per centimeter, e.g. 4 x 5 = 4 knots per cm across and 5 along, 20 per square centimeter.
The classical Mamluk carpets of Cairo (late 15th-16th centuries) are all wool with the asymmetric knot.
Mamluk carpets use S-spun yarn rather than the usual Z-spun, and their red is from lac.
Fuwwa in Kafr el-Sheikh is a center of hand-made kilim weaving (not knotted pile), dating its trade to the early 19th century.

disagreements.about: date the Fuwwa weaving trade began

says.text: Spread from 1812.
Established in 1822.
The Met attributes its examples to Cairo (some 'probably').
Many so-called Mamluk rugs are of problematic origin; one group is attributed to the Maghreb (p. 184).

museum_examples.title: Five Medallion Carpet
museum_examples.shows: museum's primary image of a classical Mamluk carpet (the model for modern 'Mamluk' designs), not a modern rug

museum_examples.title: Mamluk Carpet
museum_examples.shows: museum's primary image of a classical Mamluk carpet

museum_examples.title: Carpet
museum_examples.shows: museum's primary image of a Cairo carpet

rows.name: Rabat rugs (Moroccan urban carpets)
rows.region: Rabat, on the Atlantic coast; contemporary factory rugs are also made in Casablanca, Fez and Marrakesh.
rows.made_by: Urban workshops; contemporary factories.
rows.date_note: Woven since the 18th century; contemporary factory rugs are still woven in Rabat.

structure.kpsi_note: Stone: 40-60 symmetric knots per square inch.

design.field: A small field framed by many borders, so that about two-thirds of the rug is border; reinterpretations of Turkish models. Early Moroccan rugs follow Anatolian designs, often with an arch at both ends, more coarsely knotted and brighter than Anatolian ones.
design.border: Many borders, about two-thirds of the surface.
design.sizes: Long and narrow, to fit the main rooms of Moroccan town houses.

look_alikes.name: anatolian-village
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rabat rugs reinterpret Turkish designs but have many more borders around a small field and are coarser and brighter.

rows.trade_use: Since 1919 Moroccan rugs have carried an official 'M.A.R.O.C.' or 'Maroc' label.
rows.what_it_tells: Many borders around a small field, a long narrow shape and a 'Maroc' label point to a Rabat-type urban Moroccan rug.
rows.cautions: Older rugs have all-wool foundations; contemporary ones have cotton foundations. Only one source read for this row.

facts.text: Rabat rugs, woven since the 18th century, are long and narrow, with a small field and many borders taking about two-thirds of the rug; designs reinterpret Turkish models.
Rabat rugs have symmetric knots, 40-60 per square inch, on all-wool foundations in older rugs and cotton in contemporary ones.
Since 1919 Moroccan rugs have been labeled 'M.A.R.O.C.' or 'Maroc'.
Contemporary factory rugs are made in Rabat, Casablanca, Fez (many in Persian designs) and Marrakesh (copies of Turkish rugs).

rows.name: Middle Atlas pile rugs (incl. the ivory 'Beni Ourain' type)
rows.translit: qṭifa (Moroccan word for a pile rug, Stone)
rows.region: The Middle Atlas mountains of central Morocco (tribes named by Stone: Beni M'guild, Beni M'tir, Zaiane).
rows.made_by: Berber (Amazigh) women of Middle Atlas tribes.
rows.date_note: Moroccan rugs are not reliably dated before the 19th century. Ivory rugs with black-and-white designs reached the New York market about 1952.

structure.knot_note: Stone: Middle Atlas weavers tie the symmetric knot on four warps; the Berber knot encircles two warps twice; Beni M'guild mostly symmetric, sometimes asymmetric; Beni M'tir asymmetric; Zaiane mix symmetric and Berber knots.
structure.kpsi_note: No count for the Middle Atlas; Stone gives 15-20 per square inch for other Moroccan tribal rugs.
structure.pile_note: Coarse, thick, heavy wool (Jacobsen); some Zaiane pieces very shaggy (Stone).

design.field: Concentric diamond medallions, or vertical or horizontal stripes filled with diamonds and sawtooth designs; repeated geometric elements, often without side borders (Beni M'guild, Beni M'tir). The ivory type: ivory field with design in black and browns.
design.colors: Ivory with black and brown; red, black and white (Zaiane, Stone).
design.sizes: Long format.

look_alikes.name: bakra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: From the 1950s Indian firms copied the ivory Moroccan rugs (trade name 'Bakra'); Jacobsen says the two are not easy to tell apart.

rows.trade_use: Today the ivory long-pile type is widely sold as 'Beni Ourain' (trade usage; not in the sources read).
rows.what_it_tells: A thick, coarse, long-piled wool rug with an ivory field and dark diamond lines is consistent with Middle Atlas weaving or with an Indian copy.
rows.cautions: The name 'Beni Ourain' and its attribution to one tribal group were not found in the sources read. Indian copies have been made since the 1950s.

facts.text: Middle Atlas tribes weave pile rugs in a long format with narrow borders, with concentric diamond medallions or stripes filled with diamonds and sawtooth designs; the symmetric knot is tied on four warps.
Thick, coarse rugs with ivory fields and 'primitive' designs in black and white, woven in Morocco, appeared in the New York market about 1952.
Indian rug firms copied these ivory Moroccan rugs from the 1950s, sold under trade names such as 'Bakra', in strong, thick wool, coarsely woven.
Some Zaiane pile pieces are very shaggy and used for bedding or cloaks; their colors are red, black and white.
Most Moroccan rugs have symmetric knots; early rugs have all-wool foundations, later ones cotton.
Moroccan tribal pile rugs are coarsely knotted in thick wool.

rows.name: High Atlas rugs (incl. the 'Azilal' type)
rows.region: The High Atlas mountains of central Morocco (Ouaouzguite tribe in the High Atlas and Siroua mountains).
rows.made_by: Berber (Amazigh) women of High Atlas tribes.
rows.date_note: Moroccan rugs are not reliably dated before the 19th century.

structure.knot_note: Stone: symmetric knots on two warps; rugs mix pile and flat-woven areas.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone gives 15-20 symmetric knots per square inch for Ouaouzguite rugs.

design.field: A very narrow border around a field of wide stripes with geometric motifs; all-over diamond patterns in Ouaouzguite rugs.
design.colors: Dominant red, gold and orange.
design.sizes: Small rugs.

rows.trade_use: 'Glaoua' is a local merchants' term for High Atlas flatweaves with some pile. 'Azilal' (a High Atlas province) is a current trade name for colorful rugs on an ivory ground; it was not found in the sources read.
rows.what_it_tells: A small, coarse rug mixing pile and flat-woven bands in red, gold and orange is consistent with High Atlas weaving.
rows.cautions: Only one source read; the 'Azilal' trade type is not documented here.

facts.text: Berber tribes of the High Atlas weave small rugs of mixed pile and flat-woven structure, with symmetric knots on two warps, dominant red, gold and orange, and wide stripes of geometric motifs inside a very narrow border.
Ouaouzguite rugs are very coarse, about 15-20 symmetric knots per square inch, often with all-over diamond patterns.

rows.name: Boucherouite (Moroccan rag rugs)
rows.region: Morocco.
rows.made_by: Berber (Amazigh) women.
rows.date_note: No date found in the sources read.

structure.knot_note: Structure not described in the sources read.
structure.pile_note: Strips of old clothing and other cloth, not yarn.

design.field: Not described in the sources read.

rows.what_it_tells: A rug made from strips of recycled cloth rather than yarn, sold as Moroccan, is a boucherouite.
rows.cautions: Single source; date of origin not established. Egyptian rag rugs are flat-woven with cloth strips as weft.

facts.text: Boucherouite are Moroccan Berber rugs made from scraps of clothing and other fabric; the name is from Arabic for 'scrap'.

rows.name: Nepalese (Tibetan-style) rugs
rows.region: Kathmandu valley (Kathmandu, Patan/Lalitpur incl. Jawalakhel) and Pokhara.
rows.made_by: Tibetan refugees who arrived in 1959-60 and workshops that followed; the Jawalakhel Handicraft Center is based at the Tibetan refugee camp at Jawalakhel.
rows.date_note: Refugees from Tibet arrived in 1959-60 and began commercial weaving in camps.

structure.knot_note: Tibetan technique: a continuous pile yarn is looped around two warps and then around a gauge rod; the loops are cut and the rod removed, giving rows of tufts like overlapping shingles (Stone). Global InCH: pile length set by the rod's diameter, loops cut on the rod with a knife.
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: about 50 per square inch in refugee rugs; Global InCH: on average 45 per square inch. Makers sell '60-knot' and '100-knot' qualities (JHC); how those labels relate to knots per square inch is covered by the knot-count notation agent.
structure.pile_note: Himalayan wool (Stone).

design.field: Traditional Tibetan designs and many new ones; contemporary rugs are often carved (sculptured) after weaving.
design.colors: Bright synthetic colors in early refugee rugs.
design.sizes: Typical 3 x 6 ft.

look_alikes.name: tibetan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rugs woven in Tibet before 1959 often have red cloth edging and backing and vegetable dyes; Nepalese refugee and later rugs have cotton foundations and synthetic dyes. Importers may call Nepalese rugs 'Tibetan'.

rows.trade_use: Importers may describe these rugs as 'Tibetan' although woven in Nepal. Qualities are sold as '60-knot', '100-knot' etc. (JHC).
rows.what_it_tells: A Tibetan-technique rug (rows of cut loops, cotton foundation, Himalayan wool) with modern colors points to Nepalese production after 1960, not to old Tibet.
rows.cautions: Child and forced labor in carpet weaving is reported in Nepal (US Department of Labor, 2024); a GoodWeave label is one assurance scheme (JHC is a member). Tibetan-refugee rugs are also woven in India (Himachal Pradesh), Bhutan and Sikkim.

facts.text: Tibetan carpets are woven in Nepal by refugees from Tibet who arrived in 1959 and 1960; the main centers are Kathmandu, Pokhara and Patan.
After 1959 Tibetan refugees in Nepal, Bhutan and India began significant commercial production of rugs in the Tibetan technique.

Jawalakhel is a place in Nepal where Tibetan refugees weave rugs on cotton foundations; the Jawalakhel Handicraft Center describes itself as the Tibetan Refugee Camp and one of Nepal's largest carpet makers.
Tibetan rugs are woven by looping a supplementary yarn round warps and a gauge rod, then cutting the loops.
Nepalese refugee rugs average about 45-50 knots per square inch.
The pile is Himalayan wool on a cotton foundation; the typical size is 3 x 6 ft; early refugee rugs use bright synthetic colors.
Importers may describe Nepalese rugs as 'Tibetan'.
Galaincha rugs are made for home, tourist and export markets.
The US Department of Labor lists forced labor in carpet weaving among the worst forms of child labor in Nepal.

says.text: About 50 knots per square inch (p. 284).
On average 45 knots per square inch.
Sells '60-knot' and '100-knot' qualities (labels, unit not stated).

rows.name: Chinese rugs in Persian designs
rows.region: Silk: Nanzhao county, Nanyang, Henan (tussah silk), from the 1980s. Wool: Shandong (Shantung) and other factory regions. Beijing workshops wove some Persian-style pieces during the First World War.
rows.made_by: Factory and cooperative workshops; in Nanzhao, tens of thousands of home weavers at the peak.
rows.date_note: Persian-design silk knotting in Nanzhao began in the 1980s (Xinhua); large-scale Chinese commercial production resumed in the 1960s. Rare earlier Beijing pieces date from the First World War (Hali).

structure.knot_note: Chinese rugs use the asymmetric knot (Stone, incl. Shandong Persian-design copies).
structure.kpsi_note: Stone: Shandong Persian-design copies 100-200 asymmetric knots per square inch, short pile. Nanzhao silk: typical '210 per foot' (Xinhua); by Stone's definition of 'line' (warp pairs per foot, same count vertically) 210 line = 17.5 x 17.5 per inch = about 306 kpsi. Xinhua's top figure of 1,200 per foot would be about 10,000 kpsi and is a rare showpiece claim. Stone: silk rugs 120-300 line, wool 70-120 line.
structure.pile_note: Tussah silk in Nanzhao (Xinhua); wool in Shandong; Stone gives silk pile height 1/2 inch, wool 3/8-5/8 inch. Cotton warps are documented for Chinese wool rugs (Jacobsen p. 159); the foundation of the Nanzhao silk rugs is not given.

design.field: Copies of Persian designs (medallion, all-over, Sarouk floral sprays) as well as Chinese pictorial designs.

look_alikes.name: qom-silk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A silk rug in a Persian design may be Chinese; tussah (wild) silk and a 'line' quality on the label point to China. Sources read give no simple test.

look_alikes.name: Art silk (viscose) rugs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone's burn test: silk leaves a small ball of ash and smells of burnt feathers; cotton (incl. mercerized cotton) burns brightly to fine ash and smells of burnt paper. Rayon is cellulose like cotton, but no source read describes its burn test.

rows.trade_use: The trade uses 'Sino-' plus a Persian town name for Chinese rugs in Persian designs (names not found in the sources read).
rows.what_it_tells: A silk rug in a Persian design with a 'line' quality, very even weave and tussah silk points to Chinese production from the 1980s on.
rows.cautions: Chinese claims that Nanzhao made 80% of the world's hand-made silk carpets are the county's own, unverified. Persian-design silk rugs are also made in India, Turkey (Kayseri, Hereke) and Iran (Qom).

facts.text: Beijing workshops wove pieces in Persian styles during the First World War, when Persian carpet exports were limited; they are rare today.
Large-scale commercial rug production in China resumed in the 1960s, in cooperative factories with steel looms, chrome dyes and standard qualities measured in 'line'.
Contemporary Shandong production consists of copies of Persian designs, finely knotted (100-200 asymmetric kpsi) with a short pile.
Sarouk designs of detached floral sprays are used in rugs woven in China (as in India and Romania).
Nanzhao county (Henan) began hand-knotting carpets of local tussah silk for export in the 1980s; designs include Middle-Eastern-style 'Persian carpets' (波斯毯) and Chinese pictorials.
Nanzhao silk carpets are exported to the United States, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Dubai; the industry employs over 20,000 people.
Chinese silk rugs are made in 120-300 line qualities; 'line' is pairs of warps per foot.

rows.name: Art silk (viscose) rugs
rows.country: Various (Turkey: Kayseri documented; India and China not documented in the sources read)
rows.region: Kayseri (central Anatolia) uses rayon and mercerized cotton pile. Other centers not established in the sources read.
rows.made_by: Commercial workshops.
rows.kind: trade name (a name for a look, made in several places)
rows.date_note: Approximate. Imitation-silk pile of mercerized cotton was already in use in Asia Minor and Persia by 1913; rayon ('artificial silk') is a 20th-century fiber.

structure.knot_note: Any technique; the term describes the pile fiber, not the construction.
structure.kpsi_note: Kayseri wool rugs 80-120 kpsi; Kayseri silk up to 450 (Stone), for comparison.
structure.pile_note: Viscose/rayon is regenerated cellulose (16 CFR 303.7), usually from wood pulp; 'bamboo' textiles are almost always rayon (FTC). Mercerized cotton is cotton treated with alkali to add strength and gloss (Stone).

design.field: Any; often copies of silk Persian or Turkish (Kayseri prayer and saff) designs.

look_alikes.name: silk
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stone's burn test on a few loose fibers: silk does not easily keep a flame, leaves a small ball of ash and smells of burnt feathers; cotton (incl. mercerized cotton) burns easily to fine ash and smells of burnt paper. Rayon is regenerated cellulose (16 CFR 303.7), but no source read describes its burn test. In the US a pile-content tag is required, and a bamboo-derived fiber must be named rayon (FTC).

rows.trade_use: 'Art silk' in the trade can mean either rayon (viscose) or mercerized cotton. 'Bamboo silk' is rayon made from bamboo and must be labeled rayon in the US (FTC).
rows.what_it_tells: A shiny 'silk' rug labeled viscose, rayon, art silk or bamboo silk is a cellulose-fiber rug, not silk.
rows.cautions: Viscose loses much of its strength when wet (Swicofil), so wet cleaning and spills are risky. Mercerized-cotton and other silk imitations have been passed off as silk since at least 1920. Browning or yellowing of viscose after wetting is widely reported by cleaners but no source was read for it.

facts.text: 'Art silk' is a trade term for artificial silk or mercerized cotton.
Rayon is a manufactured fiber of regenerated cellulose (US textile labeling rule).
Most if not all 'bamboo' textiles are really rayon and must be labeled with the generic name, e.g. 'rayon made from bamboo'.
Viscose loses a great deal of strength when wet.
'Floss' is mercerized cotton polished to look like silk, sometimes called 'Turkish silk'; 'ipekli' (Turkish, 'silken') means carpets with mercerized cotton pile.
Kayseri rugs use a cotton foundation with pile of wool, rayon, mercerized cotton or, rarely, silk; many saff-design rugs have mercerized cotton pile.
By 1913 mercerized cotton was used as pile in a few districts of Asia Minor and Persia.
facts.quote: in a few of the districts of Asia Minor and Persia it is mercerised cotton or silk

facts.text: Buyers of silk rugs were warned of numerous mercerized and wool-silk imitations, some machine-made.
facts.quote: numerous mercerized and wool silk imitations, many of them not even being hand-tied but machine made

facts.text: Silk and mercerized cotton can be told apart by burning a small amount: silk leaves a small ball of ash and smells of burnt feathers, cotton burns brightly to fine ash and smells of burnt paper.
US federal rules require rugs to carry a tag stating the pile content.

says.text: Artificial silk or mercerized cotton (p. 33).
US labeling knows only generic fiber names: rayon (regenerated cellulose), lyocell, cotton etc.; 'art silk' is not a permitted fiber name.

rows.name: Japanese hand-made rugs (Imperial, Fuigi Royal, Peking)
rows.region: Not named in the sources read.
rows.made_by: Japanese commercial weaving firms (one firm made both Imperial and Fuigi Royal).
rows.date_note: Japan began weaving these about 1950; by 1969 rising costs had nearly ended imports (Fuji Royal gone; Imperials in handfuls; Peking continuing). End date approximate.

structure.knot_note: Not given.
structure.kpsi_note: No count given; Imperial described as very heavy and tightly woven (a 9 x 12 ft weighing 125-135 lb).
structure.pile_note: 100% wool pile of New Zealand or Australian wool; chrome dyes; much hand carving on Imperials; Pekings lightly lime-washed (Jacobsen).

design.field: French Savonnerie and Aubusson designs, two-corner floral sprays on a plain field (Imperial); antique Chinese designs (Peking, Fuigi Royal, some Imperials).
design.colors: Imperial: four basic soft colors, rose, light blue, green and beige. Peking: light pastel beige, tan, green and gold, known by design numbers (#200 gold, #300 beige, #500 light beige with soft blue, #600 tan, #700 green field).
design.sizes: Imperial 2 x 3 to 12 x 20 ft; Peking 2 x 4 to 6 x 9 and 8 x 10 to 12 x 20 ft; Fuigi Royal first as rounds 3 and 4 ft across.

look_alikes.name: chinese
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jacobsen says Japanese rugs in Chinese designs can be hard to tell from real Chinese rugs; a 'Peking' with a design number, or an 'Imperial' tag, points to Japan in the 1950s-60s.

look_alikes.name: Indian rugs in Savonnerie, Aubusson and Chinese designs (Indo-Savonnerie, carved one-color rugs)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: India made the same Savonnerie and Chinese designs in larger numbers; no structural test given.

rows.trade_use: Sold under trade names (Imperial, Fuigi Royal, Peking) and design numbers by New York importers.
rows.what_it_tells: An 'Imperial', 'Fuji/Fuigi Royal' or Japanese 'Peking' label points to Japanese export production of about 1950-1970.
rows.cautions: All facts from one author (Jacobsen 1962 and 1969 are not independent). Older Japanese rugs (before about 1913) had pile largely of jute and cotton, quite different from these wool rugs.

facts.text: Japan began weaving oriental rugs about 1950, most for America, in French Savonnerie/Aubusson and Chinese designs, in three qualities: Imperial, Fuigi Royal and Peking.
All three are hand-made with 100% wool pile on cotton warp and weft; the wool is from New Zealand or Australia and the dyes are chrome dyes.
The Imperial is very heavy and tightly woven with much hand carving, in rose, light blue, green and beige; a 9 x 12 ft weighs 125-135 lb.
The Fuigi Royal, first made in 1958, came first as round rugs 3 and 4 ft across and was made by the same firm as the Imperial.
Peking rugs (Japanese) were made in large numbers for one New York importer, in antique Chinese designs and pastel colors, known by design numbers.
By 1969 rising Japanese costs had nearly ended imports: the Fuji Royal had disappeared and Imperials came only in handfuls, while the Peking continued.
Around 1913 the pile of Japanese rugs was largely jute and cotton.
facts.quote: in Japan the pile is largely jute and cotton

says.text: Pile largely jute and cotton (1913, p. 30).
100% wool pile (rugs from about 1950).
Fuigi Royal.
Fuji Royal.

rows.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
other_names: Brussels (the same loom with uncut loops)
rows.country: United States; England; Belgium and other countries
rows.region: US mills in Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania (Bigelow at Clinton MA and Thompsonville CT; Shuttleworth / Mohawk at Amsterdam NY; Karagheusian at Freehold NJ; Whittall at Worcester MA; Hardwick & Magee at Philadelphia); English mills; later Belgium.
rows.made_by: Factory power looms fitted with a Jacquard pattern mechanism.
rows.date_note: Power Wilton looms were running in the US by 1878-1880 (Shuttleworth brought 14 used Wilton looms to Amsterdam NY in 1878; Whittall bought Wilton and Brussels machinery in 1880). Bigelow's power looms for Brussels (patent 1847) and for pile and cut-pile carpeting (1851-57) came earlier. Wiltons sold on their likeness to oriental rugs were advertised by 1911-12 (Whittall) and are still made.

structure.knot_note: No knots. The pile yarns run lengthwise as extra warps; the Jacquard lifts one color at a time over a flat wire, and a knife on the end of the wire cuts the loops as it is pulled out. With uncut loops the same loom makes Brussels carpet. Pile colors not needed on the face at a given point stay buried inside the rug.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.wefts_note: Two or three shots of weft for each row of pile (Brinton: three in many Wiltons for a firmer fabric; two in the fine Wiltons of c. 1919).
structure.pile_note: Worsted (smooth, combed) or woolen yarn in older rugs; polypropylene in some modern Belgian Wiltons (Stone p. 222). The number of colors in any one lengthwise line is limited by the number of 'frames' of yarn, one color per frame (CRI; Brinton: five frames usual in a Super Wilton).
structure.sides: Cut and bound edges on rugs cut from wider goods; machine binding (serging) is usual on machine-made rugs (CEPC; Stone p. 255).
structure.ends: No warp fringe of the hand-knotted kind. Where a fringe is present it is sewn on (CEPC).
structure.handle: Heavy and firm for its pile height, because unused pile yarn is buried in the body (Brinton; CRI).
structure.back: An even grid of lengthwise binding (chain) and filler (stuffer) threads crossed by weft shots; no knot bumps. How clearly the buried colors show from the back was not described in the sources read.

design.field: Copies of Persian, Turkish, Caucasian and Chinese designs, with medallions or all-over patterns.
design.colors: Few colors per lengthwise line (limited by frames), so large areas of one color are common.

look_alikes.name: Axminster rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Axminster puts all of its pile on the surface and can use far more colors; Wilton hides unused colors in the body, so it is heavier for its pile and has few colors per line (Brinton; CRI).

look_alikes.name: hand-knotted
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Part the pile: a hand-knotted rug shows the loop of a knot around the lengthwise threads at the base of each tuft; a Wilton shows none.

rows.trade_use: 'Wilton' on a label names the loom and weave, not a place. In 1934 a federal appeals court upheld an FTC order against selling rugs of a different weave as 'Wilton'.
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-made rug, usually of the 20th century. A maker's name may be woven into the back or printed on a sewn label, which can lead to the mill and a date range.
rows.cautions: Design names on labels (Kirman, Sarouk, Kashan) are pattern names, not where the rug was made; Jacobsen (1969) complained of ads naming 'Sarouk' without the word 'design'. Wilton is also the English town whose factory made hand-knotted carpets (called 'Axminster') into the 1920s (Stone p. 306), so an old 'Wilton' carpet is not always power-loomed.

facts.text: A Wilton is a pile carpet woven on a Jacquard loom: the pile yarn is looped over a wire and cut, giving a cut pile.
facts.quote: the loops of worsted yarns are cut, so that the character of the surface is velvety instead of smooth and ribbed

facts.text: If the loops are left uncut, the same kind of loom makes Brussels carpet; the two looms can be converted from one to the other.
facts.quote: The loom is practically the same for both fabrics

facts.text: In this weave the pile yarn not used on the face at a given point is carried hidden inside the body of the rug.
facts.quote: for every length of worsted that appears on the surface, four times as much is hidden in the body of the fabric

facts.text: Each pile color comes from its own 'frame' of yarn, so the colors in a Wilton are limited: a three-frame Wilton has three colors in its design.
facts.quote: Five frames of worsted are generally employed.

facts.text: Woven carpets have three sets of lengthwise threads: binding 'chain' warps, 'stuffer' warps that add bulk and stiffness, and the pile warps.
Woven Wilton is a heavy, firm fabric; three weft shots per row of pile make it firmer.
facts.quote: the treble weft shot makes a better weave and a firmer fabric

facts.text: American mills had Wilton power looms by about 1878-1880: the Shuttleworth brothers brought 14 used Wilton looms from Britain to Amsterdam NY in 1878, and M. J. Whittall bought Wilton and Brussels machinery for his Worcester mill in 1880.
In 1934 a federal appeals court upheld an FTC order that rugs of a materially different weave, sold as 'Bagdad Seamless Jacquard Wilton', could not be sold as genuine Wiltons.
facts.quote: constituted an unfair method of competition

facts.text: A 1920 'French Wilton' rug by Hardwick & Magee of Philadelphia (cotton, jute and wool) carries a maker's label on its back.
Manufacture of American machine-made rugs grew about tenfold in the decade before 1902.
facts.quote: The manufacture of American machine-made rugs has increased ten-fold in the same time.

facts.text: A machine-made copy has no knot at the base of the pile: if you part the pile of a hand-knotted rug you see the loop of each knot around the lengthwise threads; on a machine-made rug the strands are fixed to the base by the machine.

Jacobsen wrote that the federal government (the FTC) required machine-made American rugs in oriental patterns to be advertised as 'Oriental Design' rugs rather than as 'American Oriental' rugs; only hand-knotted rugs could be called oriental rugs.

rows.name: Axminster rug in an oriental design
rows.region: US and British carpet mills; Karastan's rugs (Leaksville / Eden NC) were made on modified spool Axminster looms.
rows.made_by: Factory power looms (spool or gripper Axminster).
rows.date_note: Brinton (1919) says the Axminster power loom came to England from the United States about 1878 and that cheap American Axminster flooded the British market in 1893. Karastan made spool Axminster rugs in North Carolina from 1928 until 2019-2021.

structure.knot_note: No knots. Each tuft is laid between the lengthwise threads and doubled around a crosswise weft shot, then locked by more wefts, so seen from the side it is a U, not a knot. In spool Axminster the colors are wound on spools in the order of the design and fed through small tubes; in gripper Axminster beak-like grippers take each tuft from carriers set by a Jacquard.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.wefts_note: Brinton's standard Imperial Axminster: a double chain of linen or cotton, a cotton stuffer, and three double shots of jute weft per row of tufts.
structure.pile_note: All of the pile yarn is on the surface, none buried (Brinton), which allows a nearly unlimited range of colors.
structure.sides: Machine selvage or a sewn binding.
structure.ends: No warp fringe of the hand-knotted kind; a fringe, if any, is sewn on (CEPC).
structure.handle: Firm; bends across its width but resists bending along its length (CRI).
structure.back: Flat, or ribbed where a heavier bottom weft lies across the back; the stuffer threads run straight along the length (Brinton). Karastan's modified loom pulled the pile through to the back so the pattern shows there (NC DNCR).

design.field: Copies of oriental designs; many colors possible.
design.colors: Wide range; not limited by frames.

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Wilton buries unused pile colors in the body and has few colors per line; Axminster has all pile on the face, more colors, and bends only one way (Brinton; CRI).

look_alikes.name: hand-knotted
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Part the pile: no knot loop around the lengthwise threads at the base of the tufts.

rows.trade_use: 'Axminster' on a label names the loom. The name comes from the English town of Axminster, where hand-knotted carpets were made in the 18th century.
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-made rug; with Wilton, the commonest woven machine-made rug in oriental designs in the US before tufting took over in the 1950s.
rows.cautions: An 18th-century 'Axminster carpet' from Thomas Whitty's factory is hand-knotted, not machine-made (Stone p. 36; Met 2025.725). Brinton notes the Axminster tuft is set at a slant, one more point of likeness to a hand-knotted rug, so slanting pile alone does not prove hand-knotting.

facts.text: In an Axminster the tufts are put in row by row between the lengthwise threads and held by the weft without being knotted.
facts.quote: the tuft, though inserted in the fabric mechanically, and bound down without being knotted

facts.text: All of the Axminster's pile yarn is on the surface; none is hidden in the body, unlike Wilton and Brussels.
facts.quote: none of the tuft material is hidden away or wasted in the body of the fabric

facts.text: Spool Axminster feeds the pile from spools through small tubes; another power-loom system uses mechanical fingers or grippers, controlled by a Jacquard, to take and insert each tuft.
Depending on the weave, an Axminster back is flat or ribbed; a heavier bottom weft shows across the back.
facts.quote: the bottom weft, projecting below the tuft weft, gives the back a ribbed appearance

facts.text: Axminster carpet bends only across its width (it resists bending along its length).
The Axminster power loom was brought into England from the United States about 1878.
facts.quote: The Axminster loom was introduced into England from the United States about 1878

facts.text: The name comes from the town of Axminster, England, where Thomas Whitty's factory wove hand-knotted carpets from the mid-18th century to 1835.
Karastan rugs were woven on Axminster looms modified for Marshall Field's mill in North Carolina.

A machine-made copy has no knot at the base of the pile: if you part the pile of a hand-knotted rug you see the loop of each knot around the lengthwise threads; on a machine-made rug the strands are fixed to the base by the machine.

museum_examples.licence: Public Domain (isPublicDomain true in the Met collection API)
museum_examples.title: Carpet
museum_examples.shows: A hand-knotted English Axminster carpet by Thomas Whitty, for contrast with power-loomed 'Axminster' (view not checked)

rows.name: Modern power-loomed rug in an oriental design (Belgium, Egypt, Turkey)
rows.country: Belgium; Egypt; Turkey; also France, England, Italy, Holland and others
rows.region: Belgian mills; Oriental Weavers at 10th of Ramadan City, Egypt; Merinos at Gaziantep, Turkey.
rows.made_by: Large factories with power looms (often Wilton-type).
rows.date_note: Belgian machine-made rugs in oriental designs were sold widely in US stores by the 1960s (Jacobsen 1969 reproduces a December 1968 ad; Couristan began Belgian machine-made rugs in 1964). Oriental Weavers began in 1978-79 and Merinos turned from kilims to rugs in 1983 (company texts).

structure.knot_note: No knots; woven on power looms (Stone describes Belgian production as power-loomed and names Wilton weaves).
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.pile_note: Polypropylene in some Belgian Wiltons (Stone p. 222); Couristan's Belgian machine-made rugs are 100% wool (company text). The label must give the pile fiber and the country of manufacture (US rules).
structure.sides: Machine-bound (serged) edges (CEPC; Stone p. 255).
structure.ends: Fringe, if present, is sewn on rather than being the ends of the lengthwise threads (CEPC).
structure.back: A regular machine grid with no knot bumps; the pattern may show on the back but every repeat is identical.

design.field: Persian, Turkish and Caucasian designs, often with the source name used as a pattern name.

look_alikes.name: hand-knotted
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Turn it over: no knot bumps, identical repeats, a sewn-on fringe and a machine-bound edge; the label gives the fiber and country.

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same weave family; the label (country, fiber) and date separate older American Wiltons from later imports.

rows.trade_use: Sold as 'Oriental design' or under the design's source name (e.g. 'Kashan'), with 'Made in Belgium', 'Made in Egypt' or 'Made in Turkey' on the label.
rows.what_it_tells: A machine-made rug, generally from the 1960s onward; the label usually names the country and the pile fiber.
rows.cautions: Pattern names on labels are not places of origin. Stores sometimes advertised these as 'Imported Oriental' rugs. Polypropylene (olefin) pile points to a modern rug.

facts.text: Belgium has a large modern production of power-loomed rugs, most in imitation of hand-knotted Near Eastern designs, and US department stores advertised them as 'imported oriental design' rugs in the 1960s.
Machine-made rugs in oriental designs were also imported into the US from France, England, Italy and Holland by the 1960s.
Polypropylene is used in some Wilton weaves from Belgium (and in tufted Chinese rugs).
'Olefin' is the US generic fiber name for fibers made of at least 85 percent ethylene, propylene or other olefin units, so a label reading 'olefin' usually means polypropylene.
facts.quote: composed of at least 85 percent by weight of ethylene, propylene, or other olefin units

facts.text: Olefin pile resists fading, stains and abrasion but crushes easily.
US law requires a rug's label to give the fiber content of the pile (face); the backing is exempt from the fiber disclosure.
facts.quote: backings of, and paddings or cushions to be used under, floor coverings

facts.text: Imported textile products sold in the US, rugs included, must be labeled with the country where they were made ('Made in ...'); wholly US-made goods may say 'Made in U.S.A.'.
Oriental Weavers (Egypt) was founded by Mohamed Farid Khamis, starting with a single loom; it is based at 10th of Ramadan City and makes machine-woven and tufted carpets.
Merinos (Gaziantep, Turkey) began in 1970 with two kilim looms under the Erdemoğlu family and turned to rug production in 1983; it calls itself a maker of machine-woven rugs ('dokuma makine halısı').
Couristan began selling machine-made rugs in 1964 and names Belgium as the source of its 100% wool machine-made area rugs.

Jacobsen wrote that the federal government (the FTC) required machine-made American rugs in oriental patterns to be advertised as 'Oriental Design' rugs rather than as 'American Oriental' rugs; only hand-knotted rugs could be called oriental rugs.

says.text: Home page: 'Founded in 1979 by Mohamed Farid Khamis.'
Founder page: he 'established Oriental Weavers' in 1978, 'starting with a single loom in 1979'.

rows.name: Karastan
rows.region: Leaksville, Rockingham County, North Carolina (later sources name the plant as Eden, NC); production moved to northwest Georgia from 2019.
rows.made_by: Marshall Field & Company's mills; later Fieldcrest Mills; Mohawk Industries from 1993.
rows.date_note: First Karastan off the loom April 8, 1928. Wool rug weaving in North Carolina ended between 2019 and 2021 (sources differ). The Karastan name continues on synthetic Mohawk products.

structure.knot_note: No knots. Woven on spool Axminster power looms that Eugene Clark began modifying for Marshall Field in 1926 so that the pile yarn was pulled through to the back.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.pile_note: Wool (worsted wool per the 2021 New York Times report, seen only in excerpts). Up to 50 colors.
structure.sides: Not described in the sources read.
structure.ends: Not described in the sources read.
structure.back: The pattern shows through on the back, made to look hand-knotted on both sides (NC DNCR); no knot bumps.

design.field: Reproductions of Persian and other oriental designs, sold under design names such as Kirman (the 717 Kirman of 1937 had 50 colors).
design.colors: Up to 50 colors.

look_alikes.name: hand-knotted
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The pattern shows on the back, but there are no knots: parting the pile shows no knot loop around the lengthwise threads (Jacobsen 1969; NC DNCR).

look_alikes.name: Axminster rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Karastan is an Axminster; the brand is told by its label and design numbers.

rows.trade_use: 'Karastan' is a brand, not a place. Design names such as 'Kirman 717' are pattern names.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven wool rug made in North Carolina between 1928 and about 2019-2021, in a design copied from an oriental rug.
rows.cautions: 'Karastan' sounds like a weaving region but is an invented place-like name (Stone p. 239). Because the back shows the pattern, a Karastan can be taken for hand-knotted; part the pile to look for knots. Karastan also made tufted and nylon carpet from the 1960s (Floor Focus), and Mohawk sells synthetic Karastan products after 2021, so the name alone does not date a piece.

facts.text: The first Karastan rug came off the loom on April 8, 1928.
Karastans were made by Marshall Field & Company at its Rockingham County, North Carolina mill (Leaksville; later sources say Eden).
The loom was a spool Axminster power loom that Marshall Field's engineers began modifying in 1926; Floor Focus says the Axminster equipment was bought in England.
Eugene Clark's modification pulled the pile yarn through to the back, allowing up to 50 colors and a hand-knotted look on both sides.
The trade press called them 'Mystery Rugs'; after more than five million people walked on a Kirman-design Karastan at the 1933-34 Chicago World's Fair they were sold as 'Wonder Rugs'.
The 717 Kirman design, introduced in 1937 with 50 colors, stayed the best seller for about 50 years.
Mohawk Industries bought Karastan from Fieldcrest in 1993.
Karastan added tufted carpet in the 1960s and its first nylon broadloom in 1967.
Rug-name lists include 'Karastan' as a name made to sound like a place.
In 1969 Jacobsen named Karastan, with Bigelow and Cabin Crafts, among the American makers of machine-made rugs in oriental designs.

disagreements.about: date_to (end of wool rug weaving in North Carolina)

says.text: The Eden Karastan plant closed in 2021 (93 years after 1928).

Excerpts of the 2021 New York Times report say the Axminster looms made the wool rug until 2019, when Mohawk closed that department; a 2019 Floor Daily item (excerpt only) says rug production moved to northwest Georgia from October 2019.
1935: Marshall Field merged its 24 textile mills into one operation, Fieldcrest; 1953: Fieldcrest spun off.
1953: Marshall Field sold its mill operations to Amoskeag, which formed Fieldcrest Mills, Inc.
Eugene Clark began modifying the spool Axminster loom in 1926.
Gives no year for the loom; headline dates the mill's innovation 'since 1929'.

rows.name: A. & M. Karagheusian (Gulistan)
rows.country: United States (with an operation at Tianjin, China)
rows.region: Freehold, Monmouth County, New Jersey (weaving); Roselle Park NJ (spinning, 1923); Tianjin (Tientsin), China (1925).
rows.made_by: Armenian-American brothers Arshag and Mihran Karagheusian's mills.
rows.date_note: First carpets off the Freehold looms in 1905; the Gulistan rug was introduced in 1928; oriental carpet production stopped in 1953 and the Freehold mill closed in 1964 (Baptista, NCSU).

structure.knot_note: No knots: the Freehold mill was equipped with Brussels and Wilton power looms bought in Kidderminster, England.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.pile_note: The Gulistan rug was sold on its silk-like sheen (Baptista, NCSU); how the sheen was made was not described.
structure.sides: Not described in the sources read.
structure.ends: Not described in the sources read.
structure.back: Not described in the sources read.

design.field: Persian-style designs (Gulistan).

look_alikes.name: gulistan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Older books use 'Gulistan' for hand-knotted rugs: a Persian type near Kashan and a grade of Oushak rugs from Turkey (Mumford; Lewis; Rug Primer). A machine-woven rug with no knots is the American Gulistan.

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Karagheusian made Wilton and Brussels weaves; the label tells the maker.

rows.trade_use: 'Gulistan' was Karagheusian's brand from 1928 and survives as the name of Gulistan Carpet, Inc.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven rug from Freehold NJ, 1905-1953, or a later Gulistan carpet.
rows.cautions: The firm also imported oriental rugs (from 1899) and was one of the American firms in the hand-knotted export rug trade at Tianjin, China (Stone p. 68), so a Karagheusian connection does not by itself mean machine-made. 'Gulistan' (Persian for rose garden) was a trade name for hand-knotted Persian and Turkish rugs long before 1928.

facts.text: Arshag and Mihran Karagheusian, Armenian brothers from Turkey, were importing oriental rugs in America by about 1899-1903.

In 1904 the brothers set up a carpet mill in a former shirt factory in Freehold, New Jersey, with 60 Brussels and Wilton power looms bought in Kidderminster, England; the first carpets came off the looms in 1905.
Karagheusian introduced the Gulistan rug in 1928, a Persian-style rug with a silk-like sheen.
Karagheusian had an operation at Tianjin (Tientsin), China, from 1925, and is listed among the American firms in Tianjin's export rug industry.
Oriental carpet production stopped in 1953; J. P. Stevens bought the company in 1964 and the Freehold mill closed that year.
Older books use 'Gulistan' for hand-knotted rugs: Hawley for a Persian type made near Kashan, and Mumford, Lewis and The Rug Primer for a fine grade of Oushak (Usak) rugs from western Turkey.
facts.quote: Gulistan is the Persian name for a flower garden

rows.name: Bigelow (Bigelow Carpet Co.; Bigelow-Sanford)
rows.region: Clinton, Massachusetts; Thompsonville (Enfield), Connecticut; Amsterdam, New York (Sanford); later Southern plants.
rows.made_by: Power-loom carpet mills founded on Erastus B. Bigelow's inventions.
rows.date_note: Brussels carpet on Bigelow's looms from 1849 at Clinton. Bigelow-Hartford 1914-1929; Bigelow-Sanford from 1929 (one archive says 1924); the Thompsonville plant closed in 1971. When Bigelow's oriental-design rugs began and ended was not found.

structure.knot_note: No knots; Bigelow's looms wove ingrain (flat), Brussels, Wilton, tapestry and velvet carpeting.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.back: Not described in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bigelow made Wilton and other power-loom weaves; the label names the maker.

rows.trade_use: Brand name of carpets and rugs.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-made carpet or rug; the company name on the label (Bigelow Carpet, Bigelow-Hartford, Bigelow-Sanford) narrows the date.
rows.cautions: Name changes help date a label: Bigelow-Hartford (1914-1929), Bigelow-Sanford (from 1929).

facts.text: Erastus Brigham Bigelow (1814-1879) invented power looms for carpets, including ingrain, Brussels, Wilton, tapestry and velvet carpeting, and his looms greatly increased carpet production from the 1840s.

Bigelow had power looms for ingrain carpet by 1842, patented the first Brussels power loom in 1847 and a tapestry Brussels loom in 1850, and took six patents for pile and cut-pile carpet looms in 1851-57.
In 1849 Erastus and his brother Horatio began weaving Brussels carpet on his looms at Clinton, Massachusetts; they incorporated as the Bigelow Carpet Company in 1854.
The company was Bigelow-Hartford from 1914 to 1929 and Bigelow-Sanford from 1929; the Thompsonville, Connecticut plant (carpet making there since 1828) closed in 1971.
In 1969 Jacobsen named Bigelow among the American makers of machine-made rugs in oriental designs.
Mohawk bought 'Karastan Bigelow' from Fieldcrest Cannon in 1993.

says.text: Bigelow-Hartford period 1914-1929; Bigelow-Sanford period 1929-1971.
Search excerpt of Cornell's Bigelow-Hartford Carpet Company Records finding aid: merged in 1924 with Stephen Sanford & Sons of Amsterdam NY to become Bigelow-Sanford (page not opened; 403).

disagreements.about: dates of Bigelow's Brussels and Wilton looms

says.text: First Brussels power loom patented 1847; pile and cut-pile looms 1851-57.
Search excerpt: developed his power loom for Brussels and Wilton carpets from 1845 to 1851.

rows.name: Mohawk Carpet Mills
rows.region: Amsterdam, New York; after the 1960s the South (Georgia).
rows.made_by: Mohawk Carpet Mills, formed by merger in 1920.
rows.date_note: The Mohawk name dates from the 1920 merger; the Shuttleworth mill (from 1878) and McCleary, Wallin & Crouse were earlier. Mohasco from 1956. Manufacturing in Amsterdam ended by the end of the 1960s.

structure.knot_note: No knots; Mohawk offered Wilton, Axminster, velvet and chenille weaves (Gale).
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.back: Not described in the sources read.

design.field: Mohawk's oriental-design lines were not identified in the sources read (the 1908 Shuttleworth 'Karnak' pattern is named, without a description).

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Check the label and the weave (Wilton or Axminster back).

rows.trade_use: Brand of a large US carpet maker; the modern Mohawk Industries also owns Karastan.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven rug, from Amsterdam NY between 1920 and the 1960s if the label says Mohawk Carpet Mills.
rows.cautions: Mohawk Industries today sells many kinds of rugs, including tufted and printed ones; the old Mohawk Carpet Mills label and a woven back point to the Amsterdam years.

facts.text: The Shuttleworth family began weaving carpets at Amsterdam, New York in 1878 with 14 used Wilton looms shipped from Britain, and incorporated as Shuttleworth Brothers Company in 1902.
Mohawk Carpet Mills was formed in 1920 by the merger of Shuttleworth Brothers Company and McCleary, Wallin & Crouse, both of Amsterdam NY.
Mohawk Carpet Mills offered Wilton, Axminster, velvet and chenille weaves.
Mohawk merged with Alexander Smith, Inc. in 1956 to form Mohasco Industries.
Carpet manufacturing by Mohawk in Amsterdam ended by the end of the 1960s.
Mohawk bought Karastan in 1993.

rows.name: Whittall rugs (Anglo-Persian and others)
rows.region: Worcester, Massachusetts (South Worcester; Whittall Mills off Brussels Street); a Palmer MA mill from 1891.
rows.made_by: Matthew J. Whittall's mill, from 1906 the trust M. J. Whittall Associates.
rows.date_note: Manufacturing began in 1880 on Wilton and Brussels looms (period sources via CBHL). Ads of 1911-12 promoted the woven name on the back. When the Anglo-Persian line began and when the mill closed were not settled.

structure.knot_note: No knots; Whittall's mill wove Wilton and Brussels carpet.
structure.kpsi_note: Not knotted, so knots per square inch do not apply. The power-loom trade counts pitch (pile ends in 27 inches of width) and rows or wires per inch (Stone pp. 114, 238, 306; CRI Carpet Primer).
structure.back: 1911-12 ads said the name 'Whittall's' was woven into the back of every rug; an auction listing reports 'Whittalls Anglo Persian' marked on the back of one rug.

design.field: Persian and Chinese-style designs (the 1913 catalogue is titled 'Oriental Art in Whittall Rugs').

look_alikes.name: Wilton rug in an oriental design
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Look for the woven Whittall name on the back.

rows.trade_use: 'Anglo-Persian' was a Whittall line name; it does not mean the rug was made in England or Persia.
rows.what_it_tells: An American machine-woven (Wilton-type) rug from Worcester, Massachusetts, early to mid 20th century.
rows.cautions: 'Anglo-Persian' sounds like an origin but is a line name.

facts.text: Matthew J. Whittall began making carpets on his own account in 1880 in South Worcester, Massachusetts, with machinery for Wilton and Brussels carpets; in 1906 the business passed to the trust M. J. Whittall Associates.
Whittall advertisements of 1911 and 1912 told buyers to look for the name 'Whittall's' woven into the back of the rug.
Whittall Mills in Worcester was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on March 5, 1980.

disagreements.about: number of looms at the start (1880)

says.text: Hurd (1889): seven looms.
Textile World obituary (1922) and Isaiah Thomas Lodge tribute (1928): eight looms.

rows.name: Couristan
rows.country: United States (importer and distributor; rugs made in Belgium and elsewhere)
rows.region: New York City (company); manufacture abroad.
rows.made_by: Founded by the Couri brothers; machine-made rugs from mills abroad (Belgium named).
rows.date_note: Founded 1926 as an importer of handmade Persian rugs; machine-made rugs from 1964 (company text).

look_alikes.name: Modern power-loomed rug in an oriental design (Belgium, Egypt, Turkey)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Couristan's Belgian machine-made rugs belong to this group; check the back and label.

rows.trade_use: Brand on imported rugs of several kinds: hand-knotted (early imports), machine-woven (Wilton, Axminster), hand-tufted, hand-loomed and printed.
rows.what_it_tells: A Couristan label alone does not tell how the rug was made; the back and the label's words do.
rows.cautions: The same brand has sold hand-knotted, machine-woven, hand-tufted and printed rugs.

facts.text: Couristan was founded in New York City in 1926 by the brothers Basil J., Aleer J. and George J. Couri as an importer of handmade Persian rugs.
Couristan began selling machine-made rugs in 1964, naming Belgium for its 100% wool machine-made rugs; it also sells hand-tufted, hand-loomed, digitally printed and Axminster products.

dates.title: Dates, signatures and words woven into rugs

numerals.name: Arabic-Indic digits (the digits of the Arab world and the Ottoman Empire; often called 'Arabic numerals' in old rug books)
numerals.codepoints: U+0660 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ZERO, U+0661 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ONE, U+0662 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT TWO, U+0663 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT THREE, U+0664 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FOUR, U+0665 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FIVE, U+0666 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SIX, U+0667 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SEVEN, U+0668 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT EIGHT, U+0669 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT NINE
numerals.used_on: Ottoman and Anatolian rugs until Turkey made Western digits compulsory in official use (1 June 1929); Muslim-woven Caucasian rugs; Arab-world pieces. Iranian weavers mostly used the Persian forms (next entry), but woven digits mix forms, so the shape of a 4, 5 or 6 is a hint, not proof, of where a rug was made.

woven_forms.0: ٠ a dot. Woven, it is one knot or a tiny diamond of knots, easy to miss or to take for a stray knot.
woven_forms.2: ٢ an upright with one hook at the top right, like a Latin r.
woven_forms.3: ٣ an upright with two small teeth at the top: a 2 with an extra tooth.
woven_forms.4: ٤ Arabic form: shaped like a backward 3 (an epsilon ε).
woven_forms.5: ٥ Arabic form: a small circle or loop, which a Western reader takes for a zero.
woven_forms.6: ٦ Arabic form: a hook with a downstroke, like a backward Western 7 or a small 'L' turned over.
woven_forms.9: ٩ a loop on a stem, much like a Western 9.
woven_forms.general: Knotted on a grid, curves become steps, so teeth and hooks blur. Ripley (1904) advises counting the knots that make each stroke to recover the shape.

confusions.example: Met 22.100.3: the Met's 1923 catalogue printed 1323; the Met now reads 1223. V&A T.25-1983: the last digit read as 2 or 3 (1202 or 1283).
V&A T.25-1983: third digit read as 0 or 8 (1202 or 1283).
Met 22.100.61: read 1110 in 1921, 1210 today; the 1923 catalogue says the date 'appears to have been altered by restoration'.
Poldi Pezzoli hunting carpet: 'the second digit ... can be read either 2 or 4' (929 or 949).

confusions.pair: 7 and 8 when upside down (V and Λ)
confusions.example: Inferred from the shapes only: turning a date upside down swaps ٧ and ٨. No source read reports a case.

confusions.pair: 5 read as 0 by Western readers (٥ is a circle; ٠ is a dot)
confusions.example: Inferred from the shapes; no source read reports a case.

numerals.mirrored: Dates can appear reversed (mirror image) when a weaver copied an inscription from the back of another rug (Stone, 'mirror writing'), and some dates are woven upside down (Gregorian 1987 on Armenian-inscribed rugs). Hawley and Lewis advise reading a worn date from the back, where the order of digits runs the other way. No source gives a count of how common mirrored dates are.

facts.text: Dates woven in these digits on rugs are usually years of the Muslim lunar (Hijri) calendar.
Numbers are read from left to right (largest place first), as in Western usage, even though the words around them run right to left.
Old rug books print tables of these digits and note that woven forms vary ('numerous modifications').
facts.note: Jacobsen copies Hawley's text; the OCR of every table is garbled, so shapes here are described from the Unicode reference glyphs.

facts.text: Unicode encodes the Arabic-Indic digits at U+0660–U+0669, separate from the Persian/Urdu (Eastern) set.

numerals.name: Persian (Eastern Arabic-Indic, 'extended') digits
numerals.codepoints: U+06F0 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ZERO, U+06F1 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ONE, U+06F2 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT TWO, U+06F3 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT THREE, U+06F4 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FOUR, U+06F5 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT FIVE, U+06F6 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SIX, U+06F7 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT SEVEN, U+06F8 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT EIGHT, U+06F9 EXTENDED ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT NINE
numerals.used_on: Iranian rugs (Persian), and the Persian/Urdu-writing world: Afghanistan, Pakistan and India per Unicode. On rugs: Persian city, village and tribal rugs dated in the lunar (AH) or, from 1911/1925, the solar (SH) year.

woven_forms.0: ۰ a dot, as in the Arabic set.
woven_forms.2: ۲ an upright with one hook at the top right.
woven_forms.3: ۳ an upright with two teeth at the top.
woven_forms.4: ۴ Persian form: an upright with a small double curl on its upper left; unlike the Arabic ٤.
woven_forms.5: ۵ Persian form: a pointed loop, like an upside-down heart, narrow at the top; it can be read as a 0 or an o.
woven_forms.6: ۶ Persian form: a small head with a tail swept down to the left; unlike the Arabic ٦.
woven_forms.7: ۷ a V (some local hands differ, per Unicode).
woven_forms.general: As with the Arabic set, knotting turns curves into steps. Persian and Arabic forms of 4, 5 and 6 can appear on the same rug.

facts.text: Unicode encodes a separate set of digits for Persian, Sindhi and Urdu (U+06F0–U+06F9), used in Afghanistan, India, Iran and Pakistan.
The Persian/Urdu forms of four, five, six and seven differ from the Arabic forms, and four, six and seven vary a good deal between places.
The Ardabil carpet's date is woven in these digits after the word سنه ('year'): «سنه ۹۴۶».

numerals.used_on: Armenian-inscribed Caucasian, Anatolian and Persian rugs (about 1800–1930s), Turkish rugs after the 1928–29 reforms, Soviet-era rugs, some Muslim-woven Caucasian rugs (with Hijri years), Harvard's Marasali prayer rug '1908', and modern export rugs.

woven_forms.general: Ordinary shapes, but weavers wove digits reversed, upside down, doubled, dropped or scrambled; day and month are often put between the century and the year (e.g. '19 11/7 27' for 7 Nov 1927).

A Kazak with 'Ya Huseyn' and the year 1333 in Western digits = AH 1333 (Nov 1914–Nov 1915), not AD 1333.
