facts.text: In a few cases the first or last numeral is doubled or omitted, and dates can be reversed or upside down.
Turkey made international (Western) numerals compulsory in official writing from 1 June 1929 (Law 1288 of 20 May 1928).
English rug books use 'Arabic numerals' for both Western digits and Arabic-script digits; check which is meant.

numerals.name: Armenian letter-numerals (capital letters with number values)
numerals.used_on: Armenian-era dates on 17th-century inscribed rugs; some AD years on 20th-century Caucasian rugs; manuscript colophons and gravestones
numerals.woven_forms: Written largest first and added: ՌՃԻԹ = 1000+100+20+9 = 1129. A point or stroke may follow (ՌԾԶ.). Hundreds can be written as multiplier + Ճ (ՌԲՃ եւ Կ = 1000 + 2×100 + 60 = 1260, a manuscript note). The thousands letter may be left off (a '106' read as 1706 on a ceramic).
numerals.confusions: Ի (20) vs Խ (40): the Gohar readings 1129 and 1149 differ by exactly this letter; Ghazaryan says one letter is 'sometimes confused' with another (letters lost in our OCR copy, so the pair is our inference from the arithmetic). Ռ (1000) vs Ո (600): Riegl's 651 against 1051 on the three-apsed carpet differs by exactly this letter (same inference).

facts.text: The W3C 'armenian' counter style maps 1000 to U+054C and 1 to U+0531, additive, range 1-9999.
Stone prints a table 'Armenian alphabet with numerical equivalents' for reading rug dates.
ՌԾԶ = 1056 (Armenian era) = 1607 in a dated colophon.

calendars.label: Muslim lunar (Hijri) year: AH; Persian 'qamari' (ه.ق); the usual era of woven dates before the 20th century
calendars.how_to_convert: EXACT (tabular arithmetic): AH year N begins on Julian Day JD = 1948439.5 + 354×(N−1) + floor((3 + 11×N)/30) and ends the day before year N+1 begins; turn the JD into a calendar date (Julian calendar before 15 Oct 1582, Gregorian after). Year 1 began Friday 16 July 622 (Julian). Each AH year has 354 or 355 days, so it is about 11 days shorter than a solar year and almost always straddles two AD years: write the result as a range, e.g. AH 1300 = 12 Nov 1882 – 1 Nov 1883 ('1882/83'). Real dates set by sighting the new moon can differ from the tabular ones by a day or two. QUICK ESTIMATE (old rug books): AD ≈ AH − AH/33.7 + 622 (Hawley, Stone; Jacobsen copies Hawley) or AH − AH/33 + 622 (Lewis). These land in or next to the right AD year but cannot show the straddle; use them only as a check.
worked: 946: JD of 1 Muharram 946 → 19 May 1539; year ends 7 May 1540 → '1539/40' (V&A and LACMA: 1539–40).
1247: Hawley's example: 1247 − 37 + 622 = 1832; exact range 12 Jun 1831 – 30 May 1832.
1331: Lewis's example: 1331 − 40 + 622 = 1913; exact range 11 Dec 1912 – 29 Nov 1913.
calendars.when_used: Dated rugs from the 16th century (Ardabil, AH 946) through the 20th: Persian rugs before the 1925 calendar law and often after it for religious or traditional wording; Ottoman/Anatolian prayer rugs (Ladik, Ghiordes, Kula; AH 1110–1300s); Muslim-woven Caucasian rugs (Daghestan, Shirvan, Kazak; AH 1212–1333 in the examples). Turkey's 1925 law kept the Hijri calendar for religious use.
calendars.tells_apart: On an Iranian rug a number from about 1290 to 1405 can be AH or SH, and the two readings are 38–41 years apart (AH 1300 = 1882/83; SH 1300 = 1921/22; AH 1350 = 1931/32; SH 1350 = 1971/72). A number at or below 1289 is AH, because the solar Hijri count was not in official use before 1911. A number above the current SH year (1405 in 2026) but within the AH range is AH. Lunar month names (Muharram, Rajab, Ramadan…) point to AH. On an Ottoman rug of about 1840–1925, AH and Rumi years for the same date differ by 0–3. Sources resolve the rest by style, dyes and structure, not by the number.

facts.text: The tabular Islamic calendar starts on Friday 16 July 622 (Julian), JD 1948439.5, with alternating 30- and 29-day months and 11 leap years in a 30-year cycle.
For religious purposes Muslim months begin with the first sighting of the new crescent, so real dates can differ from tabular dates.
facts.note: Met 57.5: the Met gives 14 Rajab 1280 as 26 Dec 1863; the tabular arithmetic gives 25 Dec 1863.

facts.text: Dates woven in Arabic-script digits on rugs are Hijri (Muslim) years, reckoned from the Hijra of 622.
The lunar year gains about one year on the solar year every 33.7 years; subtract 1/33.7 of the AH year and add 622.
facts.note: Jacobsen 1962/1969 copies Hawley's wording and example; not independent.

facts.text: A bare AH year covers parts of two AD years; museums write ranges such as '1210 AH/1795/96 CE' and '1287 AH (1870/71)'.
Hijri years were also written in Western digits on some Caucasian rugs (Kazak, '1333' = 1914/15, with 'Ya Huseyn').
Turkey's Law 698 (26 Dec 1925) made the Gregorian year official from 1 Jan 1926 and kept the Hijri lunar calendar for religious use.

says.text: says the Muslim year is 'thirty-three days less than ours' (an error; his 1/33 rule is still close)
lunar year gains about a year every 33.7 years (i.e. about 11 days a year)
354- or 355-day years
A.D. 1568 (wrong by about 28 years)
A.D. 1553 (wrong)

'1535 or 1540, according to inscriptions'
1298 AH catalogued as 1880 (AH 1298 began 4 Dec 1880, so nearly all of it fell in 1881)
AH 1322 catalogued as 1905 (AH 1322 ran 18 Mar 1904 – 7 Mar 1905)

disagreements.note: Catalogues pick either the starting or the ending AD year; neither is wrong, but a reader should see the range.

calendars.label: Iranian solar Hijri year: SH; Persian 'shamsi' or 'khorshidi' (ه.ش)
calendars.how_to_convert: SH year + 621 = AD year from 1 Farvardin (about 21 March) to 31 December; SH + 622 from 1 January to the end of Esfand (about 20 March). A bare SH year N therefore runs from about 21 March (N+621) to about 20 March (N+622). Months: Farvardin, Ordibehesht, Khordad, Tir, Mordad, Shahrivar (31 days each), Mehr, Aban, Azar, Dey, Bahman (30), Esfand (29, 30 in leap years). From 1911 to 1925 the same year count was used with zodiac month names (Hamal = Aries … Hut = Pisces).
worked: SH 1304 began 21 Mar 1925, so 11 Farvardin 1304 = 31 Mar 1925.
calendars.when_used: Iran's official accounting year from the General Accounts Law of 21 Safar 1329 = 2 Hut 1289 (21 Feb 1911); with Persian month names by the law of 11 Farvardin 1304 (31 Mar 1925), effective from Nowruz 1304. On rugs: Iranian rugs woven from the 1920s on may carry SH years (13xx, then 14xx from March 2021). No museum record with a woven SH date was found for this file.
calendars.tells_apart: See ah-lunar: 1290–1405 on an Iranian rug is ambiguous (38–41 years apart). Persian month names (Farvardin … Esfand) beside the year point to SH after 1925, but V&A 390-1880 shows the Persian month Khordad beside a year the V&A reads as AH (1277 = 1860/61), so a Persian month name alone is not proof. Zodiac month names point to the 1911–1925 accounting usage or to almanacs.

facts.text: The solar Hijri year with zodiac months became the official accounting calendar by Article 3 of the General Accounts Law, 21 Safar 1329 = 2 Hut 1289 SH (21 Feb 1911).
facts.note: 21 Safar 1329 = 21 Feb 1911 by the tabular arithmetic, which agrees.

facts.text: The law converting the zodiac months to Persian month names was approved on 11 Farvardin 1304 (31 March 1925), effective from Nowruz 1304.
facts.note: The 1925 year is confirmed by fourmilab_calendar; the exact day rests on Hamshahri plus the arithmetic. Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Calendars' and the University of Tehran Calendar Center pages could not be opened (403 / redirect).

facts.text: The modern Persian calendar was adopted in 1925.
The year begins at the vernal (March) equinox.
The first six months have 31 days, the next five 30, and the last 29 (30 in a leap year).
The era is counted from the Prophet's Hijra from Mecca to Medina, the same starting point as the lunar AH count.

disagreements.about: when Iran 'adopted' the solar Hijri year

says.text: official for state accounts from 1911 (zodiac months); Persian month names and the full official calendar from Nowruz 1304 (1925)
adopted in 1925

disagreements.note: Two steps, not a conflict: the SH year count existed officially from 1911.

calendars.label: Iranian 'imperial' (shahanshahi) year, 1976–1978 (UNVERIFIED in a usable source)
calendars.how_to_convert: Imperial year − 1180 = SH year; so 2535 = SH 1355 (21 Mar 1976 – 20 Mar 1977), 2536 = SH 1356 (1977/78), 2537 = SH 1357 (1978/79, until the count was dropped in late summer 1978).
calendars.when_used: Iran's official year count from March 1976 to late August or early September 1978. No source read shows it woven on a rug.
calendars.tells_apart: A woven 2535–2537 (in Persian digits) on an Iranian rug would fit this count; no other calendar on Iranian rugs gives a number in the 2500s.

calendars.label: Ottoman Rumi (fiscal, 'malî') year
calendars.how_to_convert: Up to Rumi 1332 (early 1917): the year began on 1 March and the days ran on the Julian calendar. For March-December add 584; for January and February add 585. Rumi 1 March = Gregorian 13 March in the 1800s and 14 March in the 1900s. By 1925 the year was the same as AD minus 584 for December, and the day numbers matched Gregorian ones (31 Kânunuevvel 1341 was followed by 1 Kânunusani 1926). Unverified here: the 1917 law that dropped 13 days (the day after 15 Şubat 1332 became 1 Mart 1333) and the move of New Year to 1 January from 1918 (Rumi 1334), after which +584 works all year.
calendars.when_used: Ottoman state finance and official documents: the malî year from a 1677 ferman (TDV), with TDV's worked examples from malî 1256 (= 1840); ended 31 Dec 1925 (Law 698). We found no source documenting Rumi years woven on rugs.
calendars.tells_apart: Between 1840 and 1926 a Rumi year runs 0 to 3 below the Hijri year for the same date (1840: Rumi 1256 = AH 1256; 1900: Rumi 1316 vs AH 1317/18; 1925: Rumi 1341 vs AH 1343/44). Month names Mart ... Şubat, Teşrinievvel, Kânunuevvel, Kânunusani mark a Rumi date in writing. No rug in the sources read is documented with a Rumi year.

facts.text: Julian-type 365.25-day calendars are called 'Rûmî takvim' in Turkish; the Ottoman malî year began on 1 March.
Rumi 1 March = 13 March (Gregorian) in the 1800s, 14 March in the 1900s.
Malî 1256 began on 1 March 1840 (Julian) = 9 Muharram 1256, so 1256 + 584 = 1840.

Law no. 698 (accepted 26 Dec 1925, Resmî Gazete 2 Jan 1926 no. 260): the day after 31 Kânunuevvel 1341 is 1 Kânunusani 1926; the international year count becomes official; the Hijri lunar calendar stays for religious use.
Rumi + 584 holds for December 1925 (1341) and March 1840 (1256): the two official sources agree on the same 584-year offset 85 years apart.

says.text: By the old rule tying the malî number to the Hijri year, 1288 'disappeared' (a 'sıvış yılı'); the same text calls 1 March 1872 '1 Mart 1288'.
December 1341 = December 1925, which with TDV's 1256 = 1840 leaves no room for a dropped year between 1840 and 1925.

calendars.label: Christian (Gregorian, AD) year in Western digits or, rarely, in Armenian letters
calendars.how_to_convert: Read the year as written. On Armenian-inscribed rugs, the day and month often sit between the century and the year ('19 11/7 27' = 7 Nov 1927; '18 3/10 89' = 10 Mar 1889). Before 1918 a day-and-month date from the Russian Empire was probably in the Julian calendar (Old Style), 12 days behind in the 1800s and 13 in the 1900s (not confirmed in a source read).
calendars.when_used: Armenian-inscribed Caucasian, Anatolian and Persian rugs (dated examples 1810–1938 in the Gregorian collection; Karabagh rugs of 1810–1898 in Kouymjian); Turkish rugs after the 1926–1929 reforms; Soviet-era rugs (e.g. a 1929 pictorial Karabagh); Harvard 1977.166 ('1908' three times).
calendars.tells_apart: A 4-digit Western number from 1700 to today. A Western-digit number in the 1100s–1300s on a Caucasian or Persian rug is a Hijri year written in Western digits, not an AD year (Ibrahimov's Kazak '1333'). A Western date does not by itself show an Armenian weaver.

facts.text: Law 698 (accepted 26 Dec 1925; Official Gazette 2 Jan 1926 no. 260) made the international year count official in Turkey from 1 Jan 1926: the day after 31 Kânunuevvel 1341 became 1 Kânunusani 1926.
Law 1288 (20 May 1928) made Western numerals compulsory in official writing from 1 June 1929; Law 1353 (1 Nov 1928) adopted the Latin alphabet.
Turkish rugs were often dated in Western style after Atatürk's reforms.
Dates on Armenian-inscribed rugs are often followed by ԹՎ ('year') or ԱՄԻ ('in the year').
Kouymjian's captions give Armenian-inscribed Karabagh rugs dated 26 June 1810, 1815, 1866, 1877, 8 June 1884, 6 April 1888 and 1898 (AD).
facts.note: Several are Gregorian Collection rugs, so not fully independent of gregorian_1987.

facts.text: A Gregorian date is a year counted from the birth of Christ as adjusted by Pope Gregory in 1582, as distinct from Islamic dates.

disagreements.about: does a Western-digit date point to an Armenian weaver?

says.text: Caucasian rugs with western dates are 'probably Armenian in origin'.
a western-style date is not enough, since Turkish rugs were dated in western style after Atatürk's reforms.
Hijri years in Western digits appear on Muslim-inscribed Kazaks sold as Armenian.

calendars.label: Armenian era (Great Armenian Era) year written in Armenian letters
calendars.how_to_convert: Add up the letter values (see numerals.armenian_letters), then add 551. The Armenian year had 365 days and no leap day, so its New Year slid back through the Julian calendar about one day every four years (by our calculation from a 552 epoch: early October in the 1670s, late September around 1700, end of August around 1810). A bare Armenian year therefore straddles two AD years: +551 gives the AD year that holds most of it, and the last months of the AD year before belong to the same Armenian year. When a Julian month is named, add 551 (Khachikian, followed by Grigoryan).
calendars.when_used: On the oldest inscribed Armenian rugs: the 'three-apsed' carpet (Armenian era 1051 = 1602) and the Gohar carpet (1129 or 1149 = 1680 or 1700). Later inscribed rugs (1800s-1930s) mostly give the AD year (see ad_western_digits_armenian), but some AD years are written with Armenian letters (see ad_in_armenian_letters).
calendars.tells_apart: Armenian capital letters, not digits, usually led by Ռ (1000). If letters + 551 lands in the future (e.g. ՌՋԻԸ = 1928, +551 = 2479), the weaver wrote the AD year in letters: read it without adding 551.

facts.text: Dates on Armenian rugs often appear in letter form; convert by summing the letter values and adding 551.

Kendrick & Tattersall read the Gohar inscription's date as Armenian 1129 = AD 1679; Ghazaryan gives the same inscription as 1680. Armenian year 1129 ran from about 3 Oct 1679 to 1 Oct 1680 (Julian), so both fit one reading.
Armenian-era 1051 + 551 = 1602 (the 'three-apsed' carpet).
In manuscript colophons the date is introduced by the word թվական ('year'), e.g. 'ի թվականիս հայոց ՌԾԶ' (in the Armenian year 1056 = 1607), December ԻԳ (23).

Some editors add 550 instead of 551 for dates between about 18 October and 31 December in the early 1600s, because the Armenian year then began in October; Khachikian argued +551 still applies when Julian months are named.
The day the Armenian era began (by our calculation 11 July 552, Julian) is not confirmed in a source read; the +551 rule is (Stone, Ghazaryan, Grigoryan).
facts.note: Year ranges given in this file assume the 552 epoch and a 365-day year with no leap day.

disagreements.about: +550 or +551 for the last months of the AD year

says.text: Hakobyan & Hovhannisyan add 550 for 18 Oct-31 Dec in 1604-1607; Khachikian (followed by Grigoryan) adds 551 whenever Julian month names are used.

calendars.label: AD year written with Armenian letter-numerals (no 551 added)
calendars.how_to_convert: Sum the letter values; the result is already the AD year.
calendars.when_used: Early 1900s Caucasian rugs; Gregorian's Plate 87 (Moghan, dated 1928) writes the year first in ornate Armenian numerals, then the same AD year in western digits.
calendars.tells_apart: Letter sum of 1800-1950 with Ռ (1000) + Պ (800) or Ջ (900). Adding 551 would give a year after 2350.

facts.text: On a rug dated 1928 the date is written in ornate Armenian numerals first, followed by the same Christian-calendar year in western digits.
The History Museum of Armenia describes dating on Armenian-inscribed carpets as 'often made in Armenian letters or in Arab figures' (it does not say which era the letters count from).

calendars.label: Chinese reign title with a 60-year cycle (ganzhi) year; Mongolian and Tibetan forms name an element-color and an animal
calendars.how_to_convert: 1) Find the reign's span (Qianlong 乾隆 1736–1795; Jiaqing 嘉慶 1796–1820; Daoguang 道光 1821–1850; Xianfeng 咸豐 1851–1861; Tongzhi 同治 1862–1874; Guangxu 光緒 1875–1908; Xuantong 宣統 1909–1911). 2) The cyclical sign repeats every 60 years. Stem = (AD − 4) mod 10 in 甲乙丙丁戊己庚辛壬癸; branch = (AD − 4) mod 12 in 子丑寅卯辰巳午未申酉戌亥. 3) Take the one AD year inside the reign that has the sign. Mongolian/Tibetan wording such as 'year of the blue hen' gives the element-color (blue/green = wood = 甲 or 乙; the female animal = the odd stem 乙) and the animal (hen/rooster = 酉).
worked: 乙酉 (yi-you): 1765, 1825, 1885. In Qianlong only 1765 (Qianlong 30); in Guangxu only 1885 (Guangxu 11).
'Year of the blue hen' in Guangxu (Mongolian 'Badaraghultu Tore') = 乙酉 = 1885.
calendars.when_used: Inscribed temple pillar rugs and hangings (Chinese, Mongolian, Tibetan). The V&A's pair of pillar rugs carries a Chinese Qianlong yi-you date and a Mongolian Guangxu 'blue hen' date. No reign mark (年製) woven into a Chinese pile carpet was verified (see words).
calendars.tells_apart: Chinese characters for a reign name plus two cyclical characters; or a Mongolian/Tibetan line naming a color and an animal year.

facts.text: A Chinese inscription on V&A pillar rug T.238-1928 gives the yi-you year of Qianlong, i.e. 1765; the museum dates the rug 1885 and calls the Chinese date a weaving error.
The Mongolian inscription on its pair, T.239-1928, names the year of the blue hen in the reign of Badaraghultu Tore (Guangxu), which the V&A gives as 1885.
Reign-plus-cyclical dating appears on other Qing textiles (AIC 1907.322, a Daoist vestment: the guichou year of Qianlong, i.e. 1793).
facts.note: Not a rug; shows the formula.

Mongolian date = 1885, used for both rugs

facts.text: Memorial rugs stress an exact date, as on Armenian gravestones; one rug reads '1904 IN MEMORY OF ...'.

facts.text: Inscriptions made of a palace hall's name followed by 御用 (yuyong, 'for imperial use') are recorded on Chinese carpets with silk pile, usually on a metal-thread ground, that sellers catalogue as Qing.

Sotheby's says carpets with a yuyong mark are rare.

words.meaning: 'for use (in)', as the auction houses translate it. Literally it means 'held ready for use', so a spare or reserve piece. The literal gloss is this researcher's reading, not from a source.

facts.text: Some inscribed carpets end in 備用 (beiyong) rather than 御用, for example 武英殿備用 and Jingrengong beiyong.

signatures.what_it_tells: A woven five-character line along the top edge naming a Forbidden City hall + 'for imperial use' (御用) or 'for use' (備用). It gives a place of use, never a date; the hall's naming date gives an earliest date (體和殿 got that name in the Guangxu reign, 1875–1908).

formats.how_to_read: سنه = 'year'; read the digits left to right; the year is AH unless something says otherwise.

formats.example: عمل بنده درگاه مقصود کاشانی سنه ۹۴۶
formats.how_to_read: 'Work of the servant of the threshold, Maqsud of Kashan, year 946.' The name, its place ending and the year are the facts; the humility formula is politeness.
formats.worked: As above: 1539/40.

formats.how_to_read: 'Order of Dilmaghani, (12)92.' The century is left off; supply it from the rug's style and the firm's dates.
formats.worked: [12]92 AH = 7 Feb 1875 – 27 Jan 1876 (Harvard: 1875/1876). Arithmetic alone also allows [13]92 = 1972/73.

formats.example: ۱۴ رجب المرجب … ۱۲۸ (the Met gives only the translation 'Rajab the honored [month], 14, in 128'; the Persian wording here is reconstructed)
formats.how_to_read: Day, month 'Rajab the honored', then the year. '128' has a digit missing.
formats.worked: Met reads 1280: 14 Rajab 1280 = 25 Dec 1863 by the tabular arithmetic; the Met gives 26 Dec 1863 (one day apart: sighting vs arithmetic). Other arithmetic possibilities (1128 = 1716, 1281–1289) are not excluded by the number itself; the Met's 'probably' rests on the rug.

formats.example: تاریخ هشتم خرداد سنه ۱۲۷۷ (from the V&A transliteration Ta'rikh-e hashtom-e Khordad saneh 1277)
formats.how_to_read: 'Date: 8th of Khordad, year 1277.' Khordad is the third month of the Persian solar year (about 22 May – 21 June).
formats.worked: If 1277 is AH (20 Jul 1860 – 8 Jul 1861, as the V&A reads it), Khordad falls in May–June 1861 (8 Khordad ≈ 29 May 1861). The V&A's note 'Khordad 1277 = October 1860' matches the third LUNAR month (Rabiʿ I 1277 = 17 Sep – 16 Oct 1860), not Khordad. If 1277 were SH, the date would be 1898, but the SH count was not official before 1911.

formats.pattern: two different years on one rug
formats.how_to_read: Probably the years the weaving began and ended.
formats.worked: 1324 = 25 Feb 1906 – 13 Feb 1907; 1327 = 23 Jan 1909 – 12 Jan 1910: about three years of work.

formats.example: 1182 woven four times; 1287 in both spandrels; 1908 three times
formats.how_to_read: Repetition confirms the reading; compare all copies before choosing a digit.

formats.pattern: year in a prayer-rug niche, arch apex or spandrel
formats.example: a yellow panel under the arch: ١٢١١
formats.how_to_read: Prayer rugs often put the date at the top of the niche, in a medallion at the apex, or in the spandrels.
formats.worked: Ladik 1211 = 7 Jul 1796 – 25 Jun 1797 (Kendrick: 1797).

formats.how_to_read: A digit is missing. Either the last digit (117x → 1170–1179) or the leading 1 (1117) may be left off; never pick one from the number alone.
UNVERIFIED on rugs: 2535–2537 would be the 1976–78 imperial year count; subtract 1180 for the SH year.

formats.worked: Armenian year 1129 ran about 3 Oct 1679 - 1 Oct 1680 (Julian): 'AD 1679/80'. Kendrick prints 1679, Ghazaryan 1680.
Armenian year 1149 ran about 28 Sep 1699 - 26 Sep 1700 (Julian): '1699/1700', which covers both Kouymjian's 1699 (2011) and 1700 (1992).
Ghazaryan: 1051 + 551 = 1602; Riegl read 651 + 551 = 1202. Letters are our reconstruction from the numbers.

formats.pattern: [AD year in Armenian letters] [same year in western digits]
formats.how_to_read: 1000 + 900 + 20 + 8 = 1928 AD; do not add 551 (that would give 2479)
formats.worked: Gregorian Plate 87: ornate Armenian numerals followed by the same Christian-calendar year in western digits (letters ours, from the year).

formats.how_to_read: AD year + 'year'
formats.worked: 1913 ԹՎ = in the year 1913

formats.how_to_read: century + year digits = year; month then day in the middle
26 June 1810
formats.worked: Kouymjian's caption for the same rug: 'Armenian inscription of 26 June 1810'

formats.pattern: [AD year in western digits] / [number 'in Islamic form']
formats.how_to_read: Read the western date; check the second number by Hijri and Rumi arithmetic
formats.worked: AH 1329 = 1911 and Rumi 1329 = 1913/14, neither = 1919; AH 1332 = 1913/14 and Rumi 1332 = 1916/17, neither = 1912. The pairs do not agree.

formats.pattern: [Hijri year in western digits] with Arabic-script words

formats.how_to_read: Rumi + 584 for March-December; + 585 for January-February before the 1917-18 changes
formats.worked: Kânunuevvel 1341 = December 1925 (Law 698); 1 Mart 1256 = 1 March 1840 Julian = 13 March 1840 Gregorian

formats.pattern: [hall name, usually 3 characters] + 御用 — five characters in a row
formats.how_to_read: Read the hall name (宮 gong = palace, 殿 dian = hall), then 御用 'for imperial use'. Look along the top edge, centered in the outer band. No source read states the reading direction; Qing horizontal inscriptions can run right to left, so if the line reads 用御宮仁景, reverse it. That rule is unsourced.
formats.worked: Sotheby's Paris 2022 lot 16: 景仁宮御用 = Jingren gong (Palace of Great Benevolence, one of the Six Eastern Palaces) + yuyong, 'for imperial use'. The inscription names the place it was meant for. It is not a date. Catalogued as Qing, 19th century.

formats.how_to_read: The hall name, then 備用 beiyong, which auction houses translate 'for use (in)'. Sotheby's (2018) thinks these were for more general use than 御用 pieces.
formats.worked: Sotheby's Paris 2023 lot 111: 武英殿備用 = Wuying dian (Hall of Martial Valor) + beiyong. Catalogued as Qing, 19th century.

formats.pattern: The hall name sets the earliest possible date
formats.how_to_read: Check when the hall got that name. A carpet made for a hall can't predate the hall's name, though a later inscription is always possible. The name gives an earliest date, never a latest one.
formats.worked: The Palace Museum says 体和殿 was created and named in the Guangxu reign (1875–1908). A carpet inscribed 體和殿御用 (Sotheby's Paris 2022 lot 33, catalogued '19th century') therefore points to 1875 or later. Names such as 景仁宮 (since 1535) or 太和殿 give no useful limit.

formats.how_to_read: Find a single line of Tibetan or Mongolian script across the top of a temple hanging or pillar rug. It names the donor and records the gift ('bul = offered). It doesn't give a date or the place of weaving.
formats.worked: AIC 1997.895 (pillar carpet, mid-19th century): 'donated by the monk Trinlay'. Palace Museum 新00060939: one line of Tibetan at the top, read together with a Mongolian inscription on a matching piece, meaning roughly 'devoutly offered by [a sutra teacher]'.

formats.pattern: Reign name + cyclical (ganzhi) year (no Chinese rug example verified)
formats.how_to_read: Take the reign's years (Qianlong = 1736–1795). The 60-year cycle repeats, so find the one year in that span with the named cyclical sign. Guichou years fall in 1733 and 1793, and only 1793 is within Qianlong.
formats.worked: On a Daoist vestment, not a rug: AIC 1907.322, 'the quichao [sic] year of the Qianlong [emperor] [i.e., 1793]'. No carpet with a woven ganzhi date was found.

formats.pattern: An owner's name woven in gold characters at the upper end (single report)
formats.how_to_read: This is a personal name, not a date or a workshop.
formats.worked: Leitch's plate 18 is a Qianlong-attributed silk rug with gold-thread ground. Leitch says the original owner's name was woven 'in gold characters' at the upper end.

decode_rules: 1. FIND. A date candidate is a run of 2–4 digits in ONE numeral system (Arabic-Indic ٠–٩, Persian ۰–۹, or Western 0–9), a run of Armenian capital letters, or Chinese reign/cyclical characters. Read it as a date only when it (a) sits in a cartouche, an end panel, the top of a prayer niche, a spandrel or a border panel, or (b) stands next to a date word (سنه, تاریخ, ԹՎ/թվին, ամի, 年), or (c) repeats elsewhere on the rug. Otherwise report 'a number, not read as a date'. [stone_2013 'inscription'; lewis_1920; kendrick_1922; museum examples]

2. NEVER READ AS A DATE: knot counts, sizes, stock or inventory numbers, prices, quality grades, or any number on a sewn-on label, a stamp or ink on the back. Sewn labels (e.g. 1920s–30s Chinese export firms) are not woven inscriptions. [editorial rule; hali_young_2018 on labels]

3. DO NOT READ ORNAMENT AS SCRIPT: Kufesque borders, pseudo-inscriptions and lucky characters (壽, 福, 囍) are design, not marks or dates. Crude imitation script appears on modern copies. [stone_2013 'calligraphy'/'Kufesque'; ripley_1904; kendrick_1922]
4. DIRECTION. Read Arabic-script digits left to right, largest place first, even though the words around them run right to left. [lewis_1920; stone_2013]

5. ORIENTATION. Read from the side where the surrounding letters are upright. If the digits look mirrored, the inscription may have been copied from the back of another rug (mirror writing) or you may be reading through the back: reverse the order. If upside down, rotate before reading; upside down, ٧ (V, 7) and ٨ (Λ, 8) swap (inferred from the shapes). [stone_2013 'mirror writing'; hawley_1922; lewis_1920; gregorian_1987]

6. DIGIT SHAPES. A dot is 0; a small circle is the Arabic 5 (٥), not 0; the Persian 5 (۵) is a pointed loop. Persian and Arabic 4, 5 and 6 differ, and woven pieces mix them. When a digit is unclear, give every plausible digit (2/3, 2/4, 3/4, 1/2, 0/8 are documented museum disagreements) and every resulting year. [unicode_18_ch9; vam_T_25_1983; poldi_DT_0001; aic_1948_163; met_22_100_61; met_22_100_3]

7. CALENDAR FOR ARABIC-SCRIPT DIGITS, IRANIAN RUG: ≤1289 → AH only. 1290 up to the current SH year (1405 in 2026) → give BOTH AH and SH readings with both AD ranges (they are 38–41 years apart) and say the number alone cannot decide. Above the current SH year → AH only. A lunar month name (Muharram, Safar, Rabiʿ, Jumada, Rajab, Shaʿban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhu al-Qaʿda, Dhu al-Hijja) → AH. A Persian month name (Farvardin … Esfand) → SH after 1925, but not decisive before that (V&A 390-1880 pairs Khordad with an AH year). Words قمری/ه.ق or شمسی/ه.ش, if woven, decide it (no woven example in the sources read). [hamshahri_mahha; fourmilab_calendar; vam_390_1880]

8. CALENDAR FOR ARABIC-SCRIPT DIGITS, OTTOMAN OR ANATOLIAN RUG: a year 1256–1341 may be AH or Rumi; give both (Rumi + 584 for March–December, + 585 for January–February before 1917–18). The two differ by 0–3 years. No rug in the sources read is documented with a Rumi year, so AH is the default and Rumi the alternative. [tdv_takvim_2010; tr_law_698]

9. WESTERN DIGITS: 1700 to the current year → AD. A Western-digit 11xx–13xx on a Caucasian, Persian or Turkish rug → a Hijri year written in Western digits (give the AH range). A 5-digit run such as 11838 or 19299 → probably a doubled digit; offer the 4-digit readings. Day and month may sit between century and year ('18 3/10 89' = 10 Mar 1889). [ibrahimov_2021; gregorian_1987]

10. ARMENIAN LETTERS: add the letter values (Ա=1 … Թ=9, Ժ=10 … Ղ=90, Ճ=100 … Ջ=900, Ռ=1000). If sum + 551 is later than today, the weaver wrote the AD year: read the sum as AD. Otherwise read it as an Armenian-era year: AD ≈ sum + 551, spanning two AD years (the Armenian year started in late summer or autumn in the 1600s–1800s). Watch Ի (20) / Խ (40) and Ռ (1000) / Ո (600). [stone_2013; ghazaryan_1988; gregorian_1987; w3c_css_counter_styles]

11. ALWAYS A RANGE. Report AH years as start–end dates (tabular arithmetic, ± 1–2 days for moon sighting), SH years as about 21 March – 20 March, Armenian-era years as their 365-day span, Rumi years as 1 March – end of February. Never collapse a range to one AD year without saying so. [fourmilab_calendar; met_22_100_61; vam_408_1880]

12. SHORTENED YEARS. A 2-digit year → the century was left off: offer 12xx and 13xx (AH) or 18xx/19xx (AD) as fits the script. A 3-digit year → either the last digit (117 → 1170–1179) or the leading 1 (117 → 1117) is missing: offer both. Never choose from the number alone; the catalogued readings ([12]92, 128 → 1280, 117 → 1170) rest on the rug's style. [harvard_1943_1772; met_57_5; kendrick_1922]

13. MORE THAN ONE DATE. Report each date. Two different years can be start and finish (AH 1324 and 1327 on a Kerman pictorial). Two dates in different calendars should agree; if they don't by any arithmetic, say so (Gregorian Plates 12 and 13). [kendrick_1922; gregorian_1987]

14. CHINESE: a hall name + 御用/備用 names where a carpet was meant to be used, not when or where it was made; the hall's naming date (e.g. 體和殿, Guangxu reign 1875–1908) is the earliest possible date. A reign + cyclical pair → the single year in that reign with that sign; if none fits, flag it (V&A T.238-1928). A Tibetan or Mongolian line names a donor or offering, not a place of weaving. [dpm_buildings; vam_T_238_1928; vam_T_239_1928; aic_1997_895]
15. 2500s IN PERSIAN DIGITS on an Iranian rug → possibly the 1976–78 imperial year (subtract 1180 for SH); unverified, so flag it. [see calendars.imperial-iranian]

16. WORDING OF THE ANSWER. Say 'the rug carries the date …, which reads as …'; never 'the rug was made in …'. Add the cautions that dates can be copied, added or altered and that a woven date is not proof of age. Say 'the rug carries the name X' for a signature; never treat a famous name as proof of maker, town or age. [stone_2013 'dates' and 'post knotting'; hawley_1922; mirzaei_2022_rajshomar]

17. CHRONOGRAMS. If a line of verse sits where a date would be and no digits are present, the date may be a chronogram (the sum of the letters' numerical values); flag it for a specialist rather than computing it. [stone_2013 'chronogram']

cautions.text: A woven date may be copied from an older rug the weaver worked from, so it can be earlier than the weaving.
Dates in modern rugs are often made earlier on purpose to suggest age; dates in old rugs are more often reliable.
cautions.note: Jacobsen 1962 repeats this, with the line at 1900; he copies Hawley.

cautions.text: Dates can be altered after weaving by re-knotting ('post knotting') to make a rug look older; look for fresher yarn, different knots or rewoven patches around the date.
cautions.note: Met 1923: the date on 22.100.61 'appears to have been altered by restoration'.

cautions.text: Inscriptions have been added to, inked out of, or rewoven into rugs, including Armenian inscriptions on Caucasian rugs (Ibrahimov says original Muslim inscriptions were replaced; Gregorian says Armenian ones on rugs from Turkey were inked out or woven over). Report such claims as claims.
What a date marks is not always the finish of the weaving: it may be the start, the finish (two dates on one Kerman pictorial), the commission, a gift, or a memorial (Armenian memorial rugs).
cautions.note: Hawley says the Ardabil date's position shows it was woven a little before the carpet was finished.

cautions.text: Digits are easily misread: museums have changed their readings by a century or more (Met 22.100.96: 1022 → 1210; 22.100.61: 1110 → 1210) and still give two readings for some rugs (V&A T.25-1983; Poldi Pezzoli; AIC 1948.163).

Old rug books often convert dates wrongly: the Ardabil 946 appears as 1568 (Holt), 1553 (Langton) and '942 (i.e. 1539)' (Pope); the Met's 1923 catalogue printed '1323 A.H., corresponding to 1806'. Re-do the arithmetic.
A place word in a signature ('of Kashan', 'of Kerman') tells where a person came from, not necessarily where the rug was woven.
A commission line (سفارش …) names a patron, merchant or firm, not the weaver; the firm may have ordered rugs in another town.
Famous workshop names are faked: a Mashhad expert reports fake 'Saber' and 'Khadivi' rugs every week, and the trade uses names such as Haji Jalili and Mohtasham for unsigned rugs.
Mirror-image inscriptions happen when a weaver copies an inscription from the back of a rug without reading it.
Modern copies may imitate script crudely; such characters deceive readers who don't know Arabic writing.
Weavers doubled, dropped, reversed, scrambled or upside-down-wove digits ('11838', '19299', '1992' for 1929).
A Western-digit date on a Caucasian or Turkish rug does not by itself show an Armenian weaver; scholars disagree.
Chinese palace-hall inscriptions name an intended place of use, not a date; modern copies of inscribed palace carpets exist; auction houses have misread and misprinted the characters.
Labels of 1920s–30s Chinese export firms (Nichols, Fette-Li, Karagheusian) were sewn on, not woven, and are often lost; unlabeled rugs are called by these names loosely.
Weavers seldom signed or dated antique rugs; most dated pieces readers meet are 19th–20th century.
cautions.note: AIC: carpets with inscriptions and dates are extremely rare.

cautions.text: Quick formulas from old books (AH − AH/33.7 + 622) can be a year off; a bare year always spans parts of two AD years.

The Chinese carpets with woven palace-hall inscriptions found here are silk-pile carpets, usually on metal-thread grounds. No source read links a woven hall inscription to a Ningxia wool carpet. The Palace Museum's Ningxia and Xinjiang palace carpets read online carry no inscriptions. The one HALI-reported 'Ningxia' piece with a Temple of Heaven cartouche is silk and metal thread, attributed by the auction house.

Dates for inscribed silk-and-metal 'palace' carpets vary by seller: c.1800 (Sotheby's 2018), mid-19th century (Sotheby's 2020), 19th century (Sotheby's 2015, 2022, 2023), c.1880 (Sotheby's 2019), late 19th century or earlier (Christie's NY 2016), 19th–early 20th century (Christie's), c.1900 (Grogan 2017), c.1910 under Puyi (Bonhams 2003, Dorotheum 2017). One dealer says the palace destination is 'ostensibly' given by the inscriptions and dates the silk-on-metal technique in Peking to about 1900. Chinese sources say this gold-thread weaving died out in the 1920s or after the Qing. An inscription states an intended place of use, not a weaving date, and no technical study was found.

Modern copies exist. Beijing Carpet Factory No. 5 revived gold-thread palace carpets in 2003–2005 by studying Palace Museum originals, and the Palace Museum has had copies woven for display. A Palace Museum curator recognized photos brought by a collector as the museum's own recent copies.

Readings and printed characters can be wrong. Bonhams read 'Jing … Ren' as 'in the capital' where Sotheby's and Christie's read the palace name 景仁宮, and Sotheby's printed 乾精宮 for 乾清宮. Read the woven characters yourself, and don't trust a romanization alone.
A hall name sets an earliest date only (for example, 體和殿 was named in the Guangxu reign). It never proves age, and the inscription could have been added to a later copy.

No reign mark (年制) or cyclical (ganzhi) date woven into a Chinese pile carpet was verified. Kendrick warned in 1922 that Ming attributions for silk and gold carpets have 'small justification as a rule'. Treat a reign or dynasty given by a seller as an attribution, not a reading.
Woven characters such as 壽 shou, 福 fu and 囍 xi are ornament (good wishes). They are not marks, signatures or dates and do not place or date a rug.

1920s–30s export firms (Nichols, Fette-Li, Karagheusian) marked rugs with sewn labels or emblems in the sources read, not woven names. Labels are often lost, and the trade uses 'Nichols' and 'Fette' loosely for unlabeled rugs in their style.

Tibetan, Mongolian (and, per Kendrick, Manchu) lines on temple and pillar rugs name donors and offerings. They don't name the weaving place. The Palace Museum piece came to Beijing as tribute from Tibet.
Count unknown. Roughly 20 auction appearances of hall-inscribed carpets (2003–2024) are cited across the texts read, and some may be the same carpet resold. No census was found.

No rug-specific source describes how individual Persian or Arabic digits look when woven; the shape notes come from the Unicode reference glyphs plus museum disagreements. A photo study of dated rugs (open-licence Met/AIC images) would settle it.
No source counts how often dates are mirrored or upside down.
'Lucky number' dates: no source found that says weavers wove lucky numbers as dates.
Afghanistan's use of the solar Hijri year on rugs, and Pakistani/Indian rug dates: not researched.
The Persian everyday word سال ('year'), and کار / طرح / نقشه in signatures: no woven example found.

Stone (Cyrillic rare; artels; five-year-plan rugs), Jacobsen (1929-35 imports, cotton warps), Gregorian (portrait carpets of statesmen exist; 1929 soldier rug) and Ghazaryan (Haygorg 1921) are all we have.
