values.looks_like: Checkered (quincunx) back; rug often thin and flexible.
values.points_to: Hawley: Sehna (fine cotton weft) and Hamadan (heavy cotton weft); May: Hamadan-area rugs; Stone: Lillihan, Reihan and other Arak-area village rugs, 'Ahar' in the Heriz area.

values.looks_like: Continuous weft between rows; on offset rugs one straight (cable) and one wavy (sinuous).
values.points_to: Most rugs, per Hawley.

values.looks_like: Heavier weft band; very compact.
values.points_to: Hawley: some Anatolians; Stone: early Bijar (one weft very heavy); Iranica: 'vase technique' Safavid carpets, and Kerman and Bijar today.

values.looks_like: Beaded rows of weft, number varying across the rug.
values.points_to: Hawley: Gengha, Tcherkess, Bergama and many rugs over 150 years old; Khorassan with an extra weft every few rows; Herat alternating 2 and 3.

pitfalls: Hawley counts 'crossings': his 'crosses twice' means across and back once, which modern writers call two wefts (two shoots). His 'crosses once' is one weft.
Worn backs hide the wefts; look near the ends or under a fold.

facts.text: Weavers of Sehna rugs insert only a single weft between rows, giving the back a checkered or quincunx look.
facts.quote: Weavers of Sehna rugs insert only a single thread of weft between every two rows of knots

facts.text: In almost all other rugs the weft crosses twice (across and back once) between every two rows of knots.
facts.quote: In almost all other rugs the weft crosses twice, that is, across and back once, between every two rows of knots

facts.text: When warps are offset, one weft is straight and taut (cable weft) and the other bends (sinuous weft); in some rugs the cable weft is much thicker.
Early Bijar rugs usually have three wefts, one of them very heavy, hammered down hard, which makes them very stiff; later ones have two.

features.name: Pile material
how_to_look: Part the pile and look at the yarn in daylight. Wool has a soft, slightly crimped look and a satin sheen when good; silk is very fine with a glassy, prismatic shine; mercerized cotton and viscose are glossy but often look flat, plastic or 'wet' and crush easily.
Rub a tuft between your fingers: silk feels cool and firm; viscose feels slippery and very soft; cotton pile is matte and soft and mats down.

Look at the back of a supposedly silk rug: if the warps and wefts are cotton and the back looks dull while the front shines, the pile may still be silk, but if the whole piece is unusually cheap, glossy and the pile flattens and stays flat, suspect viscose or mercerized cotton.
A burn test is the classic check but needs a loose fiber you can sacrifice; never cut from the field.

values.looks_like: Soft, slightly crimped, satin sheen when good, dull when poor.
values.points_to: Over 90 percent of pile rugs (Hawley).
values.note: See materials for kork, dead wool and Manchester wool.

values.looks_like: Fine, glassy, very sharp design detail; colors change with the light direction.
values.points_to: Fine city rugs of Persia and Turkey (Kashan, Qum, Hereke etc.), Chinese and Indian silk rugs; Turkmen use small silk highlights.

values.looks_like: Glossy but harder and flatter shine than silk.
values.points_to: Hawley: pile in a few districts of Asia Minor and Persia; Stone: Kayseri rugs may be wool, rayon, mercerized cotton or, rarely, silk.

values.looks_like: Very glossy, slippery, crushes and marks easily; colors may change or bleed when wet.
values.points_to: Modern decorative production from several countries.
values.note: Labels claiming 'bamboo silk' describe rayon in US law.

values.looks_like: Natural tan to brown, slightly coarser.
values.points_to: Hamadan borders (Hawley: a broad band of camel's hair); dyed wool or goat hair often substituted (Hawley, Stone).

values.looks_like: Wiry, lustrous, dark.
values.points_to: Mohair in some Anatolian rugs (Hawley); occasional tribal use.

values.looks_like: Bright, hard white spots in the pile.
values.points_to: Small white highlights in some Turkmen, Caucasian and Turkish rugs; allover cotton pile is uncommon because it mats (Stone).

pitfalls: Viscose, mercerized cotton and silk all shine; shine alone is not proof of silk.
Trade names on tags ('Persian silk', 'bamboo silk', 'art silk') do not state fiber content reliably.

facts.text: The wool of sheep forms the warp and weft of at least half of Oriental rugs and the pile of over ninety per cent.
facts.quote: The wool of sheep constitutes the warp and weft of at least half the Oriental rugs and the pile of over ninety per cent.

facts.text: In a few districts of Asia Minor and Persia the pile is mercerized cotton or silk.
Cotton is not generally used as an allover pile fiber because it tends to mat; undyed cotton is used for small bright white areas.
Silk imitations in mercerized cotton and 'wool silk' were already common enough in 1911-20 to mislead buyers of silk rugs.

features.name: Pile height
how_to_look: Part the pile in an unworn area (under furniture or near the border) and hold a ruler against the knots: measure from the back of the pile row to the tips.
Compare worn and unworn areas: uneven wear by color is itself a clue (see age_and_wear).

values.looks_like: Velvety, crisp outlines.
values.points_to: Hawley: Sarouk, Kashan, Tabriz; finer rugs generally (short pile goes with clear drawing).
Most village rugs.

values.looks_like: Shaggy, soft outlines.
values.points_to: Hawley: Kazak, Yuruk, Bergama, Karaman, Rhodian, Shiraz, Niris, Mosul, Kurdistan.
values.note: Hawley: long pile protects the knot foundations and wears longer.

pitfalls: Pile height is mostly a matter of how the rug was clipped and how it has worn; antiques and heavily washed rugs are often lower than when made.

facts.text: Sehna (asymmetric) knots, which allow closer weaving and clearer patterns, generally appear in rugs of shorter nap.
Long nap protects the knot foundations and so is better for durability.
facts.quote: For durability, long nap is also to be preferred to short, since it protects the foundations of the knots from wearing and becoming loose.

features.name: Pile direction (which way the nap lies)
how_to_look: Run your hand along the length of the rug: it feels smooth one way and rough the other. The smooth direction points to the end where weaving began (usually the bottom of the design).
Look from each end: the rug looks lighter and shinier from one end and darker and richer from the other.

values.looks_like: Smooth stroke one way.
values.points_to: Normal hand-knotted rug woven from bottom to top.

values.looks_like: Smooth stroke across the rug.
values.points_to: Hawley: rare rugs woven with the warps horizontal, knots in rows parallel to the sides.

pitfalls: Lewis (1920) says many imitation silk rugs can be detected because the pile leans toward the top instead of the bottom; that is a test of design orientation, not of fiber, and single-sourced.

facts.text: Knots are almost always tied from left to right and from the bottom up, and the pile leans toward the end where weaving started.
facts.quote: rubbing the hand over the pile, when it will be noticed that the knots lie on one another so as to face the same direction, which is the opposite to that in which the work of tying advanced

facts.text: An old rug looks light and glossy when the nap runs away from you and dark and rich when seen from the other end.

features.name: Spin and ply of the yarn
how_to_look: Untwist the end of a pile tuft or a fringe thread. First see how many strands (plies) are twisted together.
Hold one strand upright: if its fibers slant like the middle stroke of the letter Z it is Z-spun; like the middle of an S, S-spun.
Then look at the plied yarn the same way: most rug yarn is Z-spun singles plied together with an S twist (Z2S).

values.looks_like: Fibers slant like the middle of a Z.
values.points_to: Almost all rugs from Turkey, the Caucasus, Iran, Central Asia, India and China.

values.looks_like: Fibers slant like the middle of an S.
values.points_to: Stone: found almost exclusively in weavings from North Africa and the western Arabian peninsula (e.g. Egyptian 'Mamluk' carpets).
values.note: Unusual; worth noting if found.

pitfalls: Some yarn is hand-spun and irregular; check several strands.

facts.text: Most yarns have Z-spun singles plied with an S twist; S-spun singles are found almost only in weavings from North Africa and the western Arabian peninsula.
The ply of the yarn, and how loosely or tightly the plies are twisted, are among the indices that distinguish rugs of different districts.

features.name: Sides (edge finish along the length)
how_to_look: Look at the long edges front and back. Is the edge simply wrapped in yarn (overcast), or is there a narrow flat-woven band (selvage) built round several cords?
Count the cords at the edge by pressing along it: one cord, two, three or more bundles.
Note the wrapping color and pattern: one color, color blocks, checkerboard, or 'barber-pole' stripes; any tassels or tufts.
Check whether the wrapping is original: newer yarn of a different color or twist, a wrap that covers part of the border, or an edge that curls under suggests later rebinding.

values.looks_like: Yarn wrapped round a single edge cord.
values.points_to: Hawley: with few exceptions Persian rugs have overcast sides.

values.looks_like: Extra yarn wound over the weft-wrapped cord or several cords.
values.points_to: Hawley's type; common.

values.looks_like: Two or more cords wrapped figure-eight by the weft to make a flat band beyond the knots.
values.points_to: Hawley: Caucasian and Turkish rugs and, among Persians, Karadagh, Gorevan, Serapi, Herez, Tabriz; double selvage on Baluch and Afghan rugs.

values.looks_like: Edge wrapping in alternating colored stripes or segments.
values.points_to: Hawley: Shiraz and Niris; Stone: nomadic and tribal rugs generally; Shiraz also has small tufts of wool projecting from the sides (Hawley).

pitfalls: Sides are the first part of a rug to be replaced; much rebinding on old rugs is not original (Hawley, Lewis). A modern machine-stitched or tape binding means repair or a machine-made or tufted rug.
Hawley: rebinding done too tightly makes the sides curl.

facts.text: Sides are finished by overcasting a single cord or by wrapping two or more cords to make a selvage.
With few exceptions Persian rugs have overcast sides, while the other groups have both overcasting and selvages.
facts.quote: with few exceptions, the Persian rugs have a side finish of overcasting; and the other groups have both overcasting and selvage

facts.text: Edge finishes may be in colored segments, checkered or barber-pole stripes in nomadic or tribal rugs, sometimes with tassels, pompoms, cowries or coins attached.
In old rugs the original side finish is often gone and recent overcasting has taken its place.
facts.quote: recent overcasting of the sides may take the place of former selvage

facts.text: A simplified selvage or edge finish may suggest later production within a type.

features.name: Ends (finish at top and bottom)
how_to_look: Look at each end separately; the two often differ because one end was started and the other cut off the loom.
Is there a plain-woven band (kilim) between the last row of knots and the fringe? How wide is it, and is it plain, striped or patterned?
How is the fringe made: loose warp ends, warps knotted in groups, braided, netted, or uncut loops at one end?

Most important for the hand-knotted check: do the fringe threads run straight into the body of the rug as warps? Fold the end back and look at the back. If the fringe is a separate strip stitched or glued on under the end, it was added (on machine-made and tufted rugs, or as a repair).
Note whether the fringe is dyed (Stone: 'end dip' in some Turkish rugs).

values.looks_like: Flat-woven band beyond the pile.
other_names: elem / skirt (Turkmen, when patterned or piled)
values.points_to: Hawley: very long webs in Central Asian (Turkmen, Afghan, Baluch) rugs; moderately long in some Turkmen and Anatolian rugs and in two Persian groups (Shiraz, Niris); never in Caucasian rugs.

values.looks_like: Warp ends tied or plaited.
values.points_to: Widespread.

values.looks_like: Uncut loops of warp at the starting end.
values.points_to: Hawley: very frequent at the lower end, where the warp encircled the loom rod.

values.looks_like: A fringe strip stitched under the end; fringe threads do not continue into the rug.
values.points_to: Machine-made and tufted rugs; or a repair on a hand-knotted rug whose ends were worn (Stone calls it an unsatisfactory substitute).

pitfalls: Worn ends lose the kilim band and some rows of knots; what remains is a short fringe of bare warp (Hawley). A rug may be shorter than woven.
Do not judge the knotting method from an added fringe.

facts.text: The ends may have a plain-woven web, a heavier cord selvage, or both, and the warp of the last-finished end generally forms a fringe; the lower end often shows the loops where the warp went round the loom rod.
In old pieces the end webs have often disappeared, leaving short fringes from which some rows of knots have been lost.
facts.quote: in old pieces the webs of the ends have frequently disappeared, leaving short fringes composed of the ends of warp from which some rows of knots have been removed

facts.text: Artificial fringes may be attached to rugs with damaged ends.
The few classes with very long end webs belong to the Central Asian group; none of the Caucasian group has moderately long webs.

features.name: Handle (how it feels and folds)
how_to_look: Lift a corner and let it drape over your hand; fold it back on itself across the width and along the length.
Feel whether it is thin and floppy like cloth, firm and leathery, or stiff like a board.
Fold it gently near your ear: a crackling sound from the foundation suggests dry rot (see age_and_wear).

values.looks_like: Drapes like heavy cloth.
values.points_to: Hawley: Sehna ('always very thin'), Hamadan single-wefted rugs, Turkmen and fine silk rugs.

values.looks_like: Holds a fold, springs back.
values.points_to: Most city rugs.

values.looks_like: Resists folding; heavy.
values.points_to: Hawley and Stone: Bijar (heavy weft hammered hard, warps doubled under); other deeply offset rugs.

pitfalls: Glue or sizing applied to the back makes a rug stiffer (Jacobsen says cold-water glue sizing leaves no visible trace); latex makes it rubbery.

facts.text: Handle is the overall impression of a rug when handled: density, flexibility, thickness, softness and texture.
Dealers size rugs by wetting the back with cold-water glue to give body; once dry there is no visible trace.

features.name: The back as a whole
how_to_look: Turn the rug fully over in daylight (Hawley warns electric light misleads on color).

Is the design as clear on the back as on the front, in tiny squares of color? That is typical of a hand-knotted rug. A blurred design, a cloth or latex back, or a strict mechanical grid points to tufted or machine-made.
Look for diagonal lines across the back in plain areas (lazy lines), where the weaver worked one section at a time: a hand-weaving sign.
Hold it up to a window: thin spots and holes show as light (Hawley).
Look for repairs: patches of different texture, new knots in brighter wool, sewn rents, glue or rubbery coating, inked or painted areas, moth trails.

values.looks_like: Tiny even nodes; design crisp.
values.points_to: Fine city rugs.

values.looks_like: Lines of nodes with one node per knot recessed.
values.points_to: Offset-warp rugs.

values.looks_like: Large separate nodes, weft visible.
values.points_to: Village and tribal rugs.

values.looks_like: Canvas or scrim cloth, rubbery coating.
values.points_to: Tufted rugs, or a later backing applied to a damaged rug.

pitfalls: A shiny, worn back is common on old rugs (Lewis) and makes structure harder to read.
Painted or inked touch-ups are often done from the back over moth damage (Jacobsen).

facts.text: The back should be examined even more carefully than the front, because it shows how the knot is tied and how the warp and weft are treated.
facts.quote: The back should be even more carefully examined than the front

facts.text: Lazy lines are diagonal lines visible on the back of a knotted rug where successive rows of discontinuous wefts turn back because only part of the width was woven at a time.
Hold a rug up with the back toward you against the light to find weak spots; many rugs that look sound on the floor resemble a sieve.
Old rugs are usually somewhat shiny on the back.

features.name: Foundation color (warps and wefts together)
how_to_look: At the ends and on the back, note the colors of the warps (fringe) and wefts; plied warps of two natural shades look speckled 'salt and pepper'.

values.points_to: Most cotton foundations; many wool ones.

values.value: brown, gray or mixed natural wool
values.looks_like: Speckled or dark.
values.points_to: Tribal and nomadic rugs (Stone: warps are sometimes natural brown or black wool because it cannot be dyed for pile).

pitfalls: Dirt and age darken white foundations; cotton of poor quality darkens when wet (Hawley).

facts.text: Warp and weft are generally undyed in the body of a rug, although the end webs are very often colored.
facts.quote: Though the warp and weft are generally undyed in the body of the rug, the web of the ends is very frequently coloured.

facts.text: Nomadic rugs sometimes use naturally brown or black wool for warps.

materials.name: Sheep's wool
materials.how_to_tell: Soft, springy, slightly crimped; a good wool has a satin sheen, a poor one looks dull and harsh. A singed fiber smells of burning hair and leaves a crushable bead of ash (Stone; Lewis says a light singe on good wool brushes away without trace).
materials.where_used: Pile of the great majority of rugs; warp and weft of tribal, Turkish, Caucasian, Turkmen and many village rugs.
materials.what_it_tells: Quality varies by region and season; Hawley singles out wool from Khorasan, Kirman, Shiraz/Niriz and Anatolian uplands as long and lustrous, and Indian wool as poorer.
materials.cautions: Luster can be faked with glycerine and hot rollers (see treatments).

facts.text: Sheep's wool forms the pile of over ninety per cent of Oriental rugs and the warp and weft of at least half.
Burnt wool has a recognizable smell of burning hair; Stone adds that it barely sustains a flame and leaves ash in an elongated ball.

materials.name: Kork (fine underwool)
materials.how_to_tell: Exceptionally soft, fine, lustrous pile; cannot be confirmed by eye with certainty.
materials.where_used: Fine Persian and Turkish rugs marketed as 'kork wool'.
materials.what_it_tells: A trade claim of fine wool.
materials.cautions: Stone defines kork as the underhair of a goat or the fine belly wool of a sheep; the trade uses it loosely. Treat tags saying 'kork' as a claim.

facts.text: Kork is the underhair of a goat or the fine belly wool of a sheep.
A much finer grade of goat fleece grows next to the skin and is combed out from under the long hair.

materials.name: Dead wool (skin wool)
materials.how_to_tell: Dull, lifeless, harsh pile that does not take dye evenly and wears poorly; under a glass the fibers may show roots or tapered ends.
materials.where_used: Cheaper rugs; Hawley associates 'dead or chunam wool' with India.
materials.what_it_tells: Wool pulled from slaughtered sheepskins by chemicals or lime, not shorn.
materials.cautions: Dullness also comes from heavy chemical washing; do not decide on looks alone.

facts.text: Tabachi or dead wool is wool removed from sheepskins in a tannery by a chemical process rather than by shearing; it does not accept dyes well.
Rugs of India made of dead or 'chunam' wool look lifeless.
facts.quote: the rugs of India which are made of dead or "Chunam" wool, seem lifeless

materials.name: Imported Merino ('Manchester') wool
materials.how_to_tell: Very soft, fine, lustrous pile in some Kashan rugs; not provable by eye.
materials.where_used: Kashan (the trade's 'Manchester Kashan'); Merino wool also used in some rugs from Iran, Pakistan, China and India (Stone).
materials.date_note: Stone: Kashan rugs of Australian Merino processed in Manchester, about 1890-1930.
materials.what_it_tells: Trade name for a group of Kashan rugs.
materials.cautions: Single-sourced dates; the name is used loosely by dealers.

facts.text: 'Manchester Kashan' rugs were woven in Kashan from about 1890 to 1930 of Australian Merino wool processed in Manchester.
The introduction of Merino wool from Australia into Persian weaving was short-lived.

materials.name: Cotton
materials.how_to_tell: Smooth, matte, white or cream, soft and limp when wet; a burnt thread flares brightly, smells of burning paper and leaves a fine fragile ash (Stone).
materials.where_used: Warps and wefts of most Persian city rugs and of Indian, Pakistani and Chinese rugs; wefts of some Caucasian rugs; small bright white pile details; rarely allover pile because it mats.
materials.date_note: Old practice in foundations (Stone); increased in commercial production from the late 19th century (Hawley).
materials.what_it_tells: Combined with knot type and offset, narrows the group.
materials.cautions: Cotton foundations are vulnerable to dry rot (Stone).

facts.text: In later years cotton was widely adopted, particularly in Persian, Indian and Chinese rugs, because it is cheaper than wool, almost always as warp and weft rather than pile.
Cotton burns easily and brightly, forms a very fine ash, and its smoke smells of burnt paper.

materials.name: Mercerized cotton
materials.how_to_tell: Glossy cotton with a harder, more metallic shine than silk; burns like cotton (bright flame, paper smell, fine ash).
materials.where_used: Pile of some Turkish (e.g. Kayseri) and Persian rugs sold as silk-like; Hawley mentions it in a few districts of Asia Minor and Persia.

facts.text: Mercerized cotton is cotton treated with alkali under tension to increase strength and gloss; 'floss' is mercerized cotton polished to look like silk, sometimes called 'Turkish silk'.
In a few districts of Asia Minor and Persia the pile is mercerized cotton or silk.

materials.name: Silk
materials.how_to_tell: Very fine, strong filament with a prismatic shine that changes with the light; feels cool. A burnt fiber does not easily keep burning, smells of burnt feathers or hair and leaves a small crushable ball of ash (Stone).
materials.where_used: Pile and sometimes warps of fine city rugs (Kashan, Qum, Isfahan, Tabriz, Hereke, Chinese and Indian silk rugs); highlights in Turkmen weavings.
materials.what_it_tells: Points to a luxury workshop product.
materials.cautions: Mercerized cotton and viscose imitate it; Lewis warned in 1911-20 of 'numerous mercerized and wool silk imitations'.

facts.text: One way to tell silk from mercerized cotton is to burn a very small quantity: silk does not easily sustain a flame and smells of burnt feathers; cotton burns brightly and smells of burnt paper.
Silk rugs were still woven in a few cities of Asia Minor and Persia in the early 20th century.

materials.name: Viscose rayon ('art silk')
materials.how_to_tell: Very glossy, slippery, soft; crushes and shows footprints and water marks easily; burns like cotton (it is regenerated cellulose).
materials.where_used: Modern decorative rugs, both machine-made and hand-made.
materials.date_note: Modern; no source found here giving its first use in rugs.
materials.cautions: Labels such as 'art silk', 'bamboo silk' or 'banana silk' describe rayon in US labeling law; the FTC says products marketed as 'bamboo' textiles are rayon and must be labeled with the generic fiber name.

facts.text: 'Art silk' is a trade term for artificial silk or mercerized cotton.
Most if not all 'bamboo' textile products are really rayon and must be labeled and advertised with the proper generic fiber name, such as 'rayon made from bamboo'.

materials.name: Goat hair and mohair
materials.how_to_tell: Coarse, wiry, often dark and lustrous; mohair (Angora goat) long and silky.
materials.where_used: Side cords and sometimes warps of Afghan, Baluch and Turkmen rugs; mohair in some Anatolian rugs (Hawley).

facts.text: Tough goat hair is preferred for side selvages by weavers of Afghan, Baluch and some Turkmen rugs and is sometimes used for warp; it is very rarely used for weft unless mixed with wool.
Yarn and fabric from the fleece of the Angora goat is mohair.

materials.name: Camel hair
materials.how_to_tell: Natural tan to brown, not dyed; slightly coarser than fine wool.
materials.where_used: Hamadan-area borders and fields ('camel ground'); some Baluch and tribal rugs.
materials.cautions: Hawley says dyed wool or goat hair of similar color is often substituted; Stone says camel hair is used only rarely in pile.

facts.text: Camel hair is seldom used in rug pile.
Dyed wool or goat hair of similar color is often substituted for camel hair.
facts.quote: It is seldom woven in modern rugs, but dyed wool or goats' hair of similar colour is often substituted for it.

materials.name: Undyed natural-colored wool
materials.how_to_tell: Browns, grays and blacks that are evenly colored to the root and do not show corrosion.
materials.where_used: Outlines, grounds and warps in tribal and village rugs.
materials.what_it_tells: Black areas that are not worn down may be natural black wool rather than iron-dyed.

facts.text: The only black yarn on which time leaves no mark is wool from black sheep; natural black and brown wool and brown camel hair are durable.

materials.name: Jute
materials.how_to_tell: Coarse, hairy, golden-tan fiber, weak when wet.
materials.where_used: Some wefts (Kulah alternating wool and jute, Hawley), Indian rugs, filler in power-loomed rugs; backing cloth of tufted rugs.
materials.date_note: Stone: not used in pile rugs before the early 19th century.
materials.cautions: Jute is weakened by alkalis and bleaches (Stone).

facts.text: Jute has been used in the foundation and sometimes in the pile of Indian rugs and as filler in some power-loomed rugs; it was not used in pile rugs before the early 19th century.
In some Kulahs a wool weft alternates with a single coarser jute weft.

materials.name: Latex and glued backing cloth
materials.how_to_tell: Rubbery coating on the back, usually under a separate cloth backing; smell of rubber when new.
materials.where_used: Tufted rugs; also applied to damaged hand-knotted rugs as a repair or non-slip treatment.
materials.what_it_tells: On a tufted rug it holds the pile in; on a knotted rug it hides damage.
materials.cautions: Jacobsen: glue, 'Lastex' or non-skid substance on the back of a rug cuts resale value sharply and can hide moth damage.

facts.text: Tufted rugs are coated with latex on the back to lock the yarn in place and given additional fabric backing.
Glue, Lastex or non-skid coatings on the back of a knotted rug show at a glance from the underside and are used to hold moth-eaten areas together.

dyes.name: Madder
dyes.colors: Reds, from pink to deep brick and plum; with other dyes, oranges, browns and purples.
dyes.from: Root of Rubia tinctorum (also wild madders); coloring agents alizarin and purpurin.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: The standard rug red across Turkey, the Caucasus and Iran until synthetic reds and synthetic alizarin replaced it, mainly from the 1870s; still used, and revived in natural-dye programs.
dyes.how_to_spot: Warm, slightly varied reds that fade evenly and keep the same hue at root and tip, only lighter (Lewis). Cannot be told from synthetic alizarin by eye.
dyes.what_it_tells: Nothing about date on its own.
dyes.cautions: Madder-dyed wool can bleed a little in its first washings (Lewis, Hawley).

facts.text: Madder root yields red to brown dyes whose color depends on the mordant (alum for red, tin for orange, chrome for reddish brown, iron for purple and black).
Madder cultivation in the Caucasus collapsed within a few years of the synthetic production of alizarin; in Kuba the price fell by more than half in autumn 1873 and planters gave up the crop.
Madder was largely displaced in the 1870s by synthetic alizarin.

dyes.name: Kermes

native.translit: qermez-dāna (Iranica: general name for the insect reds)

dyes.from: Scale insect Kermes vermilio (Coccus ilicis) on the kermes oak.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Rare in rugs; Stone: costly and used only rarely.
dyes.how_to_spot: Not distinguishable from other insect reds without laboratory dye analysis.
dyes.cautions: Old books confuse kermes and cochineal (Hawley calls kermes 'cochineal (Coccus ilicis)'); Iranica notes the insect reds are often confused in sources.

facts.text: Kermes is a red dye from a scale insect that lives on oaks around the Mediterranean.
Kermes was very costly and used only rarely in rugs.
Insect reds (kermes, 'Armenian red', lac, cochineal) are frequently confused in medieval sources and modern writers sometimes use one name for all.

dyes.name: Armenian (Ararat) cochineal
dyes.from: Scale insect Porphyrophora hamelii, living on grass roots around Mount Ararat.
dyes.date_from: Ancient (Iranica: red cloth from Urartu mentioned 714 BC).
dyes.date_in_rugs: Possible in Caucasian and Armenian weaving; needs dye analysis.
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.

facts.text: 'Armenian red' from Porphyrophora hamelii is chemically similar to New World cochineal.

dyes.name: Cochineal (American)
dyes.colors: Crimson, pink, purple-red; with tin, scarlet.
dyes.from: Female scale insect Dactylopius coccus (old name Coccus cacti) from Mexico and later the Canary Islands; dye agent carminic acid.
dyes.date_from: Imported to Europe from the 16th century (Stone: as early as 1520).
dyes.date_in_rugs: Reached Persia by the end of the 16th century (English imports into Baku; via Venice); used especially for silk and for magenta-pink and crimson tones; Salimov says weavers in Azerbaijan replaced costly madder and cochineal with fuchsine after c. 1880.
dyes.how_to_spot: Bluish crimson to pink that fades toward a softer pink; laboratory confirmation needed.
dyes.what_it_tells: Its presence does not date a rug.
dyes.cautions: Holt (1901) wrongly says cochineal was 'introduced for dyeing purposes in 1856'.

facts.text: Cochineal, from a scale insect living on the cacti of Mexico, reached the Old World after the Spanish conquest of Mexico.
Cochineal was imported from the New World as early as 1520 and produced in the Canary Islands in the 1820s.
By the late 16th century the English were importing cochineal into Baku, and cochineal was among English imports to Persia in the early 17th century.
American cochineal is reported to have been exported via Venice to Persia by the end of the 16th century.
facts.quote: American cochineal is reported to have been exported via Venice to Persia by the end of the 16 th century

facts.text: Cochineal and yellow larkspur are the dyes typical of 16th-18th century Persian velvets analyzed at the Metropolitan Museum.
The effect of cochineal varies with the mordant: chromium gives purple, aluminum crimson, tin scarlet, iron gray.

says.text: 'Cochineal was introduced for dyeing purposes in 1856.'
After the conquest of Mexico it reached the Orient through Spain and supplanted kermes in a measure.
English importing cochineal into Baku by the late 16th century.

dyes.name: Lac
dyes.from: Resinous secretion of the lac insect (Kerria lacca, old name Coccus lacca) of India and Southeast Asia.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Indian carpets; also found in Persian carpets (Shibayama) and in some Turkmen weavings (not verified here).
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.
dyes.what_it_tells: Not a reliable sign of Indian origin (Shibayama).

facts.text: Lac is a red insect dye produced in India, a substitute for cochineal giving reds, crimson, terra cotta and purple according to the mordant.
Lac was thought by some to indicate Indian rather than Persian carpets, but it appears in many Persian carpets and is not a valid indicator of origin.

dyes.name: Indigo (natural)

native.translit: nīl; also rang-e kermānī, rang-e wasma (Iranica)

dyes.colors: Pale to navy blue; with yellows, greens; under madder, purples and browns.
dyes.from: Fermented leaves of Indigofera tinctoria and related plants; Persia mostly imported it from India after its own cultivation died out by the 14th century (Iranica).
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods.
dyes.how_to_spot: Deep, clear blues that fade gently; greens made with indigo plus a yellow often turn blue-green or bluish as the yellow fades (Stone, Lewis).
dyes.what_it_tells: Natural and synthetic indigo are the same compound, so blue gives no date by eye.

facts.text: The principal blues of Oriental rugs come from indigo.
When indigo is combined with a yellow to make green, the green may become bluish with time as the yellow fades.

dyes.name: Weld
dyes.from: Stalks, leaves and flowers of Reseda luteola (dyer's rocket); colorant luteolin.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods; DOBAG villagers grew it (Aramco 1991).
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.
dyes.cautions: See larkspur: Iranica identifies Persian 'esparak' as weld.

facts.text: Weld (Reseda luteola) yields a yellow dye.

dyes.name: Yellow larkspur (isparek / esparak)

native.text: isparek / esperek / esparek (spellings in Stone's cross-references)

dyes.from: Flowers of Delphinium semibarbatum (D. zalil) - or, per Iranica following Edwards, weld
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Shibayama: the most used yellow in Safavid Persia (velvets).
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.
dyes.cautions: The name is applied to different plants by different writers.

facts.text: Yellow larkspur (Delphinium semibarbatum, D. zalil) was the most used yellow dye in Persia in 16th-18th century velvets analyzed at the Metropolitan Museum.
Asburg, an ingredient of Persian-derived dye recipes, is a product of flowers of the genus Delphinium growing in the Himalayas and also sold as a powder from Afghanistan.
facts.quote: This is a product of flowers of the genus Delphinum that grows in the Himalayas. It is also obtained as a powder from Afghanistan.

facts.text: Larkspur gives a light or bright yellow.
Delphinium zalil is a source of yellow dye that may be referred to as esparek.

says.text: Esparak is weld (Reseda luteola), citing Edwards 1953 p. 32.
The common Persian yellow is yellow larkspur, Delphinium semibarbatum / D. zalil.
Delphinium zalil may be referred to as esparek.
Asburg (the same word) is a Delphinium flower from the Himalayas and Afghanistan.

dyes.name: Buckthorn ('Persian berries')
dyes.colors: Yellow; with indigo, greens (Hawley: the best Chinese greens).
dyes.from: Unripe berries of Rhamnus species (Stone: R. petiolaris).
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods; Böhmer used the limited range of R. petiolaris in central Turkey to help localize carpets (Aramco 1991).
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.

facts.text: Unripe buckthorn berries (Persian berries) yield a yellow dye with an alum mordant and, with indigo, greens.

dyes.name: Pomegranate rind
dyes.colors: Dull yellow; tannin for browns and blacks; used as a mordant.
dyes.from: Fruit rind of Punica granatum.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods.
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.

facts.text: Pomegranate rind is the best-known vegetable mordant and also gives yellow.
Pomegranate rind is still among the dye materials used around Yuntdağ.

dyes.name: Walnut husk
dyes.from: Green hulls of Juglans regia.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods.
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.

facts.text: Green walnut hulls give browns, beiges and tans, or black.

dyes.name: Oak galls, oak bark and valonia (acorn cups)
dyes.colors: Grays, browns and, with iron, black; tannins.
dyes.from: Galls and bark of oaks; acorn cups (valonia).
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods.
dyes.how_to_spot: Iron-tannin browns and blacks often show corrosion (see Iron-based browns and blacks).

facts.text: Grays and browns come from gall nuts; with iron they give black.
Valonia, pomegranate rind and sumac were the old vegetable mordants of Eastern dyers.

dyes.name: Saffron
dyes.from: Stigmas of Crocus sativus.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Doubtful in rugs: Iranica says it is not clear it continued in use as a dye; Stone says it may have been used in some early rugs of China, India and the Balkans.
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.
dyes.cautions: Popular books list it as a common rug yellow; the scholarly sources doubt it.

facts.text: Saffron was particularly costly and, though mentioned frequently in medieval sources, it is not clear that it continued to be used as a dye.
Saffron may have been used to dye some early rugs of China, India and the Balkans.

says.text: From time immemorial a beautiful yellow has been obtained from saffron.
Not clear that it continued to be used as a dye.

dyes.name: Other yellows and oranges: turmeric, safflower, henna, sumac
dyes.colors: Yellow to orange; henna reddish-brown or orange.
dyes.from: Plants (Curcuma, Carthamus tinctorius, Lawsonia inermis, Rhus).
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods.
dyes.how_to_spot: Laboratory only.
dyes.cautions: Turmeric is not fast on its own (Mumford).

facts.text: Yellow also comes from safflower, autumn vine leaves, pomegranate rind, turmeric, sumac and saffron; henna gives reddish-brown or orange.

dyes.name: Iron-based browns and blacks
dyes.colors: Dark brown and black, used for outlines.
dyes.from: Iron (filings with vinegar, ferrous sulfate, 'iron pyrites' in Hawley) combined with tannins from galls, bark or pomegranate.
dyes.date_from: Ancient.
dyes.date_in_rugs: All periods.
dyes.how_to_spot: Black and dark brown pile worn down to the knots, or eaten away, while other colors stand up in relief.
dyes.what_it_tells: Corrosion takes years of wear and is consistent with age, but it is imitated by clipping (Stone) and also happens to some modern iron-mordanted wool.

facts.text: Dyes for dark browns and black made with iron corrode the wool, so the black knots of old rugs are often worn to the warp.
facts.quote: unfortunately the dye has a corrosive effect on the wool, so that the black knots of old rugs are often worn to the warp

facts.text: Iron mordants tend to darken colors and embrittle wool.

dyes.name: Dyewoods (logwood, brazilwood, sappanwood, sandalwood)
dyes.from: Heartwood of tropical trees (Haematoxylon campechianum, Caesalpinia spp.; red sandalwood Pterocarpus santalinus).
dyes.date_from: Imported to the East in quantity in the 19th century.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Mumford: 'in recent years many reds have had for basis the dye-woods'; Salimov: fuchsine replaced red sandalwood in Azerbaijan.
dyes.how_to_spot: Reds and violets that have faded unevenly; laboratory only.

facts.text: In the late 19th century many Eastern reds were based on imported dyewoods such as Campeche (logwood) and Brazil wood.
Logwood is a red to violet dye used in Chinese rugs.

dyes.name: Mauveine (Perkin's mauve)
dyes.from: Oxidation of impure aniline from coal tar.
dyes.date_from: 1856 (Perkin's discovery at Easter, patent August 1856); factory at Greenford 1857; adopted by French dyers late 1858.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Salimov, citing Eiland 1999, reports mauveine in a Kuba rug dated '1868'.
dyes.how_to_spot: A purple or mauve that has faded badly to gray or brown on the tips while staying brighter deep in the pile.
dyes.cautions: Basic dyes like mauveine lost their color in two or three years (Piralov 1913 via Salimov).

facts.text: In 1856, 18-year-old William Henry Perkin synthesized mauve (aniline purple) from coal-tar chemicals, the first commercialized synthetic dye; he opened his factory in 1857.
Perkin filed his patent in August 1856, and French dyers adopted the color late in 1858.

says.text: Gives 1856 in 'aniline dyes' but 1853 in 'dye, synthetic' and its chronology.

dyes.name: Fuchsine (magenta)
dyes.from: Aniline with stannic chloride (Verguin); later arsenic-acid process.
dyes.date_from: 1858-59; French patent of Renard frères and Franc 8 April 1859; named magenta after the battle of 1859.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Azerbaijan: used in place of madder, cochineal and red sandalwood after c. 1880, very cheap (two zolotniks dyed a pound of yarn) (Salimov from Zedgenidze 1891).
dyes.how_to_spot: A pink or magenta that has faded to gray, tan or a pale dirty pink at the tips but stays bright at the base of the knot; often bled into adjacent white.

facts.text: Renard frères and Franc of Lyons patented fuchsine on 8 April 1859, from a process discovered by Verguin.
facts.quote: The first patent was taken out by Renard freres and Franc, of Lyons, on April 8th, 1859

facts.text: In Azerbaijan fuchsine replaced red sandalwood and costly madder and cochineal for brighter reds.

says.text: Synthesized 1857 (citing Venkataraman 1956).
Sometime between 1858 and 1859.
Patent 8 April 1859.

dyes.name: Aniline violets and blues (methyl violet, Hofmann violet, aniline blue)
dyes.from: Derivatives of fuchsine/rosaniline.
dyes.date_from: Aniline blue 1860-61; methyl violet noticed 1861, made on a large scale from 1866-67; Hofmann violets 1863.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Late 19th century.
dyes.how_to_spot: Purples that have faded to gray-brown or to pinkish tan on the surface.

facts.text: Aniline blue was first observed in 1861 (Girard and De Laire); methyl violet, noticed by Lauth in 1861, was made on a large scale from 1867; Hofmann prepared his violets in 1863.
Methyl violet is dated 1866 and malachite green 1877 by Venkataraman (as cited by Salimov).

dyes.name: Synthetic alizarin
dyes.colors: Reds (Turkey red) and, by mordant, purples and browns.
dyes.from: Anthracene from coal tar.
dyes.date_from: Structure 1868, synthesis and patents 1869 (Graebe and Liebermann with BASF; Perkin independently); commercial production from about 1869-71.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Salimov: wide use of alizarin dyes in Azerbaijani carpets not before the second quarter of the 20th century (Soviet trade organizations).
dyes.how_to_spot: Not distinguishable from madder by eye; laboratory analysis can tell (synthetic lacks madder's purpurin and other minor colorants).

facts.text: The synthesis of alizarin by Graebe and Liebermann in 1869 was the first industrial synthesis of a dye found in nature.
Two groups filed alizarin patents in 1869: Perkin, and Graebe and Liebermann working with BASF.

says.text: 'About 1870' in one entry, '1871' in its chronology.
Synthesized 1869.
Alizarin red 1868; used in Europe as a mordant red from 1871.

dyes.name: Azo dyes (acid reds, oranges, yellows; Congo red)
dyes.from: Diazotized aromatic amines coupled with phenols or amines.
dyes.date_from: First azo dyes 1860s (aniline yellow, Bismarck brown); azo dyes for wool on a manufacturing scale from 1875-78 (chrysoidine 1875, Orange II 1876, Ponceau 1878); Congo red, the first direct dye for cotton, 1884.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Stone: Ponceau 2R and Roccelline reds in 19th-century rugs, generally available about 1880. Chahardoli 2019 found Acid Red 88 and Acid Orange 7 in 14 of 18 red samples from 20th-century Iranian carpets.
dyes.how_to_spot: Bright orange-reds and scarlets that may bleed into white areas when washed, or fade to an orange-tan on the tips; often in the same rug as natural colors.
dyes.what_it_tells: Not before about 1875-78 for acid azo reds and oranges.
dyes.cautions: Many acid and direct dyes were light-fast but not wash-fast (Salimov).

facts.text: The first azo dyestuffs were introduced between 1864 and 1866, and Witt and Roussin began making azo dyes on a manufacturing scale about 1876-77.
facts.quote: The first azo-dyestuffs were introduced between 1864 and 1866.

facts.text: Chrysoidine, the first azo dye for wool, has been in use since 1875; Congo red (1884) dyes cotton by simple immersion.
Acid orange (1876), fast yellow (1877) and ponceau (1878) were the first acid azo dyes; Congo red (1884) the first and most popular direct dye.
Azo dyes were generally available about 1880; Ponceau 2R and Roccelline are red azo dyes found in 19th-century rugs.
Synthetic Acid Red 88 and/or Acid Orange 7 were found in 14 of 18 red samples from 20th-century Iranian carpets, alongside or instead of madder.

says.text: Azo dyes introduced 'about 1880'.
Chrysoidine in use since 1875.

dyes.name: Indigo carmine (soluble 'Saxon' blue)
dyes.from: Indigo dissolved in sulfuric acid (a chemically modified natural or synthetic indigo).
dyes.date_from: 18th century (not dated in sources read here).
dyes.date_in_rugs: Salimov: home dyers in Azerbaijan used 'jangyari', a fugitive blue made by dyers from blueing and sulfuric acid (Zedgenidze 1891; Khatisov 1894).
dyes.how_to_spot: Blues that have faded or run much more than ordinary indigo.
dyes.cautions: Lewis describes 'indigo dissolved in sulphuric acid' as the basis of most blues, which may confuse vat indigo with this fugitive form.

facts.text: Indigo carmine (indigotine) is a water-soluble compound of indigo formerly used as a textile dye.
In late-19th-century Azerbaijan home dyers bought 'jangyari', a fugitive blue made from blueing and sulfuric acid, instead of professional indigo vat dyeing.

dyes.name: Synthetic indigo
dyes.from: Synthesized from coal-tar chemicals (aniline or naphthalene routes).
dyes.date_from: Baeyer's first patent 1880; BASF launched 'Indigo Pure BASF' commercially in 1897.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Stone: began to be used in rug yarns in 1910 and quickly supplanted natural indigo; Salimov: spread in Azerbaijan in the early 20th century; Iranica: largely replaced the natural dye in Persia in the 20th century.
dyes.how_to_spot: Cannot be told from natural indigo by eye or, Stone says, chemically in the fiber.
dyes.what_it_tells: No dating value for an owner.

facts.text: In 1897 BASF launched synthetic 'Indigo Pure BASF' after 17 years of research.
Baeyer took out the first patent for artificial indigo in 1880.
Synthetic indigo in the fiber is chemically indistinguishable from vegetable indigo.

says.text: Gives 1880 (synthesis), 1897 (chronology) and 1910 (first use in rug yarns).
Commercial launch 1897.

dyes.name: Chrome (mordant and premetallized) dyes
dyes.from: Synthetic acid-mordant dyes fixed with potassium dichromate (chrome) or supplied already combined with chromium.
dyes.date_from: Chrome mordants came into use in the last quarter of the 19th century; acid-mordant azo 'chrome' dyes for wool were synthesized 1889-90 (Salimov, citing Venkataraman); Stone's chronology gives 1915 for 'chrome dye'.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Jacobsen: most Chinese rugs of 1921-34 used chrome dyes; India and Japan used chrome dyes exclusively by c. 1960; Iran used vegetable, aniline and chrome dyes side by side.
dyes.how_to_spot: Even, clear colors that do not run or fade much; cannot be told from good natural dyes by eye with certainty.
dyes.what_it_tells: Points to the 20th century in most rugs.
dyes.cautions: Jacobsen was a dealer who favored chrome dyes; his judgments of quality are opinion.

facts.text: Chrome dyes are synthetic dyes used with a potassium dichromate mordant; they are fast and non-fugitive.
Important acid-mordant azo dyes for wool, applied almost always with chrome mordants and so called 'chrome' dyes, were synthesized in 1889-1890.
Most Chinese rugs woven 1921-1934 used chrome dyes, and India used them exclusively for many years before 1962.

says.text: Chronology: '1915 chrome dye'.
Chrome mordanting in the last quarter of the 19th century; chrome azo dyes 1889-90.

dyes.name: Cheap imported acid dyes of the 1950s ('Swiss dyes')
dyes.from: Imported acid dyes (Jacobsen's trade name).
dyes.date_from: Jacobsen: first seen in Persian rugs around 1950-51.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Hamadan-area rugs (especially 2.5 x 4 ft), cheap Gorevan/Heriz carpets.
dyes.how_to_spot: After light washing, ivory and rose areas look bluish-white; the pile is blue below a whitened surface, partly from bleeding blue weft.
dyes.what_it_tells: Points to after c. 1950 for the rugs Jacobsen describes.

facts.text: From about 1950-51 cheap imported dyes appeared in Hamadan-district rugs and cheap Gorevan carpets, giving dirty brownish-red fields and bluish-white bleeding after a light wash.

dyes.name: Persian government bans on aniline dyes
dyes.from: Royal decrees and customs rules.
dyes.date_from: Mumford prints a law of Mozaffar al-Din Shah dated 15 Ramazan 1317 AH (c. 17 January 1900; Mumford writes 'Jan'y 1, 1900') that restates earlier bans by Naser al-Din Shah; Lewis says 1903; Kendrick says 1910; Stone credits Reza Shah.
dyes.date_in_rugs: Iranica: ineffective; synthetic dyes were used, at least in lower-grade rugs for the West, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; Eiland (via Salimov) says over half of exported Persian carpets in 1913-14 contained synthetic dyes.
dyes.how_to_spot: Not applicable.
dyes.what_it_tells: A Persian rug made after 1900 is not, because of the bans, free of synthetic dye.
dyes.cautions: The story that a dyer caught using aniline lost his right hand is repeated widely. Its earliest source here is Mumford (1900), who says only that 'in one part of Persia it was ordered long ago'; Lewis (1911) attaches it to a '1903 law' and jokes that otherwise Persia would be full of one-handed men. No Persian document for it was found.

facts.text: The law of Mozaffar al-Din Shah, signed at Tehran on 15 Ramazan 1317 AH, forbade bringing into the kingdom aniline dyes in dry or liquid form and any coloring containing aniline, ordered seizure and public burning of seized dyes, fines and a year's imprisonment, and took effect three months after signing.
facts.quote: It is forbidden to bring into the kingdom : Aniline dyes, whether in dry or liquid form, as well as all coloring materials, whether dry or liquid, into which aniline enters as a component.

facts.text: The same law states that Naser al-Din Shah had earlier forbidden the importation of aniline dyes on different occasions.
facts.quote: Our Glorious Father, Nasser ed Din Shah, ... forbade the importation of aniline dyes

facts.text: Mumford reports that the Belgian-run customs service was enforcing the 1900 law and had seized and destroyed several large consignments of aniline in its first months.
Persian government efforts to ban the import of synthetic dyes, and attempts to confiscate carpets made with them, were ineffective.
In the early 20th century the customs duty on carpet exports was charged only on carpets in which aniline-dyed yarns had been used.
Lewis (1911) says a 1903 law forbade importing chemical dyes, ordered fabrics dyed with them seized and destroyed, and decreed that a guilty dyer lose his right hand.
facts.quote: In 1903 a law was enacted by the Persian government forbidding the importation of chemical dyes

facts.text: Kendrick and Tattersall (1922) say an embargo on the import of chemical dyes in solid or liquid form was placed in Persia in 1910.
facts.quote: In 1910 an embargo was placed in Persia upon the import of chemical dyes either in solid or liquid form

facts.text: Stone says Reza Shah prohibited aniline dyes and required natural dyes, unsuccessfully.

disagreements.about: date and ruler of the ban

says.text: Law of Mozaffar al-Din Shah, 15 Ramazan 1317 AH (Jan 1900), restating earlier bans by Naser al-Din Shah (r. 1848-96).
'Rigid laws' forbid the cheaper dyes in Persia and in Smyrna.
A law of 1903, with loss of the right hand for a guilty dyer.
An embargo in 1910.
Reza Shah (r. 1925-41) prohibited them after c. 1920.
Follows Mumford: a Shah's decree of 1900.
'In one part of Persia it was ordered long ago' that a convicted dyer lose his right hand; the mandate made little impression.
Part of the 1903 law.

dyes.name: DOBAG and the natural-dye revival (Turkey)

native.text: Doğal Boya Araştırma ve Geliştirme Projesi (DOBAG)

dyes.colors: Full natural palette (madder reds, indigo blues, weld and other yellows, walnut browns).
dyes.from: Natural dyes, hand-spun wool.
dyes.date_from: 1981 (Böhmer's dye work from 1976; recipes complete by 1981; Ayvacık villages summer 1981; Yuntdağ from early 1982; cooperative at Kozaklar and Örselli 1989; Marmara University full responsibility 1988).
dyes.date_in_rugs: Rugs from 1981 on.
dyes.how_to_spot: All-wool, symmetric knot, natural dyes; sold with the project's approval or label (form of the label not verified here).
dyes.what_it_tells: A documented DOBAG rug is not before 1981.
dyes.cautions: Karavar and Öztürk report chemical dyes in some recent Yuntdağ pieces; natural-dyed modern rugs from other projects (Iran, Afghanistan, Tibet) can look 'old' but are modern.

facts.text: DOBAG (Doğal Boya Araştırma ve Geliştirme Projesi, Natural Dye Research and Development Project) began in 1981 under the school now called Marmara University Faculty of Fine Arts, in the Ayvacık (Çanakkale) and Yuntdağ (Manisa) regions.
Harald Böhmer began analyzing old rug dyes with thin-layer chromatography in 1976 and had recipes for the basic colors by 1981.
DOBAG rugs are natural-dyed, all-wool and symmetrically knotted, woven by cooperatives.
By the 1880s most of the big Turkish manufacturing networks were using synthetic dyes.

dyes.name: Natural dyes in 20th-century and modern Iran
dyes.date_from: Continuous in some areas; Iranica: vegetable dyes in common use until the 1940s; the Persian Carpet Company attempted to revive indigo cultivation.
dyes.what_it_tells: Natural dyes alone do not show that an Iranian rug is old.
dyes.cautions: The 1980s-90s revival in Fars (gabbeh and tribal rugs) is widely reported but was not verified from a source read here.

facts.text: Until the 1940s vegetable dyes continued in common use in Persian carpets (Iran Carpet Company, 1949, cited by Iranica).
Edwards observed several weaving areas still using natural dyes after World War I, supported by many late Qajar carpets without artificial dyes.
The Persian Carpet Company attempted to revive the cultivation and use of indigo in Persia.

disagreements.about: how far synthetic dyes spread in Iran

says.text: Vegetable dyes were used exclusively in Persia until about 1890; the dangerous aniline period was 1890-1910.
Synthetic dyes were noted in Persian carpets by the 1870s.
In 1876-77 cheap English dyes were well known around Kirman and 'cheap European dyes are carried into the remotest villages'.

treatments.name: Chemical washing (bleaching to soften colors)
treatments.date_from: By the 1890s-1900s; Hawley (1913) says over 90 percent of several commercial Persian types sold in the US were artificially treated.
treatments.where: Done in the East and, more heavily, in New York, London and other Western markets.
treatments.how_to_spot: All colors softened and a little indefinite, whites toned yellowish-gray, on a rug with no signs of wear (Kendrick). Pile may feel brittle or harsh; a wet rag rubbed on it may smell of acid or chlorine (Hawley; Lewis's saliva test gives a 'pungent odor'). Compare pile at the tip with the base of the knot and with the back: the back keeps stronger color.
treatments.what_it_tells: A commercial treatment, not age. A heavily washed rug often wears out faster.

facts.text: Washing methods to soften colors used lime water in the East and, in the US, ammonia, borax and soap, or chloride of lime, boracic acid, vinegar or oxalic acid, which remove the wool's natural oils.
facts.quote: Others use chloride of lime, boracic acid, vinegar, or oxalic acid, that remove some of the natural oils of the wool

facts.text: Over ninety per cent of the Kermanshahs, Sarouks, Kashans, Tabriz, Muskabads, Mahals and Gorevans sold in the US (in 1913) had been treated by some artificial process to soften colors or give an appearance of age.
facts.quote: Over ninety per cent of the Kermanshahs, Sarouks, Kashans, Tabriz, Muskabads, Mahals, and Gorevans ... have been treated by some artificial process

facts.text: If a rug is in good condition with no signs of wear yet its whites are yellowish-gray and all colors mellow and indefinite, it has very probably been washed.
Chemical washes can use lime, chlorine compounds or wood ash; harsh washes are cited as the cause of weakened, brittle fibers in some old rugs.
A trade 'washed' rug is not necessarily 'doctored': a legitimate finishing wash removes surplus dye and sets the rest.

treatments.name: Bleaching and repainting (the 'American Sarouk' treatment)
treatments.date_from: Jacobsen: about 1905 to 1955, heaviest before 1941; Hawley and Lewis already describe it in 1911-13.
treatments.where: New York and New Jersey plants (Jacobsen names Jersey City and Long Island), applied to Persian imports, above all Sarouks; also Lillihan, Arak/Sultanabad, Mahal, Kashan, Hamadan, Kirman, some Herez and Bijar.
treatments.how_to_spot: Part the pile: the color is strong at the tips but pale pink or whitish near the knot, or the paint sits on the surface and does not reach the base. The back shows a paler, different red from the front. Reds are a deep raspberry-crimson; the pile may have an artificial high gloss. A damp white cloth rubbed hard may pick up color. Painted colors fade and look 'muddy' after some years (Jacobsen).
treatments.what_it_tells: Points to a rug sold in the US market in the first half of the 20th century; it says nothing about where in Iran it was woven beyond the type.

facts.text: In the American trade, Persian rugs were chemically bleached, had colors painted back in, and were given a gloss with wax or glycerine and hot rollers (Jacobsen dates the New York plants from about 1905).
The chemicals reduced bright reds to a pale, dull pink, so reds and blues were painted back in; wax or glycerine and hot rollers then gave a silky gloss.
Some Sarouks were bleached and then painted to satisfy American color tastes; Lillihan rugs were often painted too.
Water-color paints were used to restore color where acid had acted too strongly; such rugs usually show a slight tinge of pink in the white.
facts.quote: water color paints are frequently used to restore the color in spots where the acid has acted too vigorously. Such rugs usually show a slight tinge of pink in the white.

facts.text: Jacobsen estimated that more than half of all Persian rugs imported to the US from about 1905 to 1955 were chemically washed and painted, and that rising US wages after about 1955 made painting too costly.

treatments.name: Light lime wash, 'Persian wash', 'London wash'
treatments.date_from: Lime washing of yarn or rugs in the East is old (Mumford, Hawley); Jacobsen describes the light 'New York lime wash', 'London wash' and 'Persian wash' as the usual mild finishes by c. 1960.
treatments.how_to_spot: Hard to see; colors slightly softened and even. Jacobsen notes uneven fading patches ('hairbrushes') can appear where dyes differ.

facts.text: In parts of Persia and India dyers washed yarn in lime before dyeing to brighten colors, which made it brittle.
Most Eastern washing methods, such as washing with lime water, do little real injury.
By about 1960 most new Persian rugs were given only a light lime wash, in Iran or in New York, instead of the old heavy treatment.

treatments.name: Artificial luster (glycerine or wax and hot rollers; 'lusterizing')
treatments.where: Western finishing plants; Stone notes lusterizing in contemporary Chinese rugs.
treatments.how_to_spot: A greasy or glassy sheen uniform over all colors and not matched by the feel of the wool; after washing, a lusterized rug may look dull or 'dead' (Stone).
treatments.what_it_tells: A finish, not quality or age.

facts.text: Rugs were given an artificial luster by applying glycerine or paraffin wax and passing them between hot rollers.
A lusterized rug may look exceptionally dull after it is later washed.

treatments.name: Artificial aging (street wear, sun, sea water, pumice, singeing)
treatments.date_from: Reported by 1903 (Landor, quoted by Hawley) and 1922 (Kendrick).
treatments.where: Persia and Constantinople bazaars; Western dealers.
treatments.how_to_spot: Wear in the wrong places or even over all colors; burned holes skillfully repaired; singed fiber ends (Kendrick: under a microscope the burnt, slightly swollen ends of wool fibers show); coffee-ground staining (Lewis).
treatments.what_it_tells: An apparently old rug may be new.

facts.text: New carpets were laid in crowded bazaar streets to be trampled by people and animals for days or weeks, then sold as antiques.

One factory faked antiques by soaking a new carpet in the sea to soften colors, rubbing it with pumice where wear would be expected, singeing it with a spirit flame, burning holes with hot coals and repairing them.
facts.quote: It is then taken to the sea and immersed long enough to soften and bleach the colours to the desired extent. Next it is rubbed down back and front with a pumice-stone

facts.text: Toning used chloride of lime, oxalic acid or lemon juice, and coffee grounds were used to give an old appearance.

treatments.name: Modern 'antique wash', tea wash and distressing
treatments.date_from: Late 20th century to present (not dated precisely in sources read).
treatments.how_to_spot: Muted, brownish or grayish overall tone on a rug with crisp, unworn structure; clipped low areas imitating corroded browns; abrash woven in deliberately.
treatments.what_it_tells: Decorative finish meant to look old.

facts.text: An 'antique wash' applies chemicals to soften colors and simulate an older rug.
Because etching suggests age, it is sometimes imitated by clipping in contemporary rugs.
Abrash is sometimes imitated in new commercial hand-knotted and power-loomed rugs.

treatments.name: Bleaching to change the color ('golden Afghan', 'golden Shirvan')
treatments.where: Afghan (Ersari-type) and Shirvan rugs for the Western market.
treatments.how_to_spot: Yellow or gold field where the original red still shows at the knot base, on the back or in protected areas.

facts.text: Red Afghan rugs were chemically bleached to yellow ('golden Afghan') before yellow-dyed versions were woven, and 'golden Shirvans' were made the same way.
Bleaching agents include hydrogen peroxide, sulfuric acid, ammonia, lye, and chlorine compounds.

treatments.name: Stripping and overdyeing
treatments.how_to_spot: One strong color over the whole rug with the old design faintly visible through it; back and fringe dyed too.

facts.text: Stripping is bleaching a rug so it can be dyed another color.

treatments.name: Sun fading (light damage, tip fading)
treatments.date_from: Not a treatment by itself, but also done deliberately.
treatments.how_to_spot: Pile paler at the tips than at the base; one side or end paler where the light fell.

facts.text: Colors are bleached over time by light, especially ultraviolet; tip fading is bleaching of the pile ends by light-sensitive dyes.
Exposing a new carpet to bright sunlight is one method of aging it.

treatments.name: Painting or inking worn areas
treatments.where: Dealers and jobbers of used rugs.
treatments.how_to_spot: Bare foundation (warps and wefts visible) colored to match the design; color rubs off on a damp white cloth; from the back, dye on moth-eaten or worn places.

facts.text: Threadbare parts of a pattern are tinted on the surface; Kendrick allows it for museum pieces but says the color will not last in use and re-knotting is the proper remedy.
facts.quote: One common artifice is to tint on the surface those parts of the pattern which are so threadbare as to show nothing but the foundation threads.

facts.text: Exposed foundation where the pile is worn may be painted to conceal wear.

treatments.name: Abrash (color banding) - not a treatment
treatments.how_to_spot: Bands of slightly different shade running across the rug (weft-wise), often near the top end.
treatments.what_it_tells: Shows yarn dyed in batches; common in natural-dyed and village rugs. Imitated in modern production, so it is not proof of age or of natural dye.

facts.text: Abrash is a change in color across the field and border caused by different wool or dye batches; it runs weft-wise and is more likely toward the top of a rug.
Abrash is sometimes imitated in new commercial hand-knotted and power-loomed rugs.

treatments.name: Bleeding (color run) - not a treatment
treatments.how_to_spot: A color has stained neighboring white or light areas, often after washing or a flood; reds are the usual culprits.
treatments.what_it_tells: Poorly fixed dye or poorly rinsed yarn, natural or synthetic. Not proof of synthetic dye.

facts.text: Dyes improperly fixed or inadequately washed after dyeing may bleed; some reds are particularly prone.
Fresh natural dyes can run in the first washing too, so running alone does not prove aniline.
facts.quote: when fresh they will run during the first washing in water, but afterwards they are little affected either by water or weak acids

age_and_wear.clue: Black and dark brown areas worn lower than other colors (corrosion, etching)
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Iron-based dyes have embrittled the wool over years of use; consistent with age and wear.
age_and_wear.cautions: Clipping imitates it in new rugs (Stone); natural black wool does not corrode (Hawley), so its absence proves nothing.

facts.text: Wool dyed dark brown or black with iron corrodes, so the black knots of old rugs are often worn to the warp.
Etching is sometimes imitated by clipping in contemporary rugs.

age_and_wear.clue: Each color evenly worn across the rug, but different colors worn to different heights
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Kendrick: a fairly certain sign of genuine age (at least several and probably forty or fifty years).
age_and_wear.cautions: Single source; uniform wear over all colors, or wear in odd places, suggests artificial aging.

facts.text: When each color is evenly worn throughout but the colors differ from one another in pile height, the carpet is probably at least several, and possibly forty or fifty, years old.
facts.quote: When it is seen that each separate colour is evenly worn throughout and that there are differences between the various colours

age_and_wear.clue: Color at the tip of the pile compared with the base of the knot
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Natural fading lightens a color evenly (a paler shade of the same hue); a composite color whose parts fade at different rates changes hue at the tip. A violet or pink that is gray-brown at the tip but bright at the base suggests an early synthetic dye.
age_and_wear.cautions: Hawley warns that brighter color at the base than the surface does not by itself prove aniline, because natural dyes fade too.

facts.text: A vegetable dye fades to a lighter tone of itself, while in a composite chemical color one component may vanish, leaving a changed color on the surface and the original near the warp.
facts.quote: A vegetable dye will fade into a lighter tone of itself, while in a chemical dye some one of the colors used to make up the composite color will disappear.

facts.text: It is a mistake to assume aniline dyes because the wool is brighter at the foundation than on the surface, or because color runs when wet.
facts.quote: It is a mistake, however, to assume that the dyes are aniline because the wool has a brighter colour at the surface of the nap than at the foundation

facts.text: Early basic synthetic dyes lost their color entirely within two or three years, fading to dull brown or gray.

disagreements.about: root versus tip as a test for synthetic dye

says.text: Treats the surface-versus-base difference as a way to spot chemical dyes.
Says it is a mistake to rely on it.

age_and_wear.clue: Rubbing with a damp white cloth; wetting white next to strong colors
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Color coming off freely suggests unfixed dye; old travelers and dealers used it as a test for European dyes.
age_and_wear.cautions: Freshly natural-dyed rugs can bleed in their first washing (Lewis, Hawley, Kendrick); test only on a small hidden spot and never on a valuable rug without advice.

facts.text: In 1876-77 Floyer advised testing the red and yellow of Persian carpets by rubbing hard with a wet handkerchief: madder red and the traditional yellows leave no trace, European dyes come off freely.
facts.quote: The red and yellow colours of all Persian carpets should nowadays be tested by wetting the handkerchief and rubbing the colour hard.

facts.text: Lewis advised scrubbing a spot where a bright color meets white and seeing whether the white takes color after drying; if it does, he says, the dye is aniline.
Applying a wet cloth to test whether colors are fast was standard advice to buyers of Persian rugs by the 1880s-1900s.
In a newly made vegetable-dyed rug some colors, especially blues, reds and greens, wipe off at first; after the first washing only a chemical will disturb them.

says.text: Natural reds and yellows never leave a trace; European dyes come off.
New vegetable-dyed rugs do rub off until first washed; aniline domestic carpet is comparatively fast.

age_and_wear.clue: Harsh, brittle pile that breaks or can be plucked out
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Harsh chemical washing or some early synthetic dyes; also dry rot of a cotton foundation.

facts.text: Some acid washes leave the wool so brittle that it can readily be plucked out.
Aniline-dyed fibers were said to become harsher to the touch when wet and to lose the wool's natural oil.

age_and_wear.clue: Cracking sound when the rug is folded; foundation tears easily
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Fungal rot of the cotton foundation from damp; not age as such.
age_and_wear.cautions: Salt-water damage in shipping produced similar rotten spots (Jacobsen).

facts.text: Cracking or creaking when a rug is bent indicates dry rot; test by passing a fold down the length of the rug while listening.
A rug that tears when pulled by hand on the back has salt-water damage or dry rot.

age_and_wear.clue: Cotton wefts in a Caucasian rug
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Common in rugs attributed to Kuba, Shirvan and Baku; Stone's 19th-century attributions include cotton-wefted pieces, so cotton wefts are not on their own a sign of 20th-century work.
age_and_wear.cautions: A rule that Caucasian rugs with cotton wefts date after c. 1900 is widely repeated, but no source read here states it; Stone's figures contradict it as a firm rule.

facts.text: Nineteenth-century Shirvan rugs may have cotton or wool wefts; Shirvan hex-column rugs are more likely cotton-wefted, and about a quarter of Seishour-design rugs are cotton-wefted.
Hawley (1913) says almost all Caucasian rugs have warp and weft of wool.

age_and_wear.clue: Higher knot density, wool foundation, more elaborate selvage
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Within some types, older pieces tend to be finer, wool-founded and better finished; later ones coarser, cotton-founded, with simpler edges.
age_and_wear.cautions: Tendencies within a type only; never a date.

facts.text: For some rug types a higher knot density or a wool foundation may suggest greater age, and a simplified selvage or edge finish later production.
The weave of rugs woven over 150 years ago differs from that of rugs woven 50 years ago, and cheap commercial pieces are cruder than the same classes 30 years earlier.

age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Common in Persian commercial production from the late 1930s (Iranica) or after 1945 (Jacobsen); in Khorasan much earlier.

facts.text: Joftī knotting spread in the late 1930s when production for Tehran companies and export intensified.
Very few old rugs have jufti knots; they appear in rugs woven since 1945.

age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Sets a maximum age depending on when machine-spun yarn reached the area (Stone); Stone notes that before 1924 much Tianjin rug wool was hand-spun.
age_and_wear.cautions: Owners cannot reliably tell hand- from machine-spun yarn by eye; dates by region were not found.

facts.text: A maximum age is set for rugs containing machine-spun yarn, depending on when such yarn was introduced into the area.
Machine-spun yarns appeared in Persian weaving in the later decades of the 19th century.

age_and_wear.clue: Fugitive early synthetic colors (faded purples, pinks, oranges)
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: Not before the 1860s, and in most regions not before the 1870s-80s.
age_and_wear.cautions: Their absence does not make a rug older than the 1860s: natural dyes stayed in use in many areas into the 20th century and were revived from 1981.

facts.text: Synthetic (aniline) dyes reached Eastern dyeing in the 1860s (Hawley: about 1860; Kendrick: 1865-70).
Synthetic dyes were noted in Persian carpets by the 1870s.
In Azerbaijan the mass switch from natural to aniline dyes came around 1880, most strongly in Karabagh, Kazak and Ganja and least in Kuba-Shirvan.

says.text: Introduced about 1860.
Began to be used in the East 1865-70.
By 1870 began to displace natural dyes.
Cheap English dyes well known around Kirman by 1876-77.
Mass switch in Azerbaijan about 1880; mauveine in a Kuba rug dated 1868 (citing Eiland 1999).
Most big Turkish manufacturing networks used them by the 1880s.
Vegetable dyes exclusive in Persia until about 1890; 'dangerous aniline period' 1890-1910.

age_and_wear.clue: Greens that have turned blue or blue-green
age_and_wear.what_it_tells: The yellow over-dye has faded faster than the indigo; happens with natural dyes over time.

facts.text: Because yellow dyes fade faster than indigo, greens made of indigo and yellow become blue-green with age.

age_and_wear.clue: Shiny back, ragged or newly overcast edges

facts.text: Antique rugs are usually more or less shiny on the back and their edges are somewhat ragged or have been overcast anew.

repairs.name: Reweaving and reknotting
repairs.how_to_spot: From the back, a patch where the knots are a different size, tighter or looser, or in brighter or different wool; new warps or wefts spliced in; from the front, a slightly different color that may fade differently over the years.

facts.text: Broken warp and weft threads can be mended and missing knots replaced with similar yarn.
facts.quote: Broken threads of warp and weft can be mended; missing knots can be replaced with others of similar yarn

facts.text: Rewoven areas done in new wool that matched when new often fade lighter after a few years and stand out; good repairers use old wool, for example from the back of an old saddlebag.
A little re-knotting can change a woven date and add decades or centuries to a rug's apparent age (post-knotting).

repairs.name: Rebinding (re-overcasting) the sides
repairs.how_to_spot: Edge wrapping in fresher yarn, a different twist or color; wrapping that covers part of the outer border; sides that curl under from tight rebinding; a narrow outer border missing.

facts.text: Worn sides of old rugs are often overcast anew, sometimes covering part of the border, and if overcast too tightly the sides curl under.
A common cure for curled or worn edges was to cut off a quarter to one inch along the edge and overcast it completely.

repairs.name: New fringe sewn on; ends secured
repairs.how_to_spot: A fringe strip machine-stitched or hand-sewn under the end, whose threads do not continue into the rug as warps; rows of knots lost at the ends; a binding or 'serging' along the end.

facts.text: Artificial fringes may be attached to rugs with damaged ends.
In old pieces the end webs often wear away and rows of knots are lost.

repairs.name: Glued patches, latex or cloth backing
repairs.how_to_spot: Rubbery coating, glue or a sewn cloth over areas of the back, often hiding moth damage or holes.

facts.text: Glue, Lastex or non-skid coatings on the back show at a glance from the underside and are used to make moth-eaten rugs usable.
Mechanical stabilization is preferred in conservation; any method should be reversible.

repairs.name: Painted or inked bald spots
repairs.how_to_spot: Worn areas down to the foundation colored to match the design; color comes off on a damp cloth; dye on the back over moth damage.

facts.text: Threadbare places are tinted on the surface to hide that only the foundation remains.

repairs.name: Reduced, cut-and-joined, or re-bordered rugs
repairs.how_to_spot: A seam on the back (stitching across warps, or a line where warps are joined); a design that does not balance (medallion off center, border corners that do not turn properly); borders that do not match the field's wool or knotting; one end with an incomplete border.

facts.text: Badly worn carpets are often cut up and joined into smaller pieces, the joins run along border edges or round the pattern so they are hard to see.
facts.quote: Old carpets which are badly worn, or much damaged in places, while the rest is fairly good, are often cut up and joined together again so as to make up a smaller piece of good appearance.

facts.text: Sometimes whole pieces are removed so a rug is no longer its original length, or the border is replaced by the border of another rug.

repairs.name: Sewn rents and splits
repairs.how_to_spot: From the back, stitching across a tear, often in thread of a different color.

facts.text: In many old rugs the field is full of rents that have been sewn together.

repairs.name: Sizing and straightening
repairs.how_to_spot: Not visible once dry; the rug may feel stiffer than its type.

facts.text: Crooked rugs can be straightened by loosening here and stretching there.
Dealers tacked rugs face down, wet the back with cold-water glue sizing and let them dry to make them lie flat; there is no visible trace afterwards.

dating_rules.rule: A rug containing any synthetic dye was woven no earlier than 1856, the year of the first synthetic dye.
dating_rules.applies_to: All rugs, when a dye is identified as synthetic (usually by laboratory analysis).
dating_rules.cautions: In practice synthetic dyes reached rug weaving in the 1860s-1880s depending on region; an owner cannot identify most synthetic dyes by eye.

facts.text: Perkin made the first commercial synthetic dye, mauve, in 1856.

dating_rules.rule: Fuchsine (magenta) in a rug means not before 1859.
dating_rules.applies_to: Rugs with dye analysis showing fuchsine.
dating_rules.cautions: Visual guesses of 'fuchsine pink' are unreliable.

facts.text: Fuchsine was patented on 8 April 1859.

dating_rules.rule: Synthetic alizarin identified by dye analysis means not before 1869.
dating_rules.cautions: Looks the same as madder; only analysis can tell.

facts.text: Alizarin was first synthesized and patented in 1869.

dating_rules.rule: Acid azo reds and oranges (e.g. Orange II, Ponceau) mean not before about 1876-78.
dating_rules.applies_to: Rugs with dye analysis showing these dyes.

facts.text: Acid orange (1876) and ponceau (1878) were among the first acid azo dyes for wool; azo dyes were made on a manufacturing scale from about 1876-77.

dating_rules.rule: Congo red (a direct azo dye) means not before 1884.

facts.text: Congo red, the first direct dye, dates from 1884.

dating_rules.rule: Chrome (acid-mordant azo) dyes mean not before about 1889-90.
dating_rules.cautions: Single source for the date; Stone's chronology gives 1915 for 'chrome dye'.

facts.text: Important acid-mordant azo dyes for wool, applied with chrome mordants, were synthesized in 1889-1890.

dating_rules.rule: Synthetic indigo in a rug means not before 1897, but it cannot be told from natural indigo, so this rule rarely helps.
dating_rules.applies_to: Blues, only with specialist analysis of impurities.
dating_rules.cautions: Stone says the dye in the fiber is chemically indistinguishable from vegetable indigo.

facts.text: BASF launched synthetic indigo commercially in 1897.
