dating_rules.rule: A rug made under the DOBAG natural-dye project is not before 1981.
dating_rules.cautions: Natural dyes alone do not identify a DOBAG rug.

facts.text: The DOBAG project began in 1981.

dating_rules.rule: A tufted rug with a latex-coated back is modern factory or workshop production, not a traditional knotted rug of any age.
dating_rules.applies_to: Rugs with cloth and latex backs and no knots.
dating_rules.what_it_tells: not before the modern tufting era (date not established from sources read)
dating_rules.cautions: Date of first hand-tufted rugs not established (gap).

facts.text: Tufted rugs have yarn inserted into a cotton backing and locked with latex, with an extra fabric backing.

dating_rules.rule: The full bleach-and-repaint treatment points to a rug in the US trade no earlier than about 1905 (Jacobsen) and mostly before about 1955.
dating_rules.applies_to: Persian rugs (chiefly Sarouk) with painted pile.
dating_rules.what_it_tells: not before c. 1905 for the treatment (the rug itself may be older)
dating_rules.cautions: Hawley and Lewis describe treatment by 1911-13; the start date is Jacobsen's alone.

facts.text: Chemical bleaching and painting plants were set up around New York from about 1905; the practice became too costly after about 1955.

dating_rules.rule: The Persian bans on aniline dyes (1900 and later) give no dating rule: Persian rugs made after them can contain synthetic dyes.
dating_rules.cautions: Repeated in many books as if the bans worked.

facts.text: Government efforts to ban synthetic dyes in Persia were ineffective.

gaps: Persian-language sources: the web-search budget ran out before sid.ir, magiran, noormags, Golestan-e Honar or incc.ir could be searched, and ganjineh.nlai.ir refused connection. No Persian-language text of the Qajar or Pahlavi decrees on aniline dyes was found; Mumford's 1900 English translation (from a French/Persian printed copy) is the earliest text found. Native Persian dye names come only from Encyclopaedia Iranica.

Reza Shah-era rules: Stone says Reza Shah banned aniline dyes; Iranica xii mentions the Iran Carpet Company (1935) and regulations c. 1928 but no dye law. Date and text of any 1920s-30s dye law not found.
The 'right hand cut off' penalty: no Persian primary evidence found; earliest source is Mumford (1900), who says it was ordered 'long ago' in 'one part of Persia'.
Iranian natural-dye revival (Shiraz/Fars gabbeh, Zollanvari, Abbas Sayahi, Iran National Carpet Center programs): widely reported, not verified from a source read here.

Turkish-language sources on kök boya beyond Karavar & Öztürk (2019) not reached (search budget). Böhmer's Koekboya (2002) and Oriental Rug Review (1983) article not consulted. Turkish names for weld, buckthorn (cehri), kermes, cochineal and indigo were left out because no source read here gives them.
DOBAG label or certificate: what is sewn on or attached to DOBAG rugs and how a reader can recognize one was not found in a source read here.
Chrome and premetallized dyes: no history-of-chemistry source read for first commercial chrome dyes (Stone 1915 vs Salimov 1889-90) or for premetallized dyes; history-of-chemistry check still owed.
Viscose (art silk) and mercerized cotton: no source read for when they first appear in rugs. 'Bamboo silk' warning rests on a general FTC textile notice, not a rug source.
Hand-tufted rugs: only Stone describes them; date of first production and a second source (e.g. Carpet and Rug Institute) not obtained.
Cotton wefts in Caucasian rugs 'after c. 1900': no source found for this widely repeated rule; Stone's data on 19th-century attributions contradicts it as a firm rule.
Open-left/open-right convention: no museum statement of the viewing convention (e.g. Textile Museum) was obtained; readers should treat open-side readings as tentative.
Cochineal in Caucasian rugs and lac in Turkmen rugs: dye-analysis sources (Whiting, Böhmer, Rageth, Mushak 1984) not consulted directly; Mushak is known only through Iranica's citation.
Eiland & Eiland (1998/1999) is cited second-hand through Salimov (mauveine in a Kuba rug dated 1868; over half of Persian exports in 1913-14 with synthetic dyes); not checked in the original.
Edwards, The Persian Carpet (1953), the main source on Persian dyeing and the identification of esparak as weld, was not available; known only through Iranica.
Museum examples with open images were not collected for this topic (structure details rarely have open back photographs).
